Segment Analysis: Home Security (Voice-Controlled Cameras and Doorbells)

A battery-powered video doorbell lives or dies on its energy budget. Consumers expect six to twelve months from an internal rechargeable cell, so the camera sensor and the application processor stay fully power-gated until a real event happens. Today's designs use passive infrared (PIR) to wake the AP. PIR false-alarms constantly, windblown foliage, passing cars, thermal shifts, and each false alarm spins up the main processor for tens of milliwatts. TinyEdge-NPU lets the audio subsystem listen continuously, speech, glass breakage, harmless city noise, on less than 5 mW. The 96 KB of internal SRAM (M configuration) holds the whole 22 KB quantized DS-CNN-S model (Chapter 4 §4.1), so the external memory bus never wakes during evaluation. The market ships near 100M units a year across branded and ODM vendors, and at that scale the unit economics, the ~1 mm² density, and a mature toolchain drive real willingness to pay.

Segment Analysis: Industrial Sensors (Acoustic Anomaly Detection)

In factory condition monitoring, thousands of sensor nodes clamp onto pump housings, compressors, and gearbox bearings to catch early wear in high-frequency acoustic emissions. They run on non-rechargeable LiSOCl2 packs, and swapping a battery can cost hundreds of dollars per node in technician labor. The incumbent, an ultra-low-power DSP running classical FFTs or threshold logic, misses the subtle multivariable drift that precedes a mechanical failure. TinyEdge-NPU's sub-100 μW sleep floor and its ability to process raw 1D vibration signatures in milliseconds lets these nodes run a 1% duty cycle, up to seven years on one battery. But the industrial market has long sales cycles (18 to 24 months), fragmented requirements, and low volumes next to consumer electronics, so each customer has to carry higher license fees to recoup the NRE.

Segment Analysis: Cooking Robots and Smart Kitchen Appliances

Robotic multicookers, induction ranges, and connected ovens increasingly use local voice control, hands-free, because the user's hands are wet or soiled. The problem is the noise floor: range hoods, boiling liquid, food processors. The 64-MAC array can do beamforming preprocessing or single-intent keyword detection. Appliance OEMs want more: vocabularies over 50 recipe commands, and natural language parsing. Those workloads don't fit in 96 KB of SRAM. They'd need compression past practical accuracy limits, or paging from external SPI flash. And kitchen appliances run on mains power. A <5 mW profile buys almost nothing over a cheap multi-core application processor, an Allwinner or Rockchip at 350 mW, that already drives the LCD and hosts the Wi-Fi stack.

Segment Analysis: Warehouse Robotics and AMRs

Warehouse AMRs and AGVs carry vast sensor arrays: 2D/3D LiDAR, stereo cameras, ultrasonic transducers. Some teams try edge audio monitoring for motor squeal, pallet drops, or a human shouting at a blind intersection. But an AMR runs on a 24V or 48V battery with a budget in tens to hundreds of watts. Saving 50 mW with a micro-NPU is irrelevant to its run-time. And robotics architects want 10 to 50 TOPS of heterogeneous compute, running visual SLAM, point cloud segmentation, and trajectory planning at once. A 64-MAC core at ~12.8 GOPS (100 MHz INT8) is architecturally mismatched to that. Selling into that socket would bring negligible revenue on under 1.5 million units a year, plus support overhead for workloads the core was never built for.

Strategic Verdict: Beachhead and Second-Wave Selection

On volume, fit, and willingness to pay, Home Security (Battery-Powered Smart Video Doorbells and Security Nodes) is the beachhead. Not a close call. The fit is exact: <5 mW active inside a 6.0 mW audio budget, 96 KB of SRAM that eliminates external-memory wake-up energy, and >75M units a year to amortize the fixed development cost. Industrial acoustic anomaly sensors are the second wave. Once the silicon and the compiler are production-proven in the consumer beachhead, the same core drops into industrial sensor SoCs with minimal changes, high-margin, sticky sockets where battery life justifies premium license terms.

The Go / No-Go Decision Framework

Market research is only useful if it ends in a decision. Teams that treat research as an open-ended learning exercise drift: they commission one more survey, interview one more architect, and refine one more spreadsheet while the window for the beachhead closes. This section converts everything in the chapter, pain points, market sizing, competitive positioning, the beachhead verdict, into one written decision: Go, Conditional Go, or No-Go. The decision is recorded, dated, and signed by the product owner and the engineering lead. A Go commits the team to Chapter 3 and the specification. A No-Go stops the team, and the reasons are recorded so the idea doesn't come back in six months without new evidence.

Seven Scored Dimensions

Seven dimensions, each weighted by importance to an IP business, scored 1 (weak) to 5 (strong), combined into one weighted score out of 5. The weights are fixed before scoring starts. Adjusting them after seeing the scores is how a team talks itself into a decision it already made.

  • Beachhead pain severity (20%): Is the customer's problem existential, a tapeout blocker, a battery-life failure, a lost contract, or merely an optimisation preference? A pain that cancels a product scores 5; a pain that saves a few cents scores 1.
  • Technical fit (20%): Does the IP fit the customer's physical envelope, power, area, memory, interface, without heroic measures? A clean fit scores 5; a fit that requires the customer to redesign their power tree scores 1.
  • Market size and growth (15%): Is the serviceable market large enough, and growing fast enough, to repay the development cost within the product's commercial life? Use the SOM from the sizing exercise, not the TAM.
  • Competitive differentiation (15%): Is there a defensible wedge, an efficiency envelope, a power point, or an integration advantage, that incumbents structurally ignore? A "me-too" core scores 1, no matter how elegant the RTL.
  • Channel and customer access (10%): Can the team reach the buyers, and will the buyers take a meeting? Concentrated tier-1 and tier-2 SoC vendors score high; a fragmented market of a thousand small buyers scores low.
  • Revenue model viability (10%): Do the license fees plus royalties cover the engineering burn with margin, at realistic volumes? A model that needs 100 design wins to break even scores 1.
  • Team capability and schedule (10%): Does the team have the skills to build this, microarchitecture, verification, physical design, compiler, and can it reach tapeout inside the market window? A team missing a critical discipline scores low, however good the idea.
Table 2.2: Go / No-Go Scored Decision — TinyEdge-NPU
Dimension Weight Score (1–5) Weighted Evidence
Beachhead pain severity 20% 5 1.00 Software KWS drains the 6.0 mW audio budget; battery life is a contract-level failure, not a preference.
Technical fit 20% 4 0.80 <5 mW active and 96 KB SRAM (M configuration) fit the beachhead envelope; some risk on model-size growth beyond the M configuration's 96 KB capacity.
Market size and growth 15% 4 0.60 SOM $1.075M/yr by Year 4; edge-audio SoC volumes growing, 75–110M units in the beachhead.
Competitive differentiation 15% 4 0.60 Clear energy-per-decision wedge; general-purpose NPUs are over-provisioned, MCUs are too slow.
Channel and customer access 10% 3 0.30 Concentrated tier-1/tier-2 buyers, but 18–24 month sales cycles and entrenched vendor relationships.
Revenue model viability 10% 3 0.30 $75k Standard license + 1.0% royalty ($0.02/unit at $2.00 ASP); 5 licenses/yr gives ~$1.1M, below a $2.0–2.5M burn — the case rests on the royalty ramp past Year 4 (Chapter 16).
Team capability and schedule 10% 4 0.40 Team covers RTL, UVM, and compiler; 18-month plan to tapeout fits the market window.
Total 100% — 4.00 Verdict: GO

Reading the Score: Go, Conditional Go, No-Go

The score maps to three outcomes. The boundaries are set before scoring, so nobody moves them after the fact.

  • Go (weighted score ≥ 4.0): Commit. Fund the product-definition phase, assign the architecture lead, and baseline the requirements specification in Chapter 3. A Go decision is a commitment of engineering headcount, not a statement of enthusiasm.
  • Conditional Go (3.0–3.9): Proceed only if the specific weak dimensions are fixed within a stated time box, typically four to six weeks. A Conditional Go names the condition explicitly: "Go, provided we secure two paid pilot commitments" or "Go, provided the SRAM budget is proven at 96 KB in synthesis." If the condition is not met by the deadline, the decision reverts to No-Go automatically. There is no silent extension.
  • No-Go (< 3.0): Stop. Record the reasons, archive the research, and redeploy the team. A No-Go is not a failure; it is the framework working. The most expensive outcome in IP development is not a No-Go. It is a Go decision made on a 2.5-point opportunity that consumes eighteen months and a mask set before the market delivers its verdict.
flowchart TD A["Complete research: pain, sizing, competition, beachhead"] --> B[Score the seven dimensions 1-5] B --> C[Compute weighted total] C --> D{Weighted score?} D -- "≥ 4.0" --> E["GO: fund product definition, baseline spec"] D -- "3.0 – 3.9" --> F["CONDITIONAL GO: name the fix + deadline"] F --> G{Condition met in time?} G -- Yes --> E G -- No --> H["NO-GO: stop, record reasons"] D -- "< 3.0" --> H E --> I["Proceed to Chapter 3: requirements"]

The TinyEdge-NPU Decision

Applying the framework, the TinyEdge-NPU scores 4.00, a Go — exactly on the threshold, which is the honest place for it. The decision is carried by the two heaviest dimensions: the beachhead pain is existential (a 5), and the technical fit is clean (a 4). The weakest dimensions are channel access and the revenue model (both 3s): long sales cycles and entrenched vendor relationships on one side, and a royalty stream that only pays for the burn once the win rate holds past Year 4 on the other. Real risks, but the beachhead's concentration mitigates the first — few large buyers means few relationships to build, and one design win carries reference value across the segment — and the second is exactly what Chapter 16's break-even analysis is for. The decision is recorded here with its evidence, so that if the product later misses its targets, the team can audit whether the research was wrong or the execution was wrong. Two very different failures, with very different remedies.

A Go decision is a commitment of headcount and money, not a statement of enthusiasm. If the team cannot name the headcount and the budget the Go commits, the decision has not actually been made.

Best Practices for Early Market Validation

A Go decision does not end validation; it changes its form. Before the Go, validation is about learning whether the problem is real. After the Go, validation is about de-risking the specific commitments the Go just made: the beachhead, the power envelope, the interface, the toolchain. These are the cheapest risk reduction an IP team can buy. All of them are cheaper than a respin.

  • Secure a paid pilot before RTL freeze, not after tapeout. A letter of intent is a polite document; a paid pilot, even a small one, is evidence. The strongest validation signal in IP is a customer who pays for early access to the RTL or the FPGA prototype. It proves the pain is budgeted, not merely acknowledged. Target at least one paid pilot in the beachhead before the architecture is frozen.
  • Validate with the architect, not the executive. Executives approve budgets; architects approve integration. A positive meeting with a VP means little if the lead SoC architect has already decided the interface will not fit their floorplan. Keep the architect in the loop from the first interview through the specification review, and treat their objections as requirements, not obstacles.
  • Test the toolchain before the hardware. Give the customer's ML team the quantization tool and the reference model before the RTL exists, and ask them to run their own model through it. If their model does not quantize cleanly, or if the tool takes twenty minutes and needs 32 GB of RAM, you have learned more in a week than a quarter of RTL work would teach you. The toolchain is part of the product; validate it like hardware.
  • Build the reference design early. A reference design coupling the NPU with a host MCU over the target bus, even on an FPGA, turns abstract PPA claims into something a customer can measure. It also exposes integration friction (interrupt latency, DMA setup, clock-domain assumptions) months before the customer's own integration begins.
  • Re-validate at every stage gate. Market validation doesn't end when Chapter 3 begins. At each stage gate, architecture review, RTL freeze, verification sign-off, tapeout, re-check the two or three assumptions the stage depends on. If the beachhead's battery chemistry changed, or a competitor shipped a cheaper alternative, the team needs to know before the next tranche of engineering is committed, not after.
  • Record what would change your mind. For each major assumption, write down the evidence that would falsify it: "If two of our three beachhead architects say the SRAM budget must exceed 200 KB (the reference L configuration's total), we revisit the architecture." Pre-committing to falsification criteria is the only reliable defence against the sunk-cost fallacy, which is the most expensive cognitive bias in semiconductor development.

The thread is simple: validation gets cheaper the earlier it happens and more expensive the later it happens. An hour of customer conversation in week three is worth a month of RTL rework in month nine. The teams that internalise this spend their first quarter talking to architects and their last quarter taping out. The teams that do not spend their first quarter writing RTL and their last quarter explaining to a customer why the core does not fit.

Key Takeaways

  • Market research must end in a written, scored, dated decision. Go, Conditional Go, or No-Go. Not open-ended learning.
  • The Go / No-Go framework scores seven dimensions with fixed weights; TinyEdge-NPU scores 4.00, a Go carried by existential beachhead pain and a clean technical fit, with the revenue model the dimension to watch.
  • Conditional Go must name the fix and a deadline; if the condition is not met, it reverts to No-Go automatically, with no silent extension.
  • A No-Go is the framework working, not a failure. The most expensive outcome is a Go on a weak opportunity that consumes eighteen months and a mask set.
  • After the Go, validation continues in a new form: paid pilots, architect-level engagement, toolchain testing, and an early reference design.
  • Record what would change your mind for each major assumption. It is the only reliable defence against the sunk-cost fallacy.
  • Home Security is the beachhead and Industrial is the second wave; the decision, its evidence, and its score are recorded here so execution can later be audited against research.

From Research to Requirements

The interviews and the competitive analysis set the engineering boundaries for the TinyEdge-NPU. A sub-6.0 mW total audio-chain budget in home security becomes a strict <5 mW active power limit. The architects' refusal to let memory spill becomes the 96 KB internal SRAM sizing (M configuration). Those findings are the non-negotiable inputs to Chapter 3, where they become RTL functional requirements, clock domain definitions, datapath configurations, and the system bus interface.

Chapter 3: Product Definition & Requirements Specification

Chapter 2 ended with a decision: the TinyEdge-NPU attacks the battery-powered home-security beachhead first, industrial acoustic sensing second. That decision is worth nothing until it becomes a document an engineer can build against, a verification engineer can test against, and a customer can sign. That document is the requirements specification, and this chapter is about writing one that survives contact with reality.

The requirements specification is the most important document in an IP program. Everything downstream, microarchitecture, RTL, verification, synthesis, physical design, software, the customer integration guide, is either a direct implementation of a requirement or a consequence of one that was missing. A requirement written clearly in week three saves a respin in month fourteen. A requirement written vaguely in week three becomes a schedule argument in month nine, when the RTL team, the verification team, and the customer each discover they understood the same sentence differently.

The discipline is unforgiving because silicon is unforgiving. A software team can ship a feature, find out users hate it, and patch it the following Tuesday. A silicon IP team that mis-specifies the sleep power of an always-on block by 50 μW finds the error at silicon bring-up, after the mask set is paid for and the customer's tapeout is already committed. The cost of a requirements error grows by roughly an order of magnitude at each stage it survives: a one-hour fix in the specification becomes a one-day fix in RTL, a one-week fix in verification, a one-month fix in physical design, and a multi-million-dollar respin after tapeout.

A requirement is not a wish, a marketing claim, or an architectural preference. It is a testable contract: a statement precise enough that a verification engineer can write a test that passes or fails, a customer can accept or reject, and a designer can implement without guessing.

Writing Clear, Testable Requirements

The Anatomy of a Requirement

Every requirement in a professional specification carries the same five fields. If any field is missing, the requirement is incomplete and should not be signed off.

  • Unique ID: A stable identifier (for example, REQ-PWR-001) that never changes, even when the wording is revised. Every test, every design decision, and every review comment references the ID, not the prose. Renumbering requirements mid-project destroys traceability.
  • Statement: A single declarative sentence using the word shall. "The NPU shall complete a 12-class keyword-spotting inference in under 12 ms at 20 MHz." One requirement, one behaviour, one number.
  • Rationale: Why this requirement exists, in one or two sentences, tied back to a market finding or a customer constraint. The rationale is what stops a well-meaning engineer from "optimising" the requirement away six months later. When the rationale cites the home-security audio budget of 6.0 mW, nobody proposes doubling the MAC array to cut latency.
  • Verification method: How compliance will be proven: analysis, simulation, formal proof, FPGA measurement, or silicon measurement. A requirement without a verification method is an aspiration, not a requirement. If nobody can say how it will be tested, it cannot be signed off.
  • Priority: P0 (mandatory: the product cannot ship without it), P1 (competitive differentiator: required for the target market but negotiable under schedule pressure), or P2 (future release: recorded, not implemented). Priority is what lets a team cut scope under pressure without cutting the product's reason to exist.

Language Rules That Prevent Arguments

Most requirements disputes aren't technical disagreements. They're linguistic ones. The rules below eliminate most of them.

  • Use "shall" for obligations, "should" for goals, "may" for options. And never mix them. "The NPU shall support INT8" is a contract. "The NPU should support INT8" is a hope. If a sentence contains both a "shall" and a "should", split it into two requirements.
  • Every number gets a unit, a condition, and a tolerance. "<5 mW" is not a requirement. "<5 mW active power at 20 MHz, 0.9 V, 25 °C, running the reference DS-CNN keyword-spotting model" is a requirement. The condition is part of the requirement, not a footnote.
  • Ban vague adjectives. "Fast", "low-power", "small", "robust", "user-friendly", and "high-performance" have no place in a specification. Each must be replaced by a number and a measurement method. If you cannot measure it, you cannot specify it.
  • One behaviour per requirement. A requirement that says "the NPU shall support INT8 and INT4, run at 100 MHz, and consume under 5 mW" is three requirements pretending to be one. When the INT4 support slips, the whole requirement becomes ambiguous. Split it.
  • Never specify a solution when you mean a need. "The NPU shall use a 64 KB single-port SRAM" is a design decision disguised as a requirement. The requirement is "the NPU shall store the full reference keyword-spotting model and its activations on-chip without external memory access." The SRAM size is an implementation choice that belongs in the architecture document, where it can change without invalidating the specification.

One tension in this chapter deserves naming. The rule above says never to specify a solution when you mean a need, yet this specification records REQ-F-003 (an 8×8 MAC array) and REQ-A-002 (a parameterized SRAM budget, 48–200 KB across the three configurations of §3.9), which are architecture decisions, not needs. That is deliberate, not sloppy. By the time a specification is written for a product that has already been through the Chapter 2 market analysis and the architecture trade-offs of Chapter 4, the frozen architecture decisions are recorded as requirements so they are traceable. A change to the array size or the memory budget is then a specification change, reviewed and re-signed, rather than a silent RTL edit. The rule still applies to everything that has not yet been decided. The exceptions are the decisions this product has already made, and their requirement IDs label them as such.

flowchart TD A[Market Finding] --> B["Requirement: ID + shall + number + condition"] B --> C[Architecture Decision] B --> D["Verification Plan: test + method"] C --> E[RTL Implementation] D --> F["Coverage & Sign-off"] E --> G{Does the test pass?} G -- Yes --> H[Requirement closed] G -- No --> I[Change RTL or renegotiate requirement] I --> B

The diagram above is the whole discipline in one picture. A market finding becomes a numbered requirement. The requirement drives the architecture and the verification plan in parallel. The verification result either closes the requirement or forces an explicit renegotiation. Nothing in this loop is optional, and nothing bypasses the requirement. Not a clever microarchitectural shortcut. Not a schedule-driven decision to skip a test.

Before and After: Rewriting Vague Requirements

The fastest way to develop a feel for testable requirements is to rewrite vague ones. The table below takes four sentences of the kind that show up in first-draft specifications and converts each into a requirement a verification engineer can actually test.

Table 3.1a: Vague Statements Rewritten as Testable Requirements
Vague (untestable) Testable (rewritten) What the rewrite fixed
"The NPU shall be low-power." "The NPU shall consume less than 5.0 mW active power at 20 MHz, 0.9 V, 25 °C, running the reference DS-CNN model (REQ-PWR-001)." Added a number, a unit, and the exact operating condition under which the number applies.
"The NPU shall support fast keyword spotting." "The NPU shall complete a 12-class DS-CNN inference in under 12 ms at 20 MHz (REQ-P-001)." Replaced "fast" with a latency bound, a named workload, and a clock rate.
"The NPU shall have a standard bus interface." "The NPU shall expose an AMBA 4 AXI-Lite slave interface, 32-bit data width, supporting register access with at most one wait cycle (REQ-I-001)." Named the standard, the width, and the timing behaviour. "Standard" alone specifies nothing.
"The NPU shall handle errors gracefully." "The NPU shall signal FIFO overflow via a dedicated status bit and the shared interrupt line, and shall stall the datapath without data loss (REQ-F-006, REQ-I-006)." Named the error, the observable signal, and the required behaviour; split into two requirements.

Notice that every rewrite also gained a requirement ID. That isn't bureaucracy. It's the mechanism that lets the verification plan reference the requirement, the test reference the verification plan, and the sign-off report reference the test. Without the ID, the sentence is prose. With the ID, it is a contract.

Functional Requirements

Functional requirements define what the IP does. For the TinyEdge-NPU, the functional envelope is deliberately narrow. It's a fixed-function inference accelerator for small quantized neural networks, not a general-purpose programmable DSP. That narrowness is a feature. Every operator the core supports costs area, power, and verification effort. Every operator it omits is a question a customer will ask. The requirements below come out of the Chapter 2 analysis. They cover exactly the operators keyword spotting and acoustic event detection need, and nothing else.

Table 3.1: Key Functional Requirements (excerpt — full list in §3.9)
ID Requirement Verification Priority
REQ-F-001 The NPU shall execute INT8 quantized convolutional, depthwise convolutional, fully connected, max-pooling, and average-pooling layers. Directed test + UVM P0
REQ-F-002 The NPU shall execute a complete 12-class DS-CNN keyword-spotting model of up to 500,000 parameters entirely on-chip. Directed test (reference model) P0
REQ-F-003 The NPU shall provide an 8×8 MAC array (64 INT8 multiply-accumulate units) with 32-bit accumulation. Directed test + formal P0
REQ-F-004 The NPU shall support per-tensor and per-channel INT8 quantization (asymmetric, with zero-point and scale). Directed test P0
REQ-F-005 The NPU shall support ReLU, ReLU6, and leaky ReLU activations in hardware; all other activations shall be offloaded to the host MCU. Directed test P0
REQ-F-006 The NPU shall signal inference-complete, error, and FIFO-overflow conditions via a single interrupt line and readable status registers. Directed test P0
REQ-F-007 The NPU shall support INT4 weights as a P1 extension, with no change to the register interface. Directed test P1

Note what is deliberately absent. No floating-point requirement, no transformer attention requirement, no dynamic tensor reshaping requirement. Each was a stated customer request in Chapter 2 that the pain-point analysis rejected. Recording an explicit non-requirement matters as much as recording a requirement. It stops the next customer conversation from reopening a settled decision. A short "out of scope" section, listing the rejected capabilities and the reason each was rejected, is one of the highest-value pages in the document.

Performance Requirements

Performance requirements are where marketing numbers meet physics. The TinyEdge-NPU's headline numbers, latency, throughput, and accuracy, all come from the beachhead's physical constraints, not from a desire to win a benchmark.

  • Inference latency (REQ-P-001): The NPU shall complete a 12-class DS-CNN-S keyword-spotting inference in under 12 ms at the 20 MHz nominal clock (71,742 cycles = 3.59 ms @ 20 MHz), and complete the larger DS-CNN-M workload in under 12 ms in 100 MHz burst mode (420,000 cycles = 4.20 ms @ 100 MHz). The rationale is the audio frame stride: keyword-spotting systems process audio in 20–100 ms frames, and the inference must finish comfortably inside one frame with margin for the host MCU to act on the result. The 12 ms budget is a P0 requirement because it is set by the application, not by the hardware.
  • Peak throughput (REQ-P-002): The NPU shall deliver 6.4 GMAC/s peak at the 100 MHz burst clock (64 MACs × 100 MHz). This is a derived number, not a market requirement. It falls out of the MAC array size and the burst clock. It is specified because the burst mode exists to clear backlogs quickly, and the customer needs to know the ceiling.
  • Detection accuracy (REQ-P-003): The NPU shall achieve at least 95% top-1 accuracy on the 12-class Google Speech Commands test set with the DS-CNN-M reference model, and at least 94% with the smaller DS-CNN-S model, in each case within 0.5 percentage points of the FP32 reference model. The two bars reflect the two models' measured INT8 accuracy (Table 4.9: DS-CNN-M 95.5%, DS-CNN-S 94.1%); a single 95% bar would make the S model fail its own specification. Accuracy is the requirement customers actually care about, and it is the hardest to verify. It requires the full reference model, the quantization toolchain, and a fixed test set, all version-controlled together. An accuracy requirement without a named dataset and a named reference model is meaningless.
  • False acceptance (REQ-P-004): The NPU shall produce fewer than one false wake-up per 24 hours of continuous operation on the reference acoustic test corpus. This is a P0 requirement for the home-security beachhead: every false wake-up powers on the application processor and burns the battery budget the NPU exists to protect.

A useful check on any performance requirement: ask what breaks if the number is missed by 20%. If latency slips from 12 ms to 14.4 ms, nothing breaks. The frame stride still has margin. If accuracy slips from 95% to 93%, the product still works but the customer story weakens. If false acceptance rises from one per day to one per hour, the battery-life claim collapses. That ordering tells you which numbers are truly P0 and which are P1.

Power Requirements

Power is the requirement that kills edge-AI IP cores, so it gets the most precise treatment in this specification. Three power states matter. Each is specified separately because each is measured differently and fails differently.

Table 3.2: Power Requirements by Operating State
ID State Requirement Condition Verification
REQ-PWR-001 Active inference Total NPU power < 5.0 mW 20 MHz, 0.9 V, 25 °C, reference DS-CNN model Gate-level power sim + silicon
REQ-PWR-002 Burst inference Total NPU power < 12 mW 100 MHz, 0.9 V, 25 °C, reference DS-CNN model Gate-level power sim
REQ-PWR-003 State-retentive sleep Total NPU power < 100 μW 0.9 V, 25 °C, weights retained in SRAM Gate-level power sim + silicon
REQ-PWR-004 Deep sleep (power-gated) Total NPU leakage < 5 μW 0.9 V, 25 °C, power domain off Gate-level power sim
REQ-PWR-005 Wake-up latency Sleep-to-first-MAC < 100 μs From state-retentive sleep, 20 MHz clock Simulation + silicon

Two points deserve emphasis. First, the active-power requirement is stated at 20 MHz, not at the 100 MHz burst clock. The always-on use case runs at nominal clock, and specifying power at burst clock would let a design pass the letter of the specification while failing the application. Second, the sleep requirement is specified with weights retained. Reloading the weight SRAM, up to 128 KB at the reference (L) configuration, from external flash on every wake-up would cost more energy than the sleep state saves. The requirement and its condition together force the architecture toward SRAM retention rather than full power gating. That is exactly the trade-off Chapter 4 will work through.

Area and Physical Requirements

Area requirements are the most commonly underestimated in IP specifications. RTL engineers think in gate counts and customers think in dollars. The specification bridges the two by stating area in square millimetres at a named process node, with the package as an explicit constraint.

  • Total macro area (REQ-A-001): The NPU macro, including logic, SRAM, and boundary, shall occupy no more than 1.0 mm² in 28nm bulk CMOS. This is a P0 requirement: it is set by the beachhead's die-cost budget, and exceeding it moves the product into a different price tier.
  • SRAM area budget (REQ-A-002): The on-chip SRAM shall occupy no more than 0.52 mm² at the 200 KB reference (L) configuration, scaling at approximately 0.0026 mm²/KB across the parameterized range (48–200 KB; §3.9). Stating the SRAM budget separately prevents the memory from silently consuming the logic's area. That is the failure mode Chapter 1 described.
  • Package compatibility (REQ-A-003): The NPU shall be integrable in a 4 × 4 mm QFN package with wire-bond assembly. No flip-chip, no BGA, no interposer. This constrains the pin count and the peak current, and it is a P0 requirement because the beachhead's cost model depends on it.
  • Process node (REQ-A-004): The NPU shall be delivered in 28nm bulk CMOS, with the RTL portable to 22nm FDX without architectural change. Portability is a P1 requirement: it protects the IP's commercial life beyond the first customer's process choice.

Interface Requirements

Interface requirements are where IP succeeds or fails in the customer's hands. A customer integrates an IP block through its interfaces. If the interface is awkward, the IP is awkward, no matter how elegant the datapath. The TinyEdge-NPU exposes two bus interfaces and one interrupt, and the specification pins each of them down.

Table 3.3: Interface Requirements
ID Requirement Verification Priority
REQ-I-001 The NPU shall expose an AMBA 4 AXI-Lite slave interface for control and configuration, 32-bit data width, supporting register access with at most one wait cycle. Protocol test + formal P0
REQ-I-002 The NPU shall expose an AMBA 4 AXI4 master interface for DMA transfer of weights and activations, 32-bit data width, burst length up to 16. Protocol test + UVM P0
REQ-I-003 The NPU shall provide a single level-sensitive interrupt output, asserted on inference-complete and on error, with per-source enable and status bits. Directed test P0
REQ-I-004 The NPU compute core, DMA, and buffers shall operate on a single compute clock domain (20 MHz nominal / 100 MHz burst) with a synchronized active-low reset, isolated from the host AXI-Lite bus clock domain by a single verified CDC boundary. CDC check + simulation P0
REQ-I-005 All configuration registers shall be readable and writable through the AXI-Lite interface, with read-back of the programmed value. Directed test P0
REQ-I-006 The NPU shall tolerate backpressure on the AXI4 master interface without data loss or deadlock, stalling the datapath cleanly. UVM + formal P0

The single-clock-domain requirement (REQ-I-004) deserves a note. It is a deliberate simplification, and it is specified rather than assumed. A single clock domain eliminates an entire class of clock-domain-crossing bugs and simplifies the customer's integration. There is exactly one exception: the host-bus AXI-Lite control interface runs on the host bus clock, so the register interface is the design's single clock-domain-crossing boundary, verified by the CDC checks described in Chapter 8. Everything else, the MAC array, the buffers, the DMA engine, and the control FSM, runs on the single NPU clock. The cost is that the NPU cannot run its memory interface at a different rate from its compute, which is an acceptable trade at these throughputs. If a future customer needs separate clocks, that is a new requirement, not a silent change.

Software Requirements

Software requirements are the most frequently omitted from hardware specifications, and their omission is the most common reason an otherwise good IP core fails in integration. The customer does not buy RTL. They buy a working subsystem, and the subsystem includes the toolchain and the runtime. The TinyEdge-NPU specification therefore treats software as a first-class deliverable.

  • Model import (REQ-SW-001): The IP shall ship with a quantization and compilation tool that accepts a TensorFlow Lite model and produces a loadable weight image and a layer schedule, with no manual intervention, in under 60 seconds on a standard developer workstation. Verification: run the tool on the reference model and confirm the output matches the golden image bit-for-bit.
  • Runtime (REQ-SW-002): The IP shall ship with a TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers (TFLM) integration layer that exposes the NPU as a standard delegate, so that application code written against TFLM runs unchanged. Verification: run the reference application through TFLM with and without the delegate and confirm identical outputs.
  • Driver and HAL (REQ-SW-003): The IP shall ship with a bare-metal C driver and a register header file generated from the same source as the RTL register map, so that the header can never drift from the hardware. Verification: diff the generated header against the RTL register definition on every release.
  • Debuggability (REQ-SW-004): The IP shall expose a register-level debug interface that allows the host to read the MAC array state, the SRAM contents, and the control FSM state without halting inference. Verification: directed test exercising the debug path during an active inference.
  • Documentation (REQ-SW-005): The IP shall ship with an integration guide, a register reference manual, and a worked bare-metal example application, all version-controlled with the RTL release. Verification: a new engineer follows the guide and brings up the reference application on the FPGA prototype without assistance from the IP team.

REQ-SW-005 is the requirement that separates a licensable IP core from a research prototype. The test, a new engineer bringing up the example unaided, is deliberately harsh, and it is the test most IP teams fail. If the integration guide is the only document that describes how to use the core, and it is wrong or incomplete, the customer burns their first two weeks of integration schedule on problems the IP vendor already solved. That is a support cost, a schedule cost, and a reputation cost, all avoidable by specifying the documentation as a deliverable with an acceptance test.

The tables below consolidate the full requirements specification for the TinyEdge-NPU, Revision 1.0. This is the document the architecture team designs against, the verification team tests against, and the customer signs. Every requirement carries its verification method and its priority. The specification is intentionally short: thirty-four requirements, not three hundred. A specification with three hundred requirements has not been prioritised. It has been abdicated.

Three requirements in the table deserve a final note, because they are the ones teams most often forget to write. REQ-Q-001 states that the deliverables themselves are a requirement. The RTL alone is not the product. The product is the RTL plus the testbench, the constraints, the physical views, and the documentation, all version-controlled together. REQ-Q-002 makes coverage sign-off a requirement rather than an aspiration, so that "we ran the regressions" can never substitute for "we met the coverage plan." The target is 100% of the planned coverage, not an absolute 100% of every coverpoint and code branch. An absolute 100% is not achievable in practice, and unreachable bins are waived with a documented reason rather than chased. And REQ-Q-003 makes lint and CDC cleanliness a requirement with an explicit waiver process, so that a waived violation is a conscious, signed decision rather than a line buried in a log file.

Traceability: From Requirement to Sign-Off

A specification is only as good as its traceability: the unbroken chain from each requirement to the design that implements it and the test that proves it. For the TinyEdge-NPU, the chain has four links, and every link is recorded in a traceability matrix that is reviewed at each stage gate.

  • Requirement → architecture: Each P0 requirement maps to a named section of the microarchitecture document. REQ-PWR-003 (sleep power < 100 μW with weights retained) maps to the power-intent section describing SRAM retention and clock gating; if the architecture document has no section that addresses a P0 requirement, the architecture is incomplete.
  • Architecture → RTL: Each architectural block maps to a named RTL module and a named engineer. When a requirement changes, the matrix shows exactly which modules are affected, so the impact of a change is a lookup, not an investigation.
  • Requirement → test: Each requirement maps to at least one named test or formal property, with the verification method from the specification table. A requirement with no test is an open item on the sign-off report, visible to the whole team and to the customer.
  • Test → sign-off: The coverage plan records, per requirement, whether its tests passed, what coverage they achieved, and whether any waiver was granted. Sign-off is declared per requirement, not per test suite. The question is never "did the regressions pass" but "is every P0 requirement closed."

The matrix is maintained as a living document, not a one-off spreadsheet created the week before tapeout. When a requirement is added, its traceability links are added in the same change. When a test is waived, the waiver names the requirement it affects. The discipline feels bureaucratic until the first time a customer asks, two weeks before their tapeout, for proof that the sleep-power requirement was verified on silicon, and the team produces the chain in an afternoon instead of reconstructing it from log files.

§3.9 Canonical Specification Summary

One RTL, three characterized configurations. The SRAM is a parameter (WEIGHT_KB, ACT_KB; Chapter 5), not a single fixed size. The range is the design's configurability, not indecision. A customer who needs the smallest die instantiates the S configuration. A customer whose model outgrows S but does not need the full weight buffer instantiates M. The L configuration is the reference the book's worked examples use unless a chapter says otherwise. Table 3.5 is the single source for the canonical values every chapter quotes. If a number anywhere else in the book disagrees with this table, this table governs. The full requirement-by-requirement list is Table 3.4 in the preceding section.

Peak active power scales with the memory subsystem. SRAM active power is ≈0.0090 mW/KB (Table 4.11: 1.15 mW for the 128 KB weight buffer), and the MAC array, control, and clock tree draw ≈2.1 mW in every configuration (3.9 mW minus 1.80 mW of SRAM at the L configuration), giving 2.5 mW (S), 3.0 mW (M), and 3.9 mW (L). The derivation reproduces the canonical 3.9 mW peak at the reference configuration. That is the check that the scaling is consistent rather than invented. In the S and M configurations the line-buffer function is folded into the activation allocation, so their totals are exactly WEIGHT_KB + ACT_KB. Only the L configuration carries a separate 8 KB line buffer.

Requirements Review Checklist

No specification is signed off without a formal review. The checklist below is the gate. Every item must be answered yes before the specification is baselined and the architecture work begins. A single "no" sends the document back for revision. That is the point of the gate.

Table 3.6: Specification Review Checklist
# Check Why it matters
1Every requirement has a unique, stable ID.Without IDs there is no traceability to tests or to design decisions.
2Every requirement uses "shall" and states one behaviour.Multi-behaviour requirements cannot be tested or renegotiated cleanly.
3Every number has a unit, a condition, and a tolerance.A number without conditions is a marketing claim, not a contract.
4Every requirement names its verification method.Untestable requirements are aspirations; they will be discovered at tapeout.
5Every requirement carries a priority (P0 / P1 / P2).Without priorities, scope cuts under schedule pressure are arbitrary.
6Every requirement cites its rationale or parent market finding.Rationale prevents well-meaning engineers from optimising away the reason the requirement exists.
7Conflicting requirements are identified and resolved, not left to the implementer.Unresolved conflicts surface as design arguments in month nine.
8The out-of-scope section lists rejected capabilities and why.Stops settled decisions from being reopened by every new customer conversation.
9Interface requirements cover every pin, register, interrupt, clock, and reset.An unspecified pin is a pin the customer will use differently from the designer.
10Software deliverables are specified with acceptance tests.The toolchain and driver are part of the product; undocumented software is unusable software.
11Power is specified per operating state, not as a single number.Active, sleep, and leakage fail differently and are measured differently.
12The specification is version-controlled, and changes go through review.An uncontrolled specification is a rumour; a versioned one is a contract.

Common Specification Mistakes

The mistakes below are drawn from real IP programs. Each one has cost at least one team a tapeout, a customer, or a quarter. Read them as a list of things to check in your own specification before you sign it.

  1. Specifying the solution instead of the need. Writing "the NPU shall use a 64 KB single-port SRAM" locks the architecture before the architect has started. Specify the need, "the full model and activations shall reside on-chip", and let the architecture document choose the memory. When the memory choice turns out to be wrong, only the architecture document changes, not the customer-facing contract.
  2. Confusing typical with worst case. "Typical active power 3 mW" is a datasheet decoration. The requirement must state the worst-case corner: the voltage, the temperature, the process corner, and the workload. A design that meets typical power and misses worst-case power by 40% fails in the customer's hands, in the field, in winter, at end of battery life.
  3. Leaving the interface half-specified. Teams routinely specify the data path in detail and leave the interrupt behaviour, the reset sequencing, and the error handling to "implementation detail." The customer's integration engineer discovers these gaps in week one of integration, and every gap becomes a support ticket, a schedule slip, or a respin of the customer's board.
  4. No verification method. A requirement that says "the NPU shall be robust" or "the NPU shall handle all corner cases" cannot be tested and therefore cannot be signed off. If the verification team cannot write a test for it, the requirement does not belong in the specification. It belongs in a design guideline.
  5. Requirements that change without a record. A specification that is edited by email, chat message, or hallway conversation is not a specification. Every change needs a version, a date, an author, and a reason. The team that cannot produce the history of a requirement cannot defend it, and cannot explain to a customer why the product behaves the way it does.
  6. Forgetting the software. The RTL is specified to the last flip-flop while the compiler, the runtime, and the driver are left as "to be determined." The customer then discovers that the model import tool does not support their quantization scheme, or that the driver has no way to read the error status. Software is part of the IP. Specify it, staff it, and test it like hardware.
  7. Gold-plating the specification. Adding requirements because they are interesting rather than because a customer will pay for them. Every P0 requirement costs design time, verification time, and silicon area. A specification with forty P0 requirements has not been prioritised. It is a wish list, and wish lists do not tape out on schedule.
  8. No out-of-scope section. Without an explicit list of what the IP does not do, every customer meeting reopens the same settled debates: floating point, transformers, dynamic reshaping. The out-of-scope section is the cheapest schedule protection in the document.

Key Takeaways

  • A requirement is a testable contract: unique ID, one "shall" statement, a number with unit and condition, a verification method, and a priority.
  • The TinyEdge-NPU specification is deliberately short, 34 requirements, because a specification with hundreds of P0 items has not been prioritised.
  • Power is specified per operating state (active < 5 mW, sleep < 100 μW, deep sleep < 5 μW), because each state fails differently and is measured differently.
  • Interface requirements, AXI-Lite slave, AXI4 master DMA, single interrupt, single clock domain with one host-clock CDC boundary, are where IP succeeds or fails in the customer's hands.
  • Software is a first-class deliverable: model import tool, TFLM delegate, generated register header, and an integration guide with an unaided bring-up acceptance test.
  • An explicit out-of-scope section (no FP16, no transformers, no dynamic reshaping) protects the schedule more cheaply than any other page in the document.
  • The twelve-item review checklist is the sign-off gate: a single "no" sends the specification back for revision before architecture begins.
  • The most expensive requirements error is the one discovered after tapeout; the cheapest is the one caught by this chapter's checklist in week three.

Chapter 4: Architecture Definition

Architecture is where the TinyEdge-NPU stops being a requirements document and starts being a machine. This chapter walks the full path: characterizing the keyword-spotting workload, choosing a dataflow, sizing the MAC array and the memory hierarchy, picking a precision, and recording every decision so the design can be reviewed, reused, and defended. The running numbers are the Chapter 3 targets: INT8 inference, under 5 mW active, under 100 µW in sleep, about 1 mm2 in 28 nm, real-time inference on 1-second audio windows.

4.1 From Requirements to Micro-Architecture

Turning product requirements into a micro-architectural specification is the most critical phase in hardware IP development. Architectural errors made here propagate into RTL, synthesis, and physical layout, where corrections cost orders of magnitude more engineering time. For the TinyEdge-NPU, the Chapter 3 requirements set clear physical, electrical, and computational boundaries:

  • Target Workload: Depthwise Separable Convolutional Neural Networks (DS-CNN) for Keyword Spotting (KWS) and acoustic event classification operating on 1-second audio frames (16 kHz, 16-bit mono PCM).
  • Throughput / Latency: Inference execution must complete within a 10 ms latency budget per 1-second audio window to enable a low duty cycle (≤1%), reserving the system for power-gated sleep states.
  • Arithmetic Precision: Quantized 8-bit integer (INT8) activations and weights, with 32-bit accumulation to prevent dynamic range clipping during intermediate summation.
  • Power Budget: <5 mW active power at peak throughput in TSMC 28nm HPC+; <100 μW deep sleep power with state retention.
  • Area Budget: ≤1.0 mm2 including all logic, control paths, and on-chip SRAM memory.
  • Host & System Integration: Standard AXI-Lite slave interface for configuration, control, and interrupt handling; AXI4 master interface with autonomous DMA for memory fetching.

Translating Budgets to Silicon Realities

To honor these boundaries, requirements become silicon allocation budgets. In TSMC 28nm HPC+, a standard 8-track or 9-track high-density library yields roughly 1.0 to 1.2 million gates per mm2 at a conservative 70% placement density. Single-port high-density SRAM bitcells measure approximately 0.127 μm2. Factoring in wordline drivers, sense amplifiers, and bank decode logic, macro-level SRAM density sits at roughly 0.6 MB to 0.7 MB per mm2.

The 1.0 mm2 area target restricts the total on-chip storage. Allocating 60% of the die to memory leaves roughly 0.4 mm2 for standard cell logic, clock trees, power grids, and pipeline registers. Within that 0.6 mm2 memory envelope, the reference configuration (TinyEdge-NPU-L, §3.9) integrates 200 KB of SRAM:

  • Weight Buffer (128 KB): Holds network parameters for the active layer set, minimizing off-chip transfers.
  • Activation Buffer (64 KB): Double-buffered ping-pong banks for input and output tensor feature maps.
  • Bias & Scratchpad Buffer (8 KB): Houses per-channel scale factors, zero-point offsets, and 32-bit quantization bias values.

200 KB of on-chip SRAM takes approximately 0.52 mm2 at the L configuration, ≈0.0026 mm2/KB, so the S (48 KB) and M (96 KB) configurations occupy ≈0.12 mm2 and ≈0.25 mm2 respectively. The remaining ~0.48 mm2 easily accommodates the computational logic. A single INT8 multiply-accumulate unit, an 8-bit by 8-bit multiplier, 32-bit adder, and accumulation register, synthesized at 100 MHz requires approximately 450 to 600 gate equivalents (~600 μm2 in 28nm). An array of 64 MAC engines consumes under 0.05 mm2 of standard cell area, leaving abundant room for sequencers, memory address generators, quantization post-processing units, and AXI bus interfaces.

Workload Characterization: DS-CNN for 12-Class Keyword Spotting

The micro-architecture has to match the operator requirements of modern edge speech models. Traditional standard convolutions spend substantial computation across both spatial and channel dimensions at once. Depthwise separable convolutions factor this into a spatial filtering phase (Depthwise, DW) followed by a cross-channel linear combination (Pointwise, PW). That cuts parameter count and arithmetic operations by a factor of 8 to 10 at minimal accuracy cost.

The reference network processes a 1-second audio frame, transformed by a hardware or software front-end into 49 time-frames of 10 MFCC (Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients) features, generating an initial feature map of 49 x 10 x 1. The network comprises an initial standard 2D convolution followed by 4 depthwise separable convolution blocks, an average pooling layer, and a dense projection layer producing the 12 output classes (e.g., "Silence", "Unknown", "Yes", "No", "Up", "Down", "Left", "Right", "On", "Off", "Stop", "Go").

Arithmetic intensity in this table is defined uniformly as MAC operations per byte of data moved, MACs ÷ (input bytes + weight bytes + output bytes), so that layers with different shapes can be compared on the same basis.

Table 4.1: DS-CNN-S Workload Characterization for TinyEdge-NPU (49 × 10 MFCC Input, 22,016 Weights, 12-Class Keyword Spotting)
Layer Name Type Kernel (H x W) Input Shape (H x W x C) Output Shape (H x W x C) Weights (Bytes) MAC Ops Arithmetic Intensity (MACs/Byte)
conv1 Standard 2D 10 × 4, s=(2,1) 49 × 10 × 1 20 × 7 × 64 2,560 358,400 29.84
ds_block1_dw Depthwise 3 × 3, s=(1,1) 20 × 7 × 64 20 × 7 × 64 576 80,640 4.36
ds_block1_pw Pointwise 1 × 1, s=(1,1) 20 × 7 × 64 20 × 7 × 64 4,096 573,440 26.05
ds_block2_dw Depthwise 3 × 3, s=(1,1) 20 × 7 × 64 20 × 7 × 64 576 80,640 4.36
ds_block2_pw Pointwise 1 × 1, s=(1,1) 20 × 7 × 64 20 × 7 × 64 4,096 573,440 26.05
ds_block3_dw Depthwise 3 × 3, s=(1,1) 20 × 7 × 64 20 × 7 × 64 576 80,640 4.36
ds_block3_pw Pointwise 1 × 1, s=(1,1) 20 × 7 × 64 20 × 7 × 64 4,096 573,440 26.05
ds_block4_dw Depthwise 3 × 3, s=(1,1) 20 × 7 × 64 20 × 7 × 64 576 80,640 4.36
ds_block4_pw Pointwise 1 × 1, s=(1,1) 20 × 7 × 64 20 × 7 × 64 4,096 573,440 26.05
avg_pool Global Pool 20 × 7 20 × 7 × 64 1 × 1 × 64 0 8,960 0.99
fc_out Fully Conn. 1 × 1 1 × 1 × 64 1 × 1 × 12 768 768 0.91
Total 22,016 2,984,448 13.94 (mean)

The complete DS-CNN network requires 22,016 parameters (~21.5 KB) and roughly 3.0 million Multiply-Accumulate operations (6.0 MOPs). Because the model needs only ~22 KB, the entire set of weights fits into the 128 KB weight SRAM buffer without paging from external SPI flash or system SRAM during normal operation. The activation working set peaks at the output of conv1 (20 x 7 x 64 = 8,960 bytes), which easily fits inside the 64 KB activation memory. That containment removes external bus transactions during the inference loop, preventing large energy penalties from off-chip I/O switches.

Roofline Analysis for TinyEdge-NPU

A classic Roofline model bounds attainable computational performance (P, in GMAC/s or GOPS) as a function of the operational intensity (I, in MACs/Byte) and two micro-architectural parameters: peak computational capacity (P_peak) and maximum memory bandwidth (B_mem):

P = min( P_peak,  I * B_mem )

For the TinyEdge-NPU, running at 100 MHz with an 8×8 systolic array capable of 64 INT8 MACs/cycle:

P_peak = 64 MACs/cycle * 100 MHz = 6.4 GMAC/s (12.8 GOP/s)

The on-chip activation SRAM uses a 64-bit wide read port operating at 100 MHz, yielding an internal bandwidth of 800 MB/s. The weight SRAM provides a separate 64-bit read path (800 MB/s). The system AXI4 interface is 32 bits wide running at the same 100 MHz clock, delivering a theoretical external burst transfer bandwidth of 400 MB/s.

The structural trade-off becomes obvious at the arithmetic saturation knee point, I_sat:

I_sat = P_peak / B_mem = (6.4 GMAC/s) / (0.8 GB/s) = 8.0 MACs/Byte

Table 4.1 shows the Pointwise layers at 26.05 MACs/Byte and standard convolution at 29.84 MACs/Byte. These layers run cleanly in the compute-bound regime of the roofline, at near 100% array utilization. Depthwise convolutions sit below the boundary (4.36 MACs/Byte), and Pooling/Dense operations fall deep into the memory-bound regime (0.99 and 0.91 MACs/Byte). Pointwise and standard convolutions are 2.65 million of the total 2.98 million MACs (88.9% of the compute workload), so the engine spends almost all of its execution cycles in compute-bound territory. That justifies the 8×8 array size.

Micro-Architectural Takeaway: If the model were dominated by depthwise operations, an 8×8 2D systolic array would suffer from severe starvation stalls. Because pointwise projections dominate edge acoustic networks, an 8×8 compute topology achieves high sustained utilization while staying within a 5 mW thermal envelope.

4.2 The Micro-Architecture Exploration Process

Architecture exploration is often misunderstood as an unstructured search, designers assembling arbitrary blocks in Verilog and evaluating synthesis reports. In high-reliability semiconductor IP development, it is a disciplined, multi-stage reduction process designed to reject unviable options quickly with minimal non-recurring engineering (NRE) effort.

  1. Workload Extraction: Parse targeted neural networks into directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Extract tensor shapes, layer-by-layer parameter counts, data dependencies, and operator profiles.
  2. Boundary Bounding: Define non-negotiable boundaries from the PRD: clock domain targets, dynamic power budgets, peak SRAM capacity, and process metal stack rules.
  3. First-Order Analytical Modeling: Construct a spreadsheet or Python model that maps compute loops to basic hardware topographies. Evaluate cycle counts, ideal data transfers, and memory footprints assuming 100% utilization and zero pipeline bubble overhead.
  4. Cycle-Accurate Modeling of Contested Resources: Build targeted cycle-accurate or transaction-level models (using SystemC or high-level cycle simulators) solely for contested shared structures: memory crossbars, DMA FIFO depth, and systolic pipeline fill/drain behaviors.
  5. RTL Prototyping of Critical Paths: Write synthesizable RTL for critical components (e.g., the MAC processing element, accumulator saturation trees, and local SRAM address generators) to validate timing closure at 100 MHz under worst-case PVT corners (0.9V, 125°C).

Analytical Modeling vs. Cycle-Accurate Simulation

A common pitfall is building a full cycle-accurate C++ simulator before confirming the design is viable at all. Cycle-accurate simulators are expensive to write, debug, and maintain. Split exploration between analytical calculations and cycle-accurate simulations.

Analytical modeling handles:

  • Macro memory sizing (activation double-buffering limits and weight capacities).
  • Theoretical best-case layer latency: Cycles = Layer MACs / (PE Count x Clock Frequency).
  • Static leakage estimates and dynamic power scaling: P_dyn = alpha C V squared f.
  • Maximum AXI burst durations and DMA transfer sizes.

Cycle-accurate simulation is reserved for:

  • Interleaved multi-bank SRAM access contention (bank conflict hazards).
  • Systolic array boundary conditions (pipeline drain and ramp-up cycles per kernel pass).
  • AXI bus backpressure, arbitration latency jitter, and outstanding transaction queues.
  • DMA synchronization handshakes with core sequencer interrupts.

Micro-Architectural Exploration Decisions

Every major architectural choice impacts area, performance, and verification complexity. Table 4.2 details the concrete trade-offs evaluated during the TinyEdge-NPU architecture exploration phase, with the engineering rationale behind each decision.

Table 4.2: Micro-Architectural Exploration Trade-offs for TinyEdge-NPU
Feature Area Alternative Considered Selected Architecture Micro-Architectural Rationale
Compute Topology 1D SIMD Vector (1×64 MAC lane) 2D Systolic Array (8×8 2D grid) A 1D SIMD engine requires a 64-entry crossbar to broadcast weights and activations simultaneously, dominating wire routing channels and incurring excessive parasitic capacitance. An 8×8 systolic array reuses activations horizontally and weights vertically, cutting register file read energy by 42%.
Dataflow Strategy Output-Stationary (accumulate locally) Weight-Stationary with streaming inputs In DS-CNN Pointwise layers, weights remain fixed while streaming across spatial coordinates. Pre-loading an 8×8 block of weights into PE registers eliminates weight re-fetching during spatial streaming, matching the 26.1 MACs/Byte operational intensity.
Accumulator Width 24-bit Integer Accumulation 32-bit Integer Accumulation Although 24-bit counters save ~25% accumulator register area, a 10 × 4 × 64 kernel pass accumulates K = 2,560 products; the worst case is Accum_max = K × 16,384 ≈ 41.9 × 10^6, which exceeds the 24-bit signed ceiling of 8.39 × 10^6. The general bound is B ≥ 15 + ⌈log₂K⌉ bits (27 bits for K = 2,560), so a 24-bit accumulator overflows while 32-bit accumulation covers reductions up to K = 131,072 with headroom. 32-bit width prevents catastrophic clipping overflow without requiring per-cycle saturation checks.
Activation Banking Single Monolithic 64 KB SRAM 4 × 16 KB Interleaved Sub-banks A monolithic single-port SRAM prevents concurrent reads and writes, forcing the DMA input transfer and systolic output drain to serialize. Splitting into 4 sub-banks allows ping-pong double-buffering and concurrent DMA streaming with zero stall penalties.
Quantization Post-Processing Host CPU Software Scaling Hardware Requantization Engine Soft requantization on a micro-controller requires 4 to 6 instructions per activation (shift, multiply scale factor, add zero point, clamp). Inlining a single-cycle fixed-point multiplier-shifter pipeline at the systolic array output drains activations directly to SRAM in final INT8 format.
System Bus Width 64-bit Native AXI4 Interface 32-bit AXI4 with internal packing In our target edge microcontroller SoC, the system fabric is standard 32-bit. Enforcing a native 64-bit master would mandate external asynchronous width-converters, increasing system integration overhead. The internal DMA engine packs two 32-bit words into local 64-bit bus lines natively.

Worked Example: Latency and Duty-Cycle Derivation

To confirm that the selected 8×8 array meets the latency and power requirements, here is the inference time from the analytical model. For the 2.98 MMAC DS-CNN workload on an 8×8 array (64 MACs/cycle at 100 MHz):

Ideal Compute Cycles = 2,984,448 MACs / 64 MACs/cycle = 46,632 cycles

Systolic array pipeline setup, layer configuration transitions, weight preload phases, and quantization scaling add operational overhead. Applying an empirical 65% sustained utilization factor from cycle-accurate simulations of depthwise and pointwise layers:

Actual Execution Cycles = 46,632 / 0.65 = 71,742 clock cycles
Latency at 100 MHz = 71,742 / 100,000,000 Hz = 0.717 ms (~717 microseconds)

The total inference execution time of ~0.72 ms falls well inside the 10 ms design target. Over a 1.0-second audio detection window, the computational duty cycle is:

Duty Cycle = 0.72 ms / 1000 ms = 0.072%

This low duty cycle confirms the architectural thesis. Running at 100 MHz, the active logic draws approximately 3.9 mW on the reference (L) configuration. The same DS-CNN-S inference draws ≈2.5 mW peak on the S configuration (§3.9). At the end of the 0.72 ms burst, the engine asserts an interrupt to the host CPU and enters a low-leakage state retention sleep mode drawing 65 μW. The time-averaged power consumption over the 1-second audio frame is:

P_avg = (0.717 ms × 3.9 mW + 999.283 ms × 0.065 mW) / 1000 ms
P_avg = (0.002797 mJ + 0.064953 mJ) / 1 s = 0.0678 mW = 67.8 µW

That meets the product requirements with substantial margin, confirming the micro-architectural foundation before writing synthesizable RTL.

Architecture Freeze: Criteria and Sign-off

Architecture exploration must not become an open-ended research effort. The exploration phase concludes, and the architecture is formally frozen, once four concrete criteria are satisfied. First, the analytical roofline and cycle-accurate benchmarks demonstrate that the worst-case neural layer executes within ≤70% of the maximum latency allocation (providing a 30% pipeline stall margin). Second, memory floorplans prove the 200 KB SRAM macros (L configuration) fit cleanly within the 1.0 mm2 die footprint alongside standard cell logic at ≤70% row utilization. Third, synthesized RTL prototypes of the critical path (systolic accumulator and address generators) close timing at 125 MHz in the slow-corner process library, ensuring a 25% timing guardband over the 100 MHz operational target. Fourth, the averaged system power remains under the 100 μW ceiling across all operational audio profiles. When these sign-off thresholds are met, the micro-architecture specification is baseline-frozen, and full-scale RTL implementation begins.
