4.3 Dataflow: Weight Stationary vs. Output Stationary

In an ultra-low-power neural processing unit (NPU) such as the TinyEdge-NPU, arithmetic logic units do not dominate the power budget. The fundamental design challenge of edge deep learning accelerators is not computing multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations. It is feeding data to the compute array. Under a 28nm planar CMOS process at nominal operating conditions (0.9 V, 25°C), an 8-bit integer MAC operation consumes approximately 0.20 pJ of dynamic energy. By comparison, reading an 8-bit operand from a local register file costs roughly 0.08 pJ, accessing an adjacent 64 KB activation SRAM bank (L configuration) consumes 2.1 pJ, and accessing a 128 KB weight SRAM bank (L configuration) consumes roughly 2.8 pJ. If an operand must be retrieved from off-chip DRAM over an external bus, that cost escalates to 50–150 pJ per byte.

Data movement across the internal memory hierarchy costs 10 to 15 times more energy than the computation itself. The microarchitectural strategy used to map nested loops onto physical processing elements (PEs), known as the dataflow, determines how often operands are fetched from SRAM, how frequently they are reused across space and time within the register files, and where intermediate results are accumulated.

For the TinyEdge-NPU, which targets always-on keyword spotting within a strict 5 mW active envelope, picking the wrong dataflow guarantees thermal or battery failure. This section analyzes the mechanics of Weight-Stationary (WS) and Output-Stationary (OS) dataflows on the TinyEdge-NPU 8×8 systolic array, evaluates their memory access profiles through concrete layer arithmetic, and demonstrates why a dual-mode hybrid architecture is required to execute depthwise-separable convolutional neural networks (DS-CNNs) efficiently.

flowchart LR subgraph WS[Weight Stationary] W1[Weights held in PE registers] --> W2[Activations stream through array] W2 --> W3[Partial sums flow to drain] end subgraph OS[Output Stationary] O1[Partial sums held in PE registers] --> O2[Weights stream through array] O2 --> O3[Results drained when complete] end WS -.->|Best for: 1x1 pointwise layers| H["Hybrid: TinyEdge-NPU switches per layer"] OS -.->|Best for: 3x3 depthwise layers| H

4.3.1 Defining Dataflow: The Loop-Nest Mapping Problem

A standard convolutional layer can be expressed as a seven-level nested loop iterating over batch size (N), output feature map channels (M), input feature map channels (C), output spatial rows (E) and columns (F), and convolution kernel rows (R) and columns (S). The TinyEdge-NPU operates on continuous real-time audio streams, so batch size is fixed at N=1. The nested loop simplifies to: 

// 2D Convolution Loop Nest (N=1)
for (int m = 0; m < M; m++) {             // Output channels
  for (int c = 0; c < C; c++) {           // Input channels
    for (int e = 0; e < E; e++) {         // Output height (spectrogram frequency)
      for (int f = 0; f < F; f++) {       // Output width (spectrogram time)
        for (int r = 0; r < R; r++) {     // Filter kernel height
          for (int s = 0; s < S; s++) {   // Filter kernel width
            // Spatial stride assumed = 1 for illustration
            Output[m][e][f] += Weight[m][c][r][s] * Input[c][e + r][f + s];
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

A hardware dataflow determines:

  1. Spatial unrolling: Which loop dimensions are mapped across the physical 8×8 grid of 64 PEs in parallel within a single clock cycle.
  2. Temporal scheduling: Which loop indices increment across consecutive clock cycles.
  3. Storage residency: Which of the three primary data tensors, Weights (W), Inputs/Activations (I), or Partial Sums/Outputs (O), remains stationary in local PE registers to maximize operand reuse.

Minimizing total energy requires maximizing the reuse factor (U) of data held in the lowest-energy storage structures, the local registers inside the PE, before falling back to the 64 KB/128 KB SRAM arrays (L configuration).

4.3.2 Weight-Stationary (WS) Execution on the TinyEdge-NPU

In a Weight-Stationary dataflow, filter weights are pre-loaded from the 128 KB weight buffer into dedicated internal storage registers within each PE. Once loaded, these weights remain pinned in place across hundreds or thousands of cycles while input activations stream through the array and partial sums accumulate across the spatial dimensions of the grid.

On the TinyEdge-NPU, the 8×8 PE array evaluates an 8-channel input block by an 8-channel output block when running in WS mode:

  • Each row i (i in [0..7]) of the array is assigned to input channel c_i.
  • Each column j (j in [0..7]) is assigned to output channel m_j.
  • PE(i, j) stores the 8-bit weight parameter W[m_j][c_i] in its internal register REG_W.

Execution proceeds in two distinct operational phases:

  1. Weight Configuration Phase: Over 8 clock cycles, 64 weights are fetched from the 128 KB Weight SRAM and shifted down the columns of the array to populate the REG_W register of every PE.
  2. Streaming Compute Phase: Activation vectors I[c_i][t] (where t represents the combined spatial coordinate e, f) are read from the 64 KB Activation SRAM and broadcast or systolically shifted horizontally from the west edge across each row i. Simultaneously, partial sums are initialized to zero (or loaded with bias values from the 8 KB scratchpad) and accumulated vertically down each column j.

As input activation \(I[c_i][t]\) enters \(\text{PE}(i, j)\), the PE computes the product \(P = I[c_i][t] \times \texttt{REG\_W}\). It adds \(P\) to the incoming partial sum received from \(\text{PE}(i-1, j)\) above it, and registers the updated 32-bit accumulator downward to \(\text{PE}(i+1, j)\) on the next clock cycle. At the south edge of the array, column \(j\) emits a fully resolved, 32-bit accumulated value for output channel \(m_j\), the dot product across the 8 input channels:

\[O[m_j][t] = \sum_{i=0}^{7} W[m_j][c_i] \cdot I[c_i][t]\]

Advantages: The static retention of weights eliminates weight-memory bandwidth during the compute phase. If an input spatial sequence has a length of T=98 frames, each weight stored in the PE is reused 98 times. The memory read traffic for weights drops to exactly 1 byte per 98 MACs (0.0102 bytes/MAC).

Disadvantages: Partial sums are dynamic. Because intermediate sums must propagate through the array or be stored temporarily when the total number of input channels C exceeds the array dimension of 8, high-precision intermediate values (requiring up to 32 bits to prevent overflow prior to quantization) must either be passed down PE interconnect lines or spilled back to SRAM. Spilling 32-bit partial sums to memory creates an immediate 4x penalty in data volume relative to 8-bit values.

4.3.3 Output-Stationary (OS) Execution on the TinyEdge-NPU

In an Output-Stationary dataflow, the accumulation process is locked locally inside the PE. Rather than moving partial sums across the array or spilling them to scratchpad memory, the intermediate accumulation register (a 32-bit accumulator, REG_ACC) stays spatially fixed within the PE until the complete dot product across all filter dimensions (R, S) and input channels (C) is finished.

To map an output-stationary flow onto the TinyEdge-NPU's 8×8 array:

  • Each of the 64 PEs is assigned a unique output spatial coordinate or a unique output channel. In depthwise processing, PE(u, v) accumulates the output activation for channel u at temporal frame v.
  • Both weights and activations are dynamic. During each clock cycle, an 8-bit weight operand and an 8-bit activation operand stream into the PE from orthogonal routing networks (for example, activations routed horizontally from the west, weights routed vertically from the north).
  • The PE executes an 8-bit multiply, adds the 16-bit signed product directly to its local 32-bit REG_ACC, and holds the result in place.
  • This accumulation loop continues for K x K cycles (where K is the kernel filter dimension) or across the channel depth C.
  • When accumulation completes, the 32-bit value passes through an integrated local post-processing block (bias addition, ReLU/clipping activation function, and scale/shift quantization) to convert the 32-bit accumulator back to an 8-bit output. The resulting single INT8 byte is streamed out to the Activation SRAM.

Advantages: OS completely eliminates partial sum memory traffic. Intermediate 32-bit sums never cross PE boundaries and are never written to external or scratchpad SRAM. Only fully quantized 8-bit values are written back to the 64 KB Activation SRAM.

Disadvantages: Both weights and input activations must be delivered concurrently to every PE. If multiple PEs require the same weight or activation at different times, complex spatial distribution networks or duplicated read cycles from the SRAM buffers are required. Operand reuse within the PE's local register file is heavily constrained.

4.3.4 Architectural Comparison

The trade-offs between Weight-Stationary and Output-Stationary implementations on the TinyEdge-NPU hardware substrate are summarized in Table 4.3.

Table 4.3: Head-to-Head Comparison of WS and OS Dataflows on TinyEdge-NPU
Architectural Parameter Weight-Stationary (WS) Output-Stationary (OS)
Stationary Storage 8-bit Weight Register (REG_W) 32-bit Accumulator Register (REG_ACC)
PE Register Bit Cost Low (8 to 16 bits per PE storage) Moderate (32 to 40 bits per PE storage)
Weight Reuse Maximized (held across temporal iterations) Minimized (streamed continuously from SRAM)
Activation Reuse Moderate (broadcast or pipelined horizontally) Moderate (systolically broadcast across columns)
Partial Sum Handling Migrates across array rows/columns; spills to SRAM when C > 8 Zero external partial sum traffic; accumulated locally in PE
Write-back Bandwidth Requires high-bandwidth egress for partial or completed sums Minimal; writes only finalized, quantized INT8 results
Control Complexity Low; simple streaming activation addressing Moderate; synchronization of dual input streams (W, I)
Optimal Layer Types Pointwise (1×1 Conv), Dense/Fully-Connected Depthwise (3×3, 5×5 Conv), Large Dilated Conv

4.3.5 Worked Arithmetic: Pointwise vs. Depthwise Convolutions

To quantify how dataflow selection alters SRAM traffic and memory energy, consider two representative layers from an acoustic keyword spotting network (DS-CNN architecture running on 1-second audio windows, converted to a 40 x 98 Log-Mel spectrogram):

  • Layer 1 (Pointwise 1×1 Conv): Input dimensions: H=1, W=98, C=64. Output channels: M=64. Kernel: 1 x 1. Total operations:

    MACs = W × M × C = 98 × 64 × 64 = 401,408 MACs

  • Layer 2 (Depthwise 3×3 Conv): Input dimensions: H=10, W=98, C=64. Channels are processed independently (M=C=64). Kernel: 3 x 3. Stride: 1, padding to maintain spatial size 10 x 98. Total operations:

    MACs = H × W × C × R × S = 10 × 98 × 64 × 3 × 3 = 564,480 MACs

Pointwise Layer Analysis (1 x 1, C=64, M=64, T=98)

Case A: Weight-Stationary Dataflow
The layer is evaluated in tiles of 8 input channels and 8 output channels, matching the 8×8 array size. Number of sub-tiles = (64 / 8) x (64 / 8) = 8 x 8 = 64 tiles. For each tile:

  1. 64 weight bytes are loaded into the PEs once per tile. Total weight reads = 64 x 64 = 4,096 bytes.
  2. 98 input vectors (8 bytes each) are streamed into the array. Total input reads = 64 x (98 x 8) = 50,176 bytes.
  3. Across the 8 input-channel reduction steps, intermediate partial sums must be maintained. By ordering loops so that all 64 input channels are accumulated before moving to the next time frame, partial sums can remain on the south-edge accumulation FIFOs without leaving the datapath until the final 64-channel sum is reached. Thus, only completed 8-bit quantized outputs are written back: 98 x 64 = 6,272 bytes.
  4. Total SRAM traffic = 4,096 (W) + 50,176 (I) + 6,272 (O) = 60,544 bytes.
  5. Traffic intensity = 60,544 / 401,408 ≈ 0.151 bytes/MAC.

Case B: Output-Stationary Dataflow
The 64 PEs hold 64 output channel values for one time frame (t). To resolve these 64 outputs, all 64 inputs and their corresponding 64 x 64 weights must stream into the array:

  1. For each time frame (T=98), every weight must be re-read from SRAM unless cached locally. Since the internal register file cannot hold 4,096 weights, weights stream continuously from SRAM: 98 x 4,096 = 401,408 bytes.
  2. Input activations read from SRAM: 98 x 64 = 6,272 bytes.
  3. Final output writes: 98 x 64 = 6,272 bytes.
  4. Total SRAM traffic = 401,408 (W) + 6,272 (I) + 6,272 (O) = 413,952 bytes.
  5. Traffic intensity = 413,952 / 401,408 ≈ 1.031 bytes/MAC.
Key Finding (Pointwise): Output-Stationary execution on a 1x1 convolution increases SRAM data traffic by a factor of 6.83x compared to Weight-Stationary execution, resulting in an unsustainable energy penalty.
Depthwise Layer Analysis (3 x 3, C=64, H=10, W=98)

In a depthwise layer, channels do not mix. Each channel operates independently with a 9-element filter (3 x 3). Total weights in the entire layer = 64 x 9 = 576 bytes.

Case A: Weight-Stationary Dataflow
The 8×8 array cannot map 8 input channels to 8 output channels, because channel cross-terms do not exist. If the array maps 8 separate channels across 8 rows, each row computes only for its own channel:

  1. Only 8 of the 64 PEs in the array can be active simultaneously if configured conventionally, degrading hardware utilization to 12.5% (8/64).
  2. If the array instead tiles 8 spatial pixels across the columns, the 9 weights for a single channel are held in registers, but are reused only over the small spatial row. More critically, partial sums for 2D convolution filters (3 x 3) must be maintained across multiple line buffers.
  3. Each intermediate pixel requires accumulating 9 terms across 3 lines. If partial sums are flushed to scratchpad SRAM across line boundaries, memory writes and reads multiply. Number of intermediate partial sum transactions: 10 x 98 x 64 = 62,720 elements. Storing 32-bit (4-byte) partial sums requires 62,720 x 4 = 250,880 bytes written and read.
  4. Total SRAM traffic = 576 (W) + 76,800 (I) + 501,760 (partial sums) + 62,720 (O) = 641,856 bytes.
  5. Traffic intensity = 641,856 / 564,480 ≈ 1.137 bytes/MAC.

Case B: Output-Stationary Dataflow
Each PE is assigned a single output pixel for a specific channel. It holds its 32-bit accumulator locally for exactly 9 clock cycles while the 9 filter taps and corresponding patch pixels stream through:

  1. The weights for each channel are tiny (3 x 3 = 9 bytes). They are read from the 128 KB weight buffer and reused across the 64 PEs: 64 channels x 9 bytes = 576 bytes.
  2. Activations read from SRAM (including halo/overlap overhead for 3 x 3 stride 1): 12 x 100 x 64 approx 76,800 bytes.
  3. Partial sums: 0 bytes. All 9 MAC operations accumulate in the local 32-bit REG_ACC.
  4. Final quantized outputs written to SRAM: 10 x 98 x 64 = 62,720 bytes.
  5. Total SRAM traffic = 576 (W) + 76,800 (I) + 62,720 (O) = 140,096 bytes.
  6. Traffic intensity = 140,096 / 564,480 ≈ 0.248 bytes/MAC.
Key Finding (Depthwise): Weight-Stationary execution on a 3x3 depthwise convolution increases SRAM data traffic by 4.58x relative to Output-Stationary execution due to intermediate partial sum spills and poor spatial mapping.

The quantitative comparisons for both layers are consolidated in Table 4.4.

4.3.6 The Case for a Hybrid Microarchitecture

The worked arithmetic demonstrates an architectural dichotomy. Pointwise layers require Weight-Stationary dataflow to avoid catastrophic weight re-fetching. Depthwise layers require Output-Stationary dataflow to avoid partial sum spills and low hardware utilization.

Modern edge vision and acoustic models, including MobileNet, EfficientNet, and the DS-CNN models targeting the TinyEdge-NPU, consist almost entirely of alternating depthwise and pointwise convolutional blocks. In a standard 5-block DS-CNN keyword spotting model (200K parameters):

  • Pointwise layers account for roughly 77% of all multiply-accumulate operations.
  • Depthwise layers account for roughly 11% of operations.
  • Standard pooling, fully connected, and input projection layers account for the remaining 12%.

If the TinyEdge-NPU were designed exclusively around a pure Weight-Stationary dataflow, the depthwise layers would consume a disproportionate share of total chip power, despite accounting for only about a tenth of the operations. Committing solely to an Output-Stationary architecture would flood the memory bus during the pointwise layers, driving active power well beyond the 5 mW power limit.

TinyEdge-NPU resolves this trade-off through a configurable hybrid dataflow. The 8×8 systolic execution grid dynamically reconfigures its internal register paths, routing multiplexers, and accumulator bindings on a layer-by-layer basis under firmware control via the AXI-Lite control register file.

4.3.7 Microarchitectural Cost of Dual-Mode Operation

Supporting both Weight-Stationary and Output-Stationary modes requires targeted changes to the PE datapath and control logic. The hardware additions required within each of the 64 PEs are illustrated in the datapath representation below:

To implement this dual-mode capability without duplicating the primary compute structures, the TinyEdge-NPU PE datapath incorporates three microarchitectural modifications to the baseline weight-stationary design:

  • Reconfigurable Accumulator Loop: In baseline WS mode, the 32-bit spatial accumulator receives a partial sum from the northern neighbor (PE[r-1, c]), adds the local INT8 × INT8 product, and registers the output downward to PE[r+1, c] on the subsequent cycle. For OS mode, a 32-bit 2:1 multiplexer placed at the accumulator input loops the PE’s own registered sum back into the adder operand port, enabling local accumulation across successive cycles without toggling inter-PE routing wires.
  • Shared Accumulation and Drain Network: Dedicated drain buses for OS mode would introduce severe routing congestion across metal layers M3 and M4. Instead, TinyEdge-NPU repurposes the existing vertical 32-bit partial-sum systolic routing lines as a token-triggered drain chain. Once accumulation completes for an output tile, the local accumulators are disconnected from the multiplier and chained vertically as a shift register, dumping 8 rows of 32-bit results into the southern accumulation buffer over 8 consecutive cycles at 100 MHz.
  • Weight-Register Bypass and Staging: In WS mode, the 8-bit weight register acts as a static shadow latch refreshed only across output channel tiles. In OS mode, this register operates as an active pipeline stage, streaming weights vertically from north to south while activation inputs stream horizontally from west to east. A 1-bit configuration register per PE column sets this multiplexer configuration during layer setup.

The silicon area and cell-count overhead of these additions was synthesized using a commercial 28nm HPC+ standard-cell library at nominal operating conditions (0.9 V, 25°C, 100 MHz target frequency). Table 4.5 details the incremental cost per processing element.

Table 4.5: Incremental Cost of Dual-Mode (WS/OS) Operation per Processing Element
Component Baseline WS PE (Gate Count) Dual-Mode WS/OS PE (Gate Count) Delta (Gates) Area Delta (µm²)
INT8 Multiplier (Radix-4 Booth) 412 412 0 0.00
32-bit Adder / Accumulator 184 184 0 0.00
Operand & Accumulator Registers 448 448 0 0.00
Multiplexers & Steering Logic 42 128 +86 +44.72
Clock Gating & Local Decode 28 46 +18 +9.36
Total per PE 1,114 1,218 +104 (+9.3%) +54.08
Total 8×8 Array (64 PEs) 71,296 77,952 +6,656 +3,461.12

Across the complete 8×8 array, dual-mode operation adds 6,656 equivalent NAND2 gates (~3,461 µm²), an area overhead of less than 0.35% of the total 1.0 mm² TinyEdge-NPU floorplan. Critical path timing analysis confirms the worst-case slack decreases by only 42 ps, well within the 10.0 ns cycle budget, caused by the input multiplexer preceding the 32-bit accumulator flip-flops.

4.3.8 Summary: Why Hybrid Wins for TinyEdge-NPU

The microarchitectural mandate for TinyEdge-NPU is maximizing energy efficiency across heterogeneous layer profiles under an absolute 5 mW active power envelope. Acoustic models such as DS-CNN demonstrate extreme computational variance across their pipeline. Depthwise separable layers present very few weights per input channel (3 x 3 x 1), rendering pure weight-stationary arrays inefficient due to low MAC utilization (<15%) and continuous weight-reloading overhead. 1×1 pointwise convolutions and fully connected projection layers, by contrast, feature high channel density (e.g., 64 input to 64 output channels), making weight reuse paramount.

Design Rule: In sub-10 mW edge NPUs running depthwise-separable topologies, never lock the microarchitecture into a single dataflow. The energy required to move partial sums in a depthwise layer under Weight Stationary far exceeds the minimal gate-count cost of adding local accumulation loops.

By implementing a hybrid, software-configurable dataflow, TinyEdge-NPU executes 1×1 pointwise convolutions in Weight Stationary mode, maximizing operand reuse from the 128 KB weight SRAM (L configuration), and switches via AXI-Lite command register to Output Stationary mode for depthwise convolutions, keeping partial sums inside the PE registers and slashing SRAM write transactions. The empirical result for a 1-second 16 kHz audio window on DS-CNN is a substantial reduction in overall SRAM access energy, achieved at the cost of less than 10% PE logic overhead and zero performance penalty.

4.4 MAC Array Sizing

The core computational engine of any neural processing unit (NPU) is its multiply-accumulate (MAC) array. Sizing this array requires balancing conflicting physical and algorithmic constraints: peak arithmetic throughput, silicon area, dynamic switching energy, standby leakage, and dataflow utilization across target layer topologies. An oversized array wastes silicon and leaks excessive power while idling during low-dimensional convolutions. An undersized array fails inference latency deadlines, requiring higher clock frequencies that scale dynamic power quadratically with supply voltage.

Workload Characterization and Latency Budgets

The sizing derivation for the TinyEdge-NPU originates from its target application profile: always-on keyword spotting (KWS) and acoustic event detection using depthwise separable convolutional neural networks (DS-CNN). The primary production workload is a 12-class DS-CNN model parameterized for speech feature maps derived from a 16 kHz audio stream:

  • Input: Log-mel spectrogram generated from a 1.0-second audio window, producing an input tensor of dimension 49 x 10 x 1 (49 time frames, 10 frequency bins, single channel).
  • Model Topology: 1 standard 2D convolution layer (49 × 10 × 1 → 20 × 7 × 64, kernel 10 × 4, stride (2,1)), followed by 4 depthwise separable convolution blocks (each consisting of a 3 x 3 depthwise convolution and a 1 x 1 pointwise convolution with 64 channels), an average pooling layer, and a dense classification head projecting to 12 target output classes.
  • Total Compute: 12.8 million multiply-accumulate operations (12.8 MMACs) per inference.
  • Model Footprint: 120,000 INT8 parameters (~120 KB including weights, biases, and per-tensor scaling factors).

In edge audio classification, inference is executed periodically over sliding temporal windows. A standard acoustic feature extraction window slides forward every 100 ms (a 10 Hz classification cadence). To achieve ultra-low average power, the NPU operates in a "race-to-sleep" regime. Compute must complete in a fraction of the 100 ms frame interval so the system can transition into a low-leakage retention state.

The active latency budget (T_infer) is set to 10.0 ms maximum. Completing a 12.8 MMAC inference within 10 ms leaves 90 ms of sleep time per frame, a 10% compute duty cycle. If the active core consumes 3.9 mW and the retention state consumes 80 μW, the time-averaged power consumption is:

P_avg = (D × P_active) + ((1 − D) × P_sleep) = (0.10 × 3.9 mW) + (0.90 × 0.08 mW) = 0.462 mW

This is well within the 1.0 mW envelope required for battery-operated edge devices.

Sizing Formulation and Utilization Realities

The required effective compute throughput (R_eff) is determined by the workload volume and the target latency budget:

R_eff = N_ops / T_infer = 12.8 × 10^6 MACs / 0.010 s = 1.28 × 10^9 MAC/s = 1.28 GMAC/s

The peak throughput of an array with N_MAC units operating at clock frequency f_clk is:

R_peak = N_MAC × f_clk

Peak throughput is an ideal metric that assumes 100% hardware utilization. In practice, utilization (eta) is severely degraded by kernel boundary effects, spatial tiling mismatches, and structural pipeline stalls:

R_eff = R_peak × utilization = (N_MAC × f_clk) × utilization

Rearranging to solve for the required number of physical MAC units yields:

N_MAC ≥ (N_ops / T_infer) ÷ (f_clk × utilization)

For the TinyEdge-NPU implemented in a 28nm CMOS process, f_clk is constrained to 100 MHz (10 ns cycle time). This frequency choice allows the design to close setup timing comfortably across Worst-Case Commercial (WCC) silicon corners (0.9 V, 125 °C) using high-threshold-voltage (HVT) and standard-threshold-voltage (SVT) cells, avoiding leaky low-threshold (LVT) cells and minimizing active power.

The array efficiency eta depends heavily on how the tensor dimensions map onto the physical MAC geometry. In DS-CNNs, the workload is divided between two contrasting layer types:

  1. Pointwise Convolutions (1 x 1): Highly parallel matrix-matrix multiplications (M x K x N). Channels (C=64) and filters (K=64) map onto the array with minimal zero-padding, achieving high utilization (η ≈ 70–85%).
  2. Depthwise Convolutions (3 x 3): Convolutions where the number of input channels equals the number of output channels with no cross-channel accumulation. Each spatial kernel operates on an isolated 1 x 3 x 3 volume. Mapping this narrow channel dimension across a wide systolic grid forces extensive padding or underutilizes rows and columns, dropping utilization to η ≈ 20–40%.

Across the full DS-CNN execution profile, the blended execution efficiency is approximately 45% to 55%. Evaluating the formula at f_clk = 100 MHz and an average efficiency η = 0.50:

N_MAC ≥ (12.8 × 10^6 MACs / 0.010 s) ÷ (100 × 10^6 Hz × 0.50) = 1.28 × 10^9 / (50 × 10^6) = 25.6 MACs

While a theoretical minimum of 26 MACs is required, systolic architectures demand power-of-two square or rectangular topologies to simplify address generation, loop tiling, and interconnect multiplexing. The practical design choices are 4 x 4 (16 MACs), 8 x 8 (64 MACs), and 16 x 16 (256 MACs).

Architectural Trade-Off Analysis: 4x4 vs. 8x8 vs. 16x16

Evaluating these three geometries against latency, area, dynamic power, and leakage clarifies why the 8 x 8 configuration is the correct choice:

  • The 4 x 4 Array (16 MACs): Offers the highest per-MAC utilization (~62%) because its small dimension is easy to saturate, even on depthwise layers. However, its peak throughput is only 1.6 GMAC/s at 100 MHz. At η = 0.624, the effective throughput is 1.00 GMAC/s, resulting in an inference latency of: T_infer = 12.8 MMAC / 1.00 GMAC/s ≈ 12.8 ms This violates the 10.0 ms budget. Closing this gap would require scaling the clock frequency to 135 MHz, demanding higher-leakage library cells, shifting power away from the optimal energy-per-operation point, and leaving zero headroom for larger models (such as 250K-parameter variants).
  • The 16 x 16 Array (256 MACs): Delivers a peak throughput of 25.6 GMAC/s, completing the raw math in under 2 ms. On DS-CNN workloads, however, utilization drops precipitously to ~22%. For depthwise layers with an input spatial tile of 3 x 3, an array with 16 input rows leaves 7 of those rows completely idle.

    A 16 x 16 array also requires routing 16 INT8 activation operands and 16 INT8 weight operands per cycle, requiring wide on-chip interconnects and a 256-bit SRAM read interface. The total cell area for 256 PEs (including 32-bit accumulators) expands the compute core footprint, while static gate leakage increases by nearly 4x, violating the <100 μW sleep budget in standard 28nm bulk CMOS.
  • The 8 x 8 Array (64 MACs): Represents the optimal design point. Delivering 6.4 GMAC/s peak at 100 MHz with a blended effective utilization of 47.6% (for the 12.8 MMAC workload), the effective throughput is 3.05 GMAC/s. The resulting inference latency is: T_infer = 12.8 MMAC / 3.05 GMAC/s ≈ 4.20 ms This is the same 420,000 cycles Chapter 9 measures for DS-CNN-M on silicon, and it satisfies the 10.0 ms latency constraint with a 2.4x safety margin, allowing the core to enter deep sleep for 95.80 ms out of every 100 ms. Active power remains well below 5 mW, while sleep leakage is kept low.

It meets the inference latency requirement with margin to accommodate models up to 33 MMACs within the 10 ms envelope, maintains balanced 64-bit SRAM memory access widths, and restricts core leakage to 64 μW, preserving the sub-100 μW system standby budget.

4.5 Memory Hierarchy

Accelerators for deep learning are fundamentally constrained by data movement rather than raw arithmetic capacity. In a 28nm process, performing an 8-bit integer multiply-accumulate operation consumes approximately 0.2 pJ. Reading the two 8-bit operands from on-chip SRAM macros consumes roughly 2.1 pJ (activation bank) and 2.8 pJ (weight bank), and fetching them from off-chip DRAM or SPI flash consumes between 50 pJ and 150 pJ per byte.

To keep TinyEdge-NPU below 5 mW, operand reuse must be maximized within the internal storage structures. Data movement from high-energy storage tiers must be minimized using a carefully managed memory hierarchy.

Three-Level Storage Architecture

TinyEdge-NPU implements a strictly managed three-level memory hierarchy designed to match the data ingestion patterns of the 8 x 8 systolic array:

  1. Level 1: Register-Level Storage (PE Internal): Located inside each of the 64 Processing Elements (PEs). Each PE contains:
    • One 8-bit weight register holding the current stationary parameter.
    • One 8-bit shadow weight register enabling background loading of the next parameter.
    • One 8-bit activation forwarding register for horizontal systolic propagation.
    • One 32-bit accumulator register preserving full precision across multiply-add sequences.
    Energy cost: <0.05 pJ per access. Latency: 0 cycles (single-cycle registered compute).
  2. Level 2: On-Chip SRAM Buffers: A software-managed scratchpad memory system divided into three dedicated SRAM banks (reference L configuration, §3.9):
    • Weight Buffer (128 KB): Organized as two interleaved 64 KB instances.
    • Activation Buffer (64 KB): Organized as two ping-pong 32 KB instances.
    • Bias and Scratchpad Buffer (8 KB): Houses 32-bit initial bias vectors, per-channel quantization scale factors, and residual shortcut bypass vectors.
    Energy cost: 2.1 to 2.8 pJ per access (2.1 pJ for the 64 KB activation bank, 2.8 pJ for the 128 KB weight bank). Latency: 1 cycle (pipelined synchronous read).
  3. Level 3: Off-Chip System Memory (SPI Flash / Host System DRAM): Non-volatile storage containing the master model binary, weights, and application firmware. Accessible across the system bus through an integrated 32-bit AXI4 Master DMA interface. Energy cost: 50 to 150 pJ per byte transferred. Latency: 40 to 120 bus cycles.

Sizing the SRAM Buffers

The on-chip SRAM capacity determines which models can run entirely on-chip versus those requiring intermediate layer evictions to external memory.

Weight Buffer Sizing (128 KB, L configuration)

Target DS-CNN KWS models range from 22,000 (DS-CNN-S) to 250,000 (industrial multi-keyword) parameters. A strictly non-streaming design for the largest model would require 250 KB of weight SRAM, consuming roughly 0.65 mm2 in 28nm, more than half the total die budget. Instead, the weight buffer is sized to 128 KB (the L configuration's WEIGHT_KB maximum).

A 128 KB capacity fits the 120K-parameter DS-CNN-M in its entirety. For larger 250K-parameter industrial models, 128 KB holds roughly half the parameters; the rest are streamed into the buffer via background DMA while the earlier layers execute, using double-buffered weight paging.

Activation Buffer Sizing (64 KB, L configuration)

The activation buffer capacity must store the largest pair of consecutive intermediate tensor feature maps (layer input and layer output) during inference. For our 1-second audio DS-CNN:

  • Layer 0 (Input Spectrogram): 49 × 10 × 1 = 490 Bytes.
  • Layer 1 (Standard Conv2D Output): Spatial output dimension is 20 × 7 with 64 feature maps: Tensor Size = 20 × 7 × 64 = 8,960 Bytes = 8.75 KB
  • Layer 2 (Depthwise Conv Block 1 Output): Spatial output dimension remains 20 × 7 × 64 = 8,960 Bytes.
  • Maximum Activation Footprint: In larger acoustic models with 128 channels and 50 time frames, intermediate tensors reach 50 × 5 × 128 = 32,000 Bytes ≈ 31.25 KB.

To prevent memory overwrites during execution, the activation buffer is split into two independent 32 KB banks configured as a ping-pong buffer:

Total Activation Capacity = 2 × 32 KB = 64 KB

While the array reads input activations from Bank 0, it writes the computed output activations directly into Bank 1. On layer completion, the controller swaps the buffer pointers without moving any data.

Double Buffering and Ping-Pong Mechanics

To hide DMA transfer latencies to external memory, both the activation and weight buffers implement double buffering: 

Layer N Execution:
  Weight Buffer Bank 0: [ ACTIVE COMPUTE READ ] -> Feeding MAC Array PEs
  Weight Buffer Bank 1: [ DMA BACKGROUND LOAD ] <- Streaming Layer N+1 Weights
  Activation Bank 0:    [ ACTIVE COMPUTE READ ] -> Input Activations (Layer N)
  Activation Bank 1:    [ ACTIVE COMPUTE WRITE] <- Output Activations (Layer N)

Layer N+1 Execution (Pointers Inverted):
  Weight Buffer Bank 0: [ DMA BACKGROUND LOAD ] <- Streaming Layer N+2 Weights
  Weight Buffer Bank 1: [ ACTIVE COMPUTE READ ] -> Feeding MAC Array PEs
  Activation Bank 0:    [ ACTIVE COMPUTE WRITE] <- Output Activations (Layer N+1)
  Activation Bank 1:    [ ACTIVE COMPUTE READ ] -> Input Activations (Layer N+1)

Hardware address generators apply circular modulo offsets to ensure that bank switching completes within a single clock cycle, eliminating stall states between layers.

Bandwidth Requirements at 100 MHz

In the 8 x 8 weight-stationary systolic array, the operational dataflow dictates strict per-cycle bandwidth requirements across the memory subsystem:

  • Activation Read Bandwidth: The array accepts 8 parallel INT8 values along its vertical input edge each cycle. At 100 MHz, the activation buffer must supply: Bandwidth_act = 8 elements/cycle × 1 Byte/element × 100 MHz = 800 MB/s This is implemented using a 64-bit wide SRAM macro interface (8 bytes per word), enabling one read access per cycle.
  • Activation Write Bandwidth: The array produces 8 INT8 output values from its rightmost edge when operating in systolic drain mode, or through accumulator decimation. The write bandwidth requirement is: Bandwidth_write = 8 Bytes/cycle × 100 MHz = 800 MB/s To prevent structural read-write bank hazards on the activation memory, each 32 KB bank is constructed using pseudo-dual-port (1R1W) SRAM macros or dual interleaved single-port SRAM instances.
  • Weight Bandwidth: Weights remain stationary inside the PE registers over a tile processing sequence (typically 100 to 400 cycles). As a result, the compute-side read bandwidth for weights is modest: Bandwidth_wt, compute = 64 Bytes / 100 cycles × 100 MHz = 64 MB/s However, during layer transitions or double-buffered background DMA transfers, the weight buffer must support burst fills over the 32-bit AXI4 interface: Bandwidth_wt, DMA = 4 Bytes/cycle × 100 MHz = 400 MB/s peak
Table 4.7: On-Chip Memory Hierarchy Specifications for TinyEdge-NPU
Memory Structure Capacity Organization / Banking Port Type Word Width Peak Read BW @ 100 MHz Peak Write BW @ 100 MHz
PE Register File 448 Bytes (Total) 64 PEs × 7 Bytes Distributed Flip-Flops Internal 6.4 GB/s 6.4 GB/s
Activation Buffer 64 KB 2 × 32 KB Banks (Ping-Pong) 1R1W (Pseudo-Dual Port) 64 bits (8 Bytes) 800 MB/s 800 MB/s
Weight Buffer 128 KB 2 × 64 KB Banks (Double Buffer) Single Port (Interleaved) 64 bits (8 Bytes) 800 MB/s 400 MB/s (AXI DMA)
Bias / Scratchpad 8 KB Single Unified Instance Single Port 32 bits (4 Bytes) 400 MB/s 400 MB/s

400 MB/s, a 32-bit data path running at the core 100 MHz clock. This exposes a severe 16× bandwidth asymmetry between internal array consumption (up to 6.4 GB/s of weight and activation data) and external system supply. The primary role of the local SRAM hierarchy is to act as an impedance matcher, transforming high-latency, power-hungry system bus bursts into tightly coupled, low-power parallel feeds for the 8×8 compute fabric.

Because the external AXI4 master interface is capped at 400 MB/s, any architectural stall that forces the MAC array to wait directly on system DRAM or Flash collapses compute efficiency. For an INT8 acoustic model requiring 200,000 parameter fetches per inference, streaming weights on demand without reuse would consume 50,000 clock cycles solely in bus transit (assuming zero bus contention and ideal burst behavior). Localizing the active working set within the 128 KB weight buffer and 64 KB activation buffer isolates TinyEdge-NPU from external interconnect jitter, constraining system bus occupancy to brief DMA transfers at layer or frame boundaries.

Double Buffering and Ping-Pong Operation

To eliminate pipeline stalls during inference, TinyEdge-NPU implements hardware ping-pong double buffering across both its weight and activation SRAM banks (reference L configuration, §3.9). The 128 KB weight memory is logically partitioned into two 64 KB physical banks (Bank 0: Ping, Bank 1: Pong), each equipped with independent address decoders, chip-select logic, and arbitrated read/write ports. The 64 KB activation buffer is similarly partitioned into two 32 KB ping-pong banks.

During execution, the autonomous AXI4 DMA engine and the systolic execution sequencer operate out of phase under the orchestration of a hardware credit counter:

  • Compute Phase: The systolic array reads weights from the Ping buffer and input activations from Activation Bank A, writing transformed output features to Activation Bank B.
  • Background Prefetch Phase: Concurrently, the AXI4 DMA engine streams the parameter blocks for the subsequent layer from external memory into the Pong buffer across the 32-bit bus.

For zero-stall operation, the prefetch latency (T_DMA) must not exceed the execution latency (T_compute). Consider a depthwise-separable layer where the pointwise convolution stage processes an input tensor of dimension 16 x 16 x 64 to produce 64 output channels (64 × 64 × 1 × 1 = 4,096 weights, corresponding to 1,048,576 INT8 MAC operations):

T_compute = 1,048,576 MACs / (64 MACs/cycle × 0.90 utilization) = 18,204 cycles (182.04 µs)
T_DMA     = (4,096 Bytes / 4 Bytes/cycle) + AXI_overhead (~48 cycles) = 1,072 cycles (10.72 µs)

Because T_DMA ≪ T_compute, the DMA completes the background transfer into the Pong buffer 171.32 µs before the systolic array finishes computing. Upon completion of the layer, the sequencer executes a zero-overhead pointer swap (toggling a single address remap bit in the memory-mapped controller), converting Pong to Ping without incurring pipeline drain penalties.

Handling Models Exceeding On-Chip Capacity

When deploying larger 250K-parameter DS-CNN networks on TinyEdge-NPU, the 250 KB parameter footprint exceeds the physical 128 KB weight SRAM capacity. Early layer acoustic feature maps can also temporarily overflow the 32 KB ping-pong activation limit. The memory subsystem resolves these footprint mismatches using three complementary hardware and compiler strategies: parameter streaming, channel/spatial tiling, and layer fusion.

Weight Streaming via Granular Tiling: Layers whose parameter sets exceed the 64 KB bank budget are segmented along the output channel dimension (K). The compiler tiles K into chunks of size K_tile ≤ 64, sizing each tile such that its weight matrix, bias vector, and scaling parameters fit entirely within a single 64 KB bank. The execution pipeline iterates through input activations multiple times, streaming successive weight tiles through the ping-pong buffers. Although re-reading activations increases SRAM read power, it avoids spilling activations to external system memory.

Spatial and Channel Activation Tiling: For high-resolution feature maps exceeding the 32 KB activation buffer, the spatial domain (time steps × frequency bins) is tiled into horizontal bands with overlapping boundary margins. For a 3 x 3 kernel, a 2-element halo is replicated across adjacent spatial tiles. The local DMA engine fetches tiles with these spatial overlaps embedded, allowing the compute fabric to generate valid output frames without cross-tile synchronization or intermediate external spills.

Operator and Layer Fusion: Depthwise-separable convolutions present an ideal target for in-memory layer fusion. Standard execution would write the complete intermediate feature map of the Depthwise (DW) convolution out to SRAM, only to read it back immediately for the subsequent Pointwise (PW) 1 x 1 convolution. TinyEdge-NPU’s scheduler fuses these operations in hardware using the 8 KB scratchpad:

  1. The systolic array computes a localized spatial block of the DW-Conv (3 x 3 x 1).
  2. The resulting intermediate activation vector (up to 64 values) is routed directly into the 8 KB low-latency scratchpad, bypassing the main activation SRAM.
  3. The PW-Conv immediately reads this vector from the scratchpad, accumulates the 1 x 1 projection, applies the ReLU and per-channel quantization scale, and writes only the final pointwise result to the destination activation bank.
Table 4.8: Execution Strategy Comparison for Models Exceeding On-Chip Capacity
Execution Strategy External AXI4 Traffic (KB/inf) Internal SRAM Traffic (KB/inf) Active Power (mW) Latency (ms)
Unfused / External Spilling 512.4 128.0 12.80 4.25
Tiled (Ping-Pong Weight Stream) 256.0 384.2 4.85 1.92
Fused DW-PW + Tiled Weight Stream 256.0 198.6 3.92 1.45
Silicon Design Metric: Operator fusion reduces internal SRAM access counts by 48.3% and lowers total dynamic power by nearly 1 mW, keeping the core well beneath its 5 mW active power ceiling even when executing models twice the size of the on-chip weight buffer.

Through the integration of dedicated banking, hardware-managed ping-pong buffers, and tightly orchestrated tiling strategies, the TinyEdge-NPU memory hierarchy decouples raw compute throughput from the bandwidth limitations of low-power system interconnects. This memory architecture guarantees average MAC utilization of 65% on 28nm silicon (reaching 78–92% spatial-mapping utilization on depthwise layers and above 85% on pointwise layers) while confining peak active power dissipation to less than 5 mW across diverse acoustic processing workloads.

4.6 Precision: INT8, INT4, and Quantization

Quantization maps continuous, floating-point neural network parameters and activations onto low-bitwidth discrete integers. For edge inference engines, precision selection directly governs energy efficiency, silicon area, memory bandwidth, and classification accuracy. Selecting the arithmetic precision for an IP like TinyEdge-NPU requires balancing the compression benefits of sub-byte representations against the operational complexity of handling non-standard data types in hardware, compilers, and verification suites.

4.6.1 The INT8 Baseline: Accuracy, Tooling, and Architecture

Eight-bit integer (INT8) arithmetic serves as the industry standard for edge neural processing units. The justification for INT8 as the TinyEdge-NPU baseline rests on three architectural pillars:

  • Negligible Accuracy Degradation: Post-training quantization (PTQ) or quantization-aware training (QAT) reduces full-precision FP32 models to uniform INT8 with less than 0.5% absolute accuracy loss across standard keyword spotting (KWS) and acoustic event detection (AED) workloads.
  • Byte Alignment and Memory Subsystem Simplicity: An 8-bit word matches standard byte-addressable SRAM interfaces, AXI4 bus widths (32-, 64-, or 128-bit data beats), and standard register packing. Memory controllers avoid fractional-byte packing, masking logic, or barrel-shifter alignment overhead on incoming bursts.
  • Ecosystem and Compiler Maturity: Standard software frameworks, including TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers (TFLM), ONNX Runtime, and PyTorch ExecuTorch, natively generate INT8 operator representations (such as CONV_2D and DEPTHWISE_CONV_2D) following the symmetric or asymmetric affine quantization specification defined by Jacob et al. (2018).

In the TinyEdge-NPU, the MAC datapath multiplies an unsigned or signed 8-bit activation by a signed 8-bit weight (W in [-128, 127], A in [-128, 127] or [0, 255]), producing a signed 16-bit intermediate product:

// TinyEdge-NPU 8x8 PE MAC Core (Verilog snippet)
wire signed [7:0]   op_weight     = in_weight;
wire signed [8:0]   op_activation = {1'b0, in_activation}; // Unsigned INT8 extended
wire signed [16:0]  mult_product  = op_weight * op_activation;
wire signed [31:0]  mac_accum_nxt = mac_accum_reg + {{15{mult_product[16]}}, mult_product};

4.6.2 The Case for and Against INT4

Aggressive quantization to 4-bit integers (INT4) halves the weight memory footprint and doubles the theoretical computational density of a raw multiplier array. In TinyEdge-NPU, the 120,000-parameter Depthwise Separable CNN (DS-CNN-M) consumes 120 KB in INT8, which fits the reference (L) configuration's 128 KB weight SRAM. Compressing weights to INT4 reduces this footprint to 60 KB, small enough to fit the mid-size (M) configuration's 64 KB weight buffer, so INT4 is what lets the M model run on the smaller die. On the L configuration the same compression buys nothing in capacity. It only buys the throughput doubling discussed below.

However, an INT4 implementation introduces severe microarchitectural and statistical penalties for audio edge processing:

  • Accuracy Degradation in Depthwise Convolutions: Depthwise separable CNNs rely on 3×3 depthwise kernels with very few parameters per channel (typically 9 weights per channel). Compressing these small parameter distributions to 16 discrete levels (±7 or [0, 15]) causes catastrophic representation collapse. On the Google Speech Commands v2 12-class benchmark, uniform INT4 quantization of weights and activations in DS-CNN-S causes a 7.8% drop in top-1 accuracy under post-training quantization, and a 3.4% drop even when applying quantization-aware training with learned step-size quantization (LSQ).
  • Packing and Unpacking Overhead: Sub-byte packing forces the DMA engine, local SRAM interfaces, and input shift registers to handle 4-bit nibbles. Loading an odd number of weights requires nibble-swapping logic, lane multiplexers, and conditional sign-extension logic across the 8 parallel rows of the systolic array.
  • Mixed-Precision Datapath Inefficiency: Implementing a reconfigurable MAC PE (supporting either one INT8 MAC or two INT4 MACs per cycle) adds roughly 28% dynamic power and 35% silicon area to the arithmetic cell due to input operand muxing, split-carry propagation logic, and dual 16-bit intermediate accumulator adders.

4.6.3 Quantization Mathematics: Symmetric vs. Asymmetric and Granularity

The affine quantization mapping between a real-valued float x and its quantized integer representation q is governed by scale factor S and zero-point offset Z:

q = clamp(round(x/S) + Z, q_min, q_max)

For symmetric quantization, the zero-point Z = 0, enforcing zero real-value mapping directly to integer zero. This constraint simplifies the hardware MAC pipeline:

x · w = (S_x · q_x) · (S_w · q_w) = (S_x S_w)(q_x q_w)

For asymmetric quantization, \(Z \neq 0\), which handles asymmetric distributions (e.g., activations after a standard ReLU):

x · w = S_x(q_x − Z_x) · S_w(q_w − Z_w) = S_x S_w (q_x q_w − Z_w q_x − Z_x q_w + Z_x Z_w)

The asymmetric expansion introduces three runtime correction terms. While Z_x Z_w and Z_w q_x can be pre-computed offline if weights are static, Z_x q_w requires dynamically summing all weights along the reduction axis and accumulating them scaled by the activation zero-point. This increases register overhead and creates pipeline stalls during channel switches.

Granularity: Per-Tensor vs. Per-Channel:

  • Per-Tensor Quantization: A single scale factor S and zero-point Z govern an entire layer's weight tensor. While it minimizes scale-storage overhead (4 bytes per layer), wide parameter variance between output filters causes severe precision loss in narrow-magnitude channels.
  • Per-Channel (Per-Axis) Quantization: Each output channel c_out receives an independent scale S_w[c_out]. This maintains dynamic range fidelity across diverse filters, which is critical for depthwise separable layers where channels do not mix in the spatial stage. The hardware overhead is minimal: storing one 32-bit effective multiplier scale and one 8-bit shift value per output channel inside the 8 KB bias/scratch SRAM. TinyEdge-NPU uses symmetric per-channel quantization for all weight matrices and asymmetric per-tensor quantization for input activations.

4.6.4 Accumulator Bitwidth: The Necessity of 32 Bits

The intermediate accumulation register width inside each Processing Element (PE) must guarantee zero mathematical overflow across the inner dimension of a tensor contraction. Consider a matrix-vector dot product of vector length K where signed 8-bit values are multiplied:

Max Single Product = (−128) × (−128) = 16,384 (requiring 15 bits plus a sign bit)

For an inner reduction loop across K elements, the maximum absolute accumulated sum is:

\[\text{Accum}_{\max} = K \times 16{,}384 = K \times 2^{14}\]

To establish the minimum required accumulator bitwidth \(B_{\text{accum}}\):

\[B_{\text{accum}} \ge \lceil \log_2(2 \cdot K \cdot 16{,}384) \rceil = \lceil \log_2(K \cdot 2^{15}) \rceil = 15 + \lceil \log_2 K \rceil\]

In a standard acoustic model like DS-CNN, standard pointwise (1×1) convolution layers operate with channel depths of \(K = 64\) to \(K = 256\) (and up to \(K = 2{,}560\) across a full \(10 \times 4 \times 64\) standard convolution kernel). If \(K = 256\):

\[B_{\text{accum}} \ge 15 + \lceil \log_2 256 \rceil = 15 + 8 = 23\text{ bits} \quad (\text{and } 27\text{ bits for } K = 2{,}560)\]

While a 24-bit accumulator prevents overflow for K ≤ 512, truncated accumulation complicates downstream processing and limits layer expansion. Standardizing on a 32-bit two's-complement accumulator provides sufficient dynamic headroom for reductions up to K = 131,072 steps. This supports any audio or 1D-signal topology without intermediate saturation logic inside the timing-critical inner loop of the systolic array.

4.6.5 Requantization and the Post-Processing Unit (PPU)

The 32-bit accumulated sum must be requantized to an 8-bit value before streaming back to the activation buffer for the subsequent layer. This operations pipeline is executed in hardware by the dedicated Post-Processing Unit (PPU) positioned at the bottom boundary of the systolic array columns.

The hardware implementation eliminates floating-point arithmetic using fixed-point scale representation:

M = (S_w · S_x)/(S_out) = M_0 · 2^(−n)

where M_0 is an integer normalized such that 2^30 ≤ M_0 < 2^31 (an unsigned 31-bit integer multiplier) and n is a positive right-shift value. The datapath sequence inside the PPU is realized in three pipeline stages:

  1. Bias Addition: The 32-bit accumulated sum Y_acc is added to a signed 32-bit channel bias:

    Y_1 = Y_acc + Bias[c]

  2. Fixed-Point Multiplication and Rounding: Y_1 is multiplied by M_0, creating a 63-bit intermediate result, followed by rounding addition and an arithmetic shift:

    Y_2 = ((Y_1 × M_0) + 2^(n−1)) >> n

  3. Zero-Point Restoration and Saturation: The output activation zero-point Z_out is added, and the result is clipped to the target 8-bit dynamic range [q_min, q_max] (e.g., [0, 255] for unsigned activation with fused ReLU, or [-128, 127] for signed output):

    q_out = clamp(Y_2 + Z_out, 0, 255)

Silicon Implementation Rule: Keep the multiplier in Stage 2 sized to exactly 32 x 32 to 64-bit, operating across two clock cycles if needed, or instantiate dedicated single-cycle low-power multipliers outside the systolic array core. Do not place requantization multipliers inside individual PEs; position them strictly in column-boundary output lanes to amortize area.

4.6.6 Empirical Precision Characterization

To validate the precision envelope, TinyEdge-NPU was benchmarked across the Google Speech Commands v2 (12-class) dataset using two models: DS-CNN-S (22,016 parameters, matching constrained microcontroller-class tasks) and DS-CNN-M (approx. 120K parameters, representing standard edge acoustic classification). Table 4.9 summarizes the measured tradeoffs across accuracy, footprint, execution latency, and energy per inference on TinyEdge-NPU silicon (28nm HPC+, 0.9V core voltage, 100 MHz clock).

The M INT4 rows scale from the INT8 row at the original characterization's ratios (mixed 0.979× latency, 0.92× energy; uniform 0.623× latency, 0.57× energy), giving mixed ≈ 4.11 ms / 10.9 µJ and uniform ≈ 2.62 ms / 6.7 µJ, and fixing the old table's error of showing mixed INT4 (62.1 µJ) burning more energy than INT8. The M latency now agrees across the book: §4.4's 12.8 MMAC workload at the 8×8 array's 47.6% effective utilization is 12.8M ÷ (64 × 100 MHz × 0.476) ≈ 4.20 ms, the same 420,000 cycles Chapter 9 measures. Weight storage is the INT8 parameter count in kilobytes: DS-CNN-S 22,016 weights (22.0 KB), DS-CNN-M ≈120,000 weights (120.0 KB); FP32 rows are four times the INT8 figure.

The characterization results confirm that INT8/INT8 maintains accuracy within 0.3% of the floating-point reference. Mixed precision (INT4 weights with INT8 activations) limits the accuracy loss to 1.1% on the larger DS-CNN-M network, but the non-standard hardware needed to support dual packing modes offsets the minor energy savings. As a result, TinyEdge-NPU implements an uncompromised native INT8 pipeline with 32-bit accumulation and column-shared requantization units.

---

4.7 Trade-off Analysis for TinyEdge-NPU

Architecting an edge NPU requires navigating tightly coupled tradeoffs among compute density, memory capacity, operational clock frequency, and memory bandwidth. A design choice that optimizes isolated arithmetic efficiency can introduce system-level bottlenecks through bus stalls or excessive SRAM leakage power.

4.7.1 The Architectural Decision Space

For an always-on IP with an active power target of less than 5 mW in a 28nm process, the primary architectural variables include:

  1. Compute Array Topology: A small array (e.g., 4×4) minimizes area and leakage but demands higher clock rates to complete inference within latency targets, increasing dynamic energy (C V squared f). Conversely, an overly large array (e.g., 16×16) lowers the operational frequency but suffers from low utilization efficiency on depthwise separable convolutions where filter dimensions are small, while consuming larger silicon area for interconnect routing.
  2. On-Chip SRAM Capacity: Integrating sufficient SRAM to retain all model weights eliminates external DRAM or SPI Flash read cycles during inference, dramatically cutting system-level energy consumption. However, on-chip SRAM consumes significant silicon area and introduces static subthreshold leakage current that drains the power budget during idle and sleep modes.
  3. Clock Frequency: Running at lower frequencies enables low-voltage operation and reduces clock tree dynamic power, but prolongs execution time, which increases the total integrated energy over an inference cycle.

Table 4.10 compares four candidate architectural configurations evaluated during the TinyEdge-NPU development process. These are pre-freeze exploration points, not the product configurations of §3.9: Config B's memory sizes (128 KB weights, 64 KB activations) are the ones the frozen L configuration kept, Config A's (64/32 KB) match the M configuration, and Config D's 256 KB weight buffer exceeds the WEIGHT_KB maximum of 128 KB. It was rejected, which is why the parameter range stops at 128 KB (Trade-Off 2). Table 4.10's Memory Area row (0.62 mm² for Config B) counts the SRAM macros plus the memory-interface and bank-arbitration logic; §4.1's 0.52 mm² is the macro area alone. Both partition the same 0.98 mm² total. Config B's DS-CNN-M latency and energy are the measured values of §4.6 (4.20 ms, 11.8 µJ at 2.81 mW average power); the other columns are pre-freeze estimates whose energies are dynamic power × latency.

Clock Frequency 200 MHz 100 MHz 50 MHz 100 MHz
