4.7.2 Worked Trade-Off 1: Compute Dimension and Frequency (8×8 @ 100 MHz vs. 16×16 @ 50 MHz)

To determine the optimal MAC array sizing, we evaluate two implementations that deliver equivalent or higher nominal compute performance:

  • Option 1: 8×8 array (64 PEs) clocked at 100 MHz to Peak compute = 64 × 100 MHz × 2 = 12.8 GOP/s (6.4 GMAC/s).
  • Option 2: 16×16 array (256 PEs) clocked at 50 MHz to Peak compute = 256 × 50 MHz × 2 = 25.6 GOP/s (12.8 GMAC/s).

Workload Mapping Analysis:
Consider Layer 3 of DS-CNN-M: a depthwise convolution with kernel size 3 x 3, input/output channels C = 64, and feature map dimension H x W = 25 x 10. A depthwise layer applies an independent spatial filter per channel without cross-channel summation. When running this layer on a 2D systolic array:

In the 8×8 array, the 64 channels map neatly across the array in groups of 8 channels per execution batch (64/8 = 8 iterations). Array channel utilization efficiency is near-optimal:

utilization (8×8) = valid multiply-accumulates / available array cycles = 64/64 = 100% (channel-axis mapping)

In the 16×16 array, 16 channels can be processed simultaneously along one axis. However, depthwise convolution requires 9 spatial weights per filter (3 x 3). Mapping the spatial dimension across the orthogonal 16-element array axis leaves 7 PEs unused (16 - 9 = 7 inactive PEs per row):

utilization (spatial) = (9)/(16) = 56.25%

Consequently, the effective hardware utilization drops dramatically:

utilization (16×16) = (16 channels × 9 spatial weights) / 256 PEs = 144/256 = 56.25%

Dynamic power per multiply-accumulate operation theoretically remains flat when scaling down frequency at constant supply voltage, but the static leakage power scales strictly with total silicon footprint. In the 28nm LP process, a 16×16 PE array occupies approximately 0.16 mm2 of standard-cell area compared to 0.04 mm2 for the 8×8 configuration (PE array only; the full compute cores measure 0.584 mm2 and 0.142 mm2 respectively per Table 4.6). This 4x increase in PE gate count increases baseline core leakage from 64 µW to 248 µW. The clock tree required to distribute a low-skew 50 MHz clock across a 256-PE matrix also requires more insertion buffers and wider wire routing channels than the compact 8x8 layout, clawing back roughly 30% of the dynamic clocking power savings achieved by operating at half frequency.

The decisive metric against Option 2 is PE utilization under real-world acoustic workloads. The depthwise separable convolutions (DS-CNN) that dominate keyword spotting rely on depthwise layers with small channel dimensions per group (often 16, 32, or 48 channels). When mapping a 32-channel depthwise convolution onto a 16x16 array, only two out of every sixteen rows compute valid activations, dropping hardware utilization below 35%. On the 8×8 array, depthwise-layer spatial mapping achieves 78% to 92% utilization across these same layers. The 16x16 array therefore spends significant clock cycles shifting zeroes and burning idle standby power.

Option 2 Verdict: Rejected. Doubling spatial parallelism to 16x16 while reducing clock frequency to 50 MHz inflates core silicon area by 4x, increases leakage fourfold, and degrades operational MAC efficiency down to 35% on target DS-CNN models. The 8x8 array operating at 100 MHz remains the optimal compute architecture for the TinyEdge-NPU target workload.

Trade-Off 2: On-Chip Weight Buffer Sizing (128 KB vs. 256 KB)

The second critical microarchitectural fork concerns the on-chip weight buffer capacity. The reference DS-CNN-M model for 12-keyword spotting requires 120 KB of INT8 parameters and fits the 128 KB weight buffer outright. The sizing question is set by the larger end of the model range: aggressive multi-keyword industrial models scale up to 250 KB, while smaller 10-keyword models fit within 110 KB. Designers must balance the latency and power penalties of fetching weights from off-chip non-volatile memory against the physical silicon area and standby leakage of on-chip SRAM.

In Option A (the 128 KB baseline), the on-chip weight buffer cannot hold an entire 250 KB industrial model simultaneously. The controller must double-buffer weights: while the systolic array processes the current layer from a 64 KB bank, an integrated AXI4 master DMA engine streams the subsequent layer's weights across the system bus from off-chip Flash or shared system SRAM. In Option B (a 256 KB buffer), the entire model parameter set resides on-chip after initial power-on boot, eliminating runtime DMA weight traffic entirely.

Table 4.11: Weight Buffer Sizing Trade-off (128 KB vs 256 KB)
Architecture Metric Baseline (128 KB SRAM) Expanded (256 KB SRAM) Delta / Architectural Impact
SRAM Macro Footprint (28nm) 0.33 mm2 (2x 64 KB macros) 0.67 mm2 (4x 64 KB macros) +0.34 mm2 (+100% SRAM area)
Total IP Area (Logic + Memory) 0.98 mm2 1.32 mm2 +34.7% total die area (exceeds 1.0 mm2 budget)
Standby SRAM Leakage (@ 0.9V, 25°C) 21.5 µW 43.1 µW +21.6 µW static power floor penalty
Active Memory Power (@ 100 MHz) 1.15 mW 1.38 mW +20% dynamic read power (wire parasitic loading)
External Bus Traffic per Inference 122 KB (streamed via DMA) 0 KB (steady-state resident) Saves external interconnect energy
Inference Latency (250 KB industrial DS-CNN) 6.42 ms 6.18 ms 3.7% latency reduction (DMA hidden behind compute)

Detailed performance modeling reveals that the DMA transfer latency for streaming the remaining 122 KB of weights is almost entirely hidden behind the execution of early convolutional layers. Because the systolic array takes over 2.8 ms to complete the initial feature extraction and first pointwise layers, an AXI4 DMA burst at 400 MB/s requires only 0.31 ms to populate the alternate 64 KB buffer bank, preventing core stalling.

From an energy perspective, streaming 122 KB across an on-chip system bus at 15 pJ/bit consumes approximately 14.6 µJ per inference. Evaluated at an audio inference cadence of once every 100 ms (10 inferences per second), this contributes 146 µW of average dynamic power. The streaming cost (146 µW average) exceeds the 21.6 µW leakage penalty of the larger buffer, so energy alone would favour the 256 KB option. But only for the industrial model. The reference DS-CNN-M fits the 128 KB buffer outright and streams nothing. More critically, the 0.34 mm2 silicon area penalty pushes the total IP footprint to 1.32 mm2, directly violating the product requirement of a sub-1.0 mm2 die footprint in 28nm. Area, not energy, is what kills the 256 KB option, and it is also what sets the WEIGHT_KB upper bound at 128 KB.

Weight Buffer Verdict: Retain the 128 KB baseline. Pipelining layer weights through a ping-pong banking structure via the AXI4 DMA interface hides 96% of bus latency, preserves the strict sub-1.0 mm2 area envelope, and eliminates the continuous leakage overhead of unneeded memory cells during deep standby.

Documenting the Microarchitectural Design Point

Once trade-off analyses conclude, the IP architect must freeze the microarchitectural parameters and record them definitively in the Microarchitectural Specification (MAS) and Architecture Decision Records (ADRs). For TinyEdge-NPU, this establishes an immutable baseline: an 8x8 INT8 systolic array driven at 100 MHz, backed by 128 KB of ping-pong weight SRAM, 64 KB of ping-pong activation SRAM, and 8 KB of bias/scratchpad memory (the reference L configuration, §3.9). The ADR must explicitly capture rejected alternatives, such as the 16x16 array topology and the 256 KB monolithic memory configuration, alongside the physical numbers, simulation data, and boundary conditions that drove the decision. Formalizing these boundaries early eliminates speculative scope creep during RTL implementation, anchors the verification team's coverage metrics to validated operating modes, and ensures downstream physical design proceeds against hard, achievable power and floorplan constraints.

4.8 Architecture Decision Records

Semiconductor IP cores have operational lifecycles that frequently exceed a decade. An IP block designed for a 28nm microcontroller may undergo process porting to 16nm, integration into dozens of diverse customer SoCs, and multiple derivative iterations by engineers who were not part of the original design team. When architectural decisions are preserved only as tribal knowledge, oral history degrades rapidly. The downstream result is design paralysis, where engineers fear modifying a pipeline stage or buffer allocation because "nobody knows why it was done that way", or architectural regression, where a long-discarded design choice is re-implemented only to trigger the same edge-case failures or timing bottlenecks that caused its original rejection.

An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) is a lightweight, immutable document that captures a single significant architectural decision, its context, the alternatives evaluated with quantitative metrics, the rationale for the final selection, and the anticipated trade-offs. ADRs are maintained directly in the IP core's version-controlled repository alongside the hardware description code and verification suites. By committing ADRs alongside RTL and architectural models, any modification to fundamental microarchitectural structures can be traced back to the original operational constraints and workload assumptions.

ADR Structure and Workflow

To remain useful to digital design and verification engineers, hardware ADRs must avoid vague software design patterns and focus on concrete implementation realities: clock frequency, pipeline depth, area footprints, switching power, SRAM port bandwidth, routing congestion, and verification complexity. A production hardware ADR contains six mandatory fields:

  • Title and Identifier: A sequential index and short descriptive title (e.g., ADR-004: Execution Dataflow Strategy for TinyEdge-NPU).
  • Status: Proposed, Accepted, Deprecated, or Superseded (referencing the replacing ADR).
  • Context: The engineering problem, target workloads, hardware constraints, and requirements driving the decision.
  • Options Considered: The viable architectural alternatives, each accompanied by comparative trade-off data (analytical or simulation-based).
  • Decision and Rationale: The selected alternative and the technical justification for why it was chosen over the others.
  • Consequences: The downstream impacts on RTL complexity, physical implementation, verification scope, firmware toolchains, and silicon PPA.

Complete Worked Example: ADR-004

ADR-004: Execution Dataflow Strategy for TinyEdge-NPU
Status: Accepted
Date: 2024-03-15
Author: Lead Systems Architect
Target Milestone: Microarchitecture Specification Freeze (Gate M2)

1. Context
TinyEdge-NPU is constrained to <5 mW total active power at 100 MHz in a 28nm 
logic process. The core workload is keyword spotting (KWS) and acoustic event 
detection (AED) utilizing 1D and 2D Depthwise-Separable Convolutional Neural 
Networks (DS-CNN). Standard models (e.g., 100K–250K INT8 parameters processing 
1-second windows of 16 kHz audio) consist of two alternating layer types:
  - Depthwise Convolutions: Spatial filtering per channel (e.g., 3x3 kernel, 
    channel multiplier = 1). Low operational intensity: 1.8 to 3.0 MACs per 
    byte of memory traffic.
  - Pointwise Convolutions: 1x1 convolutions mixing channel data across 
    feature maps. High operational intensity: 32 to 128 MACs per byte of 
    memory traffic.

The memory subsystem consists of a 128 KB Weight Buffer (4 banks of 32Kx8 single-port
SRAM), a 64 KB Activation Buffer (4 banks of 16Kx8 single-port SRAM), and an 8x8
systolic compute matrix (64 MACs/cycle) — the reference (L) configuration (§3.9). Accessing the on-chip SRAM consumes approximately 2.1 pJ per byte from the 64 KB activation bank and 2.8 pJ per byte from the 128 KB weight bank in this process, whereas moving data between internal PE registers consumes <0.15 pJ/bit. Dataflow selection governs memory access patterns 
and determines whether the NPU can stay within the 5 mW budget.

2. Options Considered

Option A: Pure Weight-Stationary (WS) Dataflow
Weights are read from the 128 KB buffer once and latched into PE weight registers. 
Activations are streamed horizontally across the 8x8 array; partial sums are 
accumulated vertically down the columns.
  - Advantages: Zero weight movement during compute phases; optimal energy for 
    high-channel pointwise layers.
  - Disadvantages: On depthwise layers (kernel size 3x3, channel count = 1 per filter), 
    PE weights must be replaced every 9 cycles. At 100 MHz, this demands 
    64 bytes/9 cycles = 7.11 bytes/cycle of weight read bandwidth. This saturates the 
    128 KB buffer read ports, inducing stalls and driving weight buffer access energy 
    to 2.4 mW alone (48% of total power budget). Systolic PE utilization on depthwise 
    layers drops to 28.1%.

Option B: Pure Output-Stationary (OS) Dataflow
Accumulators remain stationary within each PE to accumulate partial sums for a 
specific output activation pixel over time. Inputs (activations) and weights are 
streamed through the array simultaneously.
  - Advantages: Minimizes partial sum movement and eliminates 32-bit intermediate 
    accumulator traffic to memory. Peak PE utilization on depthwise layers reaches 87.5%.
  - Disadvantages: Requires 64 high-width (32-bit) spatial accumulator registers 
    permanently coupled to output channels. On large pointwise layers (e.g., 64x64 
    channel transformations), weights must be re-read repeatedly from the Weight Buffer 
    for each spatial patch, consuming an estimated 89 µJ per 1-second inference, 
    exceeding the energy limit.

Option C: Hybrid Dual-Mode Dataflow (Dynamically Configurable)
The 8x8 array implements a dual-mode routing mesh toggled by a 1-bit control register 
(`LAYER_CFG.DATAFLOW_MODE`) on a per-layer boundary:
  - Mode 0 (Weight-Stationary): Used for Pointwise (1x1) layers and Dense layers. 
    Weights are held in PE local registers; activations stream across rows.
  - Mode 1 (Output-Stationary / Depthwise-Optimized): Partial sums remain in PE 
    registers while weights and activations stream along systolic channels. The 
    3x3 receptive field's accumulation stays local, amortizing buffer read energy.
  - Trade-off Analysis:
    -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    Metric                     Pure WS (Opt A)  Pure OS (Opt B)  Hybrid (Opt C)
    -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    DS-CNN Active Power        4.1 mW           4.8 mW           2.8 mW
    Depthwise PE Utilization   28.1%            87.5%            84.4%
    Pointwise PE Utilization   93.8%            61.2%            93.8%
    Inference Latency (1 s)    14.2 ms          18.6 ms          9.8 ms
    PE Cell Area Overhead      Baseline         +11.2%           +4.1%
    Gate Count (NPU Core)      88K gates        98K gates        92K gates
    -------------------------------------------------------------------------

3. Decision
Adopt Option C (Hybrid Dual-Mode Dataflow). 

Rationale: Pure Weight-Stationary cannot meet the real-time latency target for the 
target 250K parameter DS-CNN model without exceeding the 5 mW ceiling during depthwise 
computations. The 4.1% silicon area penalty in the PE array (translating to ~0.009 mm2 
in 28nm) is justified by a 31.7% active power reduction (2.8 mW vs 4.1 mW) and a 31% 
reduction in total inference latency (9.8 ms vs 14.2 ms).

4. Consequences
  - Positive: Guarantees active power remains well below the 5 mW limit (<3 mW typical 
    for KWS workloads), preserving margin for on-chip system interconnect activity.
  - Negative: Microarchitecture complexity increases. The PE datapath requires two 
    additional 8-bit multiplexers and an updated register-enable network.
  - Verification Impact: Directed and constrained-random tests must explicitly verify 
    switching between Mode 0 and Mode 1 without pipeline drain deadlocks or corrupted 
    boundary states. The C++ cycle-accurate golden model must implement bit-accurate 
    internal routing for both modes.
  - Toolchain Impact: The offline model compiler must generate layer descriptor 
    packets that emit the correct `DATAFLOW_MODE` configuration bit before triggering 
    layer execution.

Note on the latencies in this ADR: ADR-004 compares dataflow options for the 250K-parameter DS-CNN model variant, not for the product's DS-CNN-M. The latencies in its table (14.2 ms, 18.6 ms, 9.8 ms) belong to that variant; the product's DS-CNN-M burst-mode latency is 4.20 ms (§4.1, Table 4.9). Do not quote the 14.2 ms figure as the TinyEdge-NPU's inference latency.

Shorter Worked Example: ADR-007

ADR-007: Compute Engine Topology and Array Dimensioning
Status: Accepted
Date: 2024-04-02
Author: Lead Microarchitect
Target Milestone: Microarchitecture Specification Freeze (Gate M2)

1. Context
The performance target is 6.4 GMAC/s at a nominal clock frequency of 100 MHz. 
This requires 64 INT8 Multiply-Accumulate operations per cycle. The design team 
must select the spatial arrangement of the MAC units: a 1D vector (1x64), a wide 
rectangular array (4x16), or a square 2D systolic array (8x8).

2. Options Considered
  - Option 1 (1x64 1D Vector): Broadcasts 1 activation byte to 64 parallel PEs, 
    requiring a 512-bit weight bus from the SRAM buffer per cycle.
  - Option 2 (8x8 2D Systolic Array): Activations stream across 8 rows; weights stream 
    or latch down 8 columns. Data buses require 64 bits for activations (8 bytes) 
    and 64 bits for weights (8 bytes).
  - Option 3 (16x4 Rectangular Array): 128-bit weight bus, 32-bit activation bus.

3. Decision
Adopt Option 2 (8x8 2D Systolic Array).

Rationale: Option 1 demands a 512-bit wide memory read interface. In 28nm, routing a 
512-bit bus across the macro causes significant local wiring congestion, requires wide 
SRAM macro multiplexing, and increases clock tree distribution power to register files. 
Option 2 requires only two 64-bit buses (one activation, one weight), which map cleanly 
to four 16-bit or two 32-bit SRAM bank configurations. Furthermore, the 8x8 geometry 
matches typical KWS layer channel dimensions (multiples of 8 or 16), ensuring array 
fill efficiency exceeds 85% on Pointwise layers.

4. Consequences
  - Positive: Tight physical floorplan (approximately 377 µm × 377 µm for the compute core). Routing density remains under 65% on Metal 3 through Metal 5.
  - Negative: Systolic skew registers are required at the array perimeter (7 cycles of 
    stagger on inputs and outputs), adding 56 flip-flops per boundary interface and 
    introducing a 9-cycle pipeline fill/drain latency per matrix tile.
  - Mitigation: The compiler tiles matrix dimensions to minimize the number of flushes, 
    keeping execution phases large enough that a 9-cycle overhead represents <0.5% of the total layer compute cycles.

4.9 Architecture Review Checklist

The architecture review is the final defensive barrier before digital design engineers transition from abstract modeling to concrete Register Transfer Level (RTL) implementation. In semiconductor IP development, starting RTL development prematurely is an expensive failure mode. An unresolved architectural ambiguity can invalidate weeks of pipeline coding, force invasive timing-closure patches, and require substantial rewrites of SystemVerilog assertions and Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) environments.

The checklist in Table 4.12 structures the evaluation into verifiable criteria. Each entry requires objective, documented evidence from cycle-accurate simulations, architectural exploration platforms, or preliminary physical prototyping before approval is granted.

Table 4.12: TinyEdge-NPU Architecture Sign-off Checklist

Category Verification Criterion & Required Artifact Sign-Off Threshold TinyEdge-NPU Status & Evidence
Workload & Algorithmic Coverage Bit-accurate execution of target production neural networks using C++/SystemC architectural model versus FP32/INT8 reference framework (TensorFlow Lite Micro). Zero mismatch across 10,000 real-world audio inference windows. Accuracy degradation <0.5% vs FP32 baseline. PASS: Evaluated on Google Speech Commands (12-label) using DS-CNN-S. Quantized INT8 top-1 accuracy is 94.1% for DS-CNN-S (baseline FP32 94.4%) and 95.5% for DS-CNN-M (baseline FP32 95.8%).
Performance Verification Cycle-accurate simulator log validating hardware execution latency, PE array utilization, and bus stall cycles on all specified layers. Real-time factor (RTF) ≤ 0.01 for 1-second audio frame (latency ≤ 10 ms). Average PE utilization ≥ 60% across entire model. PASS: At 100 MHz burst clock, DS-CNN-S completes in 0.717 ms (71,742 cycles, RTF = 0.00072) and DS-CNN-M completes in 4.20 ms (420,000 cycles, RTF = 0.0042); the larger 250K-parameter industrial variant completes in 9.8 ms (ADR-004). Average PE utilization is 65% on DS-CNN-S.
Power & Thermal Sign-off Activity-annotated power estimation (SAIF/VCD from architectural execution applied to gate-level preliminary netlist or foundry power tables). Active power < 5.0 mW at 100 MHz, 0.9V, 28nm TT corner, 25°C. Sleep/leakage power < 100 μW. PASS: Peak active power is 3.9 mW on the reference (L) configuration (2.5 mW on the S configuration, 3.0 mW on M; §3.9); average active power across DS-CNN-S is 2.81 mW on the reference hardware (1.8 mW on the S configuration). Static leakage with memory retentive sleep is 64 μW.
Area & Memory Footprint Macro placement exploration, standard-cell density estimate, and total memory macro area. Total core area ≤ 1.00 mm2 in target 28nm foundry node. Logic gate count ≤ 120k gates. PASS: Total area is 0.98 mm2 (0.21 mm2 logic + 0.52 mm2 SRAM + 0.25 mm2 periphery/routing). Logic: 0.21 mm2 (~92K gates). SRAM macros (128 KB Weight, 64 KB Activation, 8 KB Bias/Scratch, reference L configuration): 0.52 mm2 at ≈0.0026 mm2/KB.
Interface Completeness Formal bus protocol compliance checks and transaction bandwidth sizing for system control and DMA streaming paths. AXI-Lite register access ≤ 2 wait cycles. AXI4 DMA interface sustains 400 MB/s burst without backpressuring the system crossbar. PASS: CSR access latency is 1 wait cycle. 32-bit AXI4 master interface requires max 100 MB/s burst during activation swap, consuming only 25% of bus capacity.
Testability & Observability Testability review sign-off: DFT scan chain insertion model, memory BIST architecture, debug tracing registers, and hardware performance monitors. Target stuck-at fault coverage ≥ 99.0%; transition fault coverage ≥ 95.0%. 100% memory testable via production MBIST. PASS: Dual scan compression hooks planned. Embedded MBIST controller wraps all 9 SRAM instances. 4 hardware performance counters integrated into CSR block.
Configurability & Scalability Parameterized architectural boundaries specified in design specifications for derivative projects (e.g., array width, SRAM depths). Parameter propagation paths verified in architectural model; no hardcoded dimension assumptions in datapath routing logic. PASS: Array height (M) and width (N) parameterized via SystemVerilog localparam constructs; SRAM banks split across decoupled configuration packages.
Documentation & Golden Model Microarchitecture Specification (MAS), Register Abstraction Layer (RAL) definitions, and C++/SystemVerilog Golden Reference Model. MAS signed off by all leads. RAL matches register map documentation automatically generated from SystemRDL. PASS: MAS version 1.0 published. SystemRDL source generates RTL registers, UVM register model, and C firmware headers without manual edits.

Review Execution and Governance

An architecture review is not an informal technical presentation; it is a formal stage-gate review that controls engineering budget and implementation sign-off. If conducted improperly, it devolves into subjective debates about stylistic choices rather than objective evaluations of architectural fitness.

  1. Composition of the Review Board: To ensure all engineering disciplines are represented, attendance of specific stakeholders is mandatory:
    • Chief / Lead Architect (Chair): Presents evidence and defends architectural trade-offs against baseline requirements.
    • RTL Design Lead: Evaluates pipeline feasibility, clocking domain complexity, control path state-machine boundaries, and structural floorplan logic.
    • Design Verification (DV) Lead: Assesses microarchitectural observability, internal state controllability, corner-case explosion risks, and formal verification feasibility.
    • Physical Design (PD) Lead: Reviews timing closure feasibility at 100 MHz across all process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners, wire congestion, macro placement boundaries, and power grid IR-drop risks.
    • Firmware / Toolchain Lead: Verifies software-facing register maps, compiler scheduling complexity, interrupt service latency, and the cycle-accurate programming model.
  2. Mandatory Pre-Meeting Collateral: The review meeting cannot be scheduled until the following items have been published to the engineering repository at least five working days prior to the review:
    • Complete Microarchitecture Specification (MAS) detailing every pipeline stage, FIFO depth, buffer bank configuration, and state diagram.
    • Cycle-accurate, bit-accurate C++/SystemC architectural model matching the golden algorithmic output across reference test suites.
    • Preliminary synthesis report in the target 28nm standard-cell library demonstrating that the compute datapath and critical control loops meet 100 MHz timing with a minimum of 20% setup slack margin reserved for physical place-and-route.
    • Floorplan feasibility report showing preliminary macro placements for the 128 KB, 64 KB, and 8 KB SRAM blocks alongside the 8x8 PE array with pin assignments aligned to system buses.
  3. Meeting Protocol: The review should be conducted across multiple focused sessions (maximum two hours each) rather than a single prolonged marathon. Recommended session splits:
    • Session 1: Workload mapping, algorithmic fidelity, dataflow, and performance verification.
    • Session 2: Datapath microarchitecture, pipeline timing, memory subsystem, and physical feasibility.
    • Session 3: Control registers, DMA, interrupt structures, DFT/DFD, and compiler interfaces.
Definition of "Done" for Architecture Sign-off: Architectural sign-off is achieved only when every item in the Architecture Review Checklist has a documented status of PASS, zero open critical action items remain against the MAS, all related Architecture Decision Records are transitioned to Accepted, and the review board signatures are officially recorded. Only upon reaching this threshold is the design repository unlocked for active RTL microarchitecture implementation.

Key Takeaways

  • Architecture is a budgeting exercise first: the workload (DS-CNN keyword spotting) sets the MAC count, the power budget sets the clock and the array size, and the area budget sets the SRAM. TinyEdge-NPU lands on an 8×8 INT8 array at 100 MHz with 200 KB of on-chip SRAM.
  • Data movement, not arithmetic, dominates energy in a small NPU. A hybrid dataflow, weight-stationary for 1×1 pointwise layers, output-stationary for 3×3 depthwise layers, cuts SRAM access energy substantially for less than 10% extra PE logic.
  • Size the MAC array from utilization, not peak throughput. A 16×16 array looks faster on paper but drops below 35% utilization on depthwise layers and quadruples leakage; 8×8 averages 65% utilization on the target workload (78–92% spatial-mapping utilization on depthwise layers).
  • INT8 with 32-bit accumulation is the right precision baseline for keyword spotting; INT4 buys area and power only where accuracy headroom is proven by measurement, not by assumption.
  • Every architectural decision gets an ADR with the rejected alternatives and the numbers behind the choice. If a decision cannot be defended with a number, it is not ready for review.
  • Architecture is not done until the review checklist passes: workload coverage, proven performance, signed-off power and area budgets, complete interfaces, and testability hooks, all before RTL starts.

Chapter 5: RTL Design

Architecture decides what the machine does; RTL decides what the machine is. This chapter turns the TinyEdge-NPU micro-architecture from Chapter 4 into synthesizable, reusable SystemVerilog: the coding rules that keep the design clean, the parameterization strategy that makes it an IP product rather than a one-off, the four key blocks (MAC array, buffers, control FSM, AXI-Lite interface), the low-power techniques that deliver the <5 mW active and <100 µW sleep budgets, and the pitfalls and review practices that keep a small team from shipping a design that simulates fine and fails in silicon. The running numbers are the Chapter 4 decisions: an 8×8 INT8 MAC array at 100 MHz, parameterized on-chip SRAM (48–200 KB; the reference L configuration is 200 KB, 128 KB weight, 64 KB activation, 8 KB bias/scratchpad; §3.9), a hybrid dataflow, and an AXI-Lite slave plus AXI4-master DMA.

5.1 From Architecture to RTL: The Micro-Architecture Specification

RTL should never be written from a slide deck. Between the architecture document and the first line of code sits the micro-architecture specification (MAS): a document that pins down every decision the RTL author needs, so that two engineers implementing the same block produce the same hardware. For TinyEdge-NPU the MAS is about 40 pages and it answers, for every block, five questions: what are the interfaces (signals, widths, protocols, timing), what is the cycle-by-cycle behaviour, what are the corner cases, what is the reset behaviour, and how is it verified.

The single most valuable habit in this phase is to write the interface tables first. Before any datapath is coded, every block gets a table listing each port, its direction, width, clock domain, and a one-line description of its protocol (valid/ready, pulse, level, strobe). Interface tables force the architect and the RTL author to agree on the boundaries, and they become the contract the testbench checks against. Most integration bugs in small accelerators are interface bugs: a ready signal that is actually a pulse, a data bus that changes a cycle earlier than the consumer expects, a configuration register that takes effect immediately when the software model assumed it took effect at the next layer boundary. Interface tables catch those disagreements on paper, where they are cheap.

The MAS also fixes the timing contract of the design: the clock frequency (100 MHz), the reset strategy (asynchronous-assert, synchronous-deassert active-low reset rst_ni, asserted for at least 4 clocks), the pipeline depth of the MAC array (3 stages: fetch, multiply, accumulate), and the latency of each operation (a 1×1 pointwise tile of 8×8 outputs completes in 9 cycles including pipeline fill: 8 accumulation cycles, one per input channel, assuming Cin = 8, plus one cycle of pipeline fill). Writing these numbers down before coding means the verification team can build the reference model against the same contract, and the synthesis team knows the timing targets from day one.

The MAS rule: if a behaviour is not written down, it does not exist. RTL authors do not invent semantics; they implement the specification. Every time an RTL author has to guess, what happens if software writes a register mid-inference, what happens if the DMA stalls, the design has a latent bug. The MAS exists to eliminate guessing.

The TinyEdge-NPU Block Partition

Chapter 4 sized the machine; here it is partitioned into RTL blocks. The partition follows three rules: each block has one clear owner and one clear function; blocks communicate through narrow, well-defined interfaces (no block reaches into another block's internals); and the partition matches the verification plan, so each block can be tested standalone before integration.

flowchart TD subgraph HOST["Host / SoC"] CPU[Host CPU] MEM[System Memory] end subgraph NPU["TinyEdge-NPU"] AXIL["AXI-Lite Slave\nConfig & Control"] DMA[AXI4 DMA Engine] CTRL[Control FSM\nLayer Sequencer] MAC[8x8 MAC Array\nINT8, 32-bit acc] WB["Weight Buffer\n128 KB SRAM (L)"] AB["Activation Buffer\n64 KB ping-pong (L)"] SB["Scratchpad\n8 KB bias/scale (L)"] QUANT[Quantization\nRequant Unit] end CPU -->|AXI-Lite| AXIL AXIL --> CTRL DMA -->|AXI4 read| MEM DMA --> WB DMA --> AB CTRL --> MAC CTRL --> DMA WB --> MAC AB --> MAC MAC --> QUANT QUANT --> AB MAC --> SB CTRL -->|interrupt| CPU

The partition is deliberately shallow: eight blocks, one clock domain, one reset domain. A small accelerator does not need the multi-clock, multi-power-domain complexity of a large SoC. That complexity is a cost, not a feature. The only clock-domain crossing in the design is the AXI-Lite slave, which runs on the host bus clock; everything else runs on the single 100 MHz NPU clock. Keeping the CDC surface to one boundary makes the design dramatically easier to verify, to time, and to test.

5.2 Coding Guidelines for Synthesizable, Reusable IP

Reusable IP is not ordinary RTL with the comments cleaned up. It is RTL written so that a stranger, a customer engineer, a future maintainer, a synthesis tool on a different node, can use it without talking to the author. The guidelines below are the ones that matter most for a small accelerator IP. They are enforced by lint, not by goodwill: every rule has a lint check, and the lint suite runs in CI on every commit.

One clock, one reset, one style

  • Single clock per block. Every sequential block uses the same clock input, named clk_i. No derived clocks, no divided clocks inside the IP. Clock gating is done with enable signals and integrated clock-gating cells inserted by the synthesis tool, never by hand-written clock dividers.
  • Asynchronous-assert, synchronous-deassert active-low reset. Control and state flip-flops use always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni) driven by the top-level reset synchronizer so reset takes effect immediately even if the clock is gated, while release is synchronous to clk_i. Datapath pipeline registers that do not affect control state omit reset to save area and routing. Resetting a 32-bit accumulator array costs area and routing for no benefit, so accumulation registers are explicitly marked non-resettable with a waiver in the lint log.
  • No latches, ever. Every combinational always_comb block assigns every output on every path. The lint rule for incomplete case statements and missing default assignments is set to error, not warning.
  • No initial blocks, no delays, no simulation-only constructs in synthesizable code. initial, #delay, $display, and file I/O live only in testbenches. If a design needs a power-on value, it gets it from reset, not from an initial block.

Naming and structure

  • Ports carry their role in the name. _i for inputs, _o for outputs, _io for inouts. Clock is clk_i, reset is rst_ni. A signal named weight_rdata is a read-data bus; weight_rvalid is its valid flag; weight_rready is the backpressure. Anyone reading an instantiation can tell the direction and protocol from the name alone.
  • One module per file, file named after the module. tinyedge_mac_array.sv contains module tinyedge_mac_array and nothing else. This makes the file list, the synthesis scripts, and the revision history trivial to follow.
  • Parameters at the top, localparams below. Every module starts with its parameter list, then local parameters for derived constants. No magic numbers in the body: a literal 8 in the middle of a datapath is a bug waiting for the next person who changes the array size.
  • Separate datapath from control. Each block has a clearly marked datapath section (arithmetic, multiplexers, registers) and a control section (FSM, handshakes, enables). Mixing them in one always block is the fastest way to create a design that is correct by accident and wrong by the next edit.

What not to do

Anti-patternWhy it hurtsDo this instead
Combinational loops through a multiplexer chainSynthesis cannot time it; simulation can oscillateRegister the multiplexer output or restructure as a tree with a registered stage
Multi-driver nets (two always blocks driving one signal)Synthesis error or, worse, silently wrong hardwareOne driver per signal; combine with explicit priority logic in a single block
Wide combinational paths (32-bit compare chained into a 32-bit add)Becomes the critical path and kills timing at 100 MHzPipeline it: register between the compare and the add
Asynchronous reads from a register arrayInfers a large multiplexer, not a memory; area explodesUse synchronous-read SRAM macros, or register the read address
Hard-coded widths and depthsThe IP cannot be reused at a different sizeParameters with sane defaults; derive all widths from them
Clock gating by AND-ing the clock in RTLGlitch-prone, untestable, breaks scan insertionUse enable signals; let the synthesis tool insert ICG cells

The point of these rules is not pedantry. Each one exists because a real design, somewhere, failed in a way that was expensive to find. A lint-clean, guideline-conformant codebase is the cheapest insurance an IP team can buy, and it is the first thing a customer's integration team will check before they trust the deliverable.

5.3 Parameterization Strategy

An IP block that only works at one size is a design, not a product. TinyEdge-NPU is parameterized so the same RTL serves the keyword-spotting configuration the book follows and the adjacent configurations a customer might want, a smaller array for an always-on sensor, a larger one for a multi-keyword device, without forking the code. The strategy has three layers: parameters, generate blocks, and a configuration check that fails loudly at elaboration time if the parameters are inconsistent.

The parameter list

Every parameter has a default that reproduces the book's reference configuration, a documented range, and a one-line rationale. The top-level module exposes only the parameters a customer should touch; internal modules expose the full set. Parameters that interact are validated together, not one at a time.

ParameterDefaultRangeWhat it controls
MAC_ROWS / MAC_COLS8 / 84–16, power of 2PE array size; sets compute throughput and area
DATA_WIDTH88 or 4Activation/weight precision (INT8 / INT4)
ACC_WIDTH3224, 32Accumulator width; must satisfy ≥ 15 + ⌈log2(Kmax)⌉ (27 bits for K = 2,560; 32 bits default)
WEIGHT_KB12832–128Weight SRAM size in KB; sets the S/M/L configurations (32 / 64 / 128)
ACT_KB6416–64Activation SRAM size in KB (ping-pong total); S/M/L configurations (16 / 32 / 64)
LINEBUF_KB80 or 8Dedicated bias/scratchpad & line buffer in KB (8 KB for L; 0 for S/M where folded into ACT_KB)
AXI_DATA_WIDTH3232 or 64AXI-Lite / AXI4 data width
NUM_CLASSES122–64Output classes; sizes the final dense layer
ENABLE_POWER_GATING10 or 1Instantiates the sleep power switch and isolation

Two rules govern the list. First, parameters are orthogonal: changing one should not silently change the meaning of another. MAC_ROWS changes the array; it does not change the SRAM banking. Banking is derived from the array size by a formula in the code, so it always stays consistent. Second, every parameter is checked: an elaboration-time assertion verifies the range and the cross-parameter rules (for example, ACC_WIDTH >= DATA_WIDTH + 12), and a bad configuration fails the build with a readable message instead of synthesizing wrong hardware.

// Elaboration-time parameter validation — fail loudly, fail early.
initial begin
  if (MAC_ROWS != 4 && MAC_ROWS != 8 && MAC_ROWS != 16)
    $fatal(1, "MAC_ROWS must be 4, 8 or 16 (got %0d)", MAC_ROWS);
  if (ACC_WIDTH < 27)
    $fatal(1, "ACC_WIDTH (%0d) too narrow for worst-case reduction K=2560 (requires >= 27 bits)",
           ACC_WIDTH);
  if (WEIGHT_KB % 32 != 0)
    $fatal(1, "WEIGHT_KB must be a multiple of 32 KB");
end

Note that the initial block here is an elaboration-time check, not synthesizable logic. It is the one sanctioned use of initial in the RTL, and it is guarded by a lint waiver that names this exact purpose. It costs nothing in silicon, and on a design like this it typically catches misconfigurations, a wrong array size, a bank depth that is not a multiple of 32 KB, at elaboration time, before any simulation runs.

Generate blocks and the "one source of truth" rule

Replication is done with generate blocks, never by copy-pasting a module eight times. The 8×8 PE array is a nested generate of one PE module; the SRAM banks are a generate over the bank count; the requantization lanes are a generate over the output channels. If a bug is fixed in the PE, it is fixed in all 64 instances at once, because there is only one PE source. The generate variables are named, the loop bounds come from parameters, and the hierarchy names are stable so that synthesis constraints and debug probes can address a specific PE (for example, u_mac_array.gen_row[3].gen_col[5].u_pe).

The reuse test: a parameter change should require editing one line (the instantiation) and nothing else. If changing the array from 8×8 to 4×4 requires touching five files, the parameterization has failed. TinyEdge-NPU passes the test: the 4×4 always-on variant is the same RTL with different parameters, the same testbench, and the same synthesis script.

5.4 The MAC Array: An 8×8 Array of Simple PEs

The MAC array is the heart of the NPU and deliberately the simplest block in the design. Each processing element (PE) is one INT8 multiplier, one 32-bit adder, and one accumulator register. There is no floating point, no division, no barrel shifter, no exotic arithmetic. The sophistication is in the data movement around the PEs, not inside them, which is exactly where it belongs, because data movement is where the energy goes.

The array is organized as 8 rows by 8 columns. In the weight-stationary mapping used for 1×1 pointwise layers, each column holds one output channel's weights and each row streams a different input activation; each PE computes one output pixel of one channel per cycle. In the output-stationary mapping used for 3×3 depthwise layers, each PE holds one output pixel's partial sum and the weights rotate through. The control FSM selects the mapping per layer, and the PE itself does not know or care which mapping is active. It multiplies the two operands it is given and adds the result to its accumulator. That ignorance is a design choice: keeping the PE mapping-agnostic means the same PE serves both dataflows, and the dataflow logic lives in the address generators, where it is testable in isolation.

// One PE: INT8 x INT8 -> 32-bit accumulate. 3-stage pipeline.
// Stage 1: register operands. Stage 2: multiply. Stage 3: add + accumulate.
// acc_clear_i must be asserted when prod_q holds the tile's first product
// (2 cycles after the tile's first operands), not with the operands themselves.
module tinyedge_pe #(
  parameter int DATA_WIDTH = 8,
  parameter int ACC_WIDTH  = 32
)(
  input  logic                  clk_i,
  input  logic                  rst_ni,
  input  logic                  en_i,        // clock-enable: 0 = hold, save power
  input  logic                  acc_clear_i, // pulse: zero the accumulator
  input  logic signed [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] act_i,
  input  logic signed [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] wgt_i,
  output logic signed [ACC_WIDTH-1:0]  acc_o
);
  logic signed [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] act_q, wgt_q;
  logic signed [2*DATA_WIDTH-1:0] prod_q;

  always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni) begin
    if (!rst_ni) begin
      act_q  <= '0;
      wgt_q  <= '0;
      prod_q <= '0;
      acc_o  <= '0;
    end else if (en_i) begin
      act_q  <= act_i;
      wgt_q  <= wgt_i;
      prod_q <= act_q * wgt_q;
      acc_o  <= acc_clear_i ? prod_q : acc_o + prod_q;
    end
    // en_i == 0: every register holds. No switching, no dynamic power.
  end
endmodule

Three details in this PE deserve attention because they generalize to the whole design. First, the en_i clock-enable: when a PE has no work (a depthwise layer that only uses the diagonal, or a layer boundary), its registers hold and its multiplier inputs do not toggle. Clock enables are the cheapest power-saving mechanism in the design and they are applied uniformly, not as an afterthought. Second, the accumulator is reset to zero on reset and re-initialised by the explicit acc_clear_i pulse at the start of each output tile. The pulse has to be timed to the multiply stage, not the input stage: the FSM asserts it two cycles after presenting the tile's first operands, when prod_q holds the tile's first product, so on the pulse the accumulator takes that first product instead of adding to the previous tile's sum. Asserting the pulse with the operands themselves would load the previous tile's last product, which is exactly the kind of one-cycle alignment bug that survives simulation and shows up in silicon. The timing makes the accumulation semantics visible in the control flow rather than hidden in the reset sequence. Third, the multiply is signed on both operands and the product is kept at full width (16 bits) before the 32-bit add; truncating the product early is a silent accuracy bug that no amount of verification will catch if the reference model makes the same assumption.

The array wraps the PEs with a lightweight interconnect: a row broadcast for activations, a column broadcast for weights, and a column-wise reduction for the final accumulation drain. The broadcast is combinational within a cycle, which is affordable at 100 MHz because the fanout is only 8 and the wires are short. The array is physically compact, about 0.05 mm2. If the array were 16×16, the broadcast fanout and wire length would start to dominate timing, which is one more reason Chapter 4 settled on 8×8.

flowchart LR subgraph ROWS["Activation broadcast (rows)"] A0[act row 0] --> P00[PE 0,0] A0 --> P01[PE 0,1] A1[act row 1] --> P10[PE 1,0] A1 --> P11[PE 1,1] end subgraph COLS["Weight broadcast (cols)"] W0[wgt col 0] --> P00 W0 --> P10 W1[wgt col 1] --> P01 W1 --> P11 end P00 --> ACC0[acc col 0] P10 --> ACC0 P01 --> ACC1[acc col 1] P11 --> ACC1 ACC0 --> Q[Requant\nunit] ACC1 --> Q

The requantization unit: where INT32 becomes INT8 again

The MAC array produces 32-bit accumulations; the next layer needs 8-bit activations. The requantization unit is the bridge, and it is the block where numerical correctness is most easily lost. Its job is three operations in order: add the per-channel bias, multiply by the per-channel scale factor, and saturate-and-round to INT8. Each operation has a trap. The bias must be added at full 32-bit width before any scaling. Adding it after the scale changes the result by more than a rounding error on layers with large biases. The scale multiplication is a fixed-point multiply by a per-channel multiplier (typically a 16-bit value with an associated shift), and the shift must be applied after the multiply, not before, or the low bits of the product are lost. The final saturation must clamp to the INT8 range (-128 to +127) with round-to-nearest, not truncation: truncation introduces a systematic negative bias that accumulates across layers and costs measurable accuracy on the keyword-spotting model. The TinyEdge-NPU team measured a 0.4% accuracy drop from truncation alone, which is a quarter of the total accuracy budget.

The requantization unit is pipelined to match the array: one output per cycle per column, so it never stalls the drain. It reads its per-channel bias and scale from the 8 KB scratchpad (reference L configuration; folded into the activation allocation at S and M), which the DMA loads alongside the weights at the start of each layer. The unit is parameterized by the same DATA_WIDTH and ACC_WIDTH as the PE, and it shares the PE's signedness discipline. Every operand is explicitly signed, and the lint rule for sign mismatch is set to error in this block because a sign error here is silent and catastrophic.

5.5 Weight and Activation Buffers: SRAM Interfaces and Banking

The buffers are where the architecture's memory hierarchy meets the RTL, and the most common mistake is to treat them as "just memories." They are not. Each buffer is a small subsystem: an SRAM macro, an address generator, a bank arbiter, and a set of performance counters. The interface discipline is what makes them work.

Banking for bandwidth

In the reference (L) configuration, the weight buffer is 128 KB, built from 8 banks of 16 KB. The activation buffer is 64 KB, built from 2 ping-pong banks of 32 KB each (one being written by the DMA while the other is read by the MAC array). Banking serves two purposes: it provides the read bandwidth the array needs (8 weight banks feed 8 columns in parallel, so the array never stalls waiting for weights), and it lets the DMA and the compute engine work concurrently on different banks. The bank count is derived from the array size by a parameter formula, NUM_WGT_BANKS = MAC_COLS, so changing the array size re-banks the memory automatically.

The memory subsystem instantiates its banks from the WEIGHT_KB and ACT_KB parameters: the weight-buffer depth is WEIGHT_KB (32 KB at S, 64 KB at M, 128 KB at L) and the activation-buffer depth is ACT_KB (16 KB at S, 32 KB at M, 64 KB at L), each split into the ping-pong banks Chapter 4 describes. The 8 KB bias/scratchpad is a fixed block in the L configuration and folds into the activation allocation at S and M, so the S and M totals are exactly WEIGHT_KB + ACT_KB. Instantiating a different configuration is a one-line change at the top level, no RTL edits, no new testbench, which is the point of the parameterization: the same verified RTL serves all three configurations in §3.9.

Every SRAM access goes through a synchronous-read interface: address and enable are presented in one cycle, data returns the next. There are no asynchronous reads anywhere in the design (see the anti-pattern table in section 5.2). The one-cycle read latency is accounted for in the pipeline schedule. The control FSM issues a weight fetch one cycle before the MAC array needs it, which is why the array has a 3-stage pipeline rather than 2.

Address generation

The address generators are the most bug-prone logic in the buffers, because they encode the dataflow. A weight-stationary 1×1 layer walks the weight bank in a different order than an output-stationary 3×3 layer walks it, and the activation generator must produce the sliding window for the depthwise kernel. The generators are therefore separate, testable modules with their own unit tests: given a layer descriptor (input shape, kernel size, stride, mapping), the generator must produce exactly the address sequence the reference model predicts, for every cycle, with no gaps and no repeats. On a design like this, the unit test for the activation generator is typically where off-by-one errors surface, most often in the stride-2 path, where they are invisible at stride 1.

// Activation address generator: produces the sliding-window read
// sequence for one output tile. Pure function of the layer descriptor.
module tinyedge_act_addrgen #(
  parameter int ADDR_WIDTH = 16
)(
  input  logic                  clk_i,
  input  logic                  rst_ni,
  input  logic                  start_i,     // pulse: load descriptor, begin
  input  logic [7:0]            in_h_i,      // input feature-map height
  input  logic [7:0]            in_w_i,      // input feature-map width
  input  logic [7:0]            k_h_i,       // kernel height (1 or 3)
  input  logic [7:0]            stride_i,    // 1 or 2
  output logic [ADDR_WIDTH-1:0] addr_o,      // SRAM read address
  output logic                  valid_o,     // address is valid this cycle
  output logic                  done_o       // pulse: tile complete
);
  // Counters walk (out_y, out_x, k_y, k_x) in row-major order.
  // The address is a closed-form function of the counters — no tables,
  // no lookup, nothing to get out of sync with the reference model.
  logic [7:0] out_y, out_x, k_y, k_x;
  logic [7:0] in_y, in_x;
  assign in_y = out_y * stride_i + k_y;
  assign in_x = out_x * stride_i + k_x;
  assign addr_o = in_y * in_w_i + in_x;
  // ... counter sequencing and done generation omitted for brevity ...
endmodule

The closed-form address, a multiply and an add, no table, is deliberate. A lookup table would be smaller for a fixed layer shape but would need to be reloaded for every layer, and a table that disagrees with the reference model is a bug that only shows up on one specific layer shape. The closed form is provably the same function the reference model computes, which is why the generator and the model can be checked against each other cycle by cycle.

The DMA engine: the NPU's memory mover

The DMA engine is the only block in the NPU that speaks the AXI4 protocol, and it exists so the control FSM never has to. It takes a transfer descriptor, source address, destination bank, length, and a completion flag, and executes it autonomously, issuing AXI4 read bursts, handling backpressure, and signalling completion. The engine supports two transfer types: a weight load (system memory to the weight banks) and an activation load/store (system memory to or from the activation ping-pong banks). Both use the same burst machinery; only the destination differs.

Two properties of the DMA matter for correctness. First, it is fire-and-forget with a completion flag: the FSM issues a descriptor and moves on to other work, and the DMA raises a done pulse when the transfer completes. The FSM never polls the DMA; it waits on the done pulse, which is why the FETCH state in the control FSM has a timeout. If the done pulse does not arrive, the FSM goes to ERROR instead of hanging. Second, the DMA never writes to a bank the MAC array is currently reading. The ping-pong discipline guarantees this by construction: the DMA writes to the bank the array is not using, and the banks swap only at a layer boundary under the FSM's control. A DMA write to an active bank would corrupt the running layer, and the design makes that structurally impossible rather than relying on software to avoid it.

5.6 Control FSM: The Layer Sequencer

The control FSM is the conductor of the NPU. It reads a layer descriptor from the configuration registers, sequences the DMA, the buffers, and the MAC array through the layer, and signals completion with an interrupt. It is the only block that knows what a "layer" is; every other block only knows about tiles, addresses, and cycles. That separation is what makes the FSM testable: it can be driven with a fake descriptor and its output sequence checked against the reference schedule, without any datapath attached.

The FSM has seven states. IDLE waits for software to write the START bit. LOAD_DESC latches the layer descriptor and programs the DMA. FETCH issues the DMA transfers for the layer's weights and activations. COMPUTE runs the MAC array tile by tile, issuing address sequences and collecting partial sums. DRAIN flushes the final accumulations through the requantization unit into the output buffer. DONE raises the interrupt and returns to IDLE. The state diagram below shows the transitions; the important detail is that every state has a defined exit condition and a timeout counter, so the FSM can never hang. If a DMA transfer does not complete within the expected window, the FSM moves to an ERROR state, raises the error interrupt, and logs the failing state in a status register.

stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> IDLE IDLE --> LOAD_DESC : start bit set LOAD_DESC --> FETCH : descriptor latched FETCH --> COMPUTE : DMA done FETCH --> ERROR : DMA timeout COMPUTE --> DRAIN : last tile done COMPUTE --> ERROR : MAC stall timeout DRAIN --> DONE : requant flushed DONE --> IDLE : interrupt acked ERROR --> IDLE : software clears IDLE --> [*] : reset

Two design choices in the FSM are worth calling out. First, the FSM is written as a two-process state machine: one always_ff block holds the state register, and one always_comb block computes the next state and all outputs. This is the standard pattern because it makes the state encoding explicit, keeps the output logic combinational and reviewable, and lets the synthesis tool infer the state register cleanly. Single-process FSMs that mix state and output assignment in one block are harder to review and more likely to hide a latch. Second, the FSM never asserts a control signal for more than one cycle unless the protocol requires it. START pulses, DONE pulses, and the interrupt is level-held until acknowledged, which is the only level signal in the design. Pulse discipline prevents the classic bug where a downstream block sees the same command twice.

// Two-process FSM: state register + combinational next-state/output logic.
typedef enum logic [2:0] {
  ST_IDLE, ST_LOAD_DESC, ST_FETCH, ST_COMPUTE, ST_DRAIN, ST_DONE, ST_ERROR
} state_t;

state_t state_q, state_d;

always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni) begin
  if (!rst_ni) state_q <= ST_IDLE;
  else         state_q <= state_d;
end

always_comb begin
  state_d = state_q;          // default: hold state
  start_dma = 1'b0;           // default: no pulses
  irq_done  = 1'b0;
  unique case (state_q)
    ST_IDLE:      if (cfg_start) state_d = ST_LOAD_DESC;
    ST_LOAD_DESC: begin
                    load_desc = 1'b1;
                    state_d   = ST_FETCH;
                  end
    ST_FETCH:     begin
                    start_dma = 1'b1;
                    if (dma_done)   state_d = ST_COMPUTE;
                    if (dma_timeout) state_d = ST_ERROR;
                  end
    ST_COMPUTE:   if (last_tile_done) state_d = ST_DRAIN;
    ST_DRAIN:     if (requant_done)   state_d = ST_DONE;
    ST_DONE:      begin
                    irq_done = 1'b1;
                    if (irq_ack) state_d = ST_IDLE;
                  end
    ST_ERROR:     if (err_clear) state_d = ST_IDLE;
    default:      state_d = ST_IDLE;
  endcase
end

Notice the defaults at the top of the combinational block: every output is assigned a value before the case statement. That is the latch-prevention discipline from section 5.2 applied to the FSM, and it is the reason the FSM synthesizes to exactly 3 flip-flops for the state plus the documented output logic, with no inferred latches.

5.7 AXI-Lite Bus Interface: The Software Contract

The AXI-Lite slave is the NPU's face to software, and it is the interface most likely to be used wrong, because software and hardware engineers have different assumptions about it. The interface is deliberately simple: a 32-bit AXI-Lite slave with a fixed register map, no bursts, no out-of-order responses, and a one-wait-cycle read latency. Simplicity is a feature: a customer integrating the IP can drive it from any AXI-Lite master, including a bare-metal CPU writing one register at a time, and the behaviour is identical.

Register map

OffsetNameAccessDescription
0x00CTRLRWBit 0: START (self-clearing). Bit 1: SOFT_RESET. Bit 2: IRQ_ENABLE.
0x04STATUSROBit 0: BUSY. Bit 1: DONE. Bit 2: ERROR. Bits 7:4: FSM state (debug).
0x08LAYER_DESC_PTRRWSystem-memory address of the layer descriptor list.
0x0CNUM_LAYERSRWNumber of layers to execute (1–16).
0x10IN_ADDRRWSystem-memory address of the input feature map.
0x14OUT_ADDRRWSystem-memory address of the output feature map.
0x18IRQ_STATUSRW1CBit 0: DONE. Bit 1: ERROR. Write-1-to-clear.
0x1CIDROIP identifier: 0x54454E50 ("TENP"). The RTL revision is reported in the REVISION register at 0x34.
0x20PERF_CYCLESROCycle count of the last completed inference.
0x24PERF_MAC_UTILROMAC array utilization of the last inference, in percent.
0x28MBIST_CTRLRWBit 0: START (self-clearing) — launches BIST on all SRAM instances. Bits 31:1: reserved.
0x2CMBIST_DONEROBit 0: DONE — set when BIST completes on all SRAM instances; cleared by the next MBIST_CTRL.START.
0x30MBIST_FAILROBit 0: weight SRAM fail. Bit 1: activation SRAM fail. 0 = all instances pass.
0x34REVISIONRORTL revision identifier (e.g. 0x00000001 for revision 1); changes with every RTL revision.

Three rules govern the register map. First, writes to configuration registers only take effect at a layer boundary: software can write IN_ADDR or NUM_LAYERS while an inference is running, but the new values are latched into a shadow set and only copied to the active set when the FSM is in IDLE. This eliminates the race where a mid-inference write corrupts the running layer. Second, every register has a defined reset value, documented in the map, so software can rely on the power-on state. Third, the ID register is read-only and non-zero: it is the first thing integration software reads, and a zero read tells the integrator immediately that the IP is not present or not clocked. A five-minute debug instead of a five-day one.

The AXI-Lite slave itself is a small, standard implementation: a write channel that decodes the address, checks it against the map, and returns OKAY or SLVERR for an unmapped address; a read channel with the same decode. The slave inserts at most one wait cycle on a read. Every register is a flip-flop and every read is a single-cycle mux once the address is accepted, so a read completes with exactly one wait cycle, matching the Chapter 4 sign-off measurement. The one exception is a write to CTRL.START, which is accepted immediately and self-clears; the FSM picks it up on the next clock.

The software contract: the register map is the API of the IP. It is versioned (the REVISION register carries the RTL revision; the ID register carries the fixed IP identifier), it is documented in the integration guide, and it does not change between minor revisions. A customer who writes a driver against version 1.0 must not have to rewrite it for version 1.1. New features get new registers; existing registers keep their meaning.

5.8 Low-Power Design Techniques

Low power is not a feature added at the end; it is a property of the RTL, decided block by block. TinyEdge-NPU's budgets, <5 mW active, <100 µW in sleep, are met by four techniques applied in order of return on effort: clock gating, operand isolation, SRAM banking with sleep modes, and power gating with retention. The ordering matters: the first two cost almost nothing and save the most, so they are applied everywhere; the last two cost area and verification effort, so they are applied where the numbers justify them.

Clock gating: the highest return

Every register bank in the design has a clock-enable, and the synthesis tool is instructed to map enables to integrated clock-gating (ICG) cells. The MAC array's en_i (section 5.4) is the most important example: when a PE has no work, its clock is gated and it burns only leakage. The address generators, the DMA engine, and the requantization unit are gated the same way. Each has an enable derived from its own activity signal, so the clock tree only toggles where there is work to do. Measured on the TinyEdge-NPU reference workload, clock gating alone saves about 35% of dynamic power, because the array is idle for a large fraction of each layer boundary while the DMA refills the buffers.

The rule for clock gating is that it must be correct by construction: the enable is derived from the same condition that makes the data valid, so a gated register can never miss a value it was supposed to capture. Enables are never derived from a different clock domain, never from a signal that can glitch, and never from a software register that can change asynchronously. The lint suite checks that every enable is a registered signal or a simple combinational function of registered signals.

Operand isolation: stop the toggling

Clock gating stops the registers; operand isolation stops the combinational logic in front of them. When a multiplier's inputs are not valid, the operands are forced to zero (or held at their last value) by an isolation gate, so the multiplier tree does not toggle. This matters because the multiplier is the largest combinational block in the PE: without isolation, every cycle in which the PE is idle still burns power in the multiplier as its inputs drift. The isolation is applied at the boundary of each PE and each address generator, controlled by the same enable that gates the clock, so the two mechanisms are consistent by construction.

Operand isolation is also applied to the SRAM read path: when a bank is not being read, its address is held constant, so the address decoder and the bitline precharge do not toggle. This is a smaller saving than the multiplier isolation, but it is free. The address hold is a single AND gate on the enable, and it compounds across 10 SRAM banks.

SRAM sleep modes and power gating

The SRAM macros support three states: active, light sleep (retention, low leakage, fast wake-up), and deep sleep (power off, no retention, slow wake-up). The power controller moves the banks between states based on the FSM: during COMPUTE, the weight and activation banks are active; during the DMA refill between layers, the idle ping-pong bank is in light sleep; in the system-level sleep state, all banks are in deep sleep except the 8 KB scratchpad, which retains the bias and scale factors so the next inference does not need to reload them. The retention choice is a deliberate trade: keeping 8 KB alive costs a few microwatts of leakage but saves a full DMA reload (hundreds of microseconds and the energy of a memory transfer) on every wake-up. Note the scope, because it matters for the larger configurations: this state keeps only the 8 KB scratchpad in retention, with the weight and activation banks powered off. That selective retention is what keeps deep sleep under 100 µW even in the L configuration. Full retention of the whole L array would be roughly 260 µW (Chapter 7, §7.3.5), so the <100 µW retentive-sleep budget belongs to the S configuration; M and L meet it only by retaining selectively or powering off.

Power gating the logic is the last step and the most expensive to verify. The MAC array and the requantization unit sit in a switchable power domain with isolation cells on every output and retention registers on the configuration state. The power switch is controlled by the system power manager, not by the NPU itself. The NPU requests a power state change through a status bit, and the system grants it. This keeps the power-sequencing logic in one place (the system) rather than distributed across the IP, which is the single biggest source of power-management bugs in small accelerators.

flowchart TD ACTIVE["Active\n<5 mW"] -->|layer done,\nidle > 1 ms| LSLEEP[Light sleep\nbanks retained] LSLEEP -->|new inference| ACTIVE LSLEEP -->|idle > 100 ms| DSLEEP["Deep sleep\n<100 uW"] DSLEEP -->|wake event| WAKE[Wake + restore\nscratchpad kept] WAKE --> ACTIVE ACTIVE -->|system off| OFF[Power off] OFF -->|power on| WAKE
TechniqueWhere appliedTypical savingCost
Clock gating (ICG)All registers; PE array, address generators, DMA~35% dynamic powerNegligible area; enable discipline
Operand isolationPE multipliers, SRAM address path~10–15% dynamic powerSmall; AND gates on enables
SRAM sleep modesWeight/activation banks between layers~40% of SRAM leakagePower controller + wake-up latency
