5.9 Common RTL Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

Most RTL bugs are not exotic. They are the same dozen mistakes, made by every team, in every design. The table below is the TinyEdge-NPU team's living list. Every entry is a bug that was actually found, in this design or in a design the team reviewed, with the fix that prevents it recurring. New team members read it in their first week.

PitfallSymptomPrevention
Off-by-one in a counter terminal valueOne extra or one missing iteration; wrong output on the last tileCounter compares against COUNT-1, never COUNT; unit test covers the boundary tile
Reset value that software can observe but the spec does not defineDriver reads garbage after reset; works on one build, fails on the nextEvery register has a documented reset value in the register map
Handshake assumed instead of checked (using data without valid)Intermittent wrong results under backpressureValid/ready discipline: data is consumed only when valid && ready
CDC without a synchronizer (a level signal crossing domains)Metastability; works in simulation, fails in siliconTwo-flop synchronizer for single bits; async FIFO for buses; CDC lint clean
Signed/unsigned mix-up in arithmeticNegative activations interpreted as large positive valuesExplicit signed on every arithmetic operand; lint rule for width/sign mismatch
Truncation of the accumulation before the requantizationSilent accuracy loss; model and RTL disagree by 1 LSB, then divergeKeep full 32-bit accumulation until the requant unit; never truncate in the PE
Configuration change taking effect mid-operationHalf a layer computed with old parameters, half with newShadow registers; new values take effect only at a layer boundary (see 5.7)
Uninitialized memory read before the first writeX-propagation in simulation; random data in siliconInitialize or explicitly invalidate; X-propagation checks in simulation
State machine with no default and no timeoutFSM hangs; only a full reset recovers itDefault state assignment; watchdog timeout to ERROR state (see 5.6)
Parameter change that breaks a derived widthSynthesis succeeds but the hardware is wrong (truncated bus)Elaboration-time assertions on every derived width (see 5.3)

The pattern across the table is that prevention is always cheaper than detection. A counter terminal-value rule costs one line of style; finding the same bug in silicon costs a respin. The team's rule is that any bug found in verification gets a prevention entry added to this table and a lint or assertion check added to the suite, so the same class of bug cannot recur silently.

5.10 Code Review Best Practices

RTL review is the last line of defence before synthesis, and it works only if it is structured. The TinyEdge-NPU team reviews every change with two reviewers, a checklist, and a rule that the author does not choose the reviewers. The design lead assigns them, so the review is independent. The checklist below is the review gate; a change does not merge until every item is checked.

The review checklist

  • Spec conformance: every behaviour in the change traces to a line in the MAS. If there is no MAS line, the change is incomplete. Write the spec first.
  • Interface discipline: every new port follows the naming rules; every handshake is valid/ready; no block reaches into another block's internals.
  • Reset: every new register has a defined reset value (or a documented waiver); the reset sequence is simulated.
  • Clocking: no new clock, no gated clock in RTL, no combinational clock path; every enable is derived from registered signals.
  • Widths and signs: every arithmetic operation has explicit widths and signedness; no implicit truncation; no width mismatch warnings from the linter.
  • Parameters: every new constant is a parameter or a localparam; the elaboration-time checks cover the new parameter's range.
  • Testability: the change includes or updates a unit test; the test fails before the fix and passes after it (the test is run both ways).
  • Synthesis: the change has been through synthesis (not just lint) and the area/timing delta is reported in the review.
  • Documentation: the register map, the interface table, and the block diagram are updated if the change touches them.

Two practices make the review effective rather than performative. First, the review is small: changes are kept under about 300 lines, so a reviewer can hold the whole change in their head. A 2,000-line change does not get a real review; it gets a skim. Second, the review is asynchronous and written: comments are in the code-review tool, not in a meeting, so the discussion is recorded and the author can address each point. The review meeting, if one happens, is only for the points that could not be resolved in writing.

Review is a design activity, not a quality gate. The best reviews find architectural problems, a handshake that cannot work under backpressure, a parameter that cannot be what the customer needs, not typos. If a review only finds typos, the design was either already excellent or the reviewers were not reading deeply enough. The checklist exists to free the reviewers' attention for the deep questions by making the shallow ones automatic.

Key Takeaways

  • RTL starts from the micro-architecture specification, not from a slide deck. Interface tables and timing contracts are written before any datapath is coded, because most integration bugs are interface bugs.
  • Reusable IP is disciplined IP: one clock and one reset style per block, no latches, no multi-driver nets, no magic numbers, and every rule enforced by lint in CI.
  • Parameterization makes the RTL a product. Parameters have documented ranges and elaboration-time checks, generate blocks replicate the PE and the banks from a single source, and a size change should require editing one instantiation line.
  • The MAC array is deliberately simple, one INT8 multiplier, one 32-bit adder, one accumulator per PE, and mapping-agnostic, so the same PE serves both the weight-stationary and output-stationary dataflows.
  • Buffers are subsystems, not memories: banking gives the array its bandwidth, address generators are closed-form functions of the layer descriptor, and the generators are unit-tested against the reference model cycle by cycle.
  • The control FSM is a two-process state machine with defaults on every output, a timeout to an ERROR state, and pulse discipline on every command. It can never hang and it can never issue the same command twice.
  • The AXI-Lite register map is the software API: shadow registers make configuration changes take effect only at layer boundaries, every register has a documented reset value, and the ID register lets integration software detect the IP in minutes.
  • Low power is a property of the RTL: clock gating first (~35% of dynamic power), then operand isolation, then SRAM sleep modes, then power gating with retention, in that order, because the return on effort declines at each step.
  • Every bug found in verification earns a prevention entry and a lint or assertion check, so the same class of bug cannot recur silently. Review is a design activity: keep changes small, review in writing, and use the checklist to free attention for the deep questions.

Chapter 6: Design for Test (DFT)

A design that cannot be tested cannot be sold. Design for test is the discipline of building testability into the silicon from the start, so that manufacturing defects can be found quickly and cheaply: at wafer sort, at package test, and in the customer's system. For a small accelerator like TinyEdge-NPU, DFT is often treated as an afterthought, something to be "added later" once the design works. That is exactly backwards: DFT structures touch every flip-flop, every memory, and every pin in the design, and retrofitting them after the RTL is frozen is expensive, error-prone, and usually incomplete. This chapter covers the three pillars, scan, memory BIST, and boundary scan, shows how they are applied to a small accelerator, works through the coverage, area, and power trade-offs, and ends with the DFT plan for TinyEdge-NPU and the checklist the team uses at sign-off.

6.1 Why DFT Matters for a Small Accelerator

Every chip that leaves the factory has defects. A modern 28 nm process produces a small but nonzero fraction of dies with manufacturing faults: a shorted wire, an open via, a transistor that does not switch. The foundry's job is to make that fraction small; the design's job is to make it detectable. Without DFT, the only way to test a chip is to run it functionally and hope the defect shows up as a wrong output. For a neural accelerator, that hope is misplaced: most defects do not change the output of a single inference in an obvious way. A stuck bit in a weight buffer changes one weight by one LSB, which changes the classification score slightly, which may or may not flip the top-1 result. A functional test would pass a defective chip, and that chip would ship to a customer.

DFT solves this by giving the tester direct access to the internals: scan chains let the tester set and observe every flip-flop, memory BIST lets the tester exercise every SRAM bit, and boundary scan lets the tester check every pin and every board connection. With those three mechanisms, the test program can detect the overwhelming majority of manufacturing defects in seconds, at a cost of pennies per die. The economics are stark: a test that takes 2 seconds at wafer sort costs a few cents; a field return of a defective device costs tens of dollars in logistics and reputation, and a defect that escapes into a safety-relevant product costs far more.

For an IP product, DFT has a second dimension: the customer, not the IP vendor, manufactures the chip. The IP must therefore be delivered with its DFT structures intact, documented, and verifiable in the customer's flow. A customer who cannot run the IP's scan patterns in their own ATPG flow, or who cannot integrate the IP's BIST controller into their testbench, will either reject the IP or strip the DFT out. Stripping it out means the shipped silicon is untestable. DFT is part of the product, not an optional extra.

The DFT rule: testability is designed in, not tested in. Every DFT structure is specified in the architecture document, implemented in the RTL alongside the functional logic, and verified by the same testbench that verifies the function. A DFT feature added after RTL freeze is a schedule risk; a DFT feature designed in from the start is a line item.

6.2 Scan Insertion: Making Every Flip-Flop Observable

Scan is the workhorse of manufacturing test. The idea is simple: every flip-flop in the design is replaced with a scan flip-flop, which has an extra multiplexer on its input. In normal mode, the flip-flop behaves exactly as the functional design intends. In scan-shift mode, the flip-flops are connected into long shift registers, scan chains, so the tester can shift an arbitrary pattern into every flip-flop in the design, pulse the clock once to let the combinational logic react, and shift the resulting state out to be compared against the expected response. Any stuck-at fault (a net permanently tied to 0 or 1) or transition fault (a net that switches too slowly) in the combinational logic between two flip-flops will change the captured response and be detected.

Full scan and what it costs

TinyEdge-NPU uses full scan: every functional flip-flop is scannable, with no exceptions except the small set of explicitly waived registers (the free-running cycle counter used for performance measurement, which has no functional effect). Full scan is chosen because the design is small, about 45,000 flip-flops, so the area cost of the scan multiplexers is modest (roughly 4–5% of the logic area), and the coverage benefit is large: full scan with a good ATPG pattern set achieves ≥99% stuck-at coverage on the TinyEdge-NPU logic.

The scan chains are organized by clock domain and by physical region: the MAC array's flip-flops form several short chains (one per pair of PE rows), the control and DMA logic form their own chains, and the AXI-Lite registers form a separate chain. Short chains matter for test time: shifting a pattern through a chain of 1,000 flip-flops takes 1,000 shift clocks, so splitting the design into 16 chains of ~2,800 flip-flops each cuts the shift time by a factor of 16 compared to a single chain, at the cost of 16 scan-in and 16 scan-out pins (which are shared with functional pins through multiplexing in test mode). The chain balance is checked by the DFT tool, and no chain is allowed to be more than 10% longer than the average.

ATPG and fault coverage

Automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) produces the vectors that are shifted into the scan chains. The flow is: synthesize the design with scan insertion, run ATPG to generate patterns targeting stuck-at and transition faults, and simulate the patterns to confirm they detect the faults they claim to. The coverage target for TinyEdge-NPU is ≥99.0% stuck-at coverage and ≥95.0% transition coverage at 100 MHz. The residual uncovered faults are reviewed one by one: most are untestable by construction (redundant logic, tied-off configuration inputs), and each gets a waiver with a reason. A fault that is uncovered and not waived is a sign-off blocker.

Scan compression: when chains alone are not enough

Sixteen chains keep the shift time reasonable for TinyEdge-NPU, but the pattern volume, the total amount of test data the tester must store and deliver, grows with the pattern count, and transition-fault patterns are roughly twice as numerous as stuck-at patterns. For a small design the volume is manageable (a few megabits), but the team still applies scan compression: an on-chip decompressor expands a small number of tester channels into the full scan data, and a compactor compresses the responses back down. The standard approach is an XOR-based compactor and a broadcast decompressor, which typically delivers a 5–10× reduction in pattern volume at the cost of a small amount of logic and a slight loss of diagnostic resolution. When a compressed response mismatches, the compactor tells the tester that a fault was detected, but not always which chain it came from, so diagnosis needs a second, uncompressed pass. For TinyEdge-NPU the trade is worth it: the compressed pattern set fits in the tester's memory without an upgrade, and the diagnostic pass is only needed on failing dies, which are a small fraction. The compression logic itself is verified by the same scan-shift test as the chains, with an additional check that the decompressor's seed and the compactor's signature match the ATPG tool's expectation on every pattern.

Two practical points dominate scan work on a small accelerator. First, scan must be verified in the functional testbench: the testbench includes a scan-shift test that shifts a known pattern through the chains and checks it comes out the other end, which catches scan-chain ordering errors (a chain stitched in the wrong order) that ATPG cannot see. Second, clock gating and scan do not mix naively: the integrated clock-gating cells from Chapter 5 must be forced open in scan-shift mode, or the gated registers will not shift. The DFT tool inserts the test-mode override automatically, but the override is verified by simulation. A gated clock that does not open in test mode is a silent coverage killer.

6.3 Memory BIST: Testing 200 KB of SRAM (L Configuration)

SRAM does not scan. A memory's internal bitcells and sense amplifiers cannot be reached by shifting patterns through flip-flops, so memories need their own test mechanism: built-in self-test (BIST). A BIST controller sits next to each SRAM bank and, in test mode, runs a march algorithm over the memory, writing and reading patterns that detect stuck-at faults, transition faults, coupling faults between neighbouring cells, and address-decoder faults, and reports a pass/fail signature. The controller is small (a few hundred gates per bank) and it is shared where possible: one controller serves the 8 weight banks sequentially, and a second serves the 2 activation banks and the scratchpad.

March algorithms: what they catch

The standard algorithm for TinyEdge-NPU is March C-, which performs 10 operations per address (write 0, read 0, write 1, read 1, and so on, in both ascending and descending address order). March C- detects all stuck-at and transition faults, all coupling faults between cells, and most address-decoder faults, and it runs in about 10×N cycles for an N-word memory. March C- addresses words, not bytes: a 16 KB bank on a 32-bit data path holds 4,096 words, so the march is 4,096 × 10 ≈ 41,000 cycles, or 0.41 ms at 100 MHz. The two controllers run in parallel: the weight controller marches its eight 16 KB banks sequentially (8 × 0.41 ≈ 3.3 ms) while the activation controller marches its two 32 KB banks and the 8 KB scratchpad (2 × 0.82 + 0.20 ≈ 1.8 ms), so the full BIST run over all banks takes about 3.3 ms, well inside the 10 ms test-time budget and negligible in a wafer-sort test program that budgets seconds per die.

Two design decisions matter. First, the BIST controller has a bypass mode: in normal operation the controller is completely out of the path. The SRAM's functional address and data go straight through, with no multiplexer in the timing-critical read path. The BIST multiplexer sits on the address input, not the data output, so it adds no delay to the read timing. Second, the BIST signature is observable: the pass/fail result for each bank is readable through a test status register on the AXI-Lite interface, so the customer's system-level test can check the memories without entering a special test mode. This matters for field diagnostics. A device that fails in the field can be asked whether its memories are intact, which narrows the diagnosis enormously.

Repair: redundancy and the fuse decision

Testing finds bad memories; repair saves them. Each SRAM bank in TinyEdge-NPU has one spare row and one spare column. When BIST finds a faulty row or column, the failing address is recorded in a small repair register, and the memory's redundancy logic remaps accesses to the spare. The repair data is stored in on-chip fuses (or, in the testchip, in a register loaded by the tester), so the repair survives power cycles.

BIST as a field diagnostic

Memory BIST is usually described as a manufacturing test, but for TinyEdge-NPU it earns a second life as a field diagnostic. The BIST controller remains in the shipped silicon, reachable through the test status register, and the system software can run a BIST pass on demand: at boot, after a suspected soft error, or as part of a periodic health check. The march itself takes about 3 ms, and March C- is destructive: it overwrites every word it tests, so the contents are gone when the run finishes. A field run is therefore non-destructive only when the system software makes it so. Before setting MBIST_CTRL, software uses the DMA engine — the design's only AXI4 master — to save the bank contents to system memory, then runs the march, then restores the contents and reports. The save and restore add about a millisecond for the full 200 KB at 400 MB/s, on top of the 3 ms march. At boot the save is unnecessary, since the buffers are not yet populated, which is the cheapest time to run the check. This is a deliberate design decision, not an accident: the BIST controller stays small — a few hundred gates per bank, with no bus-master logic — and the save/restore lives in software, where it belongs. It is what lets a fielded device answer the question "is my memory still good" without a service visit. Soft errors from cosmic rays and alpha particles are rare at 28 nm but not zero, and a device that can test its own memory and report the result is a device that can be trusted in a product that runs unattended for years, a home-security sensor, an industrial monitor, where nobody will notice a slowly degrading memory until it causes a missed detection.

The decision to include repair is an economic one. Without repair, any bank with a single bad bitcell means a dead die. With one spare row and column per bank, a die with a handful of scattered defects can still ship, which improves the effective yield, particularly valuable on a first tape-out, when the defect density is highest and the volume is lowest. The cost is the spare rows and columns themselves (about 2% of the SRAM area) plus the fuse and remap logic. For a testchip, where every working die is precious because it is the evidence for the IP's silicon-proven status, repair is clearly worth it. For a high-volume production part, the same logic holds: a 1–2% yield improvement on a million units pays for the repair logic many times over.

6.4 Boundary Scan: Testing the Pins and the Board

Boundary scan (IEEE 1149.1 JTAG) tests what scan and BIST cannot: the connections between the chip and the outside world. Every digital I/O pin on the TinyEdge-NPU testchip gets a boundary-scan cell, a small register that can drive the pin, sample the pin, or disconnect it. The cells are chained together through the Test Access Port (TAP), a 4-pin JTAG interface (TCK, TMS, TDI, TDO), so an external tester can check that every pin is connected to the board, that no two pins are shorted, and that the board's traces are intact, without running any functional test at all.

JTAG as a debug port

Boundary scan's test role is well understood, but its debug role is what makes it indispensable on first silicon. When a testchip comes back from the fab and does not boot, the bring-up engineer has almost nothing to work with: no software runs, no waveform is visible, and the only evidence is that the device is silent. The JTAG TAP is the first tool that works in that situation, because it needs only four pins and a clock to operate. Through the TAP, the engineer can shift patterns into the scan chains and read back the state of every flip-flop, which reveals whether the reset released, whether the clock is running, and whether the control FSM reached the state it should have. On the TinyEdge-NPU testchip, the first-silicon debug flow starts with a JTAG chain-integrity test (shift a walking-ones pattern through the boundary-scan chain and confirm it comes out intact), then a scan-dump of the control registers, and only then a functional test. On a design like this, the JTAG debug flow is typically how the first silicon issues are diagnosed. For example, a reset synchronizer that releases a cycle too early, visible as the FSM starting in the wrong state, or a clock-gating enable that is asserted in test mode, visible as a block of flip-flops that would not shift. Neither would have been found by a functional test alone, because the functional test would simply have failed with no further information. The lesson is that the debug value of JTAG justifies its pins even on a design where board-level boundary scan is not strictly needed.

For the TinyEdge-NPU IP itself, boundary scan is mostly a delivery concern rather than a design concern: the IP does not contain the TAP controller (the customer's SoC provides it), but the IP must expose its boundary-scan requirements, which pins are digital, which are analog or power, and what the expected board-level connectivity is, so the customer can build the chain correctly. The IP delivery package therefore includes a Boundary Scan Description Language (BSDL) file describing the IP's pins and their boundary-scan cells, and the integration guide specifies that the IP's pins must be included in the SoC's boundary-scan chain. An IP whose pins are left out of the chain cannot be board-tested, and a board that cannot be tested is a board that ships with untested solder joints.

The testchip, which is the vehicle for the IP's silicon validation (Chapter 13), has its own TAP controller and a full boundary-scan chain, because the testchip is a standalone device that must be testable on a bare board. The testchip's JTAG chain is also the debug port: the same TAP that runs boundary scan gives the bring-up engineer access to the internal scan chains and the BIST status registers, which is how the first silicon is debugged when nothing else works.

6.5 DFT for TinyEdge-NPU: The Plan

The DFT plan for TinyEdge-NPU is a single page in the architecture document, and it is the page the customer's test engineer reads first. It states the coverage targets, the structures, the test time budget, and the interfaces. Everything the customer needs to integrate the IP's test features into their flow without reverse-engineering the RTL.

flowchart TD subgraph DFT["TinyEdge-NPU DFT structures"] SCAN[Full scan\n16 chains, ~45k FFs] BIST[MBIST\n2 controllers, 11 banks] JTAG[JTAG TAP\ntestchip only] PMON[Power monitors\n+ BIST status regs] end subgraph TEST["Test program"] ATPG[ATPG patterns\nstuck-at + transition] MARCH[March C-\nper bank] BSCAN[Boundary scan\nboard test] end SCAN --> ATPG BIST --> MARCH JTAG --> BSCAN PMON --> MARCH ATPG --> COV[Coverage sign-off\n≥99% stuck-at, ≥95% transition] MARCH --> COV BSCAN --> COV
StructureScopeCoverage targetTest time
Full scan, 16 chainsAll logic except waived perf counter≥99.0% stuck-at, ≥95.0% transition~0.5 s (ATPG, 25 MHz shift / 100 MHz capture)
MBIST, 2 controllers11 SRAM banks (8 weight, 2 activation, 1 scratchpad)100% of march-detectable faults~3.3 ms (March C-)
Boundary scan (JTAG)All digital pins (testchip); BSDL for the IP100% of pin shorts/opens~50 ms (board test)
Repair (spare row/col)Each SRAM bank1 row + 1 column per bankProgrammed once at sort

The plan also specifies what is not covered and why. The analog portions (the bandgap and the temperature sensor on the testchip) are tested functionally, not by scan, because scan cannot observe analog behaviour. The clock generator (PLL) is tested by a dedicated frequency-measurement test, not by ATPG. And the power-gating switches are tested by a leakage-measurement step, not by a logic pattern. Each of these is a deliberate, documented exclusion with its own test method, not a gap discovered at sign-off.

DFT and power gating: testing a switchable domain

The MAC array and the requantization unit sit in a switchable power domain (Chapter 7), and that domain complicates test in three specific ways that the DFT plan addresses head-on. First, scan chains must not cross a power-domain boundary while the domain is off: a scan chain that runs through a powered-down block will not shift, and worse, it can back-power the block through the scan input and produce unpredictable behaviour. The chains are therefore partitioned by domain. The switchable logic has its own chains, and the always-on control logic has its own, and the test program powers the switchable domain on before shifting its chains. Second, isolation cells must be tested: the isolation cells on the domain boundary are verified by a dedicated test that powers the domain down, drives the isolation enable, and checks that the outputs are clamped to their safe values. An isolation cell that does not isolate will corrupt the always-on logic's inputs, and the failure mode is a system hang, not a test failure. That is why the isolation test exists. Third, retention registers must be tested in both modes: the configuration state held in retention registers is checked by writing a known pattern, powering the domain down and back up, and reading the pattern back. A retention register that loses its state on power-down will silently reset the NPU's configuration, and the symptom (the NPU forgetting its layer descriptor after a sleep cycle) looks like a software bug, not a hardware fault. The DFT plan's retention test exists precisely to prevent that misdiagnosis.

6.6 Trade-Offs: Coverage, Area, and Power

DFT is never free. Every structure costs area, some cost power, and all of them cost verification effort. The trade-offs for TinyEdge-NPU are worked out explicitly, because a DFT plan that ignores its own cost is a plan that gets cut at the first schedule pressure. A cut DFT plan is worse than no plan, because the team believes the chip is testable when it is not.

ChoiceCoverage gainArea costPower costVerdict for TinyEdge-NPU
Full scan vs partial scan≥99% vs ~85% stuck-at~4–5% of logicNone in normal mode; test-mode onlyFull scan. The design is small; the extra ~14% coverage is worth 5% area.
Transition-fault ATPG in addition to stuck-at+8–10% delay-defect detectionNone (same chains)Longer test time (~2× patterns)Yes. Delay defects are the dominant escape in 28 nm; the extra test time is seconds.
MBIST per bank vs shared controllerSame fault coverageShared saves ~60% of controller areaSequential test is slower (~3.3 ms vs ~0.8 ms)Shared (2 controllers). 3.3 ms is negligible at sort.
Spare row + column per bankRecovers dies with scattered defects~2% of SRAM areaNegligibleYes. Yield improvement pays for itself, especially on the testchip.
Boundary scan on the IP vs SoC onlyBoard-level pin testCells are in the SoC, not the IPNoneBSDL + integration spec. The IP supplies the description; the SoC owns the chain.
Test points (observability) in the datapath+1–2% coverage on hard-to-reach nets<0.5% of logicNoneSelective. Added only where ATPG reports low coverage, not everywhere.

The guiding principle is that coverage is bought where it is cheapest. Full scan is cheap because the design is small. Transition ATPG is cheap because the chains already exist. Repair is cheap because SRAM area is dominated by the bitcell array, not the periphery. The expensive choices, per-bank BIST controllers, test points everywhere, are the ones that are declined, because their marginal coverage is small and their cost is real. The trade-off table is reviewed at every milestone, because the numbers change as the design grows: if the MAC array were doubled, the scan cost would double with it, and the full-scan decision would need to be revisited.

Power deserves a specific note, because DFT and low power are often in tension. Scan shift mode toggles every flip-flop on every shift clock, which draws far more current than normal operation, enough to cause IR drop that can make a good die fail test. The test program therefore limits the shift frequency (the TinyEdge-NPU scan shift runs at 25 MHz, not 100 MHz) and the DFT tool staggers the chain enables so not all chains shift simultaneously. Similarly, the BIST run is sequenced bank by bank rather than all at once, so the peak test current stays within the package's limits. These are test-program decisions, not RTL decisions, but they are specified in the DFT plan so the test engineer does not have to discover them by trial and error.

Test time is the other half of the economics, and it is where the trade-offs become concrete numbers. The full TinyEdge-NPU test program, scan (stuck-at plus transition), MBIST, boundary scan, and the leakage and frequency checks, runs in about 1.5 seconds per die at wafer sort. At a typical wafer-sort cost, that is a few cents of test cost per die. Cutting the transition-fault patterns would save about 0.4 seconds and a fraction of a cent, but it would let delay defects escape. A delay defect that escapes sort will either fail at package test (where the test costs ten times as much per die, because the die is now packaged) or escape to the field (where the cost is measured in dollars and reputation). The rule the team uses is simple: test time is bought at wafer sort, where it is cheapest, and never saved there at the cost of escapes. The one place test time is spent carefully is in the pattern count for the largest, slowest structure. That is why scan compression and the shared BIST controllers exist: they cut test time without cutting coverage, which is the only kind of test-time saving that is free.

6.7 DFT and the IP Delivery Package

A DFT plan that lives only in the vendor's repository is useless to the customer. The TinyEdge-NPU delivery package therefore includes everything the customer's test flow needs, in the formats their tools consume. The package is versioned with the IP, and a change to any DFT structure is a minor-version bump, because it can change the customer's test program.

  • Scan-inserted netlist and ATPG patterns. The gate-level netlist with scan chains inserted, the STIL/WGL pattern files, and the ATPG fault list with the coverage report. The customer re-runs ATPG in their own flow to confirm the coverage on their netlist, which may differ slightly after their own synthesis and physical design.
  • MBIST controller RTL and test vectors. The controller source, the march algorithm specification, and the expected pass/fail signatures per bank. The customer integrates the controller into their testbench and confirms the BIST run completes and reports correctly.
  • BSDL file and pin list. The boundary-scan description for the IP's pins, plus the integration guide section on including the IP in the SoC's JTAG chain.
  • DFT user guide. A short document (about 10 pages) that explains the test modes, the test-mode entry sequence, the expected test times, and the known waivers with their reasons. It is written for the customer's test engineer, not for the IP's designers, and it is reviewed by an engineer who did not design the DFT. If they cannot follow it, it is rewritten.
  • Test-mode timing constraints. SDC constraints for the test modes (scan shift clock, JTAG TCK, BIST clock), so the customer's STA flow times the test paths and does not treat them as false paths by accident.

The delivery package is verified by a customer-flow simulation: before the IP ships, the team runs the delivered patterns through a clean-room flow, a fresh synthesis, a fresh ATPG run, and a fresh BIST simulation, using only the files in the delivery package and no internal knowledge. If the clean-room flow cannot reproduce the claimed coverage, the package is incomplete and does not ship. This is the DFT equivalent of the clean-room build, and it has caught missing constraint files and stale pattern sets more than once.

6.8 DFT Planning Checklist and Best Practices

The checklist below is used at the DFT review, which happens at the same time as the architecture review, not after RTL freeze. Every item must be checked before the design is released for synthesis.

  • Coverage targets are written down (stuck-at, transition, MBIST, boundary scan) and agreed with the customer or the product team before RTL starts.
  • Every flip-flop is scannable or waived with a reason. The waiver list is short, reviewed, and in the delivery package.
  • Clock gating is test-mode aware. Every ICG cell opens in scan-shift mode; verified by simulation, not by assumption.
  • Scan chains are balanced and verified. Chain lengths within 10% of the average; a scan-shift test in the functional testbench proves the chains are stitched correctly.
  • MBIST covers every SRAM bank, including the scratchpad, and the BIST run time is budgeted in the test program.
  • Repair is decided explicitly (spare rows/columns or not) with the yield argument documented, not left as a default.
  • Boundary scan is specified for the IP (BSDL + integration guide) even though the TAP lives in the SoC.
  • Test-mode timing is constrained. SDC covers scan shift, JTAG, and BIST clocks; no test path is an accidental false path.
  • The delivery package passes a clean-room flow. Coverage is reproducible from the delivered files alone.
  • DFT is in the regression suite. Scan-shift, BIST, and JTAG tests run in CI on every RTL change, so a change that breaks testability is caught the same day.

The one-line version: DFT is a product feature with a specification, a budget, and a sign-off, the same as any functional feature. Treat it as one, and the chip will be testable. Treat it as an afterthought, and the first silicon will teach you why that was a mistake, at the worst possible time.

Key Takeaways

  • DFT is designed in from the start, not added after RTL freeze. Scan, MBIST, and boundary scan each touch every flip-flop, memory, and pin. Retrofitting them is expensive and usually incomplete.
  • Full scan is the right choice for a small accelerator: ~45,000 flip-flops, 16 balanced chains, ≥99.0% stuck-at and ≥95.0% transition coverage for about 4–5% of logic area.
  • Scan must be verified in the functional testbench (a scan-shift test proves the chains are stitched correctly), and clock-gating cells must be forced open in test mode or the coverage silently collapses.
  • Memory BIST with March C- tests all 200 KB of SRAM in about 3.3 ms, well inside the 10 ms budget. Shared controllers (one for the weight banks, one for the rest) save area at negligible test-time cost, and spare rows and columns buy back yield, especially valuable on the testchip.
  • Boundary scan is a delivery concern for the IP: the SoC owns the TAP chain, but the IP must supply the BSDL file and the integration guide, or its pins cannot be board-tested.
  • Coverage is bought where it is cheapest, full scan and transition ATPG on a small design, repair on SRAM, and the expensive options (per-bank controllers, test points everywhere) are declined where their marginal coverage is small.
  • The DFT delivery package (scan netlist and patterns, MBIST RTL and vectors, BSDL, user guide, test-mode constraints) must pass a clean-room flow: coverage reproducible from the delivered files alone, or the package does not ship.
  • DFT has a specification, a budget, and a sign-off, the same as any functional feature, with a checklist reviewed at architecture time, not after RTL freeze.

Chapter 7: Power Intent and Low-Power Verification (UPF)

The TinyEdge-NPU's entire value proposition is a power number. The active budget is under 5 mW, the sleep budget is under 100 µW, and the wake-up budget is 64 cycles. The product is a battery-powered voice interface, so those numbers are the product, not a footnote to it. The power architecture that delivers them is not a detail of the physical implementation. It is a design decision on the same level as the dataflow (Chapter 4) and the test strategy (Chapter 6), and it needs the same treatment: written down formally, reviewed, and verified, before the design is verified, not after it fails in silicon. That formal description is the power intent, written in the Unified Power Format (UPF, IEEE 1801), and this chapter is about writing it, implementing it, and proving it correct.

Power intent is the single source of truth for everything the chip does with power: which blocks are always on, which can be switched off, what happens to their outputs when they are off, what state survives a power-down, and which power state the chip is in at any moment. Synthesis reads it to insert switches, isolation cells, and retention registers. Place-and-route reads it to build the power grid and the domain fences. Simulation reads it to model power-down. Formal verification reads it to prove the retention and isolation properties. If any of those tools reads a different intent, or if the intent exists only as a slide deck and a shared understanding, the tools will faithfully implement different chips, and the difference will surface as a dead part on the bench.

7.1 Why Power Intent Is a First-Class Design Artifact

Chapter 3 states the power requirements as five lines in a table. Those five lines are the contract this chapter implements:

RequirementWhat it saysWhere it is proven
REQ-PWR-001Active power < 5.0 mW at 20 MHz, 0.9 V, 25 °CPower simulation; silicon (Chapter 13)
REQ-PWR-002Burst power < 12 mW at 100 MHzPower simulation
REQ-PWR-003State-retentive sleep power < 100 µW, weights retainedPower simulation; silicon (Chapter 13)
REQ-PWR-004Deep-sleep leakage < 5 µW, domain offPower simulation
REQ-PWR-005Wake-up latency < 100 µs (design budget: ≤ 64 cycles, 0.64 µs at 100 MHz)Simulation; silicon (Chapter 13)

Notice what the requirements do not say. They do not say how many power domains the chip has, which blocks live in each, what the isolation strategy is, or what survives a power-down. Those are architecture decisions, and they belong in the power intent, a file the tools can read, not a paragraph in a document the tools cannot. The gap between "under 100 µW in sleep" and a working chip is exactly the set of decisions this chapter records: two power domains, one PMOS header switch, clamp-to-zero isolation, 284 bits of retention, dual-rail SRAMs held at a 0.65 V retention voltage, and a power-state table with four states. None of those decisions is visible in the requirements table. All of them are visible in the UPF.

There is a second reason power intent is first-class: it is the only artifact that is consumed by every tool in the flow. The RTL describes function. The SDC describes timing. The UPF describes power, and power crosses every boundary the other two respect. A power switch sits in the netlist that synthesis produces, in the floorplan that place-and-route produces, in the testbench that simulation runs, and in the equivalence check that sign-off runs. When the UPF is wrong, the error does not stay in one tool's domain; it propagates into all of them, and each tool's output looks locally correct. The synthesis report says the switch was inserted. The simulation says the design wakes up. The silicon says it does not, because the switch the synthesis tool inserted is not the switch the simulation modelled, and the difference is a single UPF line that one flow read and the other did not.

The power-intent rule: if a power behaviour is not written in the UPF, it does not exist, no matter how carefully the RTL implies it. The UPF is the specification; the RTL is one implementation of it, and the tools check the implementation against the specification, not the other way around.

7.1.1 What happens when power intent is an afterthought

Every low-power project has a version of this story, and it always starts the same way: the functional design works, the power numbers look fine in a spreadsheet, and power intent is scheduled for "after RTL freeze, when we know what the design really looks like." Then the first power-aware simulation runs, and three things happen at once. First, the simulation finds signals floating: outputs of the powered-down block drive inputs of the always-on block, and without isolation cells those inputs sit at intermediate voltages, drawing shoot-through current and occasionally flipping the always-on logic. The isolation cells now need to be inserted in the RTL, constrained in synthesis, and placed along a floorplan that is already frozen. Second, the simulation finds state lost: configuration registers that the software wrote before sleep read back as zero after wake-up, because nobody specified retention for them, and the retention registers need a separate always-on supply rail that was never routed. Third, the power-state table turns out to have been implicit in the firmware all along, and the firmware and the hardware disagree about one transition: the firmware powers the domain down while a DMA transfer is still in flight, and the design has no defined behaviour for that case, because no one ever wrote the table down.

Each of those three failures is cheap to prevent and expensive to repair. An isolation cell specified in the UPF before RTL freeze is a line in a file. An isolation cell retrofitted after the floorplan is frozen is a re-floorplan. A retention register specified before synthesis is a cell choice. A retention register retrofitted after synthesis is a netlist edit, a new timing path, and a re-verification of everything downstream. A power-state table written before the firmware is written is a review meeting. A power-state table discovered by debugging a hang on the bench is a week. The pattern is the same as DFT, which is why this chapter follows it: the cost of a "design for X" discipline is set by when it is applied, and the cheapest time is before the RTL is frozen.

7.1.2 Why this chapter sits after DFT

DFT (Chapter 6) and power intent are the same kind of discipline, applied to different properties. Both are decided before verification, because both touch every flip-flop in the design and both are expensive to retrofit. Both are specified in the architecture document, implemented in the RTL alongside the functional logic, and verified by the same testbench that verifies the function. And the two disciplines interact directly: Chapter 6 showed that scan chains must not cross a power-domain boundary while the domain is off, that isolation cells must be tested by powering the domain down and checking the clamp, and that retention registers must be tested in both modes, powered and unpowered. None of those DFT tests can be written without the power intent, because the intent is what defines the domains, the isolation, and the retention. The DFT plan tests the power architecture; this chapter specifies it.

The ordering matters in the other direction too. The verification chapter (Chapter 8) builds a testbench that must model power-down, and a formal environment that must prove retention properties. Both need the UPF as an input: the testbench's power-aware simulation reads the UPF to know when a domain is off, and the formal tool reads it to know which registers are supposed to survive. If the UPF does not exist when verification starts, the verification team writes its own model of the power architecture, from the RTL, from a slide deck, or from a conversation, and that model will differ from the implementation in exactly the places that matter. Writing the power intent here, between DFT and verification, means the verification team inherits the specification instead of inventing it.

7.2 UPF Fundamentals: The Vocabulary

UPF (IEEE 1801) is a Tcl-based language for describing power intent. It does not describe function: it describes the power architecture around the function: which parts of the design are powered by which supplies, what happens when a supply is switched off, and which states the chip can be in. Six concepts carry almost the whole language, and the rest of this chapter is built from them.

7.2.1 Power domains

A power domain is a region of the design that shares a power supply and a power state: everything in the domain is on together or off together. Domains are the unit of power management. The TinyEdge-NPU has two: PD_AON, the always-on domain, and PD_NPU, the switchable domain. The choice of two domains, not one, not five, is itself an architecture decision, and it is worth stating why. One domain would mean no power gating at all: the whole chip would leak all the time, and the <100 µW sleep budget would be unreachable in 28 nm bulk CMOS, where a 64-MAC array and 200 KB of SRAM leak far more than 100 µW even with clock gating. Five domains, one per SRAM bank, one per MAC quadrant, one for control, would give finer-grained control and lower leakage in principle, but each additional domain adds a switch, an isolation boundary, a set of power-state transitions, and a verification burden, and the marginal leakage saving on a design this small does not pay for it. Two domains is the smallest number that meets the requirement: one domain that never sleeps, holding the wake logic and the control registers, and one domain that sleeps between inferences, holding everything that computes. The power-state table in §7.3.6 is the proof that two domains are enough: every requirement in the REQ-PWR table is met by a state of those two domains, and no requirement needs a third.

Domains are hierarchical and nestable, but the TinyEdge-NPU does not nest them: PD_AON is created with -include_scope (it contains the top level and everything not assigned elsewhere), and PD_NPU is created with an explicit element list (the MAC array, the datapath, and the accumulator). The explicit element list matters. A domain defined by exclusion, "everything that is not in PD_AON", silently absorbs every block added later, including blocks the author never intended to power-gate. An explicit element list for PD_NPU makes the intended membership visible, so a reviewer can see at a glance whether a new block belongs in the switchable domain. But the list alone does not make the tools fail: with PD_AON as the -include_scope catch-all, a block left off the list is silently absorbed into PD_AON, not reported as unassigned. Failing loudly takes one more step, an explicit-assignment check that flags any element sitting in PD_AON by default rather than by an explicit assignment. For an IP that customers will integrate and extend, that check is the right default.

7.2.2 Supply ports, supply nets, and the supply architecture

A supply port is where power enters the design (a chip pin, or a port on the IP boundary). A supply net is a named power rail inside the design, connected to a port or to the output of a power switch. A supply set is a group of related nets, a power net, a ground net, and optionally retention and standby nets, that together define what "powered" means for a domain. The distinction between ports and nets is the distinction between the IP boundary and the internal architecture: the customer supplies power at the ports, and the UPF describes how the design distributes it internally.

The TinyEdge-NPU's supply architecture has three named nets, and the naming is deliberate. VDD_AON is the always-on rail: it comes in from the package, it is never switched, and it powers PD_AON and everything that must survive a power-down (retention latches, isolation cells, SRAM retention rails). VDD_CORE is the switched rail: it is the output of the PMOS header switch, and it powers PD_NPU. VSS is the common ground: it is never switched, because switching ground (NMOS footers) would break the continuous substrate plane and inject noise into the retention latches, the reason Chapter 12 chose PMOS headers. There are also two derived rails that appear in the implementation but are not top-level supply nets: VDD_RET, the retention rail for the balloon latches, derived from VDD_AON, and the SRAM retention rail, derived the same way and clamped to the 0.65 V data-retention voltage (DRV) by internal diode regulators. The UPF names the rails the tools need to connect; the derived rails are an implementation detail of the retention cells and the SRAM macros, and they appear in the UPF only as the retention power nets of the retention and isolation strategies.

7.2.3 Power switches

A power switch is a transistor (or an array of transistors) that connects a domain's supply net to its source and can be turned off to cut the domain's power. The switch is the mechanism of power gating, and its design is a trade-off between three quantities: on-resistance (which sets the IR drop across the switch when the domain is on), turn-on time (which sets the wake-up latency), and in-rush current (which sets how violently the rail comes up). The TinyEdge-NPU uses distributed PMOS header switches with an aggregate on-resistance under 0.4 Ω, giving less than 6 mV of drop at the 18 mA peak current (Chapter 12). The switches are turned on through a 16-stage daisy chain so that the rail ramps in stages instead of all at once, capping the in-rush current at 8.5 mA; turning the whole array on simultaneously would draw over 120 mA and collapse VDD_AON hard enough to reset the always-on registers. That is the exact failure the daisy chain exists to prevent.

In UPF, a switch is declared with create_power_switch, which names the domain, the input and output supply ports, and the control signal and its sense. The control signal is the important part for verification: it is a real signal in the design (here sleep_b, driven by the power-management unit in PD_AON), and the UPF ties the switch's behaviour to it. sleep_b is asserted high to request sleep. Despite the _b suffix, the sense is defined by the UPF, not the name: the header conducts when sleep_b is low and turns off when it is high. That tie is what makes power-aware simulation possible: when the simulation drives sleep_b high, the simulator knows the switch is off, VDD_CORE is unpowered, and every cell in PD_NPU is in the off state. Without the tie, the simulator would have to guess, and it would guess wrong.

7.2.4 Isolation cells

When a domain is powered down, its outputs do not go to a defined logic value. They float, or worse, they drift to an intermediate voltage as the domain's supply collapses. A floating output driving an input in a powered domain causes shoot-through current in the receiving gate (both its PMOS and NMOS devices partially on) and can flip the receiving logic. An isolation cell sits on every signal crossing from a switchable domain into an always-on domain and clamps it to a known safe value while the source domain is off. The TinyEdge-NPU uses AND-type isolation cells clamped to ground (logic 0), powered from VDD_AON so they keep working while PD_NPU is off.

Three properties of the isolation strategy deserve attention, because all three are common sources of bugs (§7.4.4). First, isolation applies to outputs of the powered-down domain: the UPF says -applies_to outputs, and the synthesis tool inserts cells on exactly those crossings. An input to the powered-down domain does not need isolation in the same way. It is driven by the always-on side, which stays powered, but it does need to be handled: the receiving flop in the powered-down domain will see a toggling input while its supply is off, which is harmless to the flop (it has no power) but must not be allowed to back-power the domain through the input pin's protection diodes. Second, the isolation cell itself must be powered by the always-on rail. An isolation cell powered by the switched rail is off exactly when it is needed, which is the single most common UPF bug in practice and the first thing a static low-power check looks for. Third, the clamp value is a design decision, not a default: clamping to 0 is correct here because the always-on logic treats a 0 on those signals as "the NPU is idle". A 1 would look like a spurious interrupt or a false wake-up. The clamp value must match what the receiving logic expects, and that expectation must be written down, because the synthesis tool will happily clamp to the wrong value if it is told to.

7.2.5 Retention registers

Power gating the logic is only useful if the state the logic holds can be recovered cheaply. Some state can be recomputed or reloaded: the SRAM contents can be reloaded from flash, at the cost of a DMA transfer (see the OFF state in §7.3.6). Some state cannot: the layer configuration, the base memory addresses, the INT8 scale factors, and the bias offsets, 284 bits in total, are written by the host software through the control registers, and reloading them means re-running the host's configuration sequence. Those 284 bits use retention flip-flops: ordinary flip-flops with an additional "balloon" latch powered by the always-on rail. Before the domain powers down, the power-management unit asserts a SAVE signal (one cycle) that copies the flip-flop state into the balloon latch. While the domain is off, the balloon latch holds the state on VDD_AON. On wake-up, a RESTORE signal (one cycle) copies it back. The cost is the balloon latch itself, a second latch per retained bit, plus the always-on supply routing, and the benefit is that the NPU wakes up configured, with no host intervention.

The retention strategy is declared with set_retention (which registers, and which power net keeps them alive) and set_retention_control (which signals save and restore, and their sense). The save/restore sequencing is part of the power-state machine: SAVE must complete before the switch turns off, and RESTORE must complete after the switch turns on and before the isolation is released. Getting that order wrong is a silent bug. The registers restore correctly in most simulations, because the simulator's default power model often restores state for free, and it is caught by the power-aware formal checks in §7.4.2, not by functional simulation.

7.2.6 Level shifters

A level shifter translates a signal between two voltage domains: it takes a signal that swings between one supply's rails and produces a signal that swings between another's. Level shifters are needed wherever two domains run at different voltages, and, importantly, only there. The TinyEdge-NPU's two logic domains both run at the same nominal 0.90 V, so the PD_AON/PD_NPU boundary needs isolation but not level shifting: the signals on both sides swing between the same rails, and an isolation cell is sufficient. Level shifters appear in exactly two places in this design. The first is the SRAM retention boundary: in the retention state the bitcell array sits at the 0.65 V data-retention voltage while the core logic runs at 0.90 V, so the read data coming out of the array must be shifted up to the core rail on wake-up (Appendix B, ADR-004). The second is the IO boundary, where the 1.8 V or 3.3 V pad ring meets the 0.90 V core (Chapter 12). The common mistake is to insert level shifters at every domain crossing out of habit, which adds delay and area on paths that do not need them, or to omit them at the retention boundary, where the voltage difference is real but easy to miss because both sides are "the same domain" in the block diagram. The UPF declares level shifters with set_level_shifter, and the static low-power check verifies that every crossing between different supply voltages has one and that no crossing between equal voltages has one it does not need.

7.2.7 Power-state tables

A power-state table lists the legal power states of the design and, for each state, the state of every power domain and every supply net. It is the contract between the hardware and the firmware: the firmware may only request transitions the table allows, and the hardware must behave as the table says in every state the table lists. The table is also the input to power estimation: the power numbers for each state (active, nominal, retention, off) are estimated per state, and the system-level average power is the time-weighted sum over the states the product actually visits, the same calculation Chapter 4 uses for the race-to-sleep average. A state that is missing from the table is a state the firmware can request and the hardware has no defined behaviour for. A transition that is missing is a transition the firmware can attempt and the hardware will handle by accident. The TinyEdge-NPU's table has four states and is given in full in §7.3.6.

7.2.8 The commands, annotated

The seven commands below are the whole working vocabulary. Everything else in UPF 2.1 is refinement: more options on these commands, or commands that describe the same ideas for multi-voltage designs, for biasing, or for test modes. The annotated listing is a minimal two-domain example, not the TinyEdge-NPU's own UPF, which is given in full in §7.3.3, so that each command can be read on its own:

## Minimal two-domain power intent (UPF 2.1) — teaching example
create_power_domain PD_AON -include_scope
  ## PD_AON: always on. -include_scope makes it contain the top level
  ## and everything not explicitly assigned to another domain.

create_power_domain PD_NPU -elements {u_core}
  ## PD_NPU: switchable. The element list is explicit: a block added
  ## later is NOT silently absorbed into this domain.

create_supply_port VDD -direction in
create_supply_port VSS -direction in
  ## Supply ports: where power enters the IP boundary.

create_supply_net VDD_AON -domain PD_AON
create_supply_net VDD_CORE -domain PD_NPU
create_supply_net VSS -domain PD_AON
create_supply_net VSS -domain PD_NPU -reuse
  ## Supply nets: named rails inside the design. VSS is one net,
  ## shared by both domains (-reuse), because ground is never switched.

set_domain_supply_net PD_AON  -primary_power_net VDD_AON  -primary_ground_net VSS
set_domain_supply_net PD_NPU -primary_power_net VDD_CORE -primary_ground_net VSS
  ## Binds each domain to its primary power and ground nets.

create_power_switch pwr_sw -domain PD_NPU \
  -input_supply_port {in VDD_AON} -output_supply_port {out VDD_CORE} \
  -control_port {sleep_b sleep_b_ctrl} -on_state {on !sleep_b}
  ## The switch: VDD_CORE is VDD_AON passed through a header that
  ## conducts when sleep_b is low. The control signal is a real net.

set_isolation iso_out -domain PD_NPU -clamp_value 0 -applies_to outputs \
  -isolation_power_net VDD_AON -isolation_ground_net VSS
set_isolation_control iso_out -domain PD_NPU \
  -isolation_signal u_pmu/iso_en -isolation_sense high
  ## Isolation: outputs of PD_NPU are clamped to 0 while it is off.
  ## The cells run on VDD_AON, and iso_en is driven by the PMU.

set_retention ret_cfg -domain PD_NPU \
  -retention_power_net VDD_AON -retention_ground_net VSS
set_retention_control ret_cfg -domain PD_NPU \
  -save_signal {u_pmu/ret_save high} -restore_signal {u_pmu/ret_restore high}
  ## Retention: the registers in ret_cfg keep their state on VDD_AON;
  ## ret_save / ret_restore are the PMU's one-cycle strobes.

set_level_shifter ls_ret -domain PD_NPU -rule both \
  -input_supply_set {ret_ss} -output_supply_set {core_ss}
  ## Level shifter: needed only where voltages differ (here, the
  ## retention rail versus the core rail). Not needed between two
  ## domains at the same voltage.

add_power_state PD_NPU -state {ON  -supply_expr {power == FULL}} \
                         -state {OFF -supply_expr {power == OFF}}
add_power_state PD_AON -state {ON  -supply_expr {power == FULL}}
  ## Power states: the legal states, as supply expressions the
  ## tools can evaluate. The full table for this design is §7.3.6.

Two properties of this listing are worth noticing. First, every command names a real net or a real block: there are no abstract names that the implementation must later map to something. The UPF is written against the RTL hierarchy (u_core, u_pmu), and if the hierarchy changes, the UPF must change with it. That is why the UPF is checked in alongside the RTL and reviewed in the same review. Second, the listing is short: the entire power intent of a two-domain design fits on one screen. That is a feature, not a limitation. A power intent that needs pages of UPF to describe is usually a power architecture that needs simplifying, and the time to discover that is now, when the intent is a file, not later, when it is silicon.

7.3 The TinyEdge-NPU Power Intent

The fundamentals of §7.2 are generic. This section applies them to the TinyEdge-NPU: the two domains and what lives in each, the supply architecture, the annotated UPF that Chapter 12 implements, the isolation and retention strategies, and the power-state table. Everything in this section is consistent with the implementation in Chapter 12 and with the retention decision recorded in Appendix B (ADR-004); where the numbers come from a specific configuration, the configuration is named, because the SRAM is parameterized (§3.9) and the power intent must be true for all three configurations, not just the reference one.

7.3.1 The two domains and what lives in each

PD_AON (always-on)PD_NPU (switchable)
SupplyVDD_AON (0.90 V nominal, never switched)VDD_CORE (0.90 V nominal, via PMOS header switch)
ContentsPower-management unit (PMU), wake logic, control registers, isolation controller, retention controller8×8 INT8 MAC array, datapath (quantization and normalization), accumulators, configuration registers (with retention latches), SRAM banks
State in sleepFully powered; the PMU keeps running on a 32.768 kHz clockPower-gated: logic off; 284 configuration bits retained; SRAM arrays in retention
Leakage in sleep3.1 µW (AON logic) + 1.4 µW (retention latches), S configuration0.8 µW (gated logic, reverse-biased headers) + SRAM retention, S configuration
TestOwn scan chains (Chapter 6)Own scan chains, powered on before shifting (Chapter 6)

The split follows one rule: a block lives in PD_AON if and only if the chip needs it while PD_NPU is off. The wake logic must be there, because something has to detect the wake event while the compute domain is dark. The control registers must be there, because the host writes configuration while the NPU is asleep and expects it to be there when the NPU wakes. The PMU must be there, because it owns the sequencing, the switch, the isolation enable, the save/restore strobes, and sequencing cannot be owned by a block that is itself being sequenced. Everything else is in PD_NPU, including the SRAM banks: the banks are switchable logic with retention, not always-on logic, and the retention is a property of the banks (dual-rail arrays, §7.3.5), not a reason to put them in the always-on domain. Putting the SRAMs in PD_AON would have kept them powered unconditionally, which would have made the sleep budget unreachable. The banks are the largest leakage contributor in the design, and they are the reason the switchable domain exists.

One boundary case deserves a sentence, because it is the kind of thing that is decided wrong in review if it is not decided explicitly. The DMA engine and the AXI4 master interface live in PD_NPU: they move data for the compute array, and they are idle while it sleeps. The AXI-Lite slave control interface lives in PD_AON: it is the host's only way to talk to the NPU while it sleeps, and it is the design's single clock-domain crossing (Chapter 5). That split means a DMA transfer in flight when the sleep request arrives must be drained before the domain powers down. That is a power-state transition rule, and it is written in the power-state table (§7.3.6), not left to the firmware to remember.

7.3.2 Supply architecture

flowchart TD VDD_IN[VDD package pin
0.90 V nominal] --> VDD_AON[VDD_AON rail
always on] VDD_AON --> PMU[Power-management unit
PD_AON] VDD_AON --> ISO[Isolation cells
clamp to 0] VDD_AON --> RET[Retention latches
284 bits, VDD_RET] VDD_AON --> HDR[PMOS header switch
pwr_switch_core] VDD_AON --> SRAM_RET[SRAM retention rail
DRV 0.65 V] HDR -->|sleep_b low| VDD_CORE[VDD_CORE rail
switched] VDD_CORE --> MAC[8x8 MAC array] VDD_CORE --> DP["Datapath & accumulators"] VDD_CORE --> CFG[Config registers
main flops] VDD_CORE --> SRAM_PER[SRAM periphery] SRAM_RET --> SRAM_ARR["SRAM bitcell arrays
weights & activations"] PMU -->|sleep_b| HDR PMU -->|iso_en| ISO PMU -->|ret_save / ret_restore| RET VSS[VSS common ground
never switched] --> MAC VSS --> PMU VSS --> SRAM_ARR

The supply architecture has one input rail and one decision: everything that must survive a power-down hangs off VDD_AON, and everything else hangs off VDD_CORE behind the header switch. The header is a PMOS device (Chapter 12), so the switched rail is pulled up to VDD_AON through the switch when it conducts; the on-resistance is under 0.4 Ω, which keeps the IR drop under 6 mV at the 18 mA peak current, small enough that the timing sign-off at the SS/0.81 V corner (Chapter 11) does not need a separate switch-drop derating. Ground is common and never switched: a single continuous VSS plane keeps the substrate quiet and the retention latches free of back-bias shifts, which is the reason the design uses PMOS headers rather than NMOS footers.

The two derived rails are worth naming precisely, because they are where the retention story lives. VDD_RET is the retention rail for the 284 balloon latches, derived from VDD_AON inside the retention cells; it is not a package pin and not a separate supply net in the UPF. It appears only as the retention power net of the retention strategy. The SRAM retention rail is the same idea at a larger scale: each bank's bitcell array is tied to an internal rail clamped to the 0.65 V data-retention voltage by diode regulators, while the bank's periphery runs on switchable VDD_CORE and is powered down in sleep, a split that cuts SRAM leakage by 78% while preserving every weight (Chapter 12).

7.3.3 The annotated UPF

Below is the TinyEdge-NPU's power intent, adapted from the implementation UPF in Chapter 12. It is the same file the synthesis and place-and-route flows consume; the annotations are the only addition, and they explain why each line is there rather than what it does. The "what" is the command, and the "why" is the review record.

## TinyEdge-NPU Core Power Intent (UPF 2.1)
create_power_domain PD_AON -include_scope
create_power_domain PD_NPU -elements {u_mac_array u_datapath u_acc u_weight_sram u_act_sram u_dma}
  ## Two domains, no nesting. PD_AON contains the top level and
  ## everything unassigned; PD_NPU is an explicit element list that
  ## must name every switchable block — the MAC array, datapath and
  ## accumulators, both SRAM buffers, and the DMA engine (§7.3.1).
  ## A block left off this list is silently absorbed into PD_AON,
  ## not reported unassigned, so the list is checked by an
  ## explicit-assignment audit, not by the tools alone.

# Define Supply Ports and Nets
create_supply_port VDD -direction in
create_supply_port VSS -direction in

create_supply_net VDD_AON   -domain PD_AON
create_supply_net VSS       -domain PD_AON
create_supply_net VDD_CORE  -domain PD_NPU
create_supply_net VSS       -domain PD_NPU -reuse

set_domain_supply_net PD_AON  -primary_power_net VDD_AON  -primary_ground_net VSS
set_domain_supply_net PD_NPU -primary_power_net VDD_CORE -primary_ground_net VSS
  ## One ground net, shared (-reuse): VSS is never switched.

# Define Power Switch (Header) for PD_NPU
create_power_switch pwr_switch_core \
  -domain PD_NPU \
  -switch_on_condition {switch_on !sleep_b} \
  -input_supply_port {in VDD_AON} \
  -output_supply_port {out VDD_CORE} \
  -control_port {sleep_b sleep_b_ctrl}
  ## PMOS header: VDD_CORE is VDD_AON switched by sleep_b, which is
  ## driven by the PMU in PD_AON. The switch-on condition is a real
  ## net, so power-aware simulation can model the rail directly.

# Isolation Strategy: Clamp outputs of PD_NPU to 0 when sleeping
set_isolation iso_core_to_aon \
  -domain PD_NPU \
  -isolation_power_net VDD_AON \
  -isolation_ground_net VSS \
  -clamp_value 0 \
  -applies_to outputs

set_isolation_control iso_core_to_aon \
  -domain PD_NPU \
  -isolation_signal u_pmu/iso_en \
  -isolation_sense high \
  -location parent
  ## Clamp to 0: the AON logic reads 0 on these signals as "NPU idle".
  ## The cells run on VDD_AON (an isolation cell on VDD_CORE would be
  ## off exactly when it is needed). iso_en is asserted by the PMU
  ## before the switch turns off, and released after it turns on.

# Retention Strategy: Save config registers across power cycles
set_retention ret_core_cfg \
  -domain PD_NPU \
  -retention_power_net VDD_AON \
  -retention_ground_net VSS

set_retention_control ret_core_cfg \
  -domain PD_NPU \
  -save_signal    {u_pmu/ret_save    high} \
  -restore_signal {u_pmu/ret_restore high}
  ## 284 bits: layer configuration, base addresses, INT8 scale factors,
  ## bias offsets. SAVE copies them into the balloon latches (1 cycle)
  ## before power-down; RESTORE copies them back (1 cycle) after
  ## power-up. Both strobes come from the PMU, never from software.

Notice what is not in this listing. There is no set_level_shifter between PD_AON and PD_NPU, because both domains run at the same nominal 0.90 V (§7.2.6): the level shifters in this design sit at the SRAM retention boundary and at the IO boundary, and they are declared in the implementation UPF that Chapter 12 carries, not here. There is no separate power domain for the SRAMs, because the banks are switchable logic with retention, not always-on logic (§7.3.1). And there is no power-state table in the listing itself: the states are declared with add_power_state in the same file, and the table in §7.3.6 is the human-readable form of those declarations. The listing is short enough to review in a meeting, and that is a deliberate property: if the power intent cannot be reviewed in a meeting, it will not be reviewed at all.

7.3.4 Isolation at the boundary

The isolation boundary is the set of signals that cross from PD_NPU into PD_AON. On the TinyEdge-NPU there are three groups: the status and interrupt outputs (inference-complete, error flags, status bits the host polls), which clamp to 0, the value the host-side logic reads as "no interrupt pending," since a spurious interrupt would wake the host for nothing; the DMA handshake signals, clamped so that no transfer is requested while the domain is down; and the debug and trace outputs, clamped for the same reason and because a floating debug pin is a radiated-emissions problem on the board. The UPF declares all of them with one strategy (iso_core_to_aon, -applies_to outputs), and the synthesis tool inserts a cell on every crossing. The designer does not enumerate the signals by hand, and the static low-power check (§7.4.2) verifies that the tool's enumeration is complete.

The sequencing around isolation is as important as the cells. The order on power-down is: assert iso_en first, then turn the switch off. The order on power-up is the reverse: turn the switch on, restore the retained state, and only then release iso_en. Releasing isolation before the domain's outputs are valid lets garbage propagate into the always-on logic for a few cycles, usually the configuration registers' reset values, which the host misreads as a completed inference. The PMU owns this order, in hardware, not in firmware: the isolation enable is a PMU output, and the power-state machine (§7.3.6) makes the order structural. Chapter 6 tests it directly: the DFT plan powers the domain down, drives the isolation enable, and checks that every output is clamped to its safe value. A test that exists because the failure mode is a system hang, not a test failure.

7.3.5 Retention strategy per configuration

The retention strategy is the same in form for all three SRAM configurations and different in scale. In the RETENTION state, the logic in PD_NPU is power-gated, the 284 configuration bits are held in balloon latches on VDD_AON, and every SRAM bank stays in light sleep: periphery off, bitcell array clamped to the 0.65 V DRV, weights and activations preserved. The OFF state is the other option (§7.3.6): the banks go to deep sleep, powered off, no retention, except for the 8 KB scratchpad, which retains the bias and scale factors so the next inference does not need to reload them (Chapter 5). The choice between the two states is the retention-vs-power-gating decision recorded in Appendix B (ADR-004): retention costs leakage and buys a 64-cycle wake-up with no reload; power-gating the banks saves the leakage and costs a flash reload that runs to milliseconds. The design offers both states, and the product chooses per use case. But the RETENTION state is the default, because a voice interface that takes milliseconds to wake up misses the word it was woken for.

ConfigurationSRAMBanks in retention (RETENTION state)SRAM retention powerMeets REQ-PWR-003 (< 100 µW)?
S (min)48 KB (32W + 16A)All banks: 1 × 32 KB weight, 1 × 16 KB activation64.2 µWYes, total standby 69.5 µW (Chapter 12)
M (mid)96 KB (64W + 32A)All banks: 2 × 32 KB weight, 2 × 16 KB activation≈ 2× S (estimate, scales with retained array)No, exceeds 100 µW in full retention (see below)
L (reference)200 KB (128W + 64A + 8B)All banks: 4 × 32 KB weight, 4 × 16 KB activation, + 8 KB scratchpad≈ 4× S (estimate, scales with retained array)No, exceeds 100 µW in full retention (see below)

The table contains an honest limit, and it is worth stating plainly rather than smoothing over. The S configuration's sleep budget is the one the book proves: 69.5 µW total standby (0.8 µW gated logic, 64.2 µW SRAM retention, 3.1 µW AON logic, 1.4 µW retention latches, Chapter 12). Retention leakage scales, to first order, with the number of retained bitcells at a fixed DRV, so the M configuration retains at roughly twice the S figure and the L configuration at roughly four times, on the order of 130 µW and 260 µW respectively, both outside the <100 µW budget of REQ-PWR-003. The retention power numbers for M and L in the table are therefore labelled as estimates: the exact figures need the memory compiler's retention model for the larger banks, and the book does not have them. What the scaling law does establish is the consequence: the <100 µW retentive-sleep budget is a property of the S configuration, and it is the binding constraint on how much SRAM a battery-powered variant can keep in retention. A product shipping the M or L configuration has three honest options: budget more sleep power (and say so in its own requirements), retain selectively (activation banks and scratchpad in retention, weight banks powered off, with the weight reload budgeted as a DMA transfer on wake-up), or use the OFF state and accept the reload. What it cannot do is claim the S configuration's 69.5 µW for a 200 KB array. The 80 µW retention figure used in Chapter 4's average-power worked example is a planning assumption for the reference hardware, not a measured budget for the L configuration's full retention. The measured budget the book carries is the S configuration's 69.5 µW, and the two should not be quoted interchangeably.

One more detail of the retention strategy is easy to miss and matters for verification: the SRAM wake-to-read latency. The memories must support a low-voltage retention mode with a wake-to-read latency of ≤ 16 clock cycles (Appendix A), and that 16-cycle figure is a line item inside the 64-cycle wake-up budget in §7.5. A bank that takes longer to come out of retention than the budget allows is not a retention failure. The data is intact, but it is a wake-up failure, and it is caught by the same power-aware simulation that checks the rail ramp.

7.3.6 The power-state table

stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> ACTIVE : power-on reset ACTIVE --> NOMINAL : inference done,\nidle > 1 frame NOMINAL --> ACTIVE : wake event\nor new frame ACTIVE --> RETENTION : sleep request,\nDMA drained NOMINAL --> RETENTION : sleep request RETENTION --> ACTIVE : wake event\n≤ 64 cycles RETENTION --> OFF : deeper sleep\nrequested OFF --> ACTIVE : wake event\n+ flash reload ACTIVE --> OFF : shutdown\nrequested
StatePD_AONPD_NPUClockSuppliesPower (L config)Exit
ACTIVE (burst)OnOn100 MHzVDD_AON + VDD_CORE on3.9 mW peakInference done → NOMINAL or RETENTION
NOMINALOnOn20 MHzVDD_AON + VDD_CORE on< 5.0 mW (REQ-PWR-001)New frame → ACTIVE; sleep request → RETENTION
RETENTIONOnOff (logic gated; 284 bits retained; SRAMs in light sleep at DRV 0.65 V)Off for PD_NPU; AON on 32.768 kHzVDD_AON on; VDD_CORE off< 100 µW (S config: 69.5 µW)Wake event → ACTIVE in ≤ 64 cycles
OFFOnOff (logic gated; SRAMs in deep sleep except 8 KB scratchpad)Off for PD_NPU; AON on 32.768 kHzVDD_AON on; VDD_CORE off< 5 µW (REQ-PWR-004)Wake event → ACTIVE + flash reload (ms)

Four states, and the table is the whole contract. Three rules govern the transitions, and all three are enforced by the PMU in hardware, not by firmware convention. First, the ACTIVE → RETENTION transition is legal only when the DMA engine is idle: the PMU drains any in-flight transfer before asserting iso_en, because powering down mid-transfer leaves the interconnect with an unanswered request and the host with a hung bus. Second, the RETENTION → ACTIVE transition is the 64-cycle wake-up of §7.5: the PMU sequences the switch, the restore, and the isolation release in a fixed order, and the order is not configurable. Third, there is no direct transition from OFF to RETENTION: a domain that has lost its SRAM contents cannot regain them without a reload, so OFF always exits through a reload into ACTIVE. The firmware may request any state; the PMU decides whether the request is legal now, and if it is not, the request waits. It is never executed partially.
