That is what "the power-state table is the contract" means in practice: the table is implemented as a state machine, and the state machine is the only thing that can change the power state.

The two running states deserve a clarifying sentence, because the names invite confusion. NOMINAL is the 20 MHz state: the NPU is on, clocked slowly, doing background work or waiting between frames at the nominal voltage and the nominal power. ACTIVE is the 100 MHz burst state: the NPU races through an inference at full speed and then drops back to NOMINAL or RETENTION. The race-to-sleep pattern of Chapter 4 is the alternation between these two states and RETENTION: burst at 100 MHz for 0.72 ms (DS-CNN-S) or 4.2 ms (DS-CNN-M), then sleep. The average power the product achieves is set by the fraction of time in each state, which is why the power-state table and the duty-cycle calculation belong to the same discussion. The table defines the states, and Chapter 4's arithmetic weights them.

7.4 Low-Power Verification

Writing the UPF is half the work. The other half is proving that the RTL, the netlist, and the firmware all agree with it, and that the agreement holds in every power state, not just the one the functional testbench happens to exercise. Low-power verification has four layers, and they catch different bugs: power-aware simulation catches sequencing and modelling errors, power-aware formal proves the properties that simulation can only sample, equivalence checking proves the implementation matches the intent across power states, and static low-power checks catch the structural errors that no dynamic test will ever reach. A design that runs only one of the four has verified one quarter of its power architecture.

7.4.1 UPF-aware simulation

A power-aware simulation is a functional simulation with the UPF loaded: the simulator models the power domains, the switch, the isolation cells, and the retention registers, so that driving sleep_b high actually powers PD_NPU down in the simulation. Without the UPF, the simulator treats the whole design as always-on, and a test that powers the domain down and back up will pass trivially. The registers never lose their state, the outputs never float, and the design under test is not the design that will be built. With the UPF, the same test exercises the real behaviour: the outputs clamp, the non-retained registers go to X, and the retained registers survive only if the save/restore sequence ran.

Three checks carry most of the value. The first is the isolation check: in the RETENTION state, every signal crossing from PD_NPU into PD_AON must read its clamp value (0), and every input to PD_AON must be at a defined logic level, never X, never an intermediate value. The simulator's X-propagation is the instrument here: if an isolation cell is missing, the X from the powered-down driver propagates into the always-on logic, and the check fails at the first signal it touches. The second is the retention check: write a known pattern into the 284 configuration bits, power the domain down and back up, and read the pattern back. The check must be written to distinguish the two failure modes: a pattern that reads back as zero means the save never happened (or the restore never happened); a pattern that reads back as X means the retention power net was not connected, so the balloon latch itself lost power. The third is the power-sequence check: the testbench drives the sleep and wake requests through the same control interface the firmware uses (Chapter 5), and asserts the ordering: iso_en before switch-off, switch-on before RESTORE, RESTORE before isolation release, on every transition. Chapter 6's DFT tests cover the same ordering from the test side; the functional testbench covers it from the firmware side, and both must pass.

X-propagation deserves a paragraph of its own, because it is the mechanism that makes power-aware simulation honest, and the mechanism most often defeated by accident. A simulator's default is to treat unpowered logic optimistically: a flop with no power still holds its old value, and a gate with no power still computes. That default makes every power test pass and every power bug invisible. Power-aware simulation inverts the default: unpowered logic produces X, and X propagates through every gate it touches, corrupting every downstream result until an isolation cell stops it. The testbench must therefore be written to expect X in the right places (inside the powered-down domain) and to fail on X in the wrong places (anywhere in PD_AON while the domain is down). A testbench that masks X globally, a common shortcut, usually added to quiet a noisy regression, has silently disabled the entire power verification. The rule is simple: X is a signal, not noise, and the only X the testbench may tolerate is the X the UPF says should be there.

7.4.2 Power-aware formal verification

Simulation samples the power-state machine: it drives a finite set of sleep/wake sequences and checks the results. Formal verification proves properties of the machine for all sequences, which matters for power because the bug classes are sequencing bugs. They appear on the one transition the testbench never drove, usually the one where a wake event arrives while the domain is halfway through powering down. Three properties carry the argument for this design, and they are written as SystemVerilog assertions over the PMU's control signals (the same style as the properties in Chapter 8, §8.6):

// Isolation is asserted before the switch turns off, and stays
// asserted until the switch is back on and the state is restored.
p_iso_before_powerdown: assert property (
  @(posedge clk_aon) (sleep_b [*1:$] ##1 !switch_on)
    |-> $past(iso_en, 1));

// Retention save completes before power-down, and restore completes
// before isolation is released.
p_save_before_off: assert property (
  @(posedge clk_aon) $rose(switch_off) |-> $past(ret_save_done, 1));
// Restore is a 1-cycle strobe (cycle 35) and isolation releases at
// cycle 53, so $past(ret_restore_done, 1) would look at the wrong
// cycle: the check needs a sticky flag, set by the strobe and cleared
// at the next power-down.
logic ret_restore_latched;
always @(posedge clk_aon or negedge rst_ni) begin
  if (!rst_ni)               ret_restore_latched <= 1'b0;
  else if (ret_restore_done) ret_restore_latched <= 1'b1;
  else if (switch_off)       ret_restore_latched <= 1'b0;
end
p_restore_before_iso_release: assert property (
  @(posedge clk_aon) $fell(iso_en) |-> ret_restore_latched);

// The retained configuration is unchanged across a power cycle.
p_retention_holds: assert property (
  @(posedge clk_aon)
  (ret_save_done && cfg == cfg_saved) [*1:$] ##1 switch_off
  ##1 switch_on ##1 ret_restore_done |-> (cfg == cfg_saved));

The first two properties are sequencing properties: they constrain the order of events, and they are provable because the PMU implements the order as a state machine. The proof is a reachability argument over a handful of states, not a search over the datapath. The third is a data property over 284 bits, and it is provable for the same reason the retention mechanism is simple: the balloon latch is a separate storage element with its own supply, and the property reduces to "the latch's supply never goes off and the save/restore strobes fire in order." What formal does not prove is the analogue behaviour: that the rail actually reaches 0.81 V in the time the sequence allows, or that the DRV clamp actually holds the bitcells. Those are simulation and silicon measurements (§7.5, Chapter 13). Formal proves the logic of the sequence; the physics of the sequence is proven elsewhere, and the chapter does not pretend otherwise.

Two more formal applications belong here, because they are cheap on this design and commonly skipped. The first is a power-state reachability check: every state in the power-state table (§7.3.6) must be reachable, and no state outside the table must be reachable. An unreachable state is usually a dead transition in the PMU, harmless, but a sign that the table and the implementation disagree. A reachable state outside the table is a bug: the hardware can get somewhere the firmware believes is impossible, and the firmware has no defined behaviour for it. The second is an isolation completeness check, run as a static property on the RTL, before synthesis: for every port crossing from PD_NPU to PD_AON, there exists an isolation cell on the path, powered by VDD_AON, with the clamp value the receiving logic expects. An isolation cell missing from the RTL is a design error; one missing from the netlist is a tool error; the two have different owners and different fixes, and this check tells them apart.

7.4.3 Equivalence checking with UPF

Logic equivalence checking (LEC) proves that two representations of the design compute the same function: RTL against the synthesized netlist, and the synthesized netlist against the placed-and-routed netlist. With power intent, the check gains a dimension: the two representations must compute the same function in every power state, including the states where part of the design is off. A netlist that is equivalent to the RTL in the ACTIVE state but not in the RETENTION state is a netlist that loses configuration on wake-up. A conventional equivalence check, run only in the on-state, will pass it.

Power-aware equivalence checking works by loading the UPF into the equivalence tool alongside both representations, so the tool knows which cells are isolation cells, which are retention registers, and which nets are switched. The tool then checks three things the conventional check does not. First, that the isolation cells in the netlist implement the isolation strategy the UPF declares: same clamp value, same control signal, same location relative to the domain boundary. A synthesis tool that "optimizes" an isolation cell away (because its output is constant 0 while the domain is off, and the tool decided the constant could be propagated) has changed the design's behaviour in the off state, and the power-aware check catches it. Second, that the retention registers in the netlist are the registers the UPF declares: same 284 bits, same save/restore control, and that no retention register was replaced by an ordinary flop during optimization. Third, that the power switch itself is present and correctly connected: the switch is not logic, so a logic-only equivalence check cannot see it at all, and a switch connected to the wrong control signal (or to no control signal) passes every functional check while failing in silicon. The equivalence run that covers these three points is a separate run from the functional equivalence run, with its own sign-off line in the delivery package (Chapter 14), and it is run after every synthesis iteration, not once at the end, because a switch or isolation cell lost in an early iteration is far cheaper to restore than one discovered at sign-off.

7.4.4 Common bug classes

Bug classWhat happensSymptomWhat catches it
Missing isolationA signal crosses from PD_NPU to PD_AON with no isolation cellX propagates into the always-on logic in sleep; shoot-through current; occasional system hangStatic low-power check (unisolated crossing); power-aware simulation X-check (§7.4.1)
Isolation cell on the wrong supplyThe isolation cell is powered by VDD_CORE instead of VDD_AONIsolation works in simulation (which models the cell ideally) and fails in silicon (the cell is off when needed)Static low-power check (isolation power net); power-aware simulation with the UPF loaded
Retention restore failureRESTORE fires before the rail is stable, or SAVE never fired before power-downConfiguration reads back as zero or as stale values after wake-up; looks like a software bugPower-aware formal, properties p_save_before_off / p_restore_before_iso_release (§7.4.2); retention check in simulation
Level-shifter omissionA signal crosses from the 0.65 V retention rail to the 0.90 V core rail with no shifterSlow or incorrect read data on wake-up; marginal failures at the SS cornerStatic low-power check (supply-voltage crossing); SS-corner power-aware simulation
Power-switch sequencingThe switch turns on while isolation is still released, or turns off while a DMA transfer is in flightGarbage propagates into PD_AON for a few cycles; or a hung bus (Chapter 5)Power-sequence check in simulation (§7.4.1); formal sequencing properties (§7.4.2)
UPF-vs-RTL mismatchThe UPF names a block, net, or hierarchy that the RTL renamed or restructuredTools silently ignore the stale UPF lines; the implemented intent differs from the specified intentUPF lint at every RTL check-in; equivalence check with UPF loaded (§7.4.3); UPF reviewed with the RTL
Scan crossing a powered-down domainA scan chain runs through PD_NPU while it is offChain does not shift; worse, the scan input back-powers the domain unpredictablyDFT plan (Chapter 6): chains partitioned by domain, domain powered on before shifting
Clock-domain crossing on a power-control signalsleep_b or iso_en crosses from the host clock to the NPU clock without synchronizationMetastability on the switch control; the domain powers down mid-cycle or not at allCDC verification (Chapter 8, §8.3, "Clock-Domain Crossing Verification"); the control signals are in PD_AON on the AON clock by construction

Read the table as a whole and a pattern emerges: every bug class is caught by more than one layer, and no bug class is caught by simulation alone. The missing-isolation bug is the clearest case. Simulation catches it only if the testbench drives the power-down sequence and checks for X, which means the bug is caught only if someone thought to write that test. The static check catches it without any test at all, because it reads the structure. That is the argument for running all four layers: simulation catches what the tests cover, and the static and formal layers catch what the tests do not. The cost of running all four is real. The power-aware simulation runs slower than the functional simulation, and the formal properties need to be written, but the cost of the alternative is measured in the next section's currency: a wake-up that does not work, discovered on the bench.

7.4.5 Mixed-Signal Verification with a PMU Real-Number Model

Section 7.4.2 drew the boundary: formal verification proves the logic of the power sequence, that isolation releases only after restore, that save precedes power-down, but it does not prove the physics. The property p_restore_before_iso_release is a statement about two control signals; it says nothing about whether the rail actually reached 0.81 V in the 28 cycles the wake-up budget allows, or whether the header switch delivered the current without drooping below the brown-out threshold. The digital RTL has no voltage in it. This section is about the model this book uses for that voltage: a real-number model (RNM) of the PMU, written in SystemVerilog, running inside the same UVM testbench as the digital verification, and connected to the UPF flow so the sequence is checked end to end, physics included.

What a real-number model is

A real-number model is a behavioral model of an analog block written in a digital language. The PMU RNM represents the quantities the digital verification needs, the core rail voltage, the header current, the power-good and brown-out comparator outputs, as real-valued signals (wreal in SystemVerilog), computed from closed-form expressions, not transistor equations. The rail is an exponential ramp toward the nominal voltage with a time constant τ; the power-good comparator is a threshold with hysteresis; the inrush current is capacitance times the slope of the ramp. No transistors, no device models, no differential equations, just a handful of arithmetic expressions evaluated once per clock cycle, which is why the model runs at digital-simulation speed.

What it is not matters as much as what it is. It is not a circuit model: it cannot tell you whether the header transistor is sized correctly, whether the LDO is stable, or whether the bandgap drifts with temperature. Those are SPICE analyses, and the RNM takes their results as inputs, the time constant, the comparator thresholds, the decoupling capacitance, rather than reproducing them. Nor is it a substitute for the UPF intent: the RNM models the physics of the power delivery, while the UPF states what the power architecture is supposed to be. The two are connected, but neither replaces the other.

The model has four parts. The header ramp models VDD_CORE as it rises from the retention voltage (0.65 V, the DRV clamp) or from 0 V on a cold start. The power-good comparator asserts when the rail crosses 0.81 V on the way up and releases only when it falls below 0.75 V. The 60 mV of hysteresis keeps it from chattering on a slow ramp. The brown-out detector is a second, lower comparator at 0.70 V: it fires only when the rail has genuinely collapsed below the power-good release point, and it forces re-isolation. The inrush monitor computes the header current as I = Cdec × dV/dt, exposed as a real-valued signal the testbench checks against the 8.5 mA cap.

Why the power sequence needs one

There are three ways to verify a power sequence, and the RNM exists because the other two fail on this design in different ways.

The first is the timed-delay model: the testbench models power-good as "asserts N cycles after the switch turns on", a counter and a comparison, which is what most digital testbenches do by default. The problem is that it assumes the answer. A delay model cannot catch a ramp slower than the budget allows, because the delay is the budget: it asserts power-good at cycle 34 because the testbench was told to, not because the rail got there. It cannot catch a non-monotonic ramp (no rail), a comparator threshold error (no comparator), or an LDO droop when the MAC array switches on (no load). Every one of these is a real failure mode of a power switch, and the delay model is blind to all of them. It verifies the sequencer's logic against a fiction: passing tests for a design that fails on the bench.

The second is full analog co-simulation: the PMU and the power delivery modeled in Verilog-AMS or SPICE, co-simulated with the digital RTL. This is the most accurate option, and the right tool for signing off the analog itself. But it is the wrong tool for the digital regression flow this book teaches: an AMS co-simulation runs orders of magnitude slower than a digital simulation, needs analog models and a mixed-signal license, and cannot run as part of the nightly UVM regression that checks every power-state transition. Using it for the wake-up sequence would mean the sequence is checked once, by hand, on one corner. That is how the §7.4.4 sequencing bugs survive: they live on the transition nobody drove.

The RNM is the middle path, and the middle path is the point. It runs at digital-simulation speed inside the same UVM testbench, so the wake-up sequence is checked on every regression run, on every seed, alongside the functional tests, not once, by hand. And because it models the voltage, it can express the fault cases a delay model cannot: a slow ramp (τ larger than characterized), a non-monotonic ramp (a droop injected at a chosen cycle), a threshold error (the comparator trip moved), a droop under load (the ramp flattened when the MAC array switches on). Each is a parameter change or a fault injection in the testbench, not a new simulation setup, so the same testbench that checks the happy path also checks the failure modes, and the failure modes are where the power bugs live.

How the model is built

The model is written in SystemVerilog, using real-valued nets, wreal, for the analog quantities: a wreal carries a real number instead of a four-state logic value, is declared with the nettype keyword, and needs a simulator that supports real nets (VCS, Xcelium, and Questa all do). The digital signals, pwr_en, pwr_good, brown_out, stay ordinary logic, so the model plugs into the digital testbench without adapters: the sequencer drives pwr_en as a bit and reads pwr_good as a bit, exactly as it would read the real PMU.

The ramp is the heart of the model, and it is one line of arithmetic. On the retention wake-up path the rail rises from the DRV clamp (0.65 V) toward the nominal 0.90 V as a first-order exponential, V(t) = VDD − (VDD − V0)·e−t/τ, evaluated once per cycle. The time constant τ = 150 ns is a calibration parameter, and it is worth saying what sets it, because the naive answer is wrong. The naive answer is the header resistance times the decoupling capacitance, but the fully-on header resistance (Ron < 0.4 Ω, which sets the IR drop) times 4 nF gives τ ≈ 1.6 ns, a ramp that would settle in nanoseconds and draw hundreds of milliamps. The real ramp is deliberately slowed: the 16-stage daisy chain turns segments on gradually, so the resistance seen during the ramp is the staged resistance, τ/Cdec ≈ 37.5 Ω, not the fully-on Ron. The time constant is a property of the controlled turn-on, taken from the characterization rather than derived from the header.

With τ = 150 ns the numbers land inside the §7.5 budget with margin. The ramp starts at cycle 7. It crosses the 0.81 V power-good threshold about 15 cycles into the 28-cycle window, cycle 22, and by cycle 34, when the budget requires rail-stable, the model rail is at 0.86 V, 50 mV above the threshold. Peak inrush on the retention ramp is the first-cycle slope times the decoupling capacitance, about 6.4 mA, under the 8.5 mA cap. These are assertions about the model, not the silicon, the distinction the calibration section below is about.

The cold start has a different shape. The 16-stage daisy chain staggers the ramp over 1.2 µs, 16 stages at 75 ns each, and the model represents it as a linear ramp, 7.5 mV per 10 ns clock cycle, the linear average of the staircase. The average slope is 0.75 V/µs, so cold-start inrush is about 3.0 mA, again under the cap. A single exponential cannot fit both the 1.2 µs cold settling and the 8.5 mA cap. An exponential fast enough to settle in 1.2 µs would draw too much current at the start, and the staging is what makes both true. The model says so in its comments.

// pmu_rnm.sv -- Real-number model of the TinyEdge-NPU PMU.
// Behavioral model of the analog power path: header ramp, power-good
// and brown-out comparators, inrush current. It is NOT a circuit model:
// TAU, the thresholds, and C_DEC are calibration parameters, fitted to
// the analog characterization (Ch 12 extraction, Ch 13 silicon data).
// The model answers one question the digital RTL cannot: what is the
// rail voltage, and when does power-good assert?
`timescale 1ns / 1ps

nettype real wreal;  // real-valued net (IEEE 1800). If the simulator
                     // already provides wreal, drop this declaration.

module pmu_rnm #(
  parameter real VDD_NOM   = 0.90,     // nominal core rail (V)
  parameter real V_RET     = 0.65,     // retention (DRV) voltage (V)
  parameter real V_PG_RISE = 0.81,     // power-good rising trip (V)
  parameter real V_PG_FALL = 0.75,     // power-good falling trip (V)
  parameter real V_BO      = 0.70,     // brown-out trip (V)
  parameter real TAU       = 150.0e-9, // retention-ramp time constant (s)
  parameter real C_DEC     = 4.0e-9    // decoupling capacitance (F)
) (
  input  logic clk,        // 100 MHz burst clock (10 ns period)
  input  logic pwr_en,     // header enable, from the PMU sequencer
  input  logic cold_start, // 1 = ramp from 0 V, 0 = ramp from V_RET
  output wreal v_core,     // modeled core rail (V)
  output wreal i_inrush,   // modeled header current (A)
  output logic pwr_good,   // to sequencer, isolation control, assertions
  output logic brown_out   // to sequencer: forces re-isolation
);

  real v_ramp;      // modeled rail voltage
  real v_old;       // rail voltage one cycle ago
  real dv_dt;       // ramp slope (V/s)
  real i_inrush_r;  // modeled header current (A)

  assign v_core   = v_ramp;
  assign i_inrush = i_inrush_r;

  initial begin
    v_ramp    = 0.0;
    pwr_good  = 1'b0;
    brown_out = 1'b1;  // rail at 0 V is genuinely in brown-out
  end

  // Rail voltage. The retention wake-up is a first-order controlled
  // ramp: V(t) = VDD - (VDD - V0) exp(-t/TAU), evaluated once per
  // clock cycle with the exact discrete update. TAU is the *staged*
  // turn-on, not the header R_on: the 16-stage daisy chain turns
  // segments on gradually, so the resistance seen during the ramp is
  // TAU / C_DEC = 37.5 Ohm, not the fully-on R_on < 0.4 Ohm (which
  // sets the IR drop, not the ramp). The cold start is the linear
  // average of the 16-stage staircase: 0.90 V over 1.2 us, 7.5 mV
  // per 10 ns cycle. A single exponential cannot fit both the 1.2 us
  // cold settling and the 8.5 mA inrush cap; the staging is what
  // makes both true.
  // The fall is modeled as an immediate step to V_RET (or 0 V): the
  // model covers the wake-up ramp, not the power-down discharge.
  always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (!pwr_en) begin
      v_ramp    = cold_start ? 0.0 : V_RET;
      dv_dt     = 0.0;
      pwr_good  = 1'b0;
      brown_out = 1'b1;
    end else begin
      v_old = v_ramp;
      if (cold_start) begin
        if (v_ramp < VDD_NOM)
          v_ramp = v_ramp + VDD_NOM * 10.0e-9 / 1.2e-6;
        if (v_ramp > VDD_NOM)
          v_ramp = VDD_NOM;
      end else begin
        v_ramp = VDD_NOM - (VDD_NOM - v_ramp) * $exp(-10.0e-9 / TAU);
      end
      dv_dt      = (v_ramp - v_old) / 10.0e-9;
      i_inrush_r = C_DEC * dv_dt;  // I = C * dV/dt
      // Power-good with hysteresis: asserts at 0.81 V on the rising
      // edge, releases at 0.75 V on the falling edge. A single
      // threshold would chatter on a slow ramp.
      if (v_ramp >= V_PG_RISE)     pwr_good  = 1'b1;
      else if (v_ramp < V_PG_FALL) pwr_good  = 1'b0;
      // Brown-out is a level, not a latch: asserted whenever the rail
      // is below 0.70 V, including early in the ramp. The sequencer
      // masks it until power-good asserts and arms it thereafter.
      brown_out = (v_ramp < V_BO);
    end
  end

endmodule

Three details of the listing deserve emphasis. First, the comparator hysteresis: the 60 mV gap is load-bearing. Without it, a slow ramp hovering at the trip point makes power-good flicker inside one wake-up. Second, the brown-out output is a level, not a latch: it is asserted whenever the rail is below 0.70 V, including early in the ramp, so the sequencer masks it until power-good asserts and arms it thereafter. A brown-out after arming means the rail collapsed after the domain was declared good, and the only safe response is re-isolation. Third, the fall is modeled as an immediate step to the retention voltage (or to 0 V on a cold shutdown): the model covers the wake-up ramp, not the power-down discharge, and the comments say so.

Connecting the RNM to the UPF flow

The model earns its place by being connected to the UPF flow, not by sitting beside it. The connection has one rule: the same sequencer drives both. The PMU sequencer in PD_AON drives pwr_en into the RNM and reads pwr_good back out of it; the same sequencer drives the UPF power states, ACTIVE, NOMINAL, RETENTION, OFF, and the isolation and retention controls. The UPF says what the states are; the RNM says what the rail is doing between them. Driven by the same state machine, the sequence is checked end to end: the UPF transitions and the analog ramp are one verification of one sequence, not two that happen to agree.

Concretely, the wiring is three connections. The sequencer's pwr_en and cold_start go into the RNM; the RNM's pwr_good goes back into the sequencer, which waits on it before issuing the restore strobe. The restore cannot fire before the rail is stable. pwr_good also goes to the isolation control and to the assertions: the isolation-release property (p_restore_before_iso_release, §7.4.2) proves the logic of the ordering, and the RNM proves the timing, that the rail was actually above 0.81 V when the release happened, on this run, with this ramp. And i_inrush goes to the testbench, which checks it against the 8.5 mA cap on every wake-up, in every configuration (S, M, and L).

The same wiring makes the fault cases cheap. A slow ramp is τ doubled. A non-monotonic ramp is a droop injected at a chosen cycle. The testbench forces v_ramp down by 100 mV at cycle 20 and checks that power-good deasserts and the sequencer waits rather than releasing isolation into a collapsing rail. A threshold error is V_PG_RISE moved to 0.85 V, which pushes the crossing past cycle 34 and fails the rail-stable check, the check that exists to catch a comparator whose trip point drifted. A droop under load is the ramp flattened at the resume phase, expressed by raising τ. Each is a parameter override or a force in the testbench, run in the regression. The difference between a check that runs and a check that is planned.

What the RNM lets you check
CheckWhat is verifiedFault it catches
Rail-stable by cycle 34pwr_good asserts by cycle 34 of the wake-up (§7.5 budget); model rail ≥ 0.81 VSlow ramp (τ larger than characterized); header staging wrong
Isolation-release orderingiso_en releases only after pwr_good, on the same runSequencer releasing isolation into an unpowered domain
Restore after supply-goodret_restore fires only after pwr_good; 284 bits read back identicalRestore into a collapsing rail (§7.4.4 retention-restore class, with timing)
Inrush under 8.5 mAi_inrush below the cap on every wake-up, in S, M, and LRamp too fast; daisy-chain staging missing or miscalibrated
Brown-out re-isolationbrown_out after arming forces iso_en back on within one cycleMissing brown-out response; LDO droop under load

The table is the argument for the model in one place: five checks, each naming the fault it catches, and each one the delay model cannot express and the AMS flow cannot afford to run in regression. The first two are the §7.5 budget made checkable. Rail-stable by cycle 34 is a number the model produces, not a number the testbench assumes. The third closes the §7.4.4 retention-restore bug class with a timing check to go with the formal property. The fourth is the only check on the header staging in the digital flow. The fifth is the one the delay model most obviously misses, because a delay model has no brown-out at all.

Calibration and limits

The model is only as good as its parameters, and the parameters come from the analog side. τ, the comparator thresholds and hysteresis, and Cdec are fitted to the analog characterization: the header extraction and daisy-chain timing from Chapter 12, and the silicon power measurements from Chapter 13, the only measurements of the actual ramp. Refit per corner. SS at 0.81 V and FF at 0.99 V do not share a τ, and the thresholds do not move with the corner the way the rail does, and per configuration, because the decoupling capacitance differs. A model calibrated at TT and run at SS asserts the right answer for the wrong reason, and the checks pass on a ramp the silicon never produces.

And the limits are real. The RNM cannot catch transistor-level issues: a header device that is too small, an LDO that oscillates, a bandgap that drifts. Those are SPICE analyses, and the RNM takes their results as parameters rather than reproducing them. It does not model supply noise, package parasitics beyond the lumped Cdec, or temperature dependence except through the calibrated parameters. It does not replace the AMS sign-off of the analog itself, or the silicon measurements of Chapter 13, which are the final authority on whether the ramp meets the budget. What it does is move the physics of the power sequence into the digital regression, where the sequence is checked on every run.
