The claim, stated plainly: the power sequence is a mixed-signal property, and it is verified as one. The UPF states the intent, the formal properties prove the logic, and the real-number model proves the physics, in the same testbench, on the same runs, driven by the same sequencer. A wake-up that passes all three has a rail that reached 0.81 V in time, an isolation release that waited for it, and a switch under its current cap. A wake-up that passes only the first two is logically correct and physically unproven, the state §7.4.2 warned about, and the reason this section exists.

7.5 Worked Example: The Wake-Up Sequence (≤ 64 Cycles)

The wake-up budget is the sharpest test of the whole power architecture: from the wake event to the first MAC in 64 cycles, 0.64 µs at 100 MHz, with the configuration intact and the weights in place. The budget is not an aspiration; it is the design target behind REQ-PWR-005 (whose requirement is the looser < 100 µs) and the pass criterion of the sleep-and-wake-up check in Appendix D. This section traces the sequence cycle by cycle, names the budget each phase consumes, and states the check that proves each phase.

sequenceDiagram participant H as Host / audio front end participant W as Wake logic (PD_AON) participant P as PMU (PD_AON) participant S as Header switch participant R as Retention latches participant M as SRAM banks participant I as Isolation cells participant N as NPU logic (PD_NPU) H->>W: Wake event (keyword threshold) W->>P: wake_req (cycle 1) P->>S: sleep_b low (cycle 3) S->>N: VDD_CORE ramps (cycles 7-34) P->>R: ret_restore strobe (cycle 35) R->>N: 284 config bits restored P->>M: SRAM wake from retention M->>N: Banks readable (cycle 52) P->>I: iso_en released (cycle 53) P->>N: Clock resumed, FSM to FETCH N->>H: First MAC issues (cycle 64)
PhaseCyclesWhat happensBudget consumedCheck that proves it
Detect1–2Wake logic in PD_AON detects the event (audio threshold crossing or host request) and raises wake_req to the PMU2Functional test: wake event to wake_req in ≤ 2 cycles
Switch-on3–6PMU deasserts sleep_b; the header segments begin conducting in daisy-chain order4Power-aware simulation: sleep_b falls within 4 cycles of wake_req
Rail ramp7–34VDD_CORE ramps to operating voltage; PMU waits for rail-stable (VDD_CORE ≥ 0.81 V, the SS corner)28Power-aware simulation asserts rail-stable by cycle 34
Restore35–36RESTORE strobe (1 cycle) copies the 284 configuration bits from the balloon latches back into the registers, plus one settle cycle2Retention check: configuration reads back identical after wake-up (§7.4.1)
SRAM wake37–52SRAM banks exit retention; periphery powers up, arrays leave the 0.65 V DRV clamp; wake-to-read ≤ 16 cycles (Appendix A)16Power-aware simulation: SRAM macro ready-to-read asserts by cycle 52
Isolation release53–56PMU releases iso_en only after restore is confirmed; outputs of PD_NPU become valid4Formal property p_restore_before_iso_release (§7.4.2)
Resume57–64Clock to PD_NPU resumes at 100 MHz; the control FSM leaves the wake state and issues the first FETCH; the first MAC issues in cycle 648Appendix D check: wake-up recovery ≤ 64 cycles (0.64 µs at 100 MHz)
Total1–64Wake event to first MAC64

Two features of the budget deserve emphasis. The first is that the rail ramp is the long pole: 28 of the 64 cycles, nearly half the budget, belong to the power switch. That is a requirement on the switch design, not a measurement of it: the daisy chain must be staged so that VDD_CORE reaches the SS-corner operating voltage inside that 28-cycle window, and the power-aware simulation asserts rail-stable by cycle 34 on every wake-up. If the switch cannot meet the window, the wake-up budget does not stretch. The switch design changes, or the number of daisy-chain stages changes, until it does. The budget is the constraint; the implementation conforms to it.

The second is what the budget does not contain: a model reload. The 64 cycles are achievable only because the weights are already in the SRAMs (RETENTION state) and the configuration is already in the balloon latches. A wake-up from the OFF state, where the banks are in deep sleep, costs a flash reload that runs to milliseconds. That is why the OFF state is not the default wake-up path, and why Appendix B's ADR-004 rejected full shutdown as the normal sleep state. The 64-cycle figure and the retention strategy are the same decision, seen from two sides: the wake-up budget is what makes retention worth its leakage, and retention is what makes the wake-up budget achievable.

One race deserves a sentence, because it is the case the testbench most often misses. If a wake event arrives while the PMU is halfway through powering down, iso_en asserted, switch still on, or switch off but SAVE not yet complete, the PMU does not reverse direction mid-sequence. It completes the power-down, reaches the RETENTION state, and then runs the wake-up sequence from the top. The cost is a few extra cycles on that one wake-up; the benefit is that the power-state machine never occupies a state outside the table (§7.3.6), and the formal sequencing properties (§7.4.2) hold for all event orderings, not just the ones the testbench drove. A PMU that tries to be clever about the race, aborting the power-down halfway, is a PMU with a state the table does not list, and §7.4.2's reachability check exists to catch exactly that.

7.6 Power Intent Sign-Off Checklist

The checklist below is used at the power-intent review, which happens at the same time as the architecture review, not after RTL freeze, and not at sign-off. Every item must be checked before the design is released for synthesis. An item that cannot be checked is a no-go: the design does not proceed until it is resolved, because every item on this list is cheaper to fix now than in the next chapter's testbench, the synthesis flow, or the silicon.

  • The UPF is checked in with the RTL, reviewed in the same review, and lint-clean at every check-in. A UPF that names a renamed block or a restructured hierarchy is caught by lint on the day the RTL changes, not by a failed equivalence run a month later.
  • Every block is assigned to exactly one power domain, and every domain has a named owner. No unassigned elements; no block in two domains; the element list of PD_NPU is explicit, not by exclusion.
  • Every signal crossing from PD_NPU to PD_AON has an isolation cell on VDD_AON with the correct clamp value (0). The static low-power check is clean; the isolation strategy covers outputs, and the clamp value matches what the receiving logic expects.
  • All 284 retention bits save and restore. The retention check passes in power-aware simulation: a known pattern written before power-down reads back identical after wake-up.
  • The power-state table is implemented as a PMU state machine. All four states (ACTIVE, NOMINAL, RETENTION, OFF) are reachable, no state outside the table is reachable, and the DMA-drain rule on the ACTIVE → RETENTION transition is enforced in hardware.
  • Power-aware simulation passes with X-propagation on. No X anywhere in PD_AON while PD_NPU is down; isolation and retention checks green; the testbench does not mask X globally.
  • The power-aware formal properties are proven: isolation before power-down, save before off, restore before isolation release, retention holds across a power cycle, and power-state reachability (§7.4.2).
  • Power-aware equivalence is clean after every synthesis iteration: isolation cells, retention registers, and the power switch all present and correctly connected (§7.4.3).
  • Sleep power is measured in power simulation, per configuration: S configuration < 100 µW in RETENTION (budget 69.5 µW); OFF state < 5 µW; M and L configurations report their retention power explicitly rather than inheriting the S figure (§7.3.5).
  • Wake-up recovery is ≤ 64 cycles in power-aware simulation: rail-stable by cycle 34, SRAM macro ready-to-read by cycle 52, first MAC by cycle 64 (§7.5).
  • The DFT tests for the switchable domain pass (Chapter 6): scan chains partitioned by domain, the domain powered on before shifting, isolation tested by powering down, retention tested in both modes.
  • The UPF ships in the delivery package (Chapter 14) and reproduces the same intent in a clean-room flow: the customer's synthesis run from the delivered files alone produces the same switches, isolation cells, and retention registers.

The one-line version: power intent is a specification with a budget and a sign-off, the same as any functional feature, and the budget it protects is the product itself: under 5 mW awake, under 100 µW asleep, awake again in 64 cycles. Treat it as one, and the chip will wake up. Treat it as an afterthought, and the first silicon will sleep very well, and never wake up at all.

Key Takeaways

  • Power intent is a first-class design artifact: a machine-readable specification (UPF, IEEE 1801) consumed by synthesis, place-and-route, simulation, formal verification, and equivalence checking, not a slide deck and a shared understanding.
  • The TinyEdge-NPU has two power domains because two are enough: PD_AON (wake logic, control registers, PMU, always on) and PD_NPU (MAC array, datapath, SRAMs, switchable). One domain could not meet the sleep budget; five would buy little and cost a verification burden on every boundary.
  • Isolation, retention, and level shifting are three different mechanisms for three different problems: isolation clamps the outputs of a powered-down domain to a safe value; retention keeps 284 configuration bits alive on the always-on rail; level shifters are needed only where voltages differ: the SRAM retention boundary and the IO boundary, not the PD_AON/PD_NPU boundary at a common 0.90 V.
  • The power-state table (ACTIVE, NOMINAL, RETENTION, OFF) is the contract between hardware and firmware, implemented as a PMU state machine, including the rule that a DMA transfer must drain before the ACTIVE → RETENTION transition, and that there is no direct OFF → RETENTION transition.
  • Retention power scales with the retained array size: the < 100 µW retentive-sleep budget is proven for the S configuration (69.5 µW total standby), and the M and L configurations exceed it in full retention. Their retention power must be reported explicitly, not inherited from the S figure.
  • Low-power verification has four layers, power-aware simulation, power-aware formal, power-aware equivalence, and static low-power checks, and no bug class is caught by simulation alone. X-propagation is the instrument that makes power-aware simulation honest, and a testbench that masks X globally has silently disabled it.
  • The 64-cycle wake-up budget is achievable only because the weights are already in the SRAMs and the configuration is already in the balloon latches: the rail ramp takes 28 of the 64 cycles, and the budget contains no model reload. A wake-up from the OFF state costs a flash reload and runs to milliseconds.
  • Power intent has a specification, a budget, and a sign-off, with a checklist reviewed at architecture time, and the UPF ships in the delivery package, so the customer's flow reproduces the same switches, isolation cells, and retention registers from the delivered files alone.

Chapter 8: Verification Strategy

Verification is where an NPU IP earns the right to be trusted. Simulation alone cannot prove a datapath correct, and a testbench without a plan cannot tell you when you are done. This chapter works through the verification strategy for TinyEdge-NPU step by step: start with a risk-based plan, add a coverage model you can measure, build a bit-accurate golden reference model to check every number against, wrap it all in a reusable UVM testbench, and finish with formal proofs for the control paths simulation can never exhaust. The goal is not just a green regression. It is a sign-off case you can defend.

8.1 Verification Planning

The most common mistake in IP verification is also the most tempting one: start writing testbenches the moment the architecture document lands. On a tight tape-out schedule, it feels productive to have SystemVerilog classes compiling before anyone has written down what "done" means. For an edge AI processor like TinyEdge-NPU, that shortcut backfires. Subtle arithmetic saturation errors, DMA boundary crossings, and deadlocks in the ping-pong activation buffers tend to surface only late in system integration or post-silicon bring-up, when they are expensive to fix. Verification planning is the discipline of building the complete verification envelope first, deciding precisely how every requirement will be stimulated, observed, checked, and measured, before a single line of testbench infrastructure gets written.

flowchart TD PRD[Chapter 3 PRD Requirements] --> FEAT[Verification Features] FEAT --> SVA[SystemVerilog Assertions] FEAT --> COV[Functional Coverpoints] FEAT --> TEST[Directed and Random Tests] SVA --> SIGN[Sign-off Criteria] COV --> SIGN TEST --> SIGN SIGN -.-> PRD

8.1.1 Structure of the Verification Plan (vPlan)

The verification plan (vPlan) is not a static descriptive document; it is an executable, traceable contract between the system architects, digital designers, and verification engineers. A production-grade vPlan for a specialized IP must contain five distinct components for every tracked item:

  1. Feature Definition and Tracking ID: A unique tag (e.g., FEAT_DP_INT8_SAT) mapping directly back to the Product Requirements Document (PRD) or functional specification generated in early design phases. It defines the operational behavior, configuration registers involved, and modes of operation.
  2. Stimulus Strategy: The specific mechanism used to drive the design into the target state. This documents whether the stimulus originates from constrained-random transaction generation (e.g., randomized AXI transactions, random weight sparsity patterns), formal assumptions, or directed power-mode sequencing.
  3. Checks and Oracles (The Scoreboard Architecture): The mechanism that evaluates output correctness. For the TinyEdge-NPU, this distinguishes between end-to-end tensor comparison against a bit-exact Python reference model (NumPy/PyTorch-based golden output) versus transaction-level protocol assertions monitoring bus handshakes.
  4. Coverage Metrics: The quantitative proof of verification. This cross-references specific SystemVerilog functional coverage groups (covergroups), cross-coverage matrices, and assertion coverage points that demonstrate the corner cases were hit.
  5. Sign-off Criteria: The pass/fail criteria required for taped-out IP. For example, hitting 100% of defined bins without negative exclusions or manual waivers.

The Golden Rule of DV Planning: If a feature cannot be tracked by a dedicated functional coverage point or an assertion, it does not exist in the verification plan, and its operational correctness cannot be verified for tape-out sign-off.

8.1.2 Risk-Based Prioritization

Every IP project operates under finite schedule constraints. For a small footprint design like the TinyEdge-NPU, targeting roughly 75k to 100k logic gates and 48 KB of on-chip static RAM (SRAM) in the smallest (S) configuration (§3.9) in a 28nm process, attempting uniform verification coverage across every feature simultaneously leads to inefficient resource allocation. The verification environment instantiates the S configuration because it simulates fastest; the same testbench runs the reference L configuration with the WEIGHT_KB and ACT_KB parameters overridden. Verification resources must be distributed according to risk: the mathematical product of the probability of design failure (\(P_f\)) and the severity of impact (\(I_s\)) if that failure escapes to silicon.

We classify IP risk into three primary tiers:

  • Tier 1: Catastrophic Silicon Defects (Severity: High, Probability: High). Functional errors that lock the core or require a silicon respin. Examples include: accumulator overflow/saturation bugs inside the Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) array that corrupt model inference silently; DMA address wrap-around bugs that overwrite adjacent system memory; and finite state machine (FSM) deadlocks during clock gating wake-up sequences.
  • Tier 2: Protocol and Data Corruption (Severity: Moderate, Probability: Moderate). Corner-case violations that do not brick the hardware but violate system contracts. Examples include: unaligned AXI bus transfers; backpressure handling during high-latency weight buffer refreshes; and ping-pong activation buffer collisions when the execution engine runs faster than the DMA fill operation.
  • Tier 3: Non-Functional and Degraded Modes (Severity: Low, Probability: Low). Bugs that permit correct inference but incur minor performance or power penalties. Examples include: sub-optimal zero-skipping efficiency where a zero-valued activation still consumes dynamic switching power, or interrupt latency running two clock cycles longer than specified.

8.1.3 Traceability Matrix: Mapping Requirements to Verification

Traceability guarantees bidirectional alignment between functional specifications and verification execution. If an architect modifies the bias calculation pipeline in the specifications, the verification lead must instantly identify which coverpoints, assertions, and tests require updates. Table 8.1 illustrates this traceability for core features of the TinyEdge-NPU.

Req. ID Functional Requirement Summary Verification Method Check Mechanism Target Coverage Object
REQ_DP_01 Signed INT8 × INT8 multiplication with 32-bit signed accumulation, with optional INT4 mode packing two weights per byte. Constrained-random vector generation with directed corner cases. Bit-exact golden tensor scoreboard comparing RTL outputs to a C++/Python reference engine. cg_mac_math: Cover cross of operand extrema (-128, +127, 0, -1) and INT4/INT8 modes.
REQ_DP_04 Dynamic activation saturation to user-defined 8-bit clamp window: \([\text{MinVal}, \text{MaxVal}]\) with ReLU integration. Randomized clamp threshold boundaries combined with extreme accumulator outputs. Self-checking scoreboard checking boundary clamp states (\(<\text{Min}\), \(>\text{Max}\), and within bounds). cg_saturation_events: Cross of raw accumulator overflow with clamp thresholds.
REQ_MEM_02 Activation ping-pong buffer: simultaneous DMA write to Buffer B while MAC engine reads from Buffer A without memory contention. Constrained-random test interleaving high-bandwidth DMA writes with varying compute latencies. SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) monitoring Dual-Port SRAM address collision and buffer wrap flags. cg_buffer_pingpong: Cross of buffer states (Buffer A read/write, Buffer B read/write, simultaneous flip request).
REQ_DMA_05 AXI4 DMA master engine must handle arbitrary burst length terminations, wait states, and unaligned byte addresses. Randomized slave responder introducing dynamic RVALID/BVALID stalls, coupled with formal verification of bus master properties. SVA protocol suite (checking AMBA AXI4 specification compliance) and transaction scoreboard. cg_dma_transfers: Coverpoints tracking all AXI4 burst types (FIXED, INCR, WRAP), wait cycles, and alignment offsets.
REQ_PWR_03 Power down sequencing: Core logic clock-gating upon entering IDLE; dynamic power consumption <5 mW; leakage retention <100 μW (S configuration; Chapter 7, §7.3.5). Power-aware simulation using Unified Power Format (UPF 3.0) and random wake-up event generation. SVA checkers verifying that isolation cells clamp outputs to safe states before supply rail drop. cg_pwr_fsm: Transitions between ACTIVE, CLOCK_GATED, RETENTION, and OFF.

8.1.4 Effort Estimation for Small IP Cores

A common management miscalculation is assuming that a small IP core like the TinyEdge-NPU (sub-100k gates) requires only a fraction of the verification effort demanded by a full SoC. While the physical synthesis and place-and-route effort scales somewhat linearly with gate count, verification complexity scales with the state space of the concurrent modules: the MAC array, ping-pong buffers, autonomous DMA engines, and system bus interfaces running concurrently across clock and power domains.

For an IP of this scale, industry data shows that verification accounts for 55% to 65% of the total engineering effort. We use a bottom-up estimation model based on functional complexity rather than simple gate count:

gantt title TinyEdge-NPU DV Milestone Schedule - 14 Weeks dateFormat YYYY-MM-DD axisFormat Week %W section Testbench Testbench development :a1, 2026-01-05, 4w Directed tests :a2, after a1, 3w section Formal Formal property writing :b1, 2026-01-19, 4w Formal sign-off :b2, after b1, 2w section Coverage Constrained-random testing :c1, 2026-02-02, 6w Coverage closure :c2, after c1, 4w section Power Power-aware simulation :d1, 2026-02-16, 4w

The total effort for verifying the TinyEdge-NPU is approximately 32 engineer-weeks (equivalent to two dedicated verification engineers over a four-month execution window), distributed as follows:

  • Verification Environment Infrastructure (8 engineer-weeks): Constructing the Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) environment, including the register abstraction layer (UVM RAL), AXI-Lite subordinate and AXI4 manager agents, and streaming scoreboards hooked to the bit-exact Python reference model via the Direct Programming Interface (DPI-C).
  • Formal Verification of Safety and Bus Protocols (4 engineer-weeks): Deploying formal property verification (FPV) on the DMA master state machine, the activation buffer pointer management logic, and the arbiter. FPV proves safety properties (such as lack of deadlock or data corruption) mathematically without needing complex testbench stimulus.
  • Constrained-Random Test Development (10 engineer-weeks): Authoring test suites driving diverse neural network topologies (depthwise separable convolutions, fully connected layers, residual skip connections), INT4/INT8 configurations, and memory boundary conditions.
  • Coverage Closure and Bug Resolution (6 engineer-weeks): Iterating on testbench constraints to hit unexercised coverage bins, analyzing structural code coverage, and systematically eliminating holes.
  • Low-Power and Gate-Level Simulation (4 engineer-weeks): Running power-aware gate-level simulations with back-annotated Standard Delay Format (SDF) timing and UPF power state sequences to verify clock-gating logic and memory retention behavior under physical operating conditions.

8.1.5 Worked Example: TinyEdge-NPU Prioritized Feature Breakdown

The TinyEdge-NPU consists of seven critical functional domains. Applying our risk-based methodology yields the prioritized feature breakdown in Table 8.2. This ranking governs the verification schedule: high-risk elements receive dedicated UVM environments and formal proofs before low-risk elements are addressed.

Feature Domain Risk Level & Failure Mode Priority Verification Strategy & Engine
MAC Array Datapath High: Silent arithmetic overflow, broken 32-bit accumulator sign-extension, wrong bias addition, incorrect INT4 weight unpacking. P1 UVM constrained-random stimulus driving directed edge cases (alternating 0x7F/0x80 patterns, maximum negative dynamic ranges) checked lockstep via DPI-C reference model. Formal verification of saturation logic.
Activation/Weight Buffers High: Address collision in dual-port SRAM during ping-pong swap; read-during-write corruption; buffer overrun when DMA outpaces convolution execution. P1 Formal Property Verification (SVA) tracking circular pointers. High-stress concurrent UVM sequences driving asynchronous backpressure and rapid-fire buffer swaps.
DMA Engine High: AXI bus deadlock due to unhandled wait states (READY low indefinitely); unaligned burst crossing 1 KB boundaries; wrong burst termination on end-of-tensor. P1 Standard AMBA formal assertion library combined with UVM constrained-random bus responders that insert randomized wait states, error responses, and split transfers.
Control FSM & Sequencer Medium: Unreachable states or terminal lockup on invalid layer configurations; erroneous instruction decodes; missed start-of-frame triggers. P2 Exhaustive FSM state-transition coverage via constrained-random configuration sequences. Negative testing introducing illegal layer parameters to verify safe error flagging.
Power Management Logic Medium: Power domain isolation cell failure leaking current; register state corruption during retention sleep mode; clock-glitch upon wake-up switch. P2 Power-aware simulation using IEEE 1801 (UPF). Randomized power-down/power-up sequences executed across varied operational states (idle, active inferencing, DMA fill).
Bus Subordinate Interface Low: Register access errors; write-to-read latency mismatches; incorrect decode of read-only status bits. P3 Automated UVM Register Abstraction Layer (RAL) test suites (uvm_reg_hw_reset_seq, uvm_reg_bit_bash_seq, uvm_reg_access_seq).
Interrupt Generation Low: Missed interrupt clearance; pulse duration violations; interrupt line stuck high preventing subsequent host processor triggers. P3 Directed and randomized interrupt asserting/clearing sequences cross-checked with the host interrupt handler agent.

8.2 The Coverage Model

Verification completeness cannot be measured by simulation time or test pass rates. A suite of 10,000 tests that simply re-exercises the same standard execution paths provides less safety than 50 targeted tests exploring the functional boundaries of the hardware. The coverage model provides the quantitative metric that answers the ultimate project question: Are we ready to tape out?

For the TinyEdge-NPU, we implement a multi-axis coverage model spanning functional coverage, structural code coverage, and assertion coverage. Each tier addresses distinct failure modes, and none is sufficient on its own.

flowchart TD CODE[Structural Code Coverage
Line, Branch, Toggle, FSM] --> CLOSE[Coverage Closure] ASSERT[Assertion Coverage
SVA Pass and Cover] --> CLOSE FUNC[Functional Coverage
Covergroups and Coverpoints] --> CLOSE CLOSE --> SIGNOFF["Sign-off: All Three Axes at Target"]

8.2.1 Functional Coverage Metrics

Functional coverage measures how thoroughly the design features described in the vPlan have been exercised by the testbench. In the TinyEdge-NPU, functional coverage groups are organized into five primary domains:

1. Execution Opcodes and Layer Configurations

The control engine decodes layer types, activation functions, and quantization settings. The coverage model must record that every individual opcode was executed, and that opcode transitions occurred in valid and invalid sequences.

  • Layer types: 2D Convolution (CONV2D), Depthwise Separable Convolution (DW_CONV), Fully-Connected (DENSE), Max Pooling (POOL_MAX), and Average Pooling (POOL_AVG).
  • Activation modes: Linear (bypass), ReLU, and Clamped Parametric ReLU.
  • Quantization modes: Standard signed INT8 × INT8, signed INT8 × INT4 (packed weight mode), and dynamic shifting factors (0 to 15-bit downscaling).
2. Numerical Datapath and Data Patterns

Standard uniform random distribution rarely exercises datapath corner cases. The coverage model must track arithmetic boundary conditions inside the MAC units and the accumulation tree:

  • Extreme value multiplication: Crosses of operands hitting maximum positive (\(+127\)), maximum negative (\(-128\)), zero (\(0\)), and negative one (\(-1\)).
  • Accumulator saturation: Positive saturation (\(> 2^{31}-1\)), negative saturation (\(< -2^{31}\)), and near-boundary accumulation within \(\pm 10\) counts of saturation.
  • Dynamic zero-skipping: TinyEdge-NPU implements hardware activation zero-skipping to save power. The coverage model tracks zero-sparsity density from 0% (dense) to 100% (fully sparse) in 10% incremental bins to ensure the zero-bypass clock-gating logic functions correctly under all sparsity conditions.
3. Memory and Buffer States

The on-chip 32 KB weight SRAM and 16 KB ping-pong activation SRAM (S configuration) rely on precise address generators and status flags:

  • Full, empty, and almost-full/empty flag assertions.
  • Simultaneous read-during-write occurrences on independent memory banks.
  • Ping-pong pointer toggles: Validating buffer flips occurring on the cycle immediately following an execution complete flag, as well as delayed flips under backpressure.
4. DMA Burst Lengths and Address Alignment

DMA errors typically manifest on bus wrap-around boundaries and partial word alignments:

  • AXI4 burst types: FIXED, INCR (lengths 1–16), and wrapping bursts WRAP4, WRAP8, and WRAP16.
  • Address alignment: Byte-aligned (offset 0), halfword-aligned (offset 2), and unaligned (offsets 1 and 3) base addresses.
  • Cross-coverage of burst lengths against slave-induced wait states (ranging from 0 to 16 stall cycles per beat).
5. Power-State Transitions

Power control bugs are notoriously difficult to detect if state switches are not fully crossed:

  • All valid arcs between ACTIVE, CLOCK_GATED, RETENTION, and OFF.
  • Wake-up stimuli: External pin interrupt, DMA completion interrupt, and AXI bus subordinate transaction wake-up requests.

8.2.2 SystemVerilog Implementation Example

The following SystemVerilog snippet illustrates the construction of functional covergroups capturing arithmetic extremes and DMA boundary configurations for the TinyEdge-NPU:

// Covergroup capturing arithmetic corner cases within the TinyEdge-NPU MAC unit
covergroup cg_mac_datapath @(posedge clk iff rst_n);
  option.per_instance = 1;
  option.comment = "TinyEdge-NPU Datapath Mathematical Corner Cases";

  // Cover INT8 Activation inputs
  cp_act_in: coverpoint act_data_in {
    bins zero        = {8'sd0};
    bins max_pos     = {8'sd127};
    bins max_neg     = {8'sh80};
    bins neg_one     = {-8'sd1};
    bins pos_general = {[8'sd1   : 8'sd126]};
    bins neg_general = {[-8'sd127 : -8'sd2]};
  }

  // Cover INT8 Weight inputs (or packed INT4)
  cp_wt_in: coverpoint wt_data_in {
    bins zero        = {8'sd0};
    bins max_pos     = {8'sd127};
    bins max_neg     = {8'sh80};
    bins neg_one     = {-8'sd1};
    bins pos_general = {[8'sd1   : 8'sd126]};
    bins neg_general = {[-8'sd127 : -8'sd2]};
  }

  // Cover the operating precision mode
  cp_prec_mode: coverpoint cfg_precision_mode {
    bins mode_int8 = {1'b0};
    bins mode_int4 = {1'b1};
  }

  // Cover Accumulator Saturation flags
  cp_sat_status: coverpoint sat_flag_out {
    bins no_sat     = {2'b00};
    bins pos_sat_hit = {2'b01};
    bins neg_sat_hit = {2'b10};
  }

  // Cross coverage: Ensure extremes are verified across both precision modes
  cross_act_wt_prec: cross cp_act_in, cp_wt_in, cp_prec_mode;

  // Cross coverage: Ensure saturation is generated by valid combinations
  cross_sat_act: cross cp_sat_status, cp_act_in;
endgroup

// Covergroup capturing DMA transfer characteristics and bus stalls
covergroup cg_dma_engine @(posedge clk iff rst_n);
  option.per_instance = 1;

  // AXI4 burst types (AWBURST/ARBURST: FIXED=2'b00, INCR=2'b01, WRAP=2'b10)
  cp_burst_type: coverpoint burst_type_in {
    bins fixed = {2'b00};
    bins incr  = {2'b01};
    bins wrap  = {2'b10};
  }

  // AXI4 burst lengths (AWLEN/ARLEN: beats = value + 1, range 1..16)
  cp_burst_len: coverpoint burst_len_in {
    bins len1   = {0};
    bins len4   = {3};
    bins len8   = {7};
    bins len16  = {15};
    bins other  = {[1:2], [4:6], [8:14]};
  }

  // Byte alignments of DMA base source address
  cp_addr_align: coverpoint (src_addr_in[1:0]) {
    bins align_word = {2'b00};
    bins align_byte1 = {2'b01};
    bins align_half = {2'b10};
    bins align_byte3 = {2'b11};
  }

  // Stalls introduced by system memory (READY low count per transaction)
  cp_wait_states: coverpoint stall_cycles_sampled {
    bins zero_wait = {0};
    bins short_wait = {[1:3]};
    bins long_wait  = {[4:15]};
    bins max_stall  = {16};
  }

  // Cross: Burst types under varying memory stall environments
  cross_burst_stalls: cross cp_burst_type, cp_wait_states;
  // Cross: Alignment variations per burst mode
  cross_burst_align: cross cp_burst_type, cp_addr_align;
  // Cross: Burst type against length, covering WRAP4/WRAP8/WRAP16
  cross_burst_type_len: cross cp_burst_type, cp_burst_len;
endgroup

8.2.3 Structural Code Coverage

Code coverage measures how thoroughly the simulation exercised the syntactic structures of the RTL implementation. While functional coverage determines whether the design requirements were tested, code coverage highlights unexercised RTL paths, redundant logic, or untested implementation artifacts.

  • Line Coverage: Measures the execution of every printable RTL statement. In the TinyEdge-NPU, missing line coverage often points to unexercised error handling routines, such as an unhandled AXI BRESP/RRESP = SLVERR/DECERR response condition.
  • Branch and Condition Coverage: Measures whether each branch (if/else, case, ternary operations) evaluated to both TRUE and FALSE, and whether each sub-expression in a complex boolean condition (e.g., if (dma_done && !buf_full || force_flush)) toggled independently. Uncovered branches in the NPU often point to missing tests for control hazards, such as an activation buffer flip requested during a simultaneous pipeline flush.
  • Toggle Coverage: Measures whether every register and wire transitioned from \(0 \rightarrow 1\) and \(1 \rightarrow 0\). Toggle coverage is what catches structural faults: static configuration bits tied off permanently, unused bus bits, or broken register bit-fields. For the TinyEdge-NPU, 100% toggle coverage is mandated on external interface boundaries to verify there are no floating pins or undriven nets.
  • Finite State Machine (FSM) Coverage: Measures the execution of every state in an FSM (State Coverage) and every legal traversal from one state to another (Transition or Arc Coverage). For the main TinyEdge-NPU execution sequencer, 100% FSM arc coverage is non-negotiable. Any unvisited arc might hide an irrecoverable state hangup when an unexpected abort or interrupt occurs during a compute cycle.

8.2.4 Assertion Coverage

SystemVerilog Assertions (SVAs) serve a dual purpose: they act as passive inline monitors checking that rules are never violated (safety properties), and they track whether specific complex sequences occurred (liveness properties or cover property statements). Assertion coverage measures how many times these cover properties were evaluated cleanly without vacuity.

For example, to guarantee that a ping-pong buffer switch reliably occurs within two clock cycles of a convolution block ending without an intervening stall, an assertion property is established:

// Property verifying clean ping-pong switch timing.
// The buffer id is captured in a local variable at the antecedent, because
// $past() would compare against the wrong cycle on the ##2 branch.
property p_buffer_switch_latency;
  logic v; // 1-bit ping-pong buffer id, captured at the antecedent
  @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  (conv_block_done && !stall_pipeline, v = buffer_active_id) |-> ##[1:2] (buffer_active_id != v);
endproperty

a_buffer_switch_latency: assert property(p_buffer_switch_latency)
  else $error("Assertion Failed: Ping-Pong switch violated latency target!");

c_buffer_switch_latency: cover property(p_buffer_switch_latency);

Assertion coverage ensures that this temporal relationship was not just theoretically possible, but was actually stimulated and validated multiple times under different system load states.

8.2.5 Coverage Closure and Sign-off Criteria

Achieving coverage closure is the process of driving all tracked coverage metrics toward their verified targets. Unreached coverage metrics must be systematically investigated. The resolution path follows three branches:

  1. Missing Stimulus: The testbench constraints are too restrictive or the test sequences failed to generate the required scenario. The solution is writing directed tests or tuning random distribution weights.
  2. Design Defect: The coverage bin was not hit because an internal RTL bug blocks the hardware from entering that specific state or combinations of states.
  3. Unreachable Logic (Dead Code): The code cannot physically be executed due to static hardware configurations (e.g., an architectural decision tying an upper address bit to ground, or a defensive default statement in an FSM that is mathematically unreachable).

The Waiver Discipline: Unreachable code must never simply be ignored to artificially inflate overall coverage numbers. Every single waiver applied to code coverage must be documented with an unambiguous technical justification, signed off by both the design lead and the verification lead, and maintained inside version control alongside the exclusion files.

Table 8.3 defines the exact, quantified coverage sign-off gates required for the TinyEdge-NPU prior to physical tape-out.

Coverage Metric Tape-Out Sign-Off Target Allowed Waiver Policy Verification Closure Gate
Functional Coverage 100% of defined covergroups and bins Zero unmapped bins permitted. Waivers allowed only for architectural dead space (e.g., reserved INT8 opcode space) with documented microarchitecture lead approval. Sign-off regression, 50 seeds smoke, 500 nightly, 5,000+ weekend, without failures; all cross-coverage items (weight sparsity × activation quantization modes × power states) fully saturated.
Line Coverage >98% overall (>95% raw un-waived RTL) Permitted only for defensive programming traps, unmapped register bit slices, and scan-chain bypass logic. Every waived line requires an inline bug-tracker citation. Signed audit log cross-referenced against the structural RTL repository commit hash.
Branch Coverage >92% of all conditional branches Restricted to defensive default branches in synthesis-safe FSM decoders and un-triggerable hardware fault-tolerant parity traps. Automated script validation confirming that every waived branch outcome is structurally or logically unreachable during normal mission-mode operation.
Toggle Coverage >90% overall; 100% on external interfaces (AXI4-Lite, power gating, interrupts) Permitted on static mode tie-offs, upper unused address bus bits, and test-point registers. Waivers are rejected if any datapath accumulator bit remains un-toggled. Cumulative simulation database merged across dynamic functional regressions, boot-sequence tests, and scan-insertion pattern simulations.
FSM Coverage 100% reachable states; 100% reachable transitions Zero waivers on standard operational transitions. Illegal state recoveries (defensive state defaults) may be waived only if proven safe via formal equivalence checks. FSM extraction report verified against the microarchitecture control specification for MAC sequencer and DMA controllers.
Assertion Coverage 100% pass rate (zero failures); >90% cover property hits Zero tolerance for failing assertions. Unhit cover properties must be formally analyzed to confirm if the sequence represents an impossible protocol sequence. Combined dynamic SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) run logs and formal property verification (FPV) bounded proof certificates.

Achieving these quantitative metrics guarantees that the TinyEdge-NPU's INT8 datapath, dynamic clock-gating cells, and zero-skipping sparsity logic are comprehensively exercised across corner-case data distributions. But a coverage model is only as credible as the stimulus and checking mechanisms that drive it. To convert these mathematical targets into tape-out-grade silicon confidence, the verification team must integrate a golden reference model for bit-accurate numerical checking, a scalable UVM testbench architecture capable of high-throughput randomized generation, and formal verification engines to exhaustively prove control path invariants.

8.2.6 Gate-Level Simulation with SDF Back-Annotation

RTL simulation proves the design's logic; gate-level simulation proves that the logic survives synthesis. Once the RTL is mapped to a standard-cell netlist, a new class of bugs appears that RTL simulation cannot see: clock-gating cells that glitch on enable transitions, scan-chain ordering errors introduced during DFT insertion, setup and hold violations under real cell delays, and X-propagation from uninitialized flops that RTL treats as clean zeros. Gate-level simulation catches these by running the synthesized netlist with timing delays back-annotated from static timing analysis.

The flow is deliberately narrow. Synthesize the frozen RTL to a gate-level netlist, run static timing analysis to produce a Standard Delay Format (SDF) file for the worst-case corner, and simulate the netlist in VCS or Xcelium with the SDF back-annotated onto the cell instances. Run the same directed smoke tests and key layer sequences that already pass at RTL, not the full constrained-random regression, which is far too slow at gate level, first with zero delay to confirm the netlist is functionally identical to the RTL, then with SDF delays at minimum, typical, and maximum corners. The sign-off checks are: no X-values on any monitored output after reset release, no setup or hold violations reported by the simulator's timing checks, and byte-exact agreement with the reference model on every test that ran. Any mismatch is triaged as either a synthesis issue (a real bug, usually in clock gating or scan stitching) or a testbench timing artifact (for example a check sampled too close to a clock edge under SDF delays); the two are distinguished by re-running the same test in zero-delay mode.

8.3 Block-Level vs. System-Level Verification

Verifying an ultra-low-power neural processing unit such as the TinyEdge-NPU demands a disciplined partition between block-level and system-level verification environments. A common failure in domain-specific accelerator verification is attempting to validate arithmetic accuracy and microarchitectural hazard conditions exclusively inside the full subsystem testbench, which results in sluggish debug cycles, masked bugs, and unacceptably low functional coverage closure. Conversely, relying solely on block-level tests leaves system integration blind to bus contention, clock-domain crossing (CDC) synchronizer latency, DMA descriptor prefetch starvation, and host-interrupt race conditions.

The verification hierarchy must establish a strict division of responsibility: block-level environments exhaustively explore microarchitectural corner cases at high simulation bandwidth, while system-level environments validate end-to-end data pipelines, architectural transactions, and power-state transitions under software control.

flowchart TD subgraph SystemLevel ["System-Level Verification: SoC / Subsystem Environment"] HostFW[Embedded Firmware / Host Driver] -->|AXI Master / CSR Writes| BusMatrix[System Interconnect / AXI Fabric] ExtDRAM[External DRAM Memory Model] <-->|AXI DMA Bursts| BusMatrix BusMatrix <-->|Slave Port & Master DMA| NPU_Top[TinyEdge-NPU Top-Level Wrapper] NPU_Top -->|Interrupt Lines| HostFW NPU_Top -->|P-Channel / Q-Channel| PMU[Power Management Unit Model] end subgraph BlockLevel ["Block-Level Verification: Unit Testbenches"] UVM_MAC[MAC Array UVM TB] -->|Direct Drives| MAC["64-MAC Datapath (8x8)"] UVM_BUF[Buffer UVM TB] -->|Arb & Hazard Vectors| SRAM_Banks[Ping-Pong Activation/Weight SRAMs] UVM_DMA[DMA Engine UVM TB] -->|AXI Protocol Stress| DMA_Core[Scatter-Gather DMA Engine] UVM_CTRL[Control FSM UVM TB] -->|State Transition Stress| FSM[Loop-Nest Tile Controller] end BlockLevel -.->|Reusable Sequences & Checkers| SystemLevel

Block-Level Verification: Microarchitectural Exhaustion

At the block level, the environment wraps individual microarchitectural modules with dedicated Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) agents. Simulation performance is orders of magnitude faster than full-chip simulation, often reaching 10,000 to 50,000 cycles per second, enabling multi-million-cycle random stress campaigns. For TinyEdge-NPU, block-level verification isolates four critical sub-blocks:

  • MAC Array Arithmetic & Datapath: The TinyEdge-NPU uses a 64-way SIMD spatial compute datapath supporting INT8 and packed INT4 operations with 32-bit accumulators. Block-level testing drives directed and constrained-random operand sequences directly into the Processing Elements (PEs). Test benches target signed-unsigned boundary conditions (e.g., \(-128 \times -128\), \(-128 \times 127\), \(0 \times \text{saturation}\)), INT4 sign extensions within packed 8-bit bytes, zero-skipping bypass logic, and intermediate accumulator wrap-around versus saturation logic.
  • Weight and Activation Buffers (SRAMs): The IP utilizes the L configuration's two 32 KB activation banks, configured in a ping-pong structure to interleave DMA loading with matrix computation; the weight buffer is eight 16 KB banks (Chapter 5). Block-level agents model simultaneous Read-After-Write (RAW), Write-After-Read (WAR), and Write-After-Write (WAW) conditions across shared memory ports. Test suites deliberately inject bank conflict scenarios, such as the DMA writing next-layer weights to Bank 1 at the precise cycle the compute engine completes its reduction loop and toggles the ping-pong pointer.
  • Layer Loop-Nest Control FSM: A hardware sequencer manages nested convolution loops across channels (\(C\)), kernel dimensions (\(R, S\)), output feature maps (\(K\)), and spatial coordinates (\(H, W\)). Block-level verification targets FSM state transitions, checking corner-case tensor topologies: single-pixel channels (\(1 \times 1\)), asymmetric padding, dilation rates greater than spatial dimensions, and abort/reset sequences triggered mid-tile.
  • Bus Interface Units (AXI4): Dedicated protocol-compliance testbenches verify the master DMA and slave CSR interface modules. Using standard SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA), such as the Arm AXI Verification IP (VIP), the testbench checks for protocol violations: out-of-order response handling, early burst termination, backpressured WREADY/BREADY handshakes, address 4 KB boundary crossings, and unaligned narrow transfers.

System-Level Verification: Pipeline Orchestration and Software Flow

System-level verification embeds the complete TinyEdge-NPU into a representative SoC subsystem containing an embedded processor (typically a RISC-V RV32IMC or Arm Cortex-M4/M33 core), a system interconnect, an emulated external memory (SRAM/DRAM containing model weights), and a Power Management Unit (PMU). At this level, verification validates algorithmic flows, interrupt latencies, and cross-subsystem interactions that block testbenches cannot capture.

The core stimulus is an end-to-end inference of a production Keyword Spotting (KWS) neural network, such as a 12-class Depthwise Separable Convolutional Neural Network (DS-CNN) or Temporal Convolutional ResNet (TC-ResNet). The host firmware performs the identical boot sequence used in silicon:

Model card: the network under verification. The reference workload is the 12-class DS-CNN-M from Chapter 4 §4.4, targeting the Google Speech Commands keyword set ("Silence", "Unknown", "Yes", "No", "Up", "Down", "Left", "Right", "On", "Off", "Stop", "Go"). A 1-second, 16 kHz audio window is transformed into a 49 × 10 × 1 MFCC feature map, which flows through eleven layers: an initial standard 2D convolution, four depthwise separable blocks (each a 3 × 3 depthwise convolution followed by a 1 × 1 pointwise convolution, 64 channels), an average-pooling layer, and a dense projection to the 12 output classes, about 120,000 parameters (~120 KB INT8) and roughly 12.8 million multiply-accumulate operations per inference: 420,000 cycles (4.20 ms at 100 MHz) on the reference L configuration, 11.8 µJ per inference. Every coverage target, latency budget, and scoreboard check in this chapter is stated against this one network; a different model would need its own card.

  1. Program TinyEdge-NPU base registers via the 32-bit slave bus interface (clock divisor, interrupt enables, base physical addresses).
  2. Dispatch DMA channel 0 to fetch the model weights (e.g., 64 KB across four 16 KB L-configuration weight banks, across multiple layers) from external memory to the weight buffer. The weight buffer is not ping-ponged; only the activation buffer uses the ping-pong pair.
  3. Stream raw acoustic audio features, typically 40-band Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs) sampled over 10 ms frames, into the activation buffer via DMA channel 1.
  4. Trigger the hardware scheduler to execute successive layers (Standard Conv2D \(\rightarrow\) Depthwise Conv2D \(\rightarrow\) Pointwise Conv2D \(\rightarrow\) Requantization \(\rightarrow\) Fully-Connected/Softmax).
  5. Wait for the hardware interrupt line (npu_irq) asserting inference completion, service the interrupt, read back the classification vector, and confirm detection of keywords such as "Yes" or "Stop".

Beyond functional execution, system-level verification targets non-functional interactions:

  • Power-State and Clock-Gating Interactions: TinyEdge-NPU operates under an aggressive power budget (<5 mW active, <100 μW sleep in the S configuration; Chapter 7, §7.3.5). The verification environment orchestrates transitions between ACTIVE, CLOCK_GATED (logic clock-gated, SRAM retained), RETENTION (state retained at reduced supply), and OFF (power-gated, non-retentive). Stimulus checks that entering low-power states via the standard P-Channel/Q-Channel protocol, the Arm power-control handshake, in which P-Channel carries power-state requests and acknowledgements and Q-Channel is the quiescence handshake that parks the interface before the supply is cut, properly parks outstanding AXI transactions without deadlock, and that subsequent cold or warm wake-up sequences preserve or cleanly reset configuration registers.
  • Back-to-Back and Pipelined Inferences: Validating that the host can initiate inference frame \(N+1\) without waiting for frame \(N\) results to be completely cleared from the post-processing buffer, testing pipelining and boundary state reset.
  • System Deadlock Scenarios: Introducing artificial interconnect delays, cache misses on the host bus, and concurrent bus-master traffic (e.g., an emulated audio DMA competing with the NPU DMA) to expose latency-induced FIFO under-runs or scheduling deadlocks.

Divergence of Bugs Found at Each Level

The bugs exposed at block versus system level are fundamentally different in character. Block-level verification catches deterministic logic and arithmetic bugs: off-by-one sign extensions, inverted carry-lookahead bits, race conditions between parallel adder trees, pointer miscalculations in circular buffer addressing, and corner-case states in the loop counters.

System-level verification uncovers dynamic and environmental bugs: race conditions between the DMA completion interrupt and the host clearing the interrupt-status register; host firmware writing a new layer descriptor to SRAM while the NPU DMA is still streaming the tail bytes of the previous layer; deadlocks where the AXI write channel stalls waiting for a response that the system crossbar dropped due to an unexpected power-down transition; and cumulative numerical quantization drift across multi-layer pipelines.

Clock-Domain Crossing Verification: The Host-Control Boundary

TinyEdge-NPU has exactly one clock-domain crossing: the AXI-Lite slave control interface runs on the host bus clock, while the NPU core runs on its own clock. Everything else in the design is single-domain, so CDC verification is a small, sharply scoped activity. But it is not optional, because a metastability failure on the control path can corrupt a layer descriptor and silently change an inference result.

Verification proceeds in three layers. First, structural CDC checks with a dedicated CDC tool (for example Questa CDC or SpyGlass CDC) confirm that every signal crossing the boundary passes through a recognized synchronizer: two-flop synchronizers for single-bit control signals such as start and interrupt-clear, and gray-coded pointers with an asynchronous FIFO for any multi-bit data. The tool also flags the classic structural errors: combinational logic on a crossing path, reconvergent synchronized signals, and multi-bit buses crossed without a handshake. Second, metastability analysis estimates the mean time between failures (MTBF) of each synchronizer from the two clock frequencies and the flop characteristics, and the result must clear the product MTBF target with margin. Third, dynamic simulation runs CDC-aware tests: randomized host-clock phase offsets, back-to-back CSR writes straddling the boundary, and interrupt assertions during clock-gated core states, with assertions checking that no synchronized control signal glitches and that every host write eventually lands in the core-side register exactly once. A synchronizer that the structural tool cannot recognize is treated as a design bug, not a waiver.

Sequence and Component Reuse Across Environments

To prevent duplication of engineering effort, verification teams must architect components for vertical reuse. TinyEdge-NPU implements this through the following mechanisms:

  • Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) Sequence Reuse: Sequences developed to test register spaces (UVM Register Abstraction Layer - RAL) run without modification in both the block-level CSR testbench and the full subsystem testbench. Only the underlying UVM adapter and sequencer map change (from a direct register pin-wiggle sequence to an AXI VIP master sequence).
  • Scoreboard and Checker Integration: The bit-accurate reference model described in Section 8.4 is instantiated directly inside the block-level MAC and buffer testbenches, and it is also wrapped within the system-level scoreboard. In block testing, the reference model evaluates individual \(3 \times 3\) tiles on a cycle-by-cycle or transaction-by-transaction basis; at the system level, the identical model operates on an entire layer or inference graph, reading from the emulated memory and predicting the final softmax score vector.
  • SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA): Property checkers written inside the RTL or bound via interface binds, such as FIFO overflow/underflow assertions, credit-based flow control checkers (where a producer may only send when it holds a credit issued by the consumer, so the FIFO can never overflow), and valid/ready handshake invariants, remain active at all verification tiers, continuously catching protocol anomalies.

Comparison Matrix: Block-Level vs. System-Level Verification

The following table summarizes the scope, stimulus strategies, checking mechanisms, and failure profiles of the two verification levels for the TinyEdge-NPU IP:

Metric / Dimension Block-Level Verification System-Level (Subsystem/SoC) Verification
Scope Under Test Individual sub-modules: MAC Array, Activation/Weight SRAMs, Loop FSM, DMA Engine. Full TinyEdge-NPU top-level, AXI interconnect, host CPU, external memory, power controllers.
Stimulus Generation Constrained-random transaction generators, direct pin-wiggling, corner-case arithmetic drivers. End-to-end neural network workloads (KWS DS-CNN), compiled host firmware, randomized bus-traffic contention.
