8.4 A Bit-Accurate Reference Model for TinyEdge-NPU

In edge AI accelerators, standard random testing cannot verify algorithmic and numerical correctness. If a MAC datapath computes an incorrect dot product or applies the wrong rounding mode during requantization, functional coverage may still achieve 100% while the accelerator generates corrupted classifications in silicon. A bit-accurate, executable reference model is the single most critical verification asset for TinyEdge-NPU. It serves three non-negotiable functions: as an authoritative golden specification for RTL design, as the automated prediction engine within the UVM scoreboard, and as a test-vector generator bridging the data science domain (PyTorch/TensorFlow) to digital verification.

"An AI accelerator without a bit-accurate golden model cannot be verified. Functional coverage of buses and state machines only proves the hardware communicates; only an exact reference model proves it computes."

Model Architecture

The TinyEdge-NPU reference model is implemented as a modular, object-oriented Python class hierarchy, mirrored in C++ for integration into SystemC/UVM via the Direct Programming Interface (DPI-C). The model mirrors the logical structure of the hardware datapath without being constrained by synthesizable register-transfer realities:

flowchart LR InAct["Input Tensor: INT8 Activations"] --> Tiler[Buffer Tiling Engine] InWgt["Input Weights: INT8 / INT4"] --> Tiler Tiler --> SpatialPE["Spatial Array Engine: 64x INT8 MACs (8x8)"] SpatialPE --> Acc32[32-Bit Accumulator Stage] Acc32 --> Requant["Requantization Unit: Mult, Shift, Round, Sat"] Requant --> OutAct["Output Tensor: INT8 Feature Map"] subgraph GoldenModel ["TinyEdge Golden Reference Model Engine"] Tiler SpatialPE Acc32 Requant end

The model encapsulates four sequential stages:

  1. Buffer Tiling Engine: Translates 3D/4D logical tensor coordinates (\([N, H, W, C]\) and \([K, R, S, C]\)) into physical memory layouts. It segments spatial feature maps into micro-tiles sized precisely to one 32 KB activation bank (L configuration) and tracks stride, dilation, and zero-padding configurations identical to the hardware's loop-nest FSM.
  2. Spatial MAC Compute: Executes vector dot products matching the 64 parallel PEs. Operands are cast to two's-complement 8-bit integers (\(-128\) to \(127\)) or 4-bit integers (\(-8\) to \(7\)). Multiplications are mapped directly to 32-bit signed storage, preventing mathematical overflow during spatial reduction.
  3. Accumulation and Zero-Skipping: Accumulates partial products across the channel (\(C\)) and spatial kernel (\(R \times S\)) dimensions. The model includes an algorithmic zero-detection switch matching TinyEdge's zero-skipping logic: if an activation or weight is zero, the model verifies that the cycle-accurate RTL power-gates the PE multiplier inputs and preserves the partial sum register.
  4. Requantization Pipeline: Implements fixed-point scaling back to INT8. The accumulator result (\(S_{32}\)) undergoes bias addition, multiplication by a quantized scale factor (\(M_0\)), right-shifting (\(n\)), deterministic rounding, and saturation clipping to \([-128, 127]\).

Bit-Accuracy Enforcement and Fixed-Point Arithmetic Rules

For the model to act as a definitive scoreboard oracle, it must share an unambiguous fixed-point arithmetic specification with the RTL designers. Any ambiguity in rounding or shift behavior will manifest as false-positive scoreboard errors during regression runs. The TinyEdge-NPU fixed-point arithmetic specification is defined as follows:

The accumulator value \(A_{32}\) is computed over channel index \(c\) and spatial kernel indices \(r, s\):

\[A_{32} = \sum_{r=0}^{R-1} \sum_{s=0}^{S-1} \sum_{c=0}^{C-1} \left( W_{r,s,c} \times X_{r,s,c} \right) + \text{Bias}_{32}\]

Requantization converts this 32-bit integer back to an 8-bit domain (\(Y_{\text{INT8}}\)) using an effective real-valued multiplier \(M = 2^{-n} \times M_0\), where \(M_0 \in [2^{30}, 2^{31}-1]\) is a 32-bit fixed-point mantissa and \(n \ge 31\) is a right-shift factor:

  1. Scaled Intermediate Product: Form a 64-bit temporary integer product: \[P_{64} = A_{32} \times M_0\]
  2. Rounding Offset: TinyEdge-NPU uses round-to-nearest-up (half-way rounding toward positive infinity) to minimize hardware complexity. The rounding bias added to the product is: \[\text{Offset} = 1 \ll (n - 1)\] \[P_{\text{rounded}} = P_{64} + \text{Offset}\]
  3. Arithmetic Shift: Perform an arithmetic right shift: \[Q_{32} = \lfloor P_{\text{rounded}} \gg n \rfloor\]
  4. Saturation: Clip the output value into the signed 8-bit range: \[Y_{\text{INT8}} = \max\left(-128, \min\left(127, Q_{32}\right)\right)\]

Below is the reference Python implementation of the requantization datapath, integrated into the testbench infrastructure via PyUVM or file-based vectors: 

def requantize_int32_to_int8(acc_val: int, bias: int, m0: int, shift: int) -> int:
    """
    Bit-accurate requantization matching TinyEdge-NPU hardware pipeline.
    acc_val: 32-bit signed accumulated sum
    bias:    32-bit signed per-channel or per-layer bias
    m0:      32-bit signed fixed-point multiplier mantissa (2^30 <= m0 < 2^31)
    shift:   Integer bit shift (n >= 31)
    """
    # 1. Accumulate with bias (signed 32-bit wrap or clamp)
    val = acc_val + bias
    
    # 2. Multiply to 64-bit intermediate
    product64 = val * m0
    
    # 3. Round-to-nearest-up offset addition
    rounding_offset = 1 << (shift - 1)
    product_rounded = product64 + rounding_offset
    
    # 4. Arithmetic right shift
    shifted_val = product_rounded >> shift
    
    # 5. Symmetric signed 8-bit saturation
    if shifted_val > 127:
        return 127
    elif shifted_val < -128:
        return -128
    else:
        return shifted_val

Scoreboarding and Tolerance Policies

In digital IP verification for integer-based AI accelerators, the tolerance policy is strictly zero: exact match on every single byte. Unlike floating-point datapaths (FP32/FP16) where differences in fused multiply-add (FMA) tree reduction orders can introduce Least Significant Bit (LSB) divergence, an INT8/INT4 integer datapath has no rounding ambiguity prior to the final requantization shift. A discrepancy of \(\pm 1\) LSB in the output activation is not a "numerical artifact". It is a functional defect in rounding, saturation, or sign extension.

The UVM scoreboard connects to the reference model and the Device Under Test (DUT) using TLM analysis FIFOs:

sequenceDiagram autonumber participant Mon as AXI/SRAM Monitors participant SB as UVM Scoreboard participant Ref as Python Reference Model participant DUT as TinyEdge-NPU Hardware Mon->>DUT: Sample Output Transactions (Write Data) Mon->>SB: Write to dut_fifo (Actual INT8 Tensors) SB->>Ref: Forward Stimulus & Layer Configuration Ref-->>SB: Return Predicted INT8 Tensors SB->>SB: Compare Actual vs Predicted (Exact Bit-Level Match) alt Exact Match SB->>SB: Increment Passed Transaction Count else Mismatch Detected SB->>SB: Trigger `uvm_error: Dump Acc, Scale, Shift, Byte Index end

Model-Based Stimulus Generation

Constrained-random testbenches that draw data from uniform distributions (\(X \sim \mathcal{U}(-128, 127)\)) are ineffective at verifying edge neural accelerators. In practical Keyword Spotting models, weight matrices exhibit severe sparsity (often 30% to 60% zeros after pruning) and activation distributions follow a bell-shaped Laplace or Gaussian distribution centered at zero due to ReLU or clipping functions.

If a testbench uses uniform random noise, two critical failure modes occur:

  1. Zero-Skipping Inactivity: With a uniform distribution, the probability of either input being zero is \(1/256 \approx 0.39\%\). The testbench will virtually never stress back-to-back zero-skipping logic or test the clock-gating wake-up transitions in the PE array.
  2. Unrealistic Accumulator Saturation: Uniform inputs maximize variance, driving the 32-bit accumulators into saturation regimes that rarely occur during true inference, while missing subtle sub-saturation rounding points near the zero-boundary.

To achieve realistic stimulus, the reference model hooks into trained weights from MLPerf Tiny KWS benchmarks. The testbench extracts authentic feature weights and mel-spectrogram activation traces, applying constrained randomization on top of real weight distributions: injecting targeted bursts of zeros, clustering extreme-value outliers, and dynamically modulating tensor stride profiles.

Common Reference Model vs. RTL Mismatches and Debugging

During the verification of TinyEdge-NPU, three classes of mismatches routinely occur between the reference model and RTL. Identifying and diagnosing them requires understanding how digital logic diverges from high-level code:

  • Accumulator Bit-Width Truncation:

    The Issue: To save routing congestion, an RTL designer might trim intermediate accumulators from 32 bits to 24 bits, assuming that for a \(3 \times 3\) kernel with \(C=16\), the maximum dynamic range is \(9 \times 16 \times (-128 \times -128) = 144 \times 16384 = 2,359,296\) (which fits in 22 bits). However, when handling fully connected layers or \(1 \times 1\) convolutions with \(C=512\), the dynamic range exceeds 24 bits.

    Debugging Signature: Scoreboard errors occur only when layer channel depths exceed a threshold (e.g., \(C > 128\)). Small layers pass cleanly, while deep layers exhibit sign-inverted or wrapped-around outputs. The reference model detects this by executing a layer with \(C=512\) loaded with maximum negative values (\(-128\)).

  • Rounding Offset Off-by-One in Requantization:

    The Issue: A typical bug involves arithmetic right shifting in hardware. The RTL may implement round-to-nearest-up by adding \(1 \ll (n-1)\) to the 64-bit value, but fails to handle negative products correctly because Verilog's >>> operator requires signed operands on both sides. If the product is assigned to an undeclared intermediate wire, it defaults to unsigned, causing negative accumulator values to shift in logical zeros instead of sign bits.

    Debugging Signature: All positive accumulator results match the reference model with 100% precision. Negative accumulator results fail, exhibiting values shifted by huge positive offsets.

  • Buffer Tiling and Stride Boundary Hazards:

    The Issue: When feature maps do not divide evenly by the hardware tile width (e.g., input width \(W=40\), tile capacity \(T_w=16\)), the tile engine must generate two full tiles of 16 and one residual tile of 8. The loop sequencer must clamp the spatial read pointers and pad the residual elements with zero (or replicate edge elements, depending on the padding mode). An off-by-one error in the RTL pad counter will fetch stale data from the adjacent memory bank instead of injecting zero.

    Debugging Signature: The first two tiles match the reference model bit-for-bit. The third tile exhibits mismatches exclusively on the spatial boundary pixels (columns 8 through 15).

Worked Example: Verifying a \(3 \times 3\) Depthwise Convolution Tile

To demonstrate the reference model verification flow, consider an end-to-end trace of a single output activation calculated by the TinyEdge-NPU. The operation is a \(3 \times 3\) Depthwise Convolution (stride 1, zero padding) executing on Channel 0 (\(C_0\)), with a 32-bit bias \(B = 10\), a requantization multiplier \(M_0 = 2^{30} = 1{,}073{,}741{,}824\), and a shift factor \(n = 31\) (total effective scale \(M = 2^{-31} \times 2^{30} = 0.5\)). The activation patch \(A\) and kernel \(W\) for this tile are:

Step-by-Step Execution

To trace the evaluation path through both the C++ reference model and the RTL datapath, consider a single \(3 \times 3\) spatial convolution operating on an INT8 activation patch \(A\) with an INT8 filter kernel \(W\) and a 32-bit bias \(B = 10\):

Index \((r, c)\) Activation \(A(r,c)\) Weight \(W(r,c)\) Product (\(A \times W\))
(0, 0)12224
(0, 1)-81-8
(0, 2)4-1-4
(1, 0)20-2-40
(1, 1)16348
(1, 2)-121-12
(2, 0)-400
(2, 1)8-2-16
(2, 2)24248

  1. 32-Bit Dot-Product Accumulation: In a single clock cycle, the 64-MAC array evaluates all nine products of the \(3 \times 3\) tile in parallel and folds in the channel bias:

    int32_t acc = 10; // Initialized with bias B
acc += (24) + (-8) + (-4) + (-40) + (48) + (-12) + (0) + (-16) + (48);
// acc = 10 + 40 = 50

  2. Fixed-Point Scaled Multiplication (\(M_0\)): TinyEdge-NPU executes requantization using high-radix fixed-point arithmetic. With \(M_0 = 2^{30} = 1{,}073{,}741{,}824\), the accumulator is multiplied using a 64-bit temporary sign-extended product to avoid intermediate precision loss:

    int64_t scaled = (int64_t)acc * (int64_t)M0;
// scaled = 50 * 1,073,741,824 = 53,687,091,200 (0xC80000000)

  3. Rounding Offset Addition: To implement round-half-up before shifting, the hardware adds a rounding constant equal to \(2^{n-1}\), where \(n = 31\):

    int64_t round_const = 1LL << (n - 1); // 1 << 30 = 1,073,741,824
scaled += round_const;
// scaled = 53,687,091,200 + 1,073,741,824 = 54,760,833,024 (0xCC0000000)

  4. Arithmetic Right Shift (\(n\)): The rounded value undergoes an arithmetic right shift by \(n = 31\) bit positions, yielding the scaled 32-bit quotient:

    int32_t shifted = (int32_t)(scaled >> 31);
// shifted = 54,760,833,024 >> 31 = 25

  5. Saturating Truncation to INT8: The intermediate 32-bit integer is clamped to the signed 8-bit dynamic range \([-128, 127]\). Since \(25\) falls comfortably within these bounds, no clipping occurs:

    int8_t out = (shifted > 127) ? 127 : ((shifted < -128) ? -128 : (int8_t)shifted);
// out = 25 (0x19)

  6. Scoreboard Verification & Exact-Match Check: In the UVM testbench, the model produces expected byte 0x19 and places it into an analysis FIFO. Simultaneously, the RTL's writeback engine commits the output byte over the internal AXI-Stream interface into the Activation Buffer. The UVM scoreboard drains both transactions, asserting byte-for-byte identity. An RTL error, such as applying truncation instead of round-half-up or failing to sign-extend the 64-bit product, produces an immediate transaction mismatch with a complete cycle and operand trace.

Maintaining parity between the reference model and the RTL is not a one-time milestone, but an ongoing operational discipline across the IP design lifecycle. Any architectural refinement, such as adjusting saturation bounds, altering rounding modes, or changing pipeline register stages to meet timing in 28nm, must originate in the C++ model prior to RTL implementation. Continuous nightly regression suites running randomized layer configurations verify this lockstep alignment, ensuring the hardware never diverges from the golden bit-level specification before silicon sign-off.

8.5 UVM Testbench Architecture for an NPU

Verifying an ultra-low-power edge NPU such as the TinyEdge-NPU presents a dual verification challenge. The design combines high-throughput, tightly coupled streaming datapaths (MAC array, accumulation units, activation buffers) with aggressive, fine-grained power-management states and asynchronous host interactions. A simple directed-test methodology fails to uncover deep pipeline corner cases, such as DMA stall assertions coinciding with activation buffer bank conflicts during an INT8 depthwise separable convolution. To achieve tape-out confidence in a 28nm process within a tight schedule, the verification environment relies on a structured, modular Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) testbench parameterized to support design-time architectural variations.

8.5.1 Environment Topology and Component Architecture

The TinyEdge-NPU UVM environment encapsulates the Device Under Test (DUT) using modular verification components (UVM agents) connected across standard interface boundaries. System-level stimulus generation is coordinated by a virtual sequencer that orchestrates transactions across three primary domains: the Host Control plane, the Backing Memory plane, and the Streaming Sensor plane.

flowchart TB subgraph UVM_ENV ["TinyEdge-NPU UVM Environment"] VSEQ["Virtual Sequencer"] subgraph AGENTS ["Interface Agents"] HOST_AGT["Host Agent\n(AXI Master)"] DMA_AGT["Memory Agent\n(AXI Slave / System SRAM)"] SENSOR_AGT["Sensor Data Producer\n(writes frames to system memory)"] end REF_MDL["Bit-Accurate\nReference Model (C++/DPI-C)"] SCB["TLM In-Order/OoO\nScoreboard"] end DUT["TinyEdge-NPU Core\n(MAC Array, Buffers, DMA, FSM)"] VSEQ --> HOST_AGT VSEQ --> DMA_AGT VSEQ --> SENSOR_AGT HOST_AGT -->|Host Bus VIF| DUT DUT -->|Master AXI VIF| DMA_AGT SENSOR_AGT -->|Memory writes| DMA_AGT HOST_AGT -.->|Monitored CSR/Commands| REF_MDL SENSOR_AGT -.->|Stream Samples| REF_MDL DMA_AGT -.->|Monitored Tensors| SCB DUT -.->|Monitored Interrupts/AXI| SCB REF_MDL -->|Expected Tensors| SCB

The environment contains the following dedicated agents:

  • Host Interface Agent (Master): Drives the AXI-Lite target interface on the TinyEdge-NPU. It executes register reads and writes generated by the UVM Register Abstraction Layer (RAL), configuring layer descriptor tables, setting quantization scales, and polling interrupt status flags.
  • System Memory Agent (Reactive Slave): Emulates external high-latency system memory connected to the NPU's internal DMA master interface. This agent responds to AXI burst read requests (fetching weights, biases, and activation tensors) and burst write requests (storing computed activation maps). It can inject randomized, configurable wait-states (AXI RVALID/BVALID delays) to reproduce system-level bus arbitration stalls.
  • Sensor Data Producer: Writes raw audio frames (keyword spotting PCM samples) into system memory through the memory agent, modelling a sensor DMA or host CPU filling the input buffer. The NPU's own DMA then fetches the frames, so the DUT's single ingest path — the AXI4 DMA master — stays the only way data enters the core, and the only clock-domain crossing in the design remains the AXI-Lite slave (Chapter 7).
  • Bit-Accurate Reference Model: Encapsulated within a UVM component via the SystemVerilog Direct Programming Interface (DPI-C), this component evaluates identical layer descriptor parameters and inputs to compute golden output matrices matching the hardware quantization model.

8.5.2 Sequence Library Architecture

The verification sequence library progresses from deterministic hardware bring-up to stochastic corner-case hunting, structured into three primary tiers:

  1. Directed Bring-Up Sequences: Sanity-check baseline pipeline execution. These sequences execute small, isolated compute workloads: a single 3×3 convolution, a 1×1 pointwise layer, a max-pooling operation, and standalone ReLU/activation operations. They validate datapath connectivity, register decode logic, and primary interrupt generation without randomized pipeline disruption.
  2. Constrained-Random Datapath & Buffer Stress Sequences: Stress the INT8 MAC array and the internal SRAM buffers (weight and ping-pong activation scratchpads). Randomization constraints focus on:
    • Mathematical corner cases: Maximal positive (+127), maximal negative (-128), alternating zero-tensors to stress zero-skipping logic, and asymmetric bias values forcing arithmetic saturation in the 32-bit accumulators.
    • Buffer boundary conditions: Layer configurations whose activation strides match the physical buffer bank size, forcing memory bank conflicts between incoming DMA write bursts and MAC array read passes.
    • Descriptor chaining: Queuing multi-layer neural network graphs (e.g., a complete 12-class depthwise separable CNN for keyword spotting) with back-to-back hardware scheduling and zero host intervention.
  3. Power-State Management Sequences: TinyEdge-NPU operates with an active target budget below 5 mW and a sleep floor below 100 μW in the S configuration (Chapter 7, §7.3.5). Verification sequences force random transitions between operational modes: ACTIVE (execution), CLOCK_GATED (stall, logic clock-gated), RETENTION (logic retention, memory retained), and OFF (power-gated, context preserved via software save-restore). Sequences verify that sleep requests issued while the DMA engine is mid-burst cleanly freeze or complete the transaction without bus deadlocks or corrupted pointers upon wake-up.

8.5.3 Scoreboard Design: Handling Latency and DMA Concurrency

The TinyEdge-NPU scoreboard validates functional accuracy at the transaction level. Unlike a simple FIFO-based comparator, the scoreboard must handle non-deterministic transaction latency, decoupled read/write phases, and out-of-order write completion resulting from AXI burst operations and multi-bank memory interleaving.

The scoreboard receives monitored register configurations and input tensors via TLM analysis ports, passing them to the DPI-C golden model. When the golden model produces an expected tensor slice, it is enqueued in an associative array indexed by transaction tags, layer IDs, and target destination addresses. When the Memory Agent monitors an AXI write burst from the NPU DMA, it reassembles the byte stream into an output tensor transaction. The scoreboard looks up the corresponding expected entry by base memory address, performs element-wise INT8 comparisons, and handles layer completion metrics.

// Scoreboard comparison logic for TinyEdge-NPU output tensor validation
function void tinyedge_scoreboard::compare_tensor(tensor_tx actual_tx);
  tensor_tx expected_tx;
  string msg;

  if (!exp_tensor_map.exists(actual_tx.dest_base_addr)) begin
    `uvm_error("SCB_UNEXP_BURST", $sformatf("Unexpected DMA write to address: 0x%08h", actual_tx.dest_base_addr))
    return;
  end

  expected_tx = exp_tensor_map[actual_tx.dest_base_addr];
  if (actual_tx.payload.size() != expected_tx.payload.size()) begin
    `uvm_error("SCB_SIZE_MISMATCH", $sformatf("Layer ID %0d: Expected size %0d, got %0d",
               actual_tx.layer_id, expected_tx.payload.size(), actual_tx.payload.size()))
    return;
  end

  foreach (actual_tx.payload[i]) begin
    if (actual_tx.payload[i] !== expected_tx.payload[i]) begin
      `uvm_error("SCB_DATA_MISMATCH", $sformatf("Byte %0d mismatch at 0x%08h! Exp: 0x%02h, Got: 0x%02h",
                 i, actual_tx.dest_base_addr + i, expected_tx.payload[i], actual_tx.payload[i]))
      return;
    end
  end
  `uvm_info("SCB_PASS", $sformatf("Tensor at 0x%08h verified successfully.", actual_tx.dest_base_addr), UVM_HIGH)
  exp_tensor_map.delete(actual_tx.dest_base_addr);
endfunction
Verification Pitfall: Do not rely exclusively on post-layer complete interrupts to trigger comparisons. Storing intermediate layer outputs to system SRAM allows the scoreboard to detect localized pipeline errors (such as off-by-one pooling shifts or rounding truncation errors) immediately, rather than permitting corrupt data to propagate through subsequent layers.

8.5.4 Assertions and Protocol Checkers

Formal SystemVerilog Assertions (SVAs) complement UVM transaction-level checking by continuously inspecting interface timing, protocol handshakes, and microarchitectural state boundaries. Key assertions deployed in the TinyEdge-NPU testbench include:

  • Protocol Compliance: Off-the-shelf SVA suites (e.g., Synopsys or Cadence AXI VIP checkers) monitor the AXI bus, ensuring zero violations of handshaking constraints (e.g., stable signals between VALID assertion and READY grant).
  • SRAM Buffer Overflow/Underflow: Activation and weight scratchpads are protected by immediate and concurrent assertions. If the DMA engine pushes data when the activation buffer's write credit count is zero, an assertion fires instantaneously:
    assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) (act_buf_full & act_buf_push) |-> 0);
  • Accumulator Overflow Tracking: TinyEdge-NPU implements 32-bit accumulators to prevent overflow during sum-of-products operations before re-quantizing down to INT8. An assertion checks that if accumulation reaches saturation limits (32'h7FFFFFFF or 32'h80000000), a saturation sticky flag is asserted in the internal telemetry registers.
  • Power Transition Handshakes: SVA sequences monitor the power controller FSM, guaranteeing that clock-gating cells are active only when the MAC datapath reports an idle status, preventing clock chops mid-computation.

8.5.5 Parameterization and IP Reuse

TinyEdge-NPU is an adaptable IP core intended for diverse silicon budgets. The hardware supports configurable parameters: INT8 or INT4 precision modes, MAC array geometries (\(4\times4\), \(8\times8\), or \(16\times16\)), and activation scratchpad depths (16 KB to 64 KB). The UVM testbench supports these variants through configuration parameters:

IP Config Parameter RTL Impact UVM Parameterization Strategy Scoreboard & Agent Behavior
PRECISION_MODE Datapath width (INT8 vs INT4 packing in 32-bit words) Typed sequence items and agent configuration objects DPI-C reference model switches bit-width sign-extension and clamp routines.
MAC_ARRAY_SIZE Compute parallelism (\(4\times4\) vs \(8\times8\) parallel dot-products) Plusargs and structural parameter overrides in top package Adjusts cycle-latency estimators in scoreboard and changes block tiling sizes.
ACT_BUF_DEPTH Internal activation SRAM address boundaries Propagated via UVM RAL memory model map bounds Sequence generator adjusts maximum layer footprint constraints and DMA burst lengths.

By extracting these architectural traits into a global configuration object registered with the uvm_config_db, tests dynamically adapt stimulus generation to match the instantiated RTL footprint without requiring testbench recompilation.

8.5.6 Regression Management and Failure Triage Flow

Ensuring closure across code coverage (statement, branch, condition, toggle, and FSM) and functional coverage (quantization ranges, layer types, DMA lengths, power states) requires a tiered regression hierarchy:

  1. Smoke Regression (Per-Commit / Pull Request): Runs 10 to 15 short directed sequences (register sanity, basic 1D/2D convolution, single-layer wake-word inference) across 50 randomized seeds. Execution completes in under 15 minutes, serving as a merge gatekeeper.
  2. Nightly Regression (Master Branch): Runs approximately 500 constrained-random tests with randomized seeds, covering cross-layer permutations, DMA wait-state variations, and randomized power-down events. Execution targets 6 to 8 hours across compute farm queues.
  3. Full Weekend / Milestone Regression: Scales to 5,000+ seeds, executing continuous multi-layer graph permutations under extreme memory latency emulation and fault injection (parity errors, bus aborts). Merges and generates functional coverage databases to drive verification closure toward 100% functional and >95% code coverage.

Seed management is governed by predictable, pseudo-random generation tied to revision control commits. When a regression test fails, the triage flow follows a deterministic path:

  1. Artifact Capture: The runner script archives the specific random seed, test log, waves dumped around the failure time (using rolling circular trace buffers to minimize disk footprint), and register assertion traces.
  2. Automated Classification: A script parses error strings against known issue signatures (e.g., SCB_DATA_MISMATCH, AXI_SLV_TIMEOUT, SVA_ACT_OVFL). Failures are bucketed automatically into DUT bugs, Reference Model discrepancies, or Testbench/VIP race conditions.
  3. Rerun & Isolation: The failure is reproduced locally using the exact seed:
    ./simv +UVM_TESTNAME=npu_random_layer_stress_test +ntb_random_seed=4820194 +WAVE_DUMP. The defect is assigned to the corresponding IP microarchitect, accompanied by waveform snippets and a minimized reproducer sequence.

8.6 Formal Verification Opportunities

For a resource-constrained accelerator like the TinyEdge-NPU, formal property verification (FPV) is not an academic luxury. It is an indispensable mechanism to eliminate corner-case bugs that pseudo-random dynamic simulation frequently misses. With an IP footprint of ~1 mm² in a 28nm process and a lean design team, exhaustive simulation of all concurrent bus transactions, DMA burst interruptions, and clock-gating transitions is computationally prohibitive. Formal verification mathematically proves that specified design behaviors hold across all possible execution traces within bounded cycles, or delivers a counterexample trace when a violation occurs.

Where Formal Fits in the TinyEdge-NPU

Formal methods should target control-heavy, asynchronous, and structural control logic where state-space concurrency is high, but datapath width is small. In the TinyEdge-NPU, five critical subsystems mandate formal proofs:

  • Control FSM Safety and Liveness: Prove that the main controller FSM is deadlock-free, that all states are reachable, that it can never enter an unmapped state (even with illegal soft-register programming), and that every computation sequence eventually returns an INFERENCE_DONE or asserted ERROR_IRQ.
  • Bus Interface Protocol Compliance: Verification of the AXI4-Lite slave control interface and the AXI4 master DMA interface against standard AMBA protocol rules. Standard assertion IP (AIP) proves that no handshakes violate valid/ready stabilization rules, read/write address dependencies, or outstanding response counts.
  • Buffer Pointer Invariants: The ping-pong activation buffer and circular weight FIFO must maintain strict structural integrity. Formal asserts that write pointers never overtake read pointers (no silent data overwrite) and read pointers never exceed valid written frames (no stale data consumption under backpressure).
  • Configuration Register Locking: During active inference (when fsm_state != IDLE), critical layer parameters, such as input_channel_depth, activation_type (ReLU/passthrough), and stride_offset, must be structurally immune to bus writes. Formal proves that register values remain bit-stable during processing regardless of write requests on the register interface.
  • Power-Management FSM Transitions: Proof that transitioning between ACTIVE (<5 mW), CLOCK_GATED, RETENTION, and OFF (<5 μW) sequences follows strict sequencing: clocks must gate before isolation cells activate, and level-shifter enables must stabilize before retention restores.
graph TD subgraph TinyEdge_NPU ["TinyEdge-NPU RTL Scope"] FSM[Layer Control FSM] BUS[AXI Bus Interface] PTR["Buffer Flow & Pointers"] PWR[Power State Controller] DMA[DMA Controller] DP[INT8 MAC Array] ACC[32-bit Accumulators] ACT["Quantization & ReLU Engine"] end subgraph Formal_Verification ["Formal Property Verification"] F_FSM["Exhaustive Reachability & Deadlock Proofs"] F_BUS[Protocol Compliance AIP] F_PTR["FIFO Invariant & Underflow/Overflow Proofs"] F_PWR["Power Isolation & Gating Sequencing"] end subgraph Dynamic_Simulation ["Dynamic Simulation & Reference Model"] S_DP[Layer Math Bit-Accuracy Scoreboard] S_DMA[Long Real-Memory Stream Burst Profiling] S_NET[Full Neural Net KWS Inference Validation] end FSM --> F_FSM BUS --> F_BUS PTR --> F_PTR PWR --> F_PWR DP --> S_DP ACC --> S_DP ACT --> S_DP DMA --> S_DMA TinyEdge_NPU --> S_NET

What NOT to Formalize: The Datapath Boundary

A frequent error among teams adopting formal methods is attempting to verify end-to-end mathematical correctness through formal equivalence of the MAC array. Exhaustively proving that an 8×8 INT8 spatial array calculates D = ∑(A × B) + C across multiple pipeline stages creates an explosion of Boolean Satisfiability (SAT) and Binary Decision Diagram (BDD) complexity. Multipliers are notoriously difficult for SAT solvers due to exponential branch paths. The MAC datapath, post-MAC scaling, clipping, and ReLU operators should be excluded from formal engines. Bit-accurate arithmetic verification belongs strictly to constrained-random UVM simulation checked against the golden C++/Python fixed-point model.

SystemVerilog Assertion (SVA) Example: Circular Buffer Integrity

The DMA front-end staging FIFO that feeds the activation memory uses a circular credit-based indexing mechanism to support streaming keyword spotting (KWS) audio frames without stalling the DMA. The property below proves that an incoming DMA write never corrupts unread entries in that FIFO across any arbitrary stall sequence.

// Property: Staging FIFO write pointer must never overrun the read pointer.
// Staging FIFO depth is 256 entries; credit counter tracks available empty slots.
module act_buf_safety_assert #(
  parameter int ADDR_WIDTH = 8
)(
  input  logic                  clk,
  input  logic                  rst_n,
  input  logic                  wr_en,
  input  logic                  rd_en,
  input  logic [ADDR_WIDTH:0]   occupancy_count,
  input  logic                  buf_full,
  input  logic                  buf_error
);

  // Buffer full signaling rule
  property p_full_flag_exact;
    @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    (occupancy_count == 256) |-> buf_full;
  endproperty
  a_full_flag: assert property (p_full_flag_exact);

  // Write when full must instantly flag an error and drop the write
  property p_no_overflow;
    @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    (buf_full && wr_en && !rd_en) |-> ##1 (buf_error && $stable(occupancy_count));
  endproperty
  a_no_overflow: assert property (p_no_overflow);

  // Liveness: Every granted inference compute cycle guarantees eventual consumption
  property p_eventual_read;
    @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    (occupancy_count > 0) |-> strong(##[1:1024] rd_en);
  endproperty
  a_eventual_read: assert property (p_eventual_read);

endmodule

SystemVerilog Assertion (SVA) Example: Buffer Handoff Handshake

A second invariant governs the ping-pong handoff itself. When the compute engine finishes filling a buffer it raises buf_ready, and the consumer acknowledges with buf_ack. Between those two events the handoff is still in flight: if buf_ready were allowed to drop before the acknowledgement arrived, the consumer could miss the buffer entirely and the next tile would overwrite data that was never read. The property below proves the flag is held until it is acknowledged, and the companion cover property proves the handshake actually occurs. 

// Property: the buffer-ready flag must not deassert before acknowledgement.
property p_handoff_flag_held;
  @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  (buf_ready && !buf_ack) |-> ##1 buf_ready;
endproperty
a_handoff_flag_held: assert property (p_handoff_flag_held)
  else $error("Assertion Failed: buf_ready dropped before buf_ack!");

c_handoff_completed: cover property (
  @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  buf_ready ##[1:$] buf_ack
);

The Assume-Guarantee Approach and Preventing Vacuity

Formal solvers only constrain input space through assume statements. A catastrophic pitfall is an over-constrained testbench: if an assumption specifies mutually exclusive conditions or impossible environment behaviors, the solver proves all assertions trivially true because the antecedent is never satisfied, a condition known as a vacuous proof.

Engineering Rule: Never accept an unbounded formal proof without generating coverage witnesses. For every assertion, write a companion cover property ensuring the prerequisite stimulus path can be exercised.

When modeling the AXI-Lite host, do not assume wvalid and awvalid arrive simultaneously; assume only standard protocol requirements (e.g., once awvalid is high, it remains stable until awready). Periodically run formal vacuity checks using commercial EDA tooling to spot dead branches where assumptions have unintentionally zeroed out legitimate operational scenarios.

Effort vs. Payoff for a Small Team

For a team dedicated to TinyEdge-NPU, spending 80 engineering hours writing structural FPV properties on the FSM, DMA credit counters, and AMBA bridges typically pays for itself many times over compared with spending those same hours debugging multi-cycle race conditions in dynamic waveform traces. Formal proofs catch the corner cases that waveform debugging finds last, if it finds them at all. Standard bus and pointer assertions should be configured during the RTL coding phase, not retrofitted during pre-tape-out crunch.

---

8.7 Best Practices and Sign-Off Criteria

Verification sign-off is the gate through which the TinyEdge-NPU passes from an active design under verification to frozen RTL ready for logic synthesis, floorplanning, and physical layout. Hitting sign-off requires hard metrics backed by reproducible, automated test regressions.

TinyEdge-NPU Verification Sign-Off Checklist

Table 8.4 defines the mandatory gating criteria that the TinyEdge-NPU design database must satisfy before RTL freeze.

Table 8.4: TinyEdge-NPU Verification Sign-Off Checklist
Verification Domain Metric / Criterion Target Threshold Status / Closure Vehicle
Code Coverage Statement / Line Coverage >98% overall (>95% raw un-waived RTL) Regression Suite (Excluding waived debug ports)
Code Coverage Branch / Condition Coverage >92% Simulation + Formal Reachability
Code Coverage Toggle Coverage >90% overall; 100% on external interfaces Un-toggled bits must be formally proven unreachable
Functional Coverage Cross-coverage: Layers × Dimensions × Stride 100% Covergroups in UVM Agent
Functional Coverage Bus Stall Injection (DMA Wait States) 100% Error & Backpressure Sequences
Formal Properties Control FSM, AMBA, and FIFO Invariants 100% Proven (0 Failures, 0 Vacuous) Bounded proof depth ≥ 50 cycles beyond worst-case burst
Power-Aware Simulation UPF Isolation, Level Shifting, Retention Flow 100% Assertion Pass Power-Aware VCS/Xcelium with Native Low Power (NLP) assertions
Golden Reference Matching Target Inference Networks (DS-CNN, 1-Layer KWS) Zero mismatches across 10,000 real audio frames Bit-accurate comparison against fixed-point C++ model
Bug Convergence Open Severity-1 / Severity-2 Defects 0 Open Defects Jira / Bugzilla issue tracking sign-off

Common Verification Mistakes in Edge AI Accelerators

Small-footprint NPU designs frequently suffer from subtle oversights that escape standard smoke testing:

  • Weak Scoreboard Tolerances: Dynamic scoreboards that use floating-point comparisons or allow a ±1 LSB margin of error on INT8 operations hide critical accumulator overflow, asymmetric rounding, and clipping bugs. The TinyEdge-NPU scoreboard must require identical, bit-exact results against the C++ Golden Reference.
  • Neglecting Corner-Case Tensor Dimensions: Verifying only power-of-two shapes (e.g., 16×16, 32×32) masks edge-case padding failures. Hardware address generators often break when channel counts are not multiples of the MAC array vector size (e.g., 3 input channels on initial acoustic spectrogram layers).
  • Skipping Power-Aware Simulation (UPF/CPF): The TinyEdge-NPU relies on aggressive power domains. Simulating only plain RTL hides isolation clamping bugs, such as an active-high isolation cell driving a 1 onto an active-low reset tree during sleep states. Power-aware simulation with gate-level retention validation is non-negotiable.
  • The "One-Seed Fallacy": Declaring victory after a regression suite passes on seed 0. The tiered regression, 50 seeds smoke, 500 nightly, 5,000+ weekend, is required to stress concurrent FIFO backpressure, asynchronous interrupt timings, and DMA bus grants.

Feeding Tape-Out Readiness

Achieving verification sign-off directly enables the physical design flow described in Chapters 11 through 13. A clean verification sign-off ensures that logic synthesis (Chapter 11) operates on locked functional micro-architecture, avoiding costly engineering change orders (ECOs) during clock-tree synthesis and place-and-route (Chapter 12). Assertions written and proven during the verification stage are also reused as dynamic monitors during post-route timing simulations with extracted SDF delays, establishing the final confidence barrier before generating tape-out GDSII (Chapter 12).

With mathematical correctness established through formal proofs and algorithmic fidelity validated against the reference model, the digital IP is sound. However, simulation runs at kilohertz speeds, wholly inadequate for running hundreds of hours of raw acoustic sensor data. To evaluate real-time keyword spotting with operational microphones and test firmware driver interactions, the verified RTL must now transition to the prototyping lab. Chapter 9 details the FPGA prototyping strategy for the TinyEdge-NPU.

Key Takeaways

  • Write the verification plan before the testbench: prioritize features by risk, trace every feature to a requirement, and define sign-off criteria up front.
  • Close coverage on three axes at once, functional, code, and assertion, with quantified gates (for example 100% of planned functional coverpoints, >98% line, >90% toggle with justified waivers).
  • A bit-accurate reference model is the foundation of NPU verification: it is the scoreboard, the stimulus source, and the arbiter of every datapath dispute.
  • Verify at both levels: block level for arithmetic, buffers, and FSMs; system level for end-to-end inference, power-state transitions, and back-to-back runs.
  • Build the UVM testbench around transaction-level comparison against the reference model, with sequences that cover directed bring-up, constrained-random stress, and power states.
  • Use formal verification where it pays: control FSM reachability, buffer pointer invariants, bus protocol compliance, and power-state correctness, and use simulation plus the reference model for the datapath.
  • Sign off on evidence, not on effort: green regressions across seeds, coverage at target, formal proofs complete, and no open waiver without a written justification.

Chapter 9: FPGA Prototyping

Simulation proved the TinyEdge-NPU correct; it cannot prove it useful. A bit-accurate model runs at kilohertz speeds, a UVM regression finishes in minutes, and neither one has ever heard a human voice. FPGA prototyping is where the IP meets the real world: a live microphone, a real clock, a real power rail, and a user saying the wake word while a washing machine runs in the background. This chapter builds the full FPGA demo flow for TinyEdge-NPU, from board selection and RTL partitioning to a working keyword-spotting demo, and shows how to measure the three numbers that decide whether the IP is ready: latency, power, and accuracy.

9.1 When and Why to Prototype

Every IP team faces the same question after verification sign-off: is an FPGA prototype worth the weeks it costs, or should the design go straight from simulation to synthesis and tape-out? The honest answer depends on what you still do not know. Simulation answers "is the logic correct?" Prototyping answers a different set of questions that simulation cannot reach: "does it work in real time?", "does it work with real data?", "does the firmware driver actually talk to it?", and "does anyone believe the demo?"

For TinyEdge-NPU, the case for prototyping is strong on all four counts. Keyword spotting is a real-time, streaming workload: audio arrives at 16,000 samples per second whether the hardware is ready or not, and a missed frame is a missed keyword. The workload is also data-dependent in ways that are hard to simulate at scale: background noise, accents, room acoustics, and microphone characteristics all shift the effective accuracy of the model, and the only way to measure that shift is to run real audio through the real datapath. Finally, the IP's customers, SoC teams integrating it into a home-security hub or a cooking robot, will ask for a demo before they sign a license. A board that wakes on a spoken keyword is worth more than a hundred slides of simulation waveforms.

flowchart TD SIM[Simulation + UVM
Kilohertz speeds] --> Q1{What is still
unknown?} Q1 -->|Real-time behaviour| FPGA[FPGA prototype] Q1 -->|Real sensor data| FPGA Q1 -->|Firmware interaction| FPGA Q1 -->|Customer confidence| FPGA Q1 -->|Logic correctness only| SKIP[Skip prototype
Go to synthesis] FPGA --> DEMO["Live demo:
mic → keyword → action"] FPGA --> MEAS[Measured latency
power, accuracy] DEMO --> SIGN[Prototype sign-off] MEAS --> SIGN SIGN --> CH10["Chapter 11: Synthesis"]

9.1.1 What a Prototype Proves — and What It Does Not

An FPGA prototype is a functional model of the IP running on reconfigurable hardware. It proves the RTL works at speed, that the bus interfaces behave under real traffic, that the firmware driver can configure and control the IP, and that the end-to-end application, in our case keyword spotting from a live microphone, produces the right answer in the right amount of time. It also exposes a class of bugs that simulation systematically misses: clock-domain crossing issues that only appear with real asynchronous clocks, reset sequencing problems that depend on power-on timing, and interface timing violations that a testbench's idealised bus functional model never generates.

What a prototype does not prove is equally important. FPGA timing is not ASIC timing: a design that closes timing at 100 MHz on an FPGA may still fail timing at 100 MHz in 28nm, because the routing delays, the cell delays, and the clock tree are entirely different. And the FPGA's lookup-table fabric has nothing in common with the standard-cell implementation that will ship. FPGA power is not ASIC power. The static power of an FPGA is orders of magnitude higher than the target, so absolute power numbers from the board are meaningless; only relative measurements (this configuration versus that one) carry information. And FPGA area is not ASIC area: the number of LUTs and block RAMs consumed says nothing about the square millimetres the IP will occupy. The prototype is a functional and system-level validation vehicle, not a substitute for the synthesis and physical design flow in Chapters 11 and 12.

Question Simulation FPGA prototype Silicon (Ch. 13)
Is the logic functionally correct? Yes — bit-accurate, exhaustive Yes — at speed, real traffic Yes — final proof
Does it meet real-time deadlines? Approximately — cycle counts only Yes — wall-clock latency Yes — at target clock
What is the accuracy on real audio? On recorded datasets only Yes — live microphone input Yes — in the product

9.1.2 The Cost of Prototyping — and When to Skip It

Prototyping is not free. A realistic budget for the TinyEdge-NPU prototype is four to six engineer-weeks: one week for board bring-up and tool flow, one to two weeks for RTL partitioning and synthesis to the FPGA, one week for the firmware driver and demo application, and one to two weeks for measurement, debugging, and demo polish. The hardware cost is modest: a mid-range development board with an on-board audio codec and microphone input costs a few hundred dollars. But the engineering time is the real expense, and it comes directly out of the schedule between verification sign-off and tape-out.

Skip the prototype when none of the four questions in Section 9.1 applies. If the IP is a drop-in replacement for a proven block with an identical interface, if the application is fully characterised by recorded datasets, if there is no firmware driver to validate, and if the customer accepts simulation evidence, then the prototype adds schedule without adding information. For TinyEdge-NPU, none of those conditions holds: the workload is live and streaming, the data is real-world audio, there is a driver to write, and the demo is a sales asset. The prototype earns its weeks.

The Prototype Rule: Build a prototype when you have a question that only real hardware at real speed with real data can answer. If every open question can be answered in simulation, the prototype is theatre. Skip it and tape out sooner.

9.2 Choosing the Platform and Partitioning the Design

The first concrete decision is the board. For TinyEdge-NPU, the requirements are narrow and they drive the choice directly: the board needs an audio input path (a PDM microphone interface or an I2S audio codec), enough block RAM to hold the model weights and activation buffers, a processor to run the demo firmware, and a way to get data on and off the board for measurement (UART at minimum, Ethernet or USB preferred). A mid-range SoC FPGA board, an FPGA fabric with a hard ARM core on the same chip, fits best, because the ARM core runs the firmware driver and the demo application while the fabric holds the NPU. A pure-FPGA board with a soft processor is workable but slower to bring up; a high-end emulation board is overkill for a 100k-gate IP.

The board we use for the worked example in this chapter is a representative mid-range SoC FPGA development board: a Xilinx Zynq-7000 class device (or its Intel/Altera equivalent) with 512 MB of DDR, an on-board audio codec with line-in and microphone input, UART over USB, and an SD card slot. The exact board matters less than the checklist it must satisfy, and that checklist is worth writing down before ordering anything.

Requirement Why it matters for TinyEdge-NPU Minimum acceptable
Audio input Live microphone is the whole point of the demo PDM mic input or I2S codec, 16 kHz, 16-bit
Block RAM Weights + activation buffers must fit on-chip ≥ 256 KB BRAM (model is ~120 KB quantised; the ASIC SRAM is parameterized 48–200 KB, §3.9 — the FPGA BRAM requirement is a board requirement, not the ASIC size)
Hard processor Runs firmware driver and demo app without a soft core Single ARM Cortex-A9 or equivalent
Host link Logging, dataset streaming, power measurement UART over USB; Ethernet preferred
Debug access Signal capture when the demo misbehaves JTAG + on-chip logic analyser support
Power measurement Relative power comparisons between configurations Accessible core supply rail or PMBus

9.2.1 Partitioning: What Goes in the Fabric, What Stays in Software

Partitioning is the decision that determines whether the prototype is a faithful model of the IP or a misleading one. The rule is simple: everything that will be silicon goes in the fabric, and everything that is genuinely a system-level function stays in software. For TinyEdge-NPU, that means the MAC array, the weight and activation buffers, the control FSM, the DMA engine, and the register interface all go in the FPGA fabric, implemented from the same RTL that will be synthesised for the ASIC. The audio front-end, the mel-filterbank feature extraction that converts raw PCM samples into the log-mel spectrogram the model consumes, is a judgement call. In the final SoC, the filterbank may run on the NPU itself, on a small DSP, or on the host processor. For the prototype, we put the filterbank in software on the ARM core: it is not part of the IP under validation, it is easier to tune in C than in RTL, and it keeps the fabric focused on the block being proven.

The one deliberate exception is the DMA path. In the ASIC, the NPU's DMA engine fetches weights and activations from system memory over the bus. On the FPGA, the equivalent is a DMA engine in the fabric reading from the board's DDR through the SoC's high-performance AXI ports. We implement the real DMA engine, not a test harness that preloads the buffers, because the DMA behaviour under backpressure, the buffer-fill versus compute race that the verification plan worried about in Chapter 8, is exactly what the prototype is meant to exercise. A prototype that preloads its buffers proves nothing about the memory system.

9.2.2 Clocking, Resets, and the FPGA-Specific Compromises

Three compromises are unavoidable when the RTL meets the FPGA, and each must be recorded as a known deviation from the ASIC implementation so that no one mistakes a prototype result for a silicon result. First, clocking: the ASIC runs the NPU at 100 MHz in burst mode and 20 MHz nominal (Chapter 3), on a single clock domain. The wake logic lives in a separate power domain, always-on while the NPU core is power-gated, but it runs on the same clock tree, not a second clock domain. On the FPGA, we run the fabric at 100 MHz, the same speed as the ASIC burst clock, so the measured cycle counts and latencies transfer directly to silicon with no scaling: the 4.2 ms DS-CNN-M inference measured on the board is the ASIC burst-mode latency. What the FPGA cannot reproduce is the 20 MHz nominal mode. The fabric has no reason to run that slowly, so nominal-mode latencies are computed from the measured cycle counts (420,000 cycles is 21 ms at 20 MHz), not measured. The one clocking limit that matters is that the FPGA's routing cannot reliably close timing on the MAC array much above ~125 MHz, which is why the fabric runs at the burst clock and no faster; the ASIC's 100 MHz burst target is set by the power budget, not by the FPGA.

Second, memories: the ASIC uses single-port SRAM macros with specific timing and power characteristics. The FPGA implements them in block RAM, which is dual-port and has different read latency. The buffer control logic is written to be memory-agnostic: it issues a read and waits for the data valid signal. So the difference is absorbed, but the exact cycle counts for a buffer refill differ by one or two cycles between the FPGA and the ASIC. The verification plan's cycle-level checks were written against the RTL's abstract memory interface, not against a specific SRAM macro, precisely so that this difference does not invalidate the prototype.

There is a second memory deviation that matters more than the BRAM timing difference, and it is a capacity and configuration difference, not a timing one. On the prototype, the whole ~120 KB DS-CNN-M model is loaded into block RAM once at start-up and stays there; the NPU never fetches weights from DDR during an inference. The ASIC's L configuration does the same: the 120 KB model fits the 128 KB weight buffer in its entirety (§3.9, Chapter 4). So for the DS-CNN-M workload there is no weight-loading deviation at all. The streaming path exists for models that exceed the buffer (the 250 KB industrial model of Chapter 4): there the ASIC holds one layer's weights at a time and the DMA engine streams the next layer's weights from system memory while the current layer computes. The prototype never exercises that weight-streaming path, the layer-by-layer DMA traffic, the double-buffer handoff between layers, and the contention that streaming adds to the memory system, so a customer whose model exceeds the weight buffer cannot rely on the prototype's DMA numbers. The DMA measurements in Section 9.4 cover the input-tensor transfer, not the per-layer weight streaming the ASIC does for models exceeding the weight buffer. That path is validated in simulation and, for the system-level contention question, by the synthetic-traffic middle path in Chapter 10. Record the deviation wherever the DMA numbers are quoted: the prototype's DMA figures describe the input path, not the ASIC's full memory traffic.

Third, clock gating: the ASIC's aggressive clock gating, the feature that delivers the sub-100 µW sleep figure, is largely ineffective on an FPGA, where the clock network is fixed and gating a clock saves little power. The prototype therefore cannot measure the sleep power, and it cannot demonstrate the wake-up latency of the gated domains with fidelity. What it can demonstrate is the functional correctness of the power-state FSM: that the IP enters and exits each state in the right order, that the isolation and retention controls assert in the right sequence, and that no transaction is lost across a sleep-wake cycle. Power is measured properly later, on silicon (Chapter 13); the prototype proves the state machine, not the milliwatts.

The worked-example board is a Zynq-7020-class device (XC7Z020: 53,200 LUTs, 106,400 flip-flops, 140 block RAMs of 36 Kb, 220 DSP slices).

9.3 The Full FPGA Demo Flow: Microphone to Keyword

The demo is the centrepiece of the prototype, and it is worth designing it as carefully as the RTL. A good demo has a single, legible story: a person speaks, the system hears the keyword, and something visible happens within a fraction of a second. Everything in the demo flow exists to make that story true and measurable. This section builds the flow end to end for TinyEdge-NPU, from the microphone to the detection output.

9.3.1 The Pipeline, Stage by Stage

Audio enters through the PDM microphone at 16 kHz and 16-bit resolution. The ARM core's filterbank converts the raw PCM stream into log-mel spectrogram frames: 25 ms windows advanced every 10 ms, 40 mel bins per frame, giving a 40-dimensional feature vector every 10 ms. The firmware accumulates the most recent 100 frames, one second of audio, into an input tensor, quantises it to INT8 using the scale and zero-point the model was trained with, and hands it to the NPU through the DMA engine. The cadence is explicit: inference runs every 100 ms on a sliding window, each inference consuming the most recent 100 frames, so the NPU performs ten inferences per second, not one inference per second on a fresh, non-overlapping window. The NPU runs the keyword-spotting model (DS-CNN-M, a depthwise-separable convolutional network with roughly 120 KB of INT8 weights, running on the 8×8 MAC array) and returns a 12-class probability vector: eleven keywords plus a "background / unknown" class. The firmware applies a confidence threshold and a simple smoothing rule, two consecutive inferences above threshold, and raises the detection output: an LED, a UART log line, and, in the full demo, a GPIO pulse that wakes the host system.

flowchart LR MIC[PDM microphone
16 kHz, 16-bit] --> FEAT[Mel-filterbank
25 ms window, 10 ms hop
40 mel bins] FEAT --> ACC[Frame accumulator
100 frames = 1 s] ACC --> QUANT[INT8 quantise
scale + zero-point] QUANT --> DMA[DMA to NPU
input buffer] DMA --> NPU[TinyEdge-NPU
DS-CNN inference] NPU --> PROB[12-class
probabilities] PROB --> THR[Threshold +
2-frame smoothing] THR --> OUT[LED + UART log
+ GPIO wake pulse]

The end-to-end latency budget is the number the demo lives or dies by. The product-level target, not a Chapter 3 requirement, is that a keyword is detected within 500 ms of the end of the spoken word, fast enough that the user perceives the response as immediate. (Chapter 3's requirement is narrower: REQ-P-001 bounds the inference at under 12 ms at the 20 MHz nominal clock; see Section 9.4.4 for how the measured numbers relate to it.) The budget decomposes as follows: 10 ms for the final feature frame to arrive, 28 ms typical (41 ms worst case) for the DMA transfer of the input tensor, 4.2 ms for the DS-CNN-M inference, and a few milliseconds for thresholding and output, a single-pass total of 68 ms measured on the board (Table 9.1), with the remaining ~23 ms of the decomposition accounted for in Section 9.4.4. The fabric runs at 100 MHz, the same speed as the ASIC burst clock, so the measured 4.2 ms is the ASIC burst-mode inference latency. There is no scaling to apply. At the 20 MHz nominal clock the same 420,000 cycles take 21 ms, which exceeds REQ-P-001: DS-CNN-M meets the requirement only in burst mode, while the smaller DS-CNN-S (71,862 cycles, 3.6 ms at 20 MHz) meets it at nominal too. The total is far inside the 500 ms product target either way, which leaves generous headroom. And that headroom is itself a useful result, because it tells the product team the IP can afford a more accurate model without breaking the latency target.

9.3.2 Bring-Up Sequence: From Bitstream to First Detection

Bring-up is where prototypes are won or lost, and the difference between a smooth bring-up and a week of debugging is almost always the order in which things are proven. The sequence that works is deliberately boring: prove each layer before adding the next, and never debug two layers at once.

  1. Board and tools first. Load a trivial bitstream, a blinking LED, and confirm the JTAG chain, the clock, and the programming flow. If this fails, the problem is the board or the tools, not the design.
  2. Processor and UART. Boot the ARM core, print "hello" over UART, and confirm the DDR is accessible. This proves the processing system and the host link before any custom logic is involved.
  3. Register interface only. Load the full bitstream but exercise only the NPU's register interface: read the ID register, write and read back a configuration register, and confirm the values match. This proves the AXI-Lite path from the host bus clock into the NPU clock domain, the design's only clock-domain crossing (Chapter 5).
  4. DMA loopback. Program a DMA transfer from DDR to the input buffer and back, without invoking the NPU. This proves the memory path and the buffer addressing.
  5. One directed inference. Load a single known input tensor and its expected output (taken from the Chapter 8 reference model), run one inference, and compare the output vector bit-for-bit. This is the first real proof that the NPU works in hardware, and it uses the same golden vectors as the simulation regression.
  6. Streaming audio. Connect the microphone, run the filterbank, and feed live frames. Confirm the feature vectors match the offline computation for a recorded clip before trusting live input.
  7. Full demo. Enable the threshold and smoothing, speak the keyword, and watch the LED. Only now is the demo real.

Each step has a clear pass criterion and a clear suspect if it fails. Step 3 failing points at the bus or the clock crossing; step 5 failing points at the NPU datapath or the buffer contents; step 6 failing points at the audio front-end. The most common bring-up mistake is skipping steps 3 and 4 and going straight to a full inference, which leaves four possible culprits for every failure and turns debugging into guesswork.

9.3.3 The Demo Application and the Two Demo Modes

The demo runs in two modes, and both matter. Live mode is the showpiece: a person speaks into the microphone and the board responds. It is what the customer sees, and it is the mode that exposes real-world accuracy: background noise, room echo, and microphone placement all show up here and nowhere else. Replay mode is the engineering tool: the board streams a recorded dataset (the same clips used in simulation) from the SD card through the identical pipeline, so that accuracy can be measured repeatably and compared directly against the simulation numbers. Replay mode is how you know whether a live-mode failure is a hardware problem or an acoustics problem: if replay matches simulation but live does not, the hardware is fine and the room is the variable.

The demo application also implements the second workload, acoustic event detection: a glass-break, smoke-alarm, or baby-cry event detector that runs on the same NPU with a different model loaded from the SD card. The two models share the pipeline and differ only in weights and the class list, which demonstrates the IP's programmability: the same silicon runs different models without any RTL change. Switching models is a firmware operation: halt the NPU, DMA in the new weights, update the configuration registers, and resume. The switch takes under 50 ms on the prototype, which is fast enough to time-share the two workloads on a single device.

9.4 Measuring Real Latency, Power, and Accuracy

A prototype that cannot be measured is a demo, not an experiment. The three numbers that matter, latency, power, and accuracy, each need a defined measurement method, a defined instrument, and a recorded result. Without that discipline, the prototype produces anecdotes ("it felt fast") instead of evidence ("inference takes 4.2 ms at 100 MHz, measured over 1,000 runs"). This section defines the three measurements and works through the results for TinyEdge-NPU.

9.4.1 Latency: Hardware Timestamps, Not Stopwatches

Latency is measured with hardware timestamps, not with a stopwatch and not with software timers. The NPU's register interface exposes a free-running cycle counter and a start-of-inference timestamp register; the firmware reads the counter immediately before triggering an inference and immediately after the completion interrupt fires, and the difference is the inference latency in fabric clock cycles. The DMA transfer time is measured the same way, with timestamps around the DMA start and completion. The audio front-end latency, the time from a sample arriving at the microphone to the corresponding feature frame being ready, is measured by toggling a GPIO pin on sample arrival and on frame completion and observing the two edges on an oscilloscope.

The measurement is repeated 1,000 times across a representative set of inputs, because a single measurement proves nothing about the distribution. For TinyEdge-NPU, the inference latency is essentially deterministic. The model is a fixed sequence of layers with no data-dependent control flow, so the spread is small. The DMA latency, by contrast, varies with DDR contention from the ARM core, and the spread is the interesting number: the worst case, not the average, is what the system must be designed around.

9.4.2 Power: Relative Measurements and What They Can Prove

As noted in Section 9.2, the FPGA cannot measure the ASIC's absolute power. What it can measure is the relative power of different configurations, and that is genuinely useful. The method is to measure the current on the board's core supply rail, either through the board's PMBus telemetry or with a current probe on the rail, while running a fixed workload, and to compare configurations: clock gating enabled versus disabled, the 8×8 MAC array fully utilised versus half utilised, INT8 versus INT4 mode, and the NPU active versus idle. Each comparison yields a ratio, and the ratios validate or refute the architectural assumptions from Chapter 4. If disabling clock gating doubles the measured power, the gating logic is worth its area; if it changes nothing, the gating is either broken or ineffective, and that is worth knowing before tape-out.

The sleep power cannot be measured on the FPGA at all. The fabric's static power dominates by orders of magnitude, so the sub-100 µW sleep figure from Chapter 3 is validated by other means: the power-state FSM is proven functionally on the prototype, and the leakage number comes from the synthesis power analysis in Chapter 11 and the silicon measurement in Chapter 13. The prototype's job is to prove the state machine, and the measurement's job is to prove the ratios.

9.4.3 Accuracy: Live, Replay, and the Confusion Matrix

Accuracy is measured in replay mode first, because replay is repeatable. The board streams a held-out test set from Google Speech Commands, 2,000 one-second clips, balanced across the eleven keywords, background noise, and the "unknown" class, through the identical pipeline used for live audio, and the firmware logs the predicted class for each clip. The result is a confusion matrix, and the matrix is more informative than a single accuracy percentage: it shows exactly which keywords are confused with each other, which is the information the model team needs to improve the training data. The headline numbers for the TinyEdge-NPU prototype, running DS-CNN-M, are a 95.5% top-1 accuracy on the held-out set in replay mode, against 95.8% for the FP32 reference model in simulation. The 0.3-point gap is the quantisation loss between the FP32 reference model and the INT8 model the hardware runs. Not a hardware error. The RTL matches the bit-accurate INT8 golden model exactly (Chapter 8's zero-tolerance policy: a replay run scored against the INT8 golden model agrees bit-for-bit), so the 0.3 points are a float-versus-quantised model delta, and they sit inside REQ-P-003's allowance of 0.5 percentage points against the FP32 reference model.

Live accuracy is measured separately, with a scripted protocol rather than an informal demo: five speakers, each speaking each keyword ten times, in three acoustic conditions (quiet room, office background noise at roughly 50 dB SPL, and a kitchen with a running extractor fan). The live accuracy is lower than replay: 93.1% in the quiet room, 89.7% in the office, 84.2% in the kitchen. And that degradation is expected and informative: it quantifies the acoustic robustness gap and tells the product team how much margin the model needs for real deployment. The numbers also set the threshold policy: in a noisy environment, the two-frame smoothing rule from Section 9.3 is tightened to three frames, trading a few tens of milliseconds of latency for fewer false triggers.

9.4.4 Worked Measurement Results

Table 9.1 collects the headline measurements from the TinyEdge-NPU prototype. Every number in it was measured on the board by the method described in the preceding sections, and the table records the measurement method alongside the result so that the numbers are auditable. The fabric runs at 100 MHz, the same speed as the ASIC burst clock, so the FPGA results are the ASIC burst-clock results. No scaling is applied, and there is no projected-ASIC column. The one translation the reader must make is to the 20 MHz nominal clock: cycle counts are clock-independent, so a latency measured in cycles converts directly (420,000 cycles is 4.2 ms at 100 MHz and 21 ms at 20 MHz). The requirement column cites Chapter 3 where a requirement exists; the 500 ms detection figure is a product-level target, not a Chapter 3 requirement, and is labelled as such.

Metric Method FPGA result (100 MHz) Requirement (Ch. 3) Verdict
