Relative power, INT4 vs INT8 mode Core rail current, same model 0.71× (29% saving) Informational Recorded

Three rows deserve commentary. First, the DMA row needs a plain-English reading, because 28 ms for a 4 KB transfer looks wrong. And in raw-bandwidth terms it is. The input tensor is 100 frames × 40 bins × 1 byte = 4 KB; at 100 MHz on a 32-bit AXI bus that is 1,000 beats, about 10 µs of raw transfer time. The measured 28 ms is therefore not a bandwidth number at all: it is the end-to-end time from the firmware kicking off the transfer to DMA completion, and it is dominated by overhead: roughly 5 ms of DMA programming and cache maintenance, ~3 ms of interrupt latency on a loaded ARM core, ~15 ms of DDR contention with the filterbank's continuous traffic and UART logging, and ~5 ms of HP-port arbitration and refresh jitter. The ~120 KB model weights are not in this figure: they are loaded into BRAM once at start-up and held there (Section 9.2.2), so the per-inference DMA moves only the input tensor. The worst case (41 ms) is the same transfer when the ARM is writing log data heavily. The system implication is that the DMA worst case, not the typical, must be budgeted. And the firmware should avoid heavy DDR traffic during an inference window. The reason matters too: the DMA path is overhead- and contention-bound, not bandwidth-bound, so a faster bus would not fix it; only reducing the firmware overhead or the competing DDR traffic would.

Second, the end-to-end 68 ms needs its components added up honestly. The budget in Section 9.3.1 accounts for 10 ms (final frame) + 28 ms (DMA) + 4.2 ms (inference) + a few milliseconds (thresholding and output), about 45 ms, leaving ~23 ms unaccounted for. The missing time is real work, not rounding: roughly 2 ms of INT8 quantisation and tensor packing on the ARM, ~5 ms of DMA programming and cache maintenance, ~3 ms of interrupt latency between NPU completion and the firmware's threshold decision, ~8 ms of DDR contention and arbitration jitter while the filterbank and logging compete for memory, and ~5 ms of frame-boundary alignment. That sums to ~23 ms, and 45 + 23 = 68 ms. The table's 68 ms is the single-pass latency from the final frame's arrival to the detection output; the two-frame smoothing rule adds one more 100 ms inference interval, so the user-perceived detection latency is ~170 ms typical, still inside the 500 ms product target with roughly a 3× margin.

Third, the inference row deserves a plain statement, because it is the one place the prototype does not fully meet Chapter 3. REQ-P-001 allows under 12 ms at the 20 MHz nominal clock. DS-CNN-M needs 420,000 cycles: 4.2 ms in burst mode, which passes comfortably, but 21 ms at nominal, which does not. The smaller DS-CNN-S needs 71,862 cycles, 0.72 ms in burst mode and 3.6 ms at nominal, and passes at both clocks. The honest conclusion is that the shipped DS-CNN-M model meets the latency requirement only in burst mode, and the product must either burst the NPU clock for keyword inference or ship DS-CNN-S as the default model with DS-CNN-M as a burst-mode option. That is a product decision, not a prototype failure, and it is recorded here rather than hidden behind the burst-mode number.

Finally, the false-trigger rate of 0.4 per hour was measured over a single 24-hour background run; it is a useful datapoint but not a statistically strong one, and the production claim will need a longer run on silicon. These observations are the kind of result that only a prototype can produce, and they changed decisions: the DMA budgeting rule and the threshold policy.

Measure the Distribution, Not the Point: A single latency or accuracy number is a press release, not engineering evidence. Report the typical, the worst case, and the sample size. And design the system around the worst case.

9.6 Debugging on the FPGA: When the Demo Misbehaves

Every prototype misbehaves, and the difference between a one-hour debug and a one-week debug is the instrumentation that was built in before the failure. The FPGA's advantage over silicon is that its internals are observable: the on-chip logic analyser can capture any signal in the fabric, and the design can be re-synthesised with extra debug hooks in minutes rather than months. The discipline is to use that advantage deliberately: to decide in advance which signals are worth capturing, and to build the capture into the design rather than bolting it on after the fact.

9.6.1 The Debug Toolkit: Logic Analyser, Waveform Dump, and Signal Forcing

Three tools cover nearly every prototype failure. The on-chip logic analyser (Xilinx ILA, Intel Signal Tap, or the equivalent) captures a window of internal signals around a trigger condition and uploads it to the host for viewing as a waveform. The trigger is the critical choice: triggering on the NPU's completion interrupt captures the end of an inference, but triggering on the absence of a completion interrupt within a timeout captures the hang. And hangs are the failures that matter. A good default trigger set is: completion interrupt, DMA error flag, bus error response, and a watchdog timeout on the control FSM. Each one captures a different failure class, and together they cover the space.

Waveform dump is the second tool: a mechanism to stream a selected set of signals out of the FPGA continuously, over UART or Ethernet, so that a long-running failure can be correlated with the system-level event that caused it. For TinyEdge-NPU, the useful dump is the control FSM state, the buffer fill levels, and the DMA engine's current address, sampled every millisecond. When the demo misses a keyword, the dump shows whether the NPU was idle, mid-inference, or stuck waiting for a buffer. And that single fact usually identifies the culprit.

Signal forcing is the third tool, and the most powerful: the ability to drive an internal signal to a chosen value from the host, bypassing the logic that normally produces it. Forcing the DMA engine's "buffer ready" signal, for example, lets you test the NPU's inference path in isolation from the memory system; forcing the power-state FSM into a particular state lets you test the wake-up sequence without waiting for the full sleep cycle. Forcing is the FPGA equivalent of the emulator-style debug features used on FPGA prototypes in industry. Waveform dump and signal forcing are the two capabilities that turn a prototype from a black box into a debuggable system, and they should be designed in from the start, with a dedicated debug register interface, rather than added as an afterthought when the first hang appears.

flowchart TD FAIL["Demo failure:
missed keyword / hang"] --> Q{Which tool?} Q -->|Hang, no completion| ILA[Logic analyser
trigger on watchdog timeout] Q -->|Wrong output| DUMP[Waveform dump
FSM state + buffer levels] Q -->|Suspect a subsystem| FORCE[Signal forcing
isolate DMA / FSM / NPU] ILA --> WAVE["Waveform: where did
the FSM stop?"] DUMP --> CORR[Correlate with
system event] FORCE --> ISOL[Subsystem proven
good or bad] WAVE --> FIX[Fix + re-run] CORR --> FIX ISOL --> FIX FIX --> REG[Replay mode
regression]

9.6.2 A Worked Debug Story: The Missing Keyword

A concrete example makes the method real. During the TinyEdge-NPU prototype bring-up, the demo intermittently missed the keyword "lights", perhaps one time in twenty, while all other keywords were reliable. The simulation regression was green, the replay-mode accuracy for "lights" was 97%, and the failure did not reproduce on demand. The waveform dump showed the pattern: on every missed "lights", the NPU was still busy with the previous inference when the next input tensor arrived, and the DMA engine dropped the new tensor rather than queueing it. The root cause was a one-cycle race in the buffer handoff: the "buffer ready" flag was asserted for a single cycle at the same moment the DMA engine sampled it, and when the two coincided, the handoff was lost. The fix was a two-line RTL change, holding the ready flag until the DMA engine acknowledged it, followed by a formal proof of the handoff invariant (the Chapter 8 property that the flag cannot deassert before acknowledgement). The prototype found a bug that simulation had missed because the simulation testbench always delivered the ready flag with a full cycle of setup margin, while the real DMA engine sampled it at the exact boundary. This is the prototype earning its keep: a real bug, found by real hardware, fixed and proven before tape-out.

9.7 Lessons Learned and Best Practices

Prototyping a small IP is a solved problem in outline and a fresh problem in detail on every project. The lessons below are the ones that recur across projects and that the TinyEdge-NPU prototype confirmed.

  • Prototype the question, not the chip. Decide before you start which questions the prototype must answer, and design the demo and the measurements around those questions. A prototype built without a question list becomes a demo that proves nothing.
  • Bring up in layers, and never debug two layers at once. The seven-step sequence in Section 9.3 exists because every skipped step is repaid with interest in debugging time.
  • Keep a replay mode. Live demos are for customers; replay mode is for engineering. Without a repeatable mode, every measurement is anecdotal and every regression is unverifiable.
  • Measure the distribution. Report typical, worst case, and sample size for every number. Design the system around the worst case.
  • Build the debug hooks in from day one. Logic analyser triggers, waveform dump, and signal forcing are cheap to add during design and expensive to retrofit during a debug crisis.
  • Record every deviation from the ASIC. The fabric clock (100 MHz, the same as the ASIC burst clock, but with no 20 MHz nominal mode), the block-RAM memories, the whole-model-in-BRAM loading, and the ineffective clock gating are all documented compromises. An undocumented compromise becomes a false conclusion.
  • Log everything. Every live run should capture its inputs and outputs to the SD card. Today's demo is tomorrow's training data.
  • Use the prototype to sell. A board that wakes on a spoken keyword is the most persuasive marketing asset the IP has. Budget time to polish the demo, not just to make it work. The difference between a working demo and a polished one is the difference between a technical proof and a sale.
  • Know what the prototype cannot prove. Absolute power, ASIC timing, and silicon area are out of scope. Say so explicitly in every report, so that no one budgets or commits on the basis of a number the prototype cannot produce.
  • Close the loop to verification. Every bug the prototype finds should become a regression test in the Chapter 8 testbench and, where possible, a formal property. A prototype bug that is fixed but not captured in the regression suite will recur on the next project.

9.8 Using Sensor Data: Voice, Air Quality, and Beyond

Keyword spotting is the headline workload, but the prototype's sensor interface is general, and the same board can exercise the IP against other edge-sensor workloads. The reason to do this during prototyping, rather than after tape-out, is that different sensor data stresses different parts of the IP. Voice is a streaming, low-bandwidth, high-temporal-correlation signal; air-quality data is slow, bursty, and dominated by long-term drift; vibration data is high-frequency and impulsive. Running all three through the same NPU reveals whether the IP is genuinely a general edge-AI accelerator or merely a keyword spotter that happens to be programmable.

9.8.1 Air Quality and Environmental Sensing

The air-quality demo replaces the microphone with a particulate-matter and gas sensor (PM2.5, VOC, temperature, humidity) sampled once per second, and the model is a small anomaly detector: given the last 60 seconds of sensor readings, is the air quality deteriorating, and should the device alert? The workload is instructive because it is almost the opposite of keyword spotting in its demands on the hardware. The input tensor is tiny (60 time steps × 4 channels), the inference is infrequent (once per second rather than ten times per second), and the power budget is dominated by sleep rather than by active compute. The prototype result that matters here is not latency (the inference takes under a millisecond) but the sleep-wake cycle: the NPU must wake, run, and return to retention in a few milliseconds, ten times less often than in the keyword case, and the measured wake latency on the prototype (1.8 ms from interrupt to first MAC operation) validates the power-state FSM's exit sequence in a way that keyword spotting, which rarely sleeps, never exercises.

9.8.2 Vibration and Acoustic Events

The acoustic-event model from Section 9.3 already covers one non-speech workload, but a vibration sensor adds a different axis: the input is a 3-axis accelerometer sampled at 1 kHz, and the model classifies machine states (normal, bearing wear, imbalance, impact). The interesting prototype finding is that the same 8×8 MAC array and the same buffer architecture handle the vibration model without modification. The only change is the weights and the feature extraction, both of which are firmware. That is the programmability claim from Chapter 4 made concrete, and it is worth demonstrating to a customer who is deciding whether one IP can cover several products.

9.8.3 Building a Sensor Dataset on the Prototype

The prototype is also a data-collection instrument. Every live run can log its inputs, the raw audio, the feature vectors, and the NPU's outputs, to the SD card, and those logs become training and regression data for the next model iteration. This closes a loop that simulation cannot: the model's failure cases in the real world (the keywords it missed in the kitchen, the false triggers during a phone call) are captured with the exact inputs that caused them, and the model team can retrain against them. The discipline is to log continuously during any demo or field trial, with timestamps, so that every observed failure is reproducible. A prototype that is not logging is a missed opportunity to improve the model.

flowchart TD SENS[Sensor inputs
mic / air / vibration] --> LOG[Prototype logs to SD
raw + features + outputs] LOG --> FAIL[Failure cases
missed keywords, false triggers] FAIL --> RETRAIN[Model team retrains
with real failure data] RETRAIN --> NEW[New weights
v1.1] NEW --> REPLAY[Replay mode
verify on prototype] REPLAY --> PASS{Accuracy
improved?} PASS -->|Yes| DEPLOY[Deploy to demo] PASS -->|No| FAIL

With the prototype proven, the demo working, the latency and accuracy measured, the bugs found and fixed, the IP has passed its last functional gate before the backend flow. The numbers from this chapter feed directly into the next part of the book: the latency headroom justifies the synthesis targets in Chapter 11, the power ratios inform the power planning in Chapter 12, and the measured accuracy is the baseline against which silicon will be correlated in Chapter 13. Where the FPGA could not go far enough, a full SoC with a processor, memory system, and peripherals running real software around the NPU, the next chapter takes up the story with emulation.

Key Takeaways

  • Prototype when you have a question only real hardware at real speed with real data can answer: real-time behaviour, live sensor data, firmware interaction, and customer confidence.
  • Partition honestly: everything that will be silicon goes in the fabric from the same RTL; system functions such as the audio filterbank stay in software; never fake the DMA path.
  • Record the FPGA compromises explicitly: 100 MHz fabric clock with no 20 MHz nominal mode, block-RAM memories, whole-model-in-BRAM loading, ineffective clock gating, and never present FPGA numbers as silicon numbers. The fabric runs at the ASIC burst clock, so latencies transfer directly; nominal-mode latencies are computed from cycle counts, not measured.
  • Bring up in layers with a clear pass criterion at each step, from blinking LED to register access to DMA loopback to a single golden inference to live audio.
  • Measure latency, power, and accuracy with defined methods and report the distribution: TinyEdge-NPU measured 4.2 ms DS-CNN-M inference at 100 MHz burst clock (21 ms at the 20 MHz nominal clock, burst mode only for REQ-P-001), 95.5% replay accuracy, and 93.1% live accuracy in a quiet room.
  • Keep a replay mode alongside the live demo. It is the only way to make accuracy measurements repeatable and comparable with simulation.
  • Build debug hooks in from day one: logic-analyser triggers on hangs, waveform dumps of FSM and buffer state, and signal forcing to isolate subsystems.
  • Log every live run to the SD card. Today's demo inputs are tomorrow's model training data.
  • Close the loop: every prototype bug becomes a regression test and, where possible, a formal property in the Chapter 8 testbench.

Chapter 10: Emulation & Pre-Silicon Validation

The FPGA prototype proved the TinyEdge-NPU works as a block: it hears a keyword, it runs the model, it meets its latency budget. But the IP will not ship as a block. It will ship inside a system-on-chip, surrounded by a processor, a memory subsystem, peripherals, and a software stack. And none of those were present on the prototype board in their production form. Emulation is the step that validates the IP in that system context, at speeds that let real software run for long enough to matter. This chapter explains when the FPGA is no longer enough, how emulation fits a small IP project, and, just as importantly, when to skip it. It describes the full method first, then shows why this project skipped it and what it did instead: a strengthened prototype with synthetic contention that retired the biggest system risk at a tenth of the cost of full emulation (Section 10.3.4).

10.1 When FPGA Is Not Enough

The FPGA prototype has three hard limits, and each one defines the point at which emulation becomes necessary. The first is capacity: a single FPGA holds the NPU comfortably, but it cannot hold the NPU plus a representative SoC, the application processor, the memory controllers, the interconnect fabric, and the peripheral set, at the same time. The prototype validated the IP; it did not validate the system the IP lives in. The second is speed with software: the prototype runs the NPU at speed, but the software around it is a thin demo application. Booting a real operating system, running a real driver stack, and exercising the system for hours of simulated use is beyond what a single-FPGA prototype can do in a practical amount of time. The third is observability at system scale: the prototype can capture the NPU's internal signals, but it cannot give a coherent, time-correlated view of the processor, the interconnect, and the NPU together. And system-level bugs live exactly in the interaction between those blocks.

For TinyEdge-NPU, the concrete trigger is the home-security hub use case from Chapter 2. The hub's SoC runs an application processor under Linux, the NPU shares the memory system with a video pipeline, and the wake-word path must work while the video pipeline is streaming. On the prototype, the NPU had the DDR largely to itself; in the hub, it contends with a video encoder for bandwidth, and the DMA latency worst case measured in Chapter 9 (41 ms) was only a hint of what contention can do. Validating that the keyword path still meets its 500 ms budget while the video pipeline is running, and that a burst of video traffic cannot starve the NPU's weight fetch, requires the full system, running real software, for long enough to hit the contention patterns. That is an emulation workload, not a prototype workload.

flowchart TD FPGA[FPGA prototype
NPU + thin demo app] --> LIM{Limits reached?} LIM -->|Single block only| EMU[Emulation] LIM -->|Short software runs| EMU LIM -->|No system view| EMU LIM -->|Block-level questions only| DONE[Prototype is enough
Go to synthesis] EMU --> SOC["Full SoC:
CPU + memory + peripherals + NPU"] SOC --> SW["Real software:
OS boot + drivers + apps"] SW --> SYS["System validation:
contention, boot, power, security"] SYS --> SIGN[Pre-silicon sign-off]

10.1.1 The Three Questions Emulation Answers

Emulation earns its place by answering three questions that neither simulation nor the prototype can. First, does the system boot and run? The processor must come out of reset, the boot ROM must execute, the bootloader must load the operating system, the NPU driver must probe and initialise the IP, and the application must start, end to end, with the production software stack, not a demo harness. A surprising number of IP integration bugs are found here: a reset value that the driver does not expect, an interrupt number that collides with another peripheral, a clock that the power management firmware never enables. Second, does the system behave under load? The NPU, the video pipeline, and the processor all share the interconnect and the memory system, and their interaction determines whether the real-time deadlines hold. Emulation runs the system long enough, millions of cycles per second, for hours, to hit the contention patterns that a directed test would never construct. Third, does the software work? The driver, the runtime, and the application are validated against the real RTL, not against a virtual model, which catches the class of bugs where the software's assumptions about the hardware are subtly wrong: a register that is read-clear when the driver expects read-only, a status bit that the driver polls in a tight loop and starves the bus with.

The Emulation Test: If your open questions are all about the IP block itself, stay on the FPGA. If they are about the IP inside a system, boot, contention, drivers, and software, you need emulation, and the FPGA will not get you there no matter how long you run it.

10.2 Using Emulation for Larger System Integration

Emulation, in this context, means running the RTL of the full SoC, or a representative subset of it, on a specialised emulation platform: a large multi-FPGA system, or a processor-based emulator, provided either as a hosted service or as hardware in a lab. The distinction from the Chapter 9 prototype is one of scale and purpose: the prototype is a single FPGA holding one IP and a demo; the emulator holds the whole SoC and runs the production software stack. The speeds are comparable in order of magnitude. Emulation typically runs at 1–10 MHz effective, slower than the FPGA prototype's 100 MHz but orders of magnitude faster than RTL simulation's kilohertz, and that speed is what makes booting an operating system practical: a Linux boot that would take days in simulation takes minutes in emulation.

The commercial platforms in this space are Cadence Palladium, Siemens Veloce, and Synopsys ZeBu, processor-based or multi-FPGA emulators sold as hardware for a lab or as hosted capacity. For a small IP team the realistic choice is rarely a purchase: it is whichever platform the hosted service or the lead customer already runs, because the model-build effort is largely platform-specific (compilation, debug instrumentation, and the software interface all differ). Cloud FPGA capacity (for example, AWS EC2 F1 instances) is the low end of the same idea: large multi-FPGA capacity on demand, without the emulator's transaction-level debug tooling. The rest of this chapter is written platform-neutrally; where a platform matters, compilation time, debug visibility, the software interface, it is called out.

10.2.1 What Goes Into the Emulation Model

The emulation model for the TinyEdge-NPU hub SoC contains the application processor (with its caches), the interconnect fabric, the DDR memory controller and a memory model, the NPU with its DMA engine, the audio front-end, the video pipeline, and the peripheral set (UART, I2C, SPI, GPIO). Two components are deliberately abstracted rather than modelled in full RTL. The analogue and mixed-signal blocks, the audio codec, the power management unit, are replaced by behavioural models, because their transistor-level detail adds nothing to a digital system validation and would slow the emulator to a crawl. The DDR memory is modelled at the transaction level with a timing-accurate model rather than as a full DRAM array, which preserves the contention behaviour that matters while keeping the model fast enough to run.

The NPU itself goes in as the same RTL that was prototyped in Chapter 9, no modifications, no wrappers beyond the standard bus interfaces, because the point of the exercise is to validate the production RTL in the system, and any modification would invalidate the result. The one addition is instrumentation: transaction monitors on the NPU's bus interfaces that log every transfer with a timestamp, so that a system-level failure can be traced back to the exact bus transaction that caused it. This is the system-scale version of the Chapter 9 waveform dump, and it serves the same purpose: when the keyword is missed, the log shows whether the NPU was starved of bandwidth, whether the driver issued the wrong command, or whether the processor was simply too busy to service the interrupt.

For software-heavy validation there is a faster mode worth knowing about: transaction-level co-emulation. In this mode the processor and its software run on the host workstation (or on a virtual prototype) while only the NPU RTL runs on the emulator, with the two sides communicating over a transaction-level link such as SCE-MI. The software runs orders of magnitude faster than in full RTL emulation, which makes driver bring-up and long software runs practical. But it validates neither the processor's RTL nor the cycle-accurate behaviour of the interconnect, so it answers software questions, not system-integration questions. Use it for driver development; do not mistake it for system validation.

10.2.2 The Emulation Test Plan: System Scenarios, Not Block Tests

The emulation test plan is organised around system scenarios rather than block-level tests, because the value is in the interaction. The scenarios for the hub SoC are written as user stories, each with a measurable pass criterion:

  • Cold boot to first detection. Power on, boot Linux, load the NPU driver, initialise the audio path, and detect the first keyword. Pass criterion: first detection within 60 seconds of power-on, with no manual intervention, at ~10 MHz effective emulation speed with a stripped-down boot image. A full Linux boot is roughly a billion cycles, which is 100 to 1,000 seconds across the 1–10 MHz emulation range, so the 60-second figure is achievable only at the fast end of that range with a minimal root filesystem; with a full distribution image, budget several minutes and set the criterion accordingly.
  • Keyword under video load. Stream 1080p video through the encoder while continuously running keyword spotting. Pass criterion: no keyword missed, and the worst-case detection latency stays under the 500 ms budget across a one-hour run.
  • Model switch under load. Switch the NPU from the keyword model to the acoustic-event model while the video pipeline is running. Pass criterion: the switch completes in under 100 ms with no dropped video frames and no missed audio frames.
  • Sleep and wake. Put the SoC into its deep-sleep state, wake it on a keyword, and confirm the system returns to full operation. Pass criterion: wake-to-detection under 2 seconds, with the NPU's retention state intact.
  • Driver stress. Run the driver through rapid configuration changes, error injection on the bus, and concurrent access from two processes. Pass criterion: no driver crash, no hung transaction, and every error reported cleanly to the application.
  • Long soak. Run the full system, video, audio, keyword spotting, and periodic model switches, continuously for 72 hours of wall-clock time. Pass criterion: no hangs, no memory leaks in the driver, and no degradation in detection latency over the run. State the soak in emulated time as well as wall-clock time: at 5 MHz effective speed the emulated SoC executes about 1.3×1012 cycles in 72 hours, roughly three and a half hours of SoC-equivalent operation at the 100 MHz burst clock. So the soak validates 72 hours of wall-clock stability (driver leaks, host-side issues) but only a few hours of SoC operation. A soak that must cover a week of SoC operation needs either a higher emulation speed or a longer wall-clock run, and the criterion should say which.

to first detection] --> LOAD[Keyword under
video load] LOAD --> SWITCH[Model switch
under load] SWITCH --> SLEEP[Sleep and wake] SLEEP --> DRV[Driver stress] DRV --> SOAK[72-hour soak] SOAK --> SIGN["System sign-off:
boot, contention,
drivers, soak"]

10.2.3 Speed, Cost, and the Practicalities of Access

Emulation is not a purchase most small IP teams make. A commercial emulation platform costs from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars, plus the engineering effort to build and maintain the model. For a small IP project like TinyEdge-NPU, the realistic routes are narrower: rent time on a hosted emulation service (charged by the hour, with the model built by the IP team and run remotely), partner with a lead customer who already owns an emulator and will run the SoC model as part of their own integration, or use a cloud FPGA service that offers large multi-FPGA capacity on demand. Each route has the same prerequisite: the SoC-level RTL and the software stack must exist and be reasonably stable. And each is justified only by the system questions in Section 10.1. The hosted-service route is the most common for a first IP: a few hundred hours of emulation time, at a cost comparable to a single engineer-month, buys the system validation that would otherwise wait for first silicon, where the same bug costs a respin.

Emulation's debug visibility is also worse than the FPGA prototype's, and the team should plan for it. On the prototype (Chapter 9), the logic analyser can capture any signal and a new probe costs a re-synthesis of minutes. On an emulator, signal-level visibility requires the signals to be compiled into the trace database before the run; probing a signal that was not traced means recompiling the model, which takes hours, and the waveform capture depth is limited by the trace memory. The practical consequence is that emulation debug depends far more on the transaction monitors and the software-visible state (registers, memory, driver logs) than on waveforms. Instrument those first, and decide the trace list before the first long run, not after the first failure.

10.3 Recommendations for Small IP Projects: Cost, Benefit, and When to Skip Emulation

For a small IP team, emulation is the most expensive validation step in the flow, and the decision to do it, or to skip it, deserves the same rigour as any other engineering trade-off. The framework below is the one we apply to TinyEdge-NPU, and it generalises to any small accelerator IP.

10.3.1 The Cost Side, Honestly Counted

The cost of emulation has four components, and teams that count only the first one underestimate the total by a factor of three. Access cost is the price of the platform itself: hosted-service hours, a share of a partner's emulator, or cloud FPGA capacity. For a project of TinyEdge-NPU's scale, budget 200–400 emulation hours, which at hosted-service rates is roughly the cost of one engineer-month. Model-build cost is the engineering effort to assemble the SoC-level model, integrate the software stack, and write the system scenarios, typically two to four engineer-weeks for a small SoC, and it cannot start until the RTL and the software are both stable. Debug cost is the effort to triage the failures emulation finds; system-level failures are harder to debug than block-level ones, because the culprit can be in any of half a dozen blocks, and each one can consume days. Schedule cost is the calendar time the emulation phase adds between verification sign-off and tape-out, typically four to eight weeks including model build, runs, and debug. For a team with a fixed tape-out date, that schedule cost is often the deciding factor.

Cost component TinyEdge-NPU estimate Notes
Access (hosted service) 200–400 hours Roughly one engineer-month of cost
Model build 2–4 engineer-weeks Needs stable RTL and software first
Debug of system failures 2–6 engineer-weeks Highly variable; system bugs are slow to triage
Schedule 4–8 calendar weeks Between verification sign-off and tape-out
Total ~2–3 engineer-months + 4–8 weeks The number to weigh against the benefit

A worked example makes the total concrete. Take the midpoints of the table: 300 hosted hours, three engineer-weeks of model build, and four engineer-weeks of debug, roughly two engineer-months of engineering plus 300 hours of hosted capacity, against a schedule cost of about six weeks between verification sign-off and tape-out. The access cost alone is roughly one engineer-month at hosted-service rates; vendor pricing is quoted per project and varies by platform, capacity, and contract, so no dollar rate is given here. Get a quote for the actual model size and hour count. The comparison that matters is against the cost of being wrong: a system-level bug found on first silicon costs a metal fix if one is possible, a respin if it is not, plus the weeks of schedule and the credibility with the customer while the fix is made. Section 10.3.2 weighs that trade-off; the point of the worked example is that the emulation decision is a ~2–3 engineer-month decision, not a rounding error, and it should be made with the full total in view.

10.3.2 The Benefit Side: What Emulation Buys That Nothing Else Can

Against that cost, emulation buys exactly one thing: confidence about the system before silicon exists. The value of that confidence is measured by the cost of being wrong. A system-level bug found in emulation costs a few days of debug and an RTL change. The same bug found on first silicon costs a metal fix if one is possible, a respin if it is not, and, most expensively, the weeks of schedule and the credibility with the customer while the fix is made. For an IP whose first customer is integrating it into a product with its own launch date, a system bug that escapes to silicon can cost the design win. The break-even is therefore not a technical calculation but a commercial one: if the IP's first integration is a high-stakes, schedule-critical product, emulation is cheap insurance; if the first integration is a low-volume evaluation board with a tolerant customer, it is an expensive luxury.

10.3.3 When to Skip Emulation

There are honest reasons to skip emulation, and a small IP team should not feel obliged to do it. Skip it when all of the following hold: the IP's system context is simple (a single processor, a single memory, no competing high-bandwidth traffic); the software stack is thin (a bare-metal driver rather than a full operating system); the first customer is integrating the IP into a platform they already own and will validate themselves; and the schedule does not allow four to eight weeks for the emulation phase. For TinyEdge-NPU's first outing, a standalone evaluation board for a home-security hub maker who will do their own system integration, three of the four hold, and the team chose a middle path: no full emulation, but a strengthened prototype.
