10.3.4 The Middle Path: Synthetic Contention on the Prototype

The middle path is worth describing in detail, because it is the pragmatic choice for most small IP projects. And for TinyEdge-NPU it is the choice the team actually made. Instead of a full SoC emulation, the team extended the Chapter 9 prototype in two ways. First, a second DMA engine was added to the fabric to generate synthetic competing traffic, a programmable bandwidth hog that mimics the video pipeline's memory access pattern, with configurable burst size and duty cycle. Second, the firmware driver was exercised against a bus functional model of the processor's memory system that introduced realistic latency and backpressure, rather than the idealised model used in simulation. Together, these two additions answered the most important system question: does the keyword path hold its deadline under contention? They did it at a tenth of the cost of full emulation.

The contention generator is a small piece of RTL, and its design is the whole point. It is a DMA engine like the NPU's own, but its descriptors are programmed to reproduce the video pipeline's traffic shape: large sequential writes (1080p frame buffers, tens of kilobytes per burst) issued at a configurable duty cycle, so the team can sweep the competing load from 0% to 100% of the high-performance port's bandwidth and record the NPU's detection latency at each step. The generator shares the DDR with the NPU through the same interconnect the SoC will use, so the arbitration behaviour is real. The NPU's DMA waits behind the video-pattern bursts exactly as it would wait behind a real encoder. The bus functional model for the driver is the software-side complement: it stalls the processor's memory accesses with realistic latency distributions instead of returning data immediately, which exposes the driver bugs (a status bit polled in a tight loop, a timeout set too short) that an idealised model hides.

The measurement uses the same hardware-timestamp method as Chapter 9, and the headline result is a single worked number. The baseline single-pass detection latency is 68 ms (Table 9.1: 10 ms frame + 28 ms DMA + 4.2 ms inference + ~23 ms of quantisation, setup, interrupt, and contention overhead + a few milliseconds of thresholding and output). Under maximum synthetic contention the same measurement rises to 112 ms, a 44 ms penalty, decomposed as follows: the DMA transfer grows from 28 ms to ~70 ms (+42 ms), because the NPU's DMA is lower priority than the video-pattern traffic and spends most of the extra time waiting for arbitration, not moving data; and interrupt latency grows by ~2 ms as the ARM core stalls on DDR. The inference itself is unchanged at 4.2 ms. Compute is contention-free; only the memory path slows. Including the two-frame smoothing confirmation, the user-perceived detection latency rises from ~170 ms to ~212 ms, still inside the 500 ms product target with more than a 2× margin. The sweep also showed where the knee is: latency stays near baseline up to roughly 70% utilisation of the high-performance port, then rises steeply as DMA queueing dominates. That single measurement retired the biggest system risk, the keyword path under video load, without an emulator, and it set the system rule that the NPU's DMA must not be the lowest-priority master on the port.

10.3.5 If You Do Emulate: A Short Checklist

  • Start the model build early. The SoC model and the software stack take weeks to assemble; begin them as soon as the RTL is feature-complete, not after verification sign-off, or the emulation phase lands on the critical path.
  • Write system scenarios, not block tests. The value is in boot, contention, driver stress, and soak, the scenarios from Section 10.2.2, not in re-running block-level tests at system speed.
  • Instrument before you need it. Bus transaction monitors with timestamps, and a way to correlate a system failure with the transaction that caused it, are the difference between a day of debug and a week.
  • Budget debug time, not just run time. The emulation runs themselves are the cheap part; triaging system-level failures is where the weeks go.
  • Decide the exit criteria in advance. Which scenarios must pass, and what happens if one fails late? A pre-agreed criterion prevents the emulation phase from expanding indefinitely.
  • Feed every finding back to verification. Like the prototype bugs in Chapter 9, every emulation finding should become a regression test or a formal property, so the next project starts from a stronger base.

Emulation is the last pre-silicon validation gate, and for a small IP it is an optional one, justified by system complexity and commercial stakes, not by habit. Whether the team emulates fully, takes the middle path of synthetic contention, or skips it with eyes open, the decision should be recorded with its reasoning, because the next project's team will ask the same question. With the system validated, by emulation, by the strengthened prototype, or by a conscious decision to defer it to the lead customer's integration, the IP is ready for the backend flow. Chapter 11 takes the verified, prototyped RTL and turns it into a netlist: synthesis, constraints, and static timing analysis.

Key Takeaways

  • The FPGA proves the block; emulation proves the block inside a system: boot, contention, drivers, and real software running for hours.
  • Emulation answers three questions nothing else can: does the system boot and run, does it behave under load, and does the software actually work against the real RTL.
  • Build the emulation model from the production RTL with behavioural models only for analogue blocks and DRAM; add bus transaction monitors with timestamps before the first run.
  • Organise the test plan around system scenarios: cold boot, keyword under video load, model switch under load, sleep and wake, driver stress, and a 72-hour soak, each with a measurable pass criterion.
  • Count the full cost honestly: access, model build, debug, and four to eight weeks of schedule, totalling roughly two to three engineer-months for a small IP.
  • Skip emulation when the system context is simple, the software is thin, and the first customer will validate the integration themselves. And say so explicitly, with the reasoning recorded.
  • Consider the middle path: synthetic competing traffic plus a realistic bus model on the prototype can retire the biggest system risk, the deadline under contention, at a tenth of the cost of full emulation.
  • Whatever the choice, feed every finding back into the Chapter 8 regression suite and formal properties.

Chapter 11: Synthesis, Constraints & Static Timing Analysis

This chapter takes the TinyEdge-NPU from RTL to a synthesized, timing-closed netlist. The worked examples use the S configuration (48 KB SRAM: 32 KB weights + 16 KB activations; §3.9). Synthesis and static timing analysis are where an NPU design either becomes shippable IP or remains a lab curiosity: the constraints you write, the way you structure the MAC array, and the discipline of your sign-off flow decide what every future customer actually receives.

11.1 Introduction: Where IP Becomes Silicon or Remains a Lab Curiosity

Every semiconductor engineering team has witnessed a "phantom" IP block: an accelerator core that achieves flawless functional verification in an RTL simulator, sails through zero-delay behavioral regressions, and demonstrates state-of-the-art throughput in cycle-accurate architectural models, yet never ships in volume. Invariably, these designs die in the physical implementation flow. They either fail static timing closure across target Process, Voltage, and Temperature (PVT) corners, consume three times their allotted leakage budget due to pathological sizing loops, or self-destruct on the tester because an improperly constrained cross-clock handshake caused catastrophic meta-stability.

For an ultra-low-power edge processor like the TinyEdge-NPU, the synthesis and Static Timing Analysis (STA) boundary is where abstract mathematical intent meets the brutal physics of 28nm CMOS. Operating within an envelope of <5 mW active power at 100 MHz and <100 μW standby leakage across ~1 mm², there is zero margin for over-design. In deep sub-micron regimes, dynamic power is aggressively governed by capacitive charging (\(P_{dyn} = \alpha C V_{dd}^2 f\)), but total silicon footprint and leakage power (\(P_{leak} = I_{leak} V_{dd}\)) are determined largely by how hard the logic synthesis and physical optimization engines must work to meet your timing constraints.

flowchart LR A[RTL Design] --> B[SDC Constraints] B --> C[Synthesis] C --> D[Static Timing Analysis] D --> E[Physical Silicon] D -->|violations| B C -->|restructure| A

If you under-constrain the design, omitting external PCB traces, neglecting clock skew uncertainty, or applying overzealous false paths, the synthesis engine will insert small, high-resistance, low-drive standard cells (e.g., X1 or X0.5 inverters and gates). The resulting layout will pass a naive timing check, but the actual silicon will violate hold times at fast-cold corners or setup times at slow-hot corners, yielding dead silicon or dismal wafer yields. Conversely, if you over-constrain the design, applying unachievable input delays, excessive clock uncertainties, or failing to declare multi-cycle arithmetic pipelines, the synthesis engine panics. It maps logic into aggressive, leaky multi-threshold (Low-\(V_t\) or Extreme-Low-\(V_t\)) cells, inflates buffer trees, inserts parallel drive stages, and turns your 0.95 mm² footprint into a 1.4 mm² thermal radiator that blows past the 5 mW power ceiling.

As an IP provider, your delivery vehicle is not just the synthesizable Verilog or SystemVerilog source. Your primary deliverable to the SoC integration team is an airtight, portable Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) package. The SDC contract defines the boundary assumptions: what the SoC host must provide in drive strength and arrival time, what the NPU guarantees at its interfaces, and which internal paths are mathematically decoupled from the single-cycle clock. In this chapter, we develop the discipline required to bridge this chasm, using the TinyEdge-NPU as our living reference.

---

11.2 Writing Robust SDC Constraints for an NPU

Modern machine learning accelerators exhibit heterogeneous timing behaviors: massive parallel compute arrays (8×8 INT8 matrix engines) switching simultaneously, high-density SRAM macros with fixed setup and access times, synchronous low-bandwidth control registers (AXI-Lite), and ultra-low-frequency always-on (AON) power-management blocks. Constraining such a design requires a disciplined approach to clock architectures, I/O boundaries, and timing exceptions.

11.2.1 Clocks, Uncertainty, and Jitter Budgeting

The TinyEdge-NPU features two distinct asynchronous clock domains:

  • clk_core: The primary computation clock, running at a nominal 100 MHz (\(T_{clk} = 10.0\text{ ns}\)) within the switchable core power domain. It drives the 8×8 INT8 MAC array, the weight decoder, activation buffers, and the AXI-Lite slave interface.
  • clk_aon: The always-on low-power clock, sourced from an on-chip RC oscillator or real-time clock (RTC), running at a nominal 32.768 kHz or 1 MHz (\(T_{clk} = 1.0\text{ }\mu\text{s}\) in our implementation). It controls the wake-up sequencer, power-switch controller, and interrupt aggregation logic.

A common mistake in constraint design is modeling a clock as a mathematically pure edge. Real clocks exhibit phase jitter, duty-cycle distortion (DCD), and clock network insertion delay skew. In SDC, we model these non-idealities using set_clock_uncertainty and set_clock_transition.

flowchart LR A[Clock Period 10 ns] --> B[Combinational Delay] B --> C[Setup Margin] C --> D[Clock Uncertainty] D --> E[Positive Slack Means Pass]

Clock uncertainty must be partitioned into two distinct physical components: jitter (a cycle-to-cycle variation that affects both pre-CTS synthesis and post-CTS signoff) and skew (spatial variations across the clock tree). Prior to Clock Tree Synthesis (CTS), the clock uncertainty value represents the sum of expected clock tree skew plus phase jitter. Post-CTS, the physical clock tree is fully propagated; thus, the uncertainty parameter must be dialed down in your signoff script to represent only the random jitter and margin components:

# Pre-CTS Budgeting (Synthesis Phase)
# Setup uncertainty: 200ps jitter + 250ps expected skew = 450ps
set_clock_uncertainty -setup 0.450 [get_clocks clk_core]
# Hold uncertainty: 150ps expected skew margin
set_clock_uncertainty -hold  0.150 [get_clocks clk_core]

# Post-CTS Signoff Budgeting (STA Phase)
# Clock tree is propagated; skew is physically calculated by the tool.
# Setup uncertainty: only residual PLL jitter + margin
set_clock_uncertainty -setup 0.150 [get_clocks clk_core]
set_clock_uncertainty -hold  0.050 [get_clocks clk_core]

For generated clocks, such as clock gating cells or internal frequency dividers, you must rely on the cell library's Integrated Clock Gating (ICG) functional arcs. If your design utilizes an architectural clock divider (for instance, stepping the core clock down to 50 MHz for an ultra-low-power sensor interface mode), you must explicitly use create_generated_clock referencing the master clock source pin. Relying on the tool to infer generated clocks through logic gates risks broken clock tree tracing and phase inversion errors.

11.2.2 Input/Output Boundary Constraints

An NPU IP block is a tenant within a larger customer SoC. The core does not interface with the outside world in a vacuum; it interfaces through pad cells, crossbar interconnects, and intermediate logic levels. If you fail to specify I/O constraints, synthesis treats input pins as infinitely fast sources and output pins as driving zero capacitance, resulting in undersized boundary cells that fail miserably upon SoC integration.

AXI-Lite Control Interface

The AXI-Lite interface operates synchronously to clk_core. A careful IP specification budgets the total cycle time (\(10.0\text{ ns}\)) between the upstream SoC interconnect and the NPU boundary. We allocate a standard 60/40 timing split:

  • External SoC budget: 60% of cycle time (\(6.0\text{ ns}\)) for upstream register clock-to-Q, routing across the SoC fabric, and logic stages in the interconnect crossbar.
  • NPU internal budget: 40% of cycle time (\(4.0\text{ ns}\)) for internal setup time, input buffering, and address decode logic.
# AXI-Lite Input Constraints (Setup max = 6.0ns, Hold min = 1.0ns)
set_input_delay -clock clk_core -max 6.0 [get_ports {s_axi_awaddr[*] s_axi_awvalid s_axi_wdata[*] s_axi_wvalid s_axi_araddr[*] s_axi_arvalid}]
set_input_delay -clock clk_core -min 1.0 [get_ports {s_axi_awaddr[*] s_axi_awvalid s_axi_wdata[*] s_axi_wvalid s_axi_araddr[*] s_axi_arvalid}]

# AXI-Lite Output Constraints (Downstream takes up to 4.0ns setup; min hold = 0.5ns)
set_output_delay -clock clk_core -max 4.0 [get_ports {s_axi_awready s_axi_wready s_axi_bvalid s_axi_arready s_axi_rvalid s_axi_rdata[*]}]
set_output_delay -clock clk_core -min 0.5 [get_ports {s_axi_awready s_axi_wready s_axi_bvalid s_axi_arready s_axi_rvalid s_axi_rdata[*]}]
Embedded SRAM Macros

The TinyEdge-NPU integrates a 32 KB Weight SRAM and a 16 KB Activation SRAM (S configuration, §3.9). These are not standard cell logic; they are pre-compiled, hard macro blocks delivered via foundry memory compilers. In our floorplan, these SRAMs are internal to the IP, but their timing arcs dictate the core's maximum performance. SRAM interfaces exhibit asymmetric, demanding timing characteristics:

  • Setup requirements: Macro address (ADDR), write enable (CEN, WEN), and write data (D) pins require substantial setup margins, frequently 1.2 ns to 1.8 ns in a 28nm low-power process.
  • Clock-to-Q access times (\(T_{access}\)): Output read data (Q) is not available immediately; the internal sense amplifiers require \(2.5\text{ ns}\) to \(3.5\text{ ns}\) following the rising clock edge to drive valid data.

When synthesis compiles the MAC logic that consumes Q, it has only \((T_{clk} - T_{access} - T_{setup\_MAC})\) remaining in the cycle. If \(T_{access} = 3.2\text{ ns}\), clock uncertainty is \(0.45\text{ ns}\), and register setup is \(0.2\text{ ns}\), the logic paths from the SRAM output ports down into the INT8 multiplier trees have only \(10.0 - 3.2 - 0.45 - 0.2 = 6.15\text{ ns}\) of physical logic propagation budget. Constraints must preserve every picosecond of this path; synthesizing the core without properly characterizing these macro timing models via .lib files will lead to catastrophic setup violations.

11.2.3 Timing Exceptions Discipline

Timing exceptions, false paths and multicycle paths, are the sharpest razor in digital design. Used correctly, they save vast silicon area and milliwatts of dynamic power. Used incorrectly, they mask real design flaws, leading to silicon that must be permanently down-clocked or completely respun. The cardinal engineering rule of timing exceptions is: Exceptions must represent physical, architectural reality, never an escape mechanism to suppress timing violations.

flowchart TD subgraph CORE[Core Domain 100 MHz] A[Control FSM] --> B[Config Registers] end subgraph AON[Always-On Domain 32 kHz] C[Wake Controller] --> D[Power State] end A -->|CDC false path| C C -->|CDC false path| B
False Paths

A path is false if it is structurally impossible for a signal transition to propagate along that path and be latched by the receiving clock edge during valid functional operation. In the TinyEdge-NPU, two primary categories of paths qualify as false:

  1. Static Configuration Registers: Hyperparameters such as cfg_activation_type (ReLU, ReLU6, Pass-through), cfg_conv_stride, and cfg_weight_base_addr are written via the AXI-Lite interface prior to initiating a tensor computation. Once the NPU_START bit is strobed, these registers remain completely static throughout hundreds of thousands of compute cycles until the NPU_DONE interrupt fires. Synthesis must not size up these nets to meet a 100 MHz single-cycle path into the MAC arithmetic control logic.
  2. Asynchronous Reset and Power-State Handshakes: Signals crossing between the switchable clk_core domain and the always-on clk_aon domain (e.g., pwr_ack, iso_ctrl_n, and asynchronous reset assertions) are synchronized through multi-stage flip-flop synchronizers. While the functional transfer is critical, the precise cycle-to-cycle edge relationship between the original driver and the first synchronizer flip-flop cannot be guaranteed. These paths are declared false, shifting the verification burden to CDC (Clock Domain Crossing) analysis tools to guarantee MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures).
Warning: Never apply wildcards across full hierarchical modules, such as set_false_path -to [get_cells u_power_ctrl/*]. This can inadvertently turn synchronous reset networks, clock-gate enables, and internal state machine paths into unconstrained logic, blinding your static timing reports to real functional failures.
Multicycle Paths (MCP)

A multicycle path instructs STA to expand the timing window beyond one clock cycle for setup, while modifying the hold relationship accordingly. In TinyEdge-NPU, there are two prime candidates for multicycle paths:

  1. Accumulator Drain and Post-Processing Requantization: In an INT8 convolution, MAC accumulation is carried out at high speed in 32-bit registers over many sequential cycles (e.g., accumulating across 64 input channels). Only when a channel reduction terminates does the core trigger the post-processing pipeline: taking the 32-bit accumulated sum, multiplying by a fixed-point quantization scale factor (\(M_0\)), adding an output zero-point offset (\(Z_3\)), applying an activation clamp, and saturating to INT8. This requantization path is heavily arithmetic. Rather than inserting a deep, pipeline-register stage that costs power and flip-flop area, the architecture assigns this datapath two full clock cycles, enabled by an architectural state machine strobe (requant_en).
  2. Weight-Load Burst Sequencer: During SRAM block-fetch configurations, multi-cycle address calculation and bank pre-charge enables follow an alternating cadence, permitting two full clock cycles for SRAM address stabilization before the memory latch activates.

When declaring a multicycle path for setup, you must almost always adjust the hold path. Under default SDC rules, if you declare a setup multicycle of \(N\) cycles without adjusting hold, the tool assumes the hold check must be performed against the edge immediately preceding the new setup edge, meaning the hold check moves from cycle 0 to cycle \(N-1\)! For a two-cycle path, failing to specify -hold 1 forces the tool to check hold at cycle 1 instead of cycle 0, requiring the physical synthesis tool to insert hundreds of redundant delay buffers to delay data by an entire clock period.

# Correct Two-Cycle MCP Specification:
set_multicycle_path 2 -setup -from [get_pins u_mac_array/accum_reg[*]/C] \
                             -to   [get_pins u_post_proc/requant_out_reg[*]/D]
set_multicycle_path 1 -hold  -from [get_pins u_mac_array/accum_reg[*]/C] \
                             -to   [get_pins u_post_proc/requant_out_reg[*]/D]
flowchart LR A[Launch Edge Cycle N] --> B[Logic Delay Two Cycles] B --> C[Setup Capture Cycle N plus 2] A --> D[Hold Check Cycle N plus 1] D --> C
Clock Groups and Exception Discipline

When multiple clocks exist on an SoC, the default behavior of STA is to evaluate timing between every possible permutation of clock edges across all domains. Because clk_core (100 MHz) and clk_aon (1 MHz) share no common harmonic integer relationship and their phase relationship is completely arbitrary, any timing path between them is physically meaningless. We decouple them globally using set_clock_groups:

set_clock_groups -asynchronous \
  -group [get_clocks clk_core] \
  -group [get_clocks clk_aon]

Using set_clock_groups -asynchronous commands the timing engine to instantly ignore all timing paths spanning these two clock domains in either direction. It is functionally equivalent to applying a bi-directional set_false_path between the clocks, but it is executed much earlier in the analysis graph compilation, significantly reducing timing graph memory overhead and synthesis runtime.

---

11.3 Complete Worked SDC for the TinyEdge-NPU

Below is the complete, production-grade SDC constraint file for the TinyEdge-NPU core IP. It is structured systematically: establishing process environments, instantiating clock objects, asserting drive and load boundary assumptions, and applying rigorous timing exceptions. Every segment includes inline architectural rationale.

################################################################################
# Design Constraints (SDC) for TinyEdge-NPU
# Target Technology: GlobalFoundries / TSMC 28nm Low-Power CMOS
# Operating Condition: Worst-Case Slow-Slow (SSG), 0.81V, 125C (Setup signoff)
#                      Fast-Fast (FFG), 0.99V, -40C (Hold signoff)
# Nominal Core Frequency: 100 MHz (10.0 ns period)
# Always-On Frequency:    1.0 MHz (1000.0 ns period)
################################################################################

# ==============================================================================
# 1. Environment & Operating Assumptions
# ==============================================================================
set_units -time ns -resistance kOhm -capacitance pF -voltage V -current mA

# Model the drive capability of an upstream driving pin (e.g., standard BUFF_X4)
set_driving_cell -lib_cell BUFX4_LVT [get_ports {s_axi_* pwr_req_i aon_rst_n_i core_rst_n_i}]

# Model realistic downstream capacitive loading on NPU output pins
# Standard 28nm standard-cell input capacitance is roughly 1-3 fF (0.001-0.003 pF)
# We set an external load ceiling of 20 fF to represent SoC routing track capacitance
set_load 0.020 [all_outputs]

# Heavy load on interrupt and event lines traversing back across the SoC
set_load 0.050 [get_ports {npu_irq_o pwr_ack_o}]

# ==============================================================================
# 2. Clock Definitions
# ==============================================================================

# Master Compute Clock: 100 MHz (10.0 ns)
create_clock -name clk_core \
  -period 10.000 \
  -waveform {0.000 5.000} \
  [get_ports clk_core_i]

# Always-On Management Clock: 1.0 MHz (1000.0 ns)
create_clock -name clk_aon \
  -period 1000.000 \
  -waveform {0.000 500.000} \
  [get_ports clk_aon_i]

# Slew rate (transition time) on input clock ports to reflect clock tree buffers
set_input_transition 0.080 [get_ports clk_core_i]
set_input_transition 0.250 [get_ports clk_aon_i]

# ==============================================================================
# 3. Clock Network Modeling (Pre-CTS Budgets)
# ==============================================================================

# Setup uncertainty: Phase jitter (150ps) + Target insertion skew (250ps) + margin (50ps)
set_clock_uncertainty -setup 0.450 [get_clocks clk_core]
# Hold uncertainty: Skew variation between adjacent local leaf sinks
set_clock_uncertainty -hold  0.150 [get_clocks clk_core]

# Uncertainty for the ultra-slow AON domain
set_clock_uncertainty -setup 5.000 [get_clocks clk_aon]
set_clock_uncertainty -hold  1.000 [get_clocks clk_aon]

# Define clock domain relationships: clk_core and clk_aon are fully asynchronous
set_clock_groups -asynchronous \
  -group [get_clocks clk_core] \
  -group [get_clocks clk_aon]

# ==============================================================================
# 4. Input / Output Delays: AXI-Lite Slave Interface (clk_core)
# ==============================================================================
# The external host interconnect claims 60% of setup cycle (6.0ns).
# The external host claims a minimum clock-to-Q/flight delay of 1.0ns for hold.

set AXI_INPUTS [get_ports { \
  s_axi_awaddr[*] \
  s_axi_awprot[*] \
  s_axi_awvalid   \
  s_axi_wdata[*]  \
  s_axi_wstrb[*]  \
  s_axi_wvalid    \
  s_axi_bready    \
  s_axi_araddr[*] \
  s_axi_arprot[*] \
  s_axi_arvalid   \
  s_axi_rready    \
}]

set_input_delay -clock clk_core -max 6.000 $AXI_INPUTS
set_input_delay -clock clk_core -min 1.000 $AXI_INPUTS

# Output responses must meet downstream setup constraints.
# Downstream logic requires 4.0ns setup margin; generates 0.5ns minimum hold.
set AXI_OUTPUTS [get_ports { \
  s_axi_awready \
  s_axi_wready  \
  s_axi_bresp[*] \
  s_axi_bvalid  \
  s_axi_arready \
  s_axi_rdata[*] \
  s_axi_rresp[*] \
  s_axi_rvalid  \
}]

set_output_delay -clock clk_core -max 4.000 $AXI_OUTPUTS
set_output_delay -clock clk_core -min 0.500 $AXI_OUTPUTS

# ==============================================================================
# 5. Input / Output Delays: Always-On Domain (clk_aon)
# ==============================================================================
# Extremely wide cycles allow relaxed multi-nanosecond budgets.

set_input_delay  -clock clk_aon -max 50.000 [get_ports pwr_req_i]
set_input_delay  -clock clk_aon -min  5.000 [get_ports pwr_req_i]

set_output_delay -clock clk_aon -max 50.000 [get_ports pwr_ack_o]
set_output_delay -clock clk_aon -min  5.000 [get_ports pwr_ack_o]

# Interrupt line is registered in clk_core, routed to external SoC interrupt controller
set_output_delay -clock clk_core -max 4.500 [get_ports npu_irq_o]
set_output_delay -clock clk_core -min 0.500 [get_ports npu_irq_o]

# ==============================================================================
# 6. Timing Exceptions: False Paths
# ==============================================================================

# 6.1 Asynchronous Resets
# The resets are asserted asynchronously and deasserted synchronously through 
# specialized reset-synchronizer macros (u_rst_sync_*).
set_false_path -from [get_ports core_rst_n_i]
set_false_path -from [get_ports aon_rst_n_i]

# 6.2 Power Management Handshake Crossings
# Handshake bits from the Core power domain entering AON synchronizers
set_false_path -to [get_pins -hierarchical *u_sync_core_to_aon*/d_in_reg[0]/D]
set_false_path -to [get_pins -hierarchical *u_sync_aon_to_core*/d_in_reg[0]/D]

# 6.3 Static Configuration Registers (Decoupled from runtime inference)
# These registers are written during the AXI initialization phase and remain 
# locked while the MAC execution sequencer (u_ctrl_fsm/state != IDLE) is active.
set_false_path -from [get_pins -hierarchical u_regs/cfg_layer_dim_reg[*]/C]
set_false_path -from [get_pins -hierarchical u_regs/cfg_act_type_reg[*]/C]
set_false_path -from [get_pins -hierarchical u_regs/cfg_quant_scale_reg[*]/C]
set_false_path -from [get_pins -hierarchical u_regs/cfg_quant_offset_reg[*]/C]

# ==============================================================================
# 7. Timing Exceptions: Multicycle Paths
# ==============================================================================

# 7.1 Requantization & Saturation Pipeline
# The INT32 accumulation array feeds the requantization scaling unit.
# The compute FSM asserts 'requant_enable' every alternating cycle per channel.
# Setup is extended to 2 cycles (20.0 ns); Hold is advanced by 1 cycle (cycle 0).
set_multicycle_path 2 -setup \
  -from [get_pins -hierarchical u_mac_array/acc_reg_*/C] \
  -to   [get_pins -hierarchical u_post_proc/requant_stage1_reg_*/D]

set_multicycle_path 1 -hold \
  -from [get_pins -hierarchical u_mac_array/acc_reg_*/C] \
  -to   [get_pins -hierarchical u_post_proc/requant_stage1_reg_*/D]

# 7.2 Weight SRAM Address Staging
# Complex address generation with stride and dilation logic runs over a 2-cycle 
# evaluation cadence before driving the SRAM macro chip-select and address latches.
set_multicycle_path 2 -setup \
  -from [get_pins -hierarchical u_addr_gen/w_addr_calc_reg_*/C] \
  -to   [get_pins -hierarchical u_weight_sram/sram_inst/A*]

set_multicycle_path 1 -hold \
  -from [get_pins -hierarchical u_addr_gen/w_addr_calc_reg_*/C] \
  -to   [get_pins -hierarchical u_weight_sram/sram_inst/A*]

Design Rule Constraints (DRCs) enforce electrical feasibility across the standard-cell fabric regardless of whether the operating frequency is 100 MHz or 1 GHz. In 28nm planar and FinFET-adjacent nodes (such as 28nm HPC+), thin-oxide logic gates display steep short-circuit (\(I_{sc}\)) power penalties when driven by degraded signal transitions. Routing interconnect resistance per unit length increases dramatically at the lower metal layers (\(M_1\) through \(M_3\)), making early slews and capacitance caps essential to prevent delay divergence between pre-layout synthesis and post-route physical sign-off.

# ==============================================================================
# 8. Design Rule Constraints (DRCs)
# ==============================================================================

# Global maximum transition limit for data paths (28nm standard-cell limit: 250 ps)
# Restricts signal slew to prevent excessive dynamic/leakage power and crosstalk sensitivity
set_max_transition 0.250 [current_design] -data_path

# Dedicated maximum transition on clock networks prior to Clock Tree Synthesis (CTS)
# Tighter slew limits on clock paths ensure clean clock edges and preserve local OCV margins
set_max_transition 0.100 [get_clocks {clk_core clk_axi}] -clock_path

# Global maximum capacitance constraint to limit interconnect loading on internal nets
# Overrides conservative library defaults to enforce dense 28nm buffer insertion
set_max_capacitance 0.035 [current_design]

# Specific port-level output capacitance cap for TinyEdge-NPU external interfaces
# Reflects a realistic SoC interconnect load (~30 fF) on AXI-Lite and interrupt pins
set_max_capacitance 0.030 [all_outputs]

# Maximum fanout limit to control net branching before placement
# Prevents high-fanout broadcast lines (e.g., mac_enable, weight_load_en) from
# developing unwieldy RC trees during initial logic synthesis
set_max_fanout 16 [current_design]

# Designate reset and scan signals as ideal networks during front-end synthesis
# These will be buffered into balanced distribution trees during physical implementation
set_ideal_network [get_ports {rst_n_core rst_n_axi scan_enable}]

Why These Specific Design-Rule Constraints Matter for the TinyEdge-NPU

The limits below are SDC design-rule constraints (set_max_transition, set_max_capacitance, set_max_fanout) applied during synthesis, not the physical layout DRC checks of Chapter 12. They bound what the synthesis tool may build, so that the netlist handed to place-and-route is already within the electrical envelope the back end assumes.

  • Data Slew (set_max_transition 0.250): In ultra-low-power regimes (<5 mW active budget), dynamic short-circuit dissipation caused by slow, ramped transitions can account for up to 15% of total power. Constraining transition times to 250 ps forces the synthesis compiler to downsize oversized gates and insert appropriately sized repeaters along wide activation buses running between the 16 KB activation SRAM and the 8×8 MAC array.
  • Clock Transition (set_max_transition 0.100): A loose clock slew introduces substantial edge-rate variability across Process, Voltage, and Temperature (PVT) corners. Enforcing a strict 100 ps cap ensures the clock distribution network will not suffer from excessive local on-chip variation (OCV) derating during static timing analysis.
  • Capacitance (set_max_capacitance 0.035): Thin-wire metal layers in 28nm can exhibit electromigration (EM) failure over time if forced to drive highly capacitive nodes. Setting a 35 fF cap limits wire-length excursions on local accumulation paths inside the INT8 dot-product engines.
  • Fanout (set_max_fanout 16): The NPU features several control signals that broadcast across all 64 processing elements simultaneously, most notably the weight-stationary register enables and the INT8 accumulation clear signals. Capping logical fanout at 16 ensures the logic synthesis tool constructs a coarse, early buffer tree instead of generating an unroutable single-driver star topology.

11.3.9 SDC Sign-Off and Timing Sanity Checks

An unchecked SDC is an active liability. Syntax errors, conflicting multicycle paths, unconstrained ports, or floating clocks will result in optimistic timing reports where critical timing violations slip through undetected into tape-out. Before committing the netlist to place-and-route (P&R), the constraints must be audited using an automated validation flow.

flowchart TD A["RTL & SDC Input"] --> B[check_timing Analysis] B --> C{Unconstrained
Endpoints / Clocks?} C -- Yes --> D["Flag Critical Errors & Fix SDC"] D --> B C -- No --> E[report_exceptions Audit] E --> F{Overridden or
Invalid Exceptions?} F -- Yes --> G[Refine False / Multicycle Paths] G --> E F -- No --> H[report_analysis_coverage] H --> I["SDC Sign-Off Complete for P&R"]

The following Tcl audit script executes inside the STA tool (such as Synopsys PrimeTime or Cadence Tempus) to validate constraint completeness for the TinyEdge-NPU design database:

# ==============================================================================
# 9. Timing Constraint Integrity and Audit Script
# ==============================================================================

# 1. Structural timing checks
# Verify that all flip-flop clock pins receive a legitimate clock source,
# identify undriven input ports, and flag combinatorial timing loops.
check_timing -verbose > reports/timing_check_structural.rpt

# 2. Check for unconstrained endpoints and inputs
# Any unconstrained register pin or output port is a severe sign-off hazard.
set unconstrained_endpoints [all_registers -data_pins -no_clock]
if {[llength $unconstrained_endpoints] > 0} {
    puts "CRITICAL ERROR: Detected [llength $unconstrained_endpoints] unconstrained sequential endpoints!"
}

# 3. Audit timing exceptions for shadowing and invalid targeting
# Validates that set_false_path and set_multicycle_path expressions explicitly match
# actual design objects and have not been nullified by conflicting constraints.
report_exceptions -ignored     > reports/exceptions_ignored.rpt
report_exceptions -overshadowed > reports/exceptions_overshadowed.rpt

# 4. Clock domain and clock relationship audits
# Verify that no clocks exist without sinks and confirm generated clock dividers
report_clocks -skew -attributes > reports/clock_network_audit.rpt
check_clock_tree               > reports/clock_tree_integrity.rpt

# 5. Coverage assertion
# Confirm that 100% of all register-to-register, in-to-reg, reg-to-out, 
# and in-to-out paths are accounted for by setup and hold checks.
report_analysis_coverage       > reports/timing_analysis_coverage.rpt

The worked SDC developed throughout this chapter constitutes the foundational contract for the TinyEdge-NPU. By defining accurate, non-conflicting clock definitions, conservative I/O timing envelopes for the AXI-Lite interface, precise CDC boundaries, physical SRAM boundary constraints, and realistic 28nm design rules, this single constraint file guides the entire back-end toolchain. Moving from initial logic synthesis through physical floorplanning, Clock Tree Synthesis (CTS), and sign-off Static Timing Analysis, maintaining this constraint set guarantees that the synthesized gate netlist reliably realizes the sub-5 mW, 100 MHz performance target in silicon.

11.4 Synthesis Strategies and Optimization

Synthesis transforms register-transfer-level (RTL) descriptions into an optimal gate-level netlist bound to a target semiconductor foundry's standard cell and macro libraries. For an edge AI processor like the TinyEdge-NPU, synthesis is not a hands-off, "push-button" translation. The design must pack an 8×8 array of multiply-accumulate (MAC) engines, local activation ping-pong buffers, and memory interfaces into an area footprint of roughly 1.0 mm2 in a 28nm planar CMOS process, while dissipating fewer than 5 mW of active dynamic power at 100 MHz.

To satisfy these aggressive constraints, synthesis requires deliberate compile flows, fine-grained control over datapath generation, explicit resource management, disciplined register retiming, and accurate black-box modeling of SRAM macros.

Compile Flow: Top-Down vs. Bottom-Up for IP Reuse

A recurring architectural question during synthesis planning is whether to compile the design flat (top-down) or hierarchically (bottom-up).

flowchart TD subgraph TD1[Top-Down Flat Compile] A1[Whole NPU RTL] --> B1[Single Synthesis Run] end subgraph BU[Bottom-Up Hierarchical] A2[PE Tile RTL] --> B2[Compile Tile Once] B2 --> C2[Assemble 8 by 8 Array] end

In a top-down flow, the entire design hierarchy, from the top-level AXI-Lite register bank down through the activation routing and the individual Processing Elements (PEs), is read into the synthesis tool and optimized concurrently: 

# Typical Top-Down Compile Script (Synopsys Design Compiler / Fusion Compiler)
read_verilog -sv [glob ./rtl/*.sv]
current_design tinyedge_npu_top
link
read_sdc ../constraints/tinyedge_npu_top.sdc

# Compile with boundary optimization and auto-ungrouping
compile_ultra -gate_clock -scan

Top-down synthesis offers global visibility. The synthesis engine can optimize across sub-module boundaries, eliminating redundant inverter stages between the controller and the MAC array, merging status flags, and propagating constants transparently. However, for the TinyEdge-NPU, a completely flat compile has significant drawbacks: runtimes are high, and the tool often makes suboptimal local decisions across the highly regular 64-element PE array by structuring functionally identical PEs differently based on asymmetric wire loads near the boundaries.

A bottom-up (hierarchical) flow compiles the core computing element, the single INT8 MAC PE, independently. Once hardened into a clean, optimized netlist, the PE is marked as an untouchable design or exported as an intermediate design format (such as a .ddc or structural netlist with a dedicated timing interface model): 

# Compile Leaf Processing Element
current_design tinyedge_pe
link
read_sdc ../constraints/tinyedge_pe.sdc
compile_ultra -gate_clock
set_dont_touch [get_designs tinyedge_pe]

# Switch to Top-Level Context
current_design tinyedge_npu_top
link
compile_ultra -gate_clock -no_autoungroup

The bottom-up methodology guarantees identical internal cell layouts, predictable pin placements, and uniform parasitics across all 64 PEs. It also accelerates synthesis iterations: tuning an accumulator or an INT8 multiplier takes seconds rather than hours. However, hard boundaries prevent cross-boundary optimizations. If the controller presents a static configuration bit to the PE, the bottom-up engine cannot sweep away the corresponding configuration flop or gate.

For the TinyEdge-NPU, a hybrid compile flow delivers the best result:

  • The PE array is synthesized hierarchically as a standardized leaf cell (tinyedge_pe) to lock down datapath timing, minimize standard cell entropy, and establish structural consistency.
  • The memory controllers, DMA engines, and bus wrappers (AXI-Lite) are synthesized top-down around the hardened core, allowing the synthesis tool to freely optimize control logic, clock-gating insertion, and bus arbitration boundaries.

Optimization Targets: Balancing Area, Timing, and Power

In a 28nm library (such as TSMC 28HPC+ or Samsung 28LPP), standard cell offerings span multiple threshold voltages (\(V_t\)): High-\(V_t\) (HVT), Standard-\(V_t\) (SVT), and Low-\(V_t\) (LVT). Channel length variants (e.g., 28nm nominal, 32nm, or 35nm optical gate length extensions) also allow precise throttling of sub-threshold and gate-leakage currents.

Optimization Target Synthesis Engine Directives TinyEdge-NPU Application
Timing (Max Performance) set_cost_priority -delay
group_path -weight 5.0		 Restricted strictly to the MAC tree carry-propagate paths and high-fanout accumulator feedback nets to prevent excessive leakage.
Dynamic Power compile_ultra -gate_clock
set_dynamic_optimization true		 Aggressive multi-bit clock gate (MBCG) insertion. Fused registers share enable logic across 16-bit and 32-bit internal buses.
Leakage Power set_leakage_optimization true
set_target_library_subsets -hvt		 Target >85% HVT / SVT usage. Force HVT cells on all AXI-Lite registers, slow configuration state machines, and inactive sleep control logic.
Area compile_ultra -area_high_effort_script Operator sharing and cell-footprint reclamation applied to activation routing muxes and DMA address generators.

Because active power must remain under 5 mW at 100 MHz, dynamic power optimization cannot be an afterthought during physical design. Synthesis must instantiate integrated clock gating (ICG) cells natively. For TinyEdge-NPU, we instruct the tool to target minimum bit-widths of 4 for clock gates, preventing an explosion of tiny, inefficient single-bit ICGs: 

# Clock Gating Configuration for Dynamic Power Control
set_clock_gating_style -positive_edge_logic integrated:POST_CG \
                       -control_point before \
                       -minimum_bitwidth 4 \
                       -max_fanout 32 \
                       -observation_point false

Preventing Area Explosion in the 8×8 MAC Array

An 8×8 array contains 64 independent INT8 multipliers and 64 32-bit accumulators. Implemented naively in behavioral RTL: 

// Naive RTL resulting in explosive logic synthesis
logic signed [7:0]  weight_reg, act_reg;
logic signed [31:0] accum_reg;

always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
  if (!rst_n) begin
    accum_reg <= '0;
  end else if (accum_enable) begin
    accum_reg <= accum_reg + (weight_reg * act_reg);
  end
end

If unconstrained, the synthesis engine infers discrete arithmetic components: an independent signed 8-bit multiplier followed by a 32-bit sign-extension block, feeding a discrete 32-bit carry-propagate adder (CPA). Synthesizing 64 such topologies creates severe area and routing bloat:

  • Datapath Structuring: Rather than synthesizing discrete arithmetic operators, use specialized datapath generators (such as Synopsys DesignWare Building Blocks or equivalent synthetic arithmetic operators). Instruct the tool to synthesize a merged Multiply-Accumulator (MAC) primitive that fuses the product reduction tree directly into the accumulator's carry-save adder (CSA) stages. This avoids carry propagation between the multiplier product and the accumulator.
  • Synthetic Architecture Selection: Explicitly direct the synthesis tool to use low-area Wallace tree or Booth-encoded architectures instead of high-speed, high-area non-uniform structures (like carry-lookahead arrays).
# Direct synthesis tool to build area-efficient arithmetic structures
set_dp_smartmesh true
set_attribute [get_designs *tinyedge_pe*] optimize_for_speed false
set_app_var hlo_resource_allocation area

Resource Sharing vs. Throughput

Resource sharing trades silicon area for operational cycles. In the TinyEdge-NPU, weights remain stationary in the PE local registers for a sequence of cycles while activations stream across columns.

A common pitfall is attempting to share arithmetic hardware between disparate pipelines. For example, sharing a single 32-bit adder between the MAC accumulator and the PE's non-linear activation unit (e.g., a ReLU or requantization scaling stage). This creates long combinational feedback paths and requires wide multiplexers on the adder inputs:

flowchart TD subgraph UNS[Unshared Pipelines] A1[MAC Array] --> B1[Requant Unit A] A2[MAC Array] --> B2[Requant Unit B] end subgraph SHR[Over-Shared Architecture] C1[MAC Array] --> D1[Shared Mux] D1 --> E1[Single Requant Unit] end

The multiplexer logic and cross-coupled control often consume more silicon area than the adder gates saved, while introducing significant routing congestion. The optimal strategy for the TinyEdge-NPU is zero resource sharing within the inner loop of the PE. Dedicate an unshared, highly compact multiplier-accumulator per PE, and place requantization and scaling outside the array as a shared pipelined resource at the activation buffer boundaries.

Register Retiming: Dos and Don'ts

Register retiming moves registers across combinational logic gates to balance pipeline path delays without altering functional latency.

Retiming Rule of Thumb for Edge NPUs: Retime internal datapath pipelines only within strictly bound hierarchical modules. Never apply global retiming across module interfaces, SRAM boundaries, or logic domains subject to formal verification or testability constraints.

Do:

  • Apply retiming locally within the MAC engine if an intermediate pipeline stage is placed between the INT8 multiplication array and the 32-bit accumulation stage: 
    # Safe, constrained local retiming
set_optimize_registers true -designs [get_designs tinyedge_pe]
  • Use retiming to let the tool shift internal pipeline latches across the Carry-Save reduction tree, automatically evening out bit-slice delay disparities.

Don't:

  • Do not permit register retiming across the AXI-Lite register interfaces or control registers. Retiming changes the naming scheme of flip-flops, complicating functional verification and silicon bring-up.
  • Do not retime logic driving asynchronous reset pins, clock-gating enables, or multi-cycle memory start signals.
  • Do not retime without generating formal guidance files. When using tools like Synopsys Formality or Cadence Conformal, retiming without an export log (e.g., Formality Setup File .svf) breaks automated Logic Equivalence Checking (LEC).

Handling SRAM Macros as Black Boxes

The TinyEdge-NPU uses a 32 KB weight SRAM and a 16 KB activation SRAM. In 28nm technologies, these memories are instantiated as hard IP compile macros generated by a memory compiler, not synthesized from RTL registers.

During synthesis, the compiler must treat these instances as black boxes. They contain no internal gate definitions in the RTL, but their timing, power, and pin interface behavior must be fully characterized via a standard timing library (.lib):

flowchart TD A[Control Logic] --> B[Pipeline Flops] B --> C[SRAM Wrapper] subgraph WRAP[Black-Box Macro Boundary] C --> D[SRAM Macro] end E[BIST Controller] --> F[BIST Mux] F --> D
// Instantiation of the 16KB Activation SRAM Wrapper
module sram_act_16k_wrapper (
    input  logic        clk,
    input  logic        cs_n,
    input  logic        we_n,
    input  logic [11:0] addr,
    input  logic [31:0] wdata,
    output logic [31:0] rdata
);

    // Hard macro instantiation
    TS1N28HPC_SP_4096X32_BM u_macro (
        .CLK  (clk),
        .CEB  (cs_n),
        .WEB  (we_n),
        .A    (addr),
        .D    (wdata),
        .Q    (rdata),
        .BWEB ('0)
    );
endmodule

To synthesize logic surrounding these macros correctly:

  • Read Timing Models Early: Ensure the target_library and link_library variables include the explicit .db files for all compiler corners (e.g., ts1n28hpc_4096x32_ss0p9v125c.db). If missing, the synthesis tool marks pins as unconstrained, leading to unbuffered output paths and setup violations in static timing analysis.
  • Isolate Macro Interfaces: Wrap all memory macros in a dedicated RTL boundary that houses the Built-In Self-Test (BIST) muxes, scan-isolation logic, and bypass routes. Never interlock combinational random logic into the address decoder nets upstream of the macro pins without registering them first.
---

11.5 Timing Closure Challenges in MAC Arrays and Memory Interfaces

Static Timing Analysis (STA) verifies that every synchronous path in a design meets both setup and hold requirements across all manufactured process corners, operating voltages, and temperatures (PVT). For the TinyEdge-NPU, running at 100 MHz (a 10.0 ns cycle time) might appear trivial compared to GHz-class application processors. However, achieving zero-margin, low-power closure at 28nm presents unique physical challenges.

The Critical Path: 8×8 Adder Trees and Accumulator Feedback

The primary combinational critical path runs through the MAC pipeline. In an INT8 signed multiply-accumulate operation, the arithmetic engine evaluates:

\[\text{Accumulator}[31:0] \leftarrow \text{Accumulator}[31:0] + \sum_{k=0}^{7} (W_k \times A_k)\]

When unpipelined, data cascades through:

  1. Clock-to-Q delay of the input activation and weight registers (\(\sim 0.25\text{ ns}\)).
  2. Booth encoder and partial-product generation logic (\(\sim 0.60\text{ ns}\)).
  3. Wallace/Carry-Save Tree reduction of partial products (\(\sim 1.10\text{ ns}\)).
  4. Accumulation stage: adding the 16-bit intermediate product to the 32-bit running sum (\(\sim 1.35\text{ ns}\)).
  5. Setup time into the destination accumulator flip-flop (\(\sim 0.15\text{ ns}\)).
flowchart LR A[Weight SRAM Read] --> B[MAC Multiply] B --> C[Adder Tree] C --> D[Accumulator Register] D -->|feedback path| B

The tightest path is often the accumulator feedback loop:

\[T_{\text{cycle}} \ge T_{\text{clk2q}} + T_{\text{accum\_adder}} + T_{\text{mux\_control}} + T_{\text{setup}} + T_{\text{margin}}\]

Because the running sum must be updated every clock cycle to preserve maximum throughput without insertion of bubble states, this path cannot be broken up simply by adding pipeline registers without redesigning the NPU's scheduling state machine. If sign-extension logic for the INT8 product is left unoptimized, the sign bit must propagate across all 32 bits of the accumulator adder, creating a high-fanout net right in the critical path.

Weight Broadcast Fanout and Wire Delay

In the TinyEdge-NPU's weight-stationary flow, weights are broadcast row-wise, while activations are broadcast column-wise. A single 8-bit activation net originates at the memory controller register and drives eight distinct PEs across the physical array.

Within the array, each bit routes to the multiplier logic of every PE along the line. This introduces an immediate logical fanout of 8, but physically, the wire must span across standard cell rows (approximately 300 to 500 μm of interconnect length). In 28nm interconnect stacks (typically 1P8M or 1P9M with thin lower metal layers \(M_1\) through \(M_4\)), high-resistance thin-pitch wires introduce substantial RC delays:

\[R_{\text{wire}} \approx 0.3 - 0.8\ \Omega/\mu\text{m}, \quad C_{\text{wire}} \approx 0.15 - 0.25\ \text{fF}/\mu\text{m}\]

An unbuffered 500 μm run can easily exhibit an RC flight time of over 0.8 ns, causing substantial transition-time degradation (slew > 0.4 ns) at the leaf pins, which drastically inflates cell internal delays.

SRAM Read-to-MAC Timing

Interfacing the MAC array directly to the activation SRAM is one of the most common sources of timing failure. Consider the access timing metrics for a representative 28nm single-port SRAM macro at the worst-case slow corner (SSG, 0.81V, 125°C):

  • Access Time (\(T_{\text{clk}\to\text{Q}}\)): \(1.85\text{ ns}\) from clock pin assertion.
  • Output Wire RC: \(\sim 0.40\text{ ns}\) across the macro routing channel.
  • Data Setup Time (\(T_{\text{setup}}\)) of PE inputs: \(\sim 0.10\text{ ns}\).

If the activation read data flows straight out of the SRAM macro directly into the combinational input of the PE array within the same cycle, the remaining timing budget for the entire MAC datapath is:

\[T_{\text{avail}} = 10.0\text{ ns} - (1.85\text{ ns} + 0.40\text{ ns} + 0.10\text{ ns}) = 7.65\text{ ns}\]

While 7.65 ns seems generous for a simple INT8 multiply, if any muxing logic, zero-skipping logic, or activation-clamping gating is introduced between the SRAM output pins and the PE input register, the timing margin erodes quickly once clock skew and on-chip variations are factored in.

Clock Skew, OCV, and Margins at 28nm

At advanced planar nodes like 28nm, simple flat deratings (e.g., adding a flat 10% uncertainty) no longer accurately reflect real-world physical behavior. Timing analysis must account for On-Chip Variation (OCV), typically modeled via Advanced OCV (AOCV) or Parametric OCV (POCV).

Variation manifests as:

  • Sytematic Variations: Lithographic optical proximity effects, optical flare, and chemical-mechanical polishing (CMP) thickness variations.
  • Random Variations: Random Dopant Fluctuation (RDF) and Line-Edge Roughness (LER), which dominate transistor threshold variation at small geometries.

In static timing scripts, derating factors are applied unequally to launching paths versus capturing paths: 

# Standard Setup Derating (Late Path / Early Path) under POCV/AOCV
set_timing_derate -early 0.95 -data
set_timing_derate -late  1.05 -data
set_timing_derate -early 0.95 -clock
set_timing_derate -late  1.05 -clock

The impact on setup slack (\(S_{\text{setup}}\)) is expressed as:

\[S_{\text{setup}} = (T_{\text{clk\_period}} + T_{\text{clk\_capture\_early}}) - (T_{\text{clk\_launch\_late}} + T_{\text{data\_late}} + T_{\text{setup}})\]

For a 10.0 ns cycle, late clock tree insertion delays (e.g., 1.5 ns insertion with 5% variation) and early capture shifts can consume 150–300 ps. Combined with 100 ps of phase jitter from the on-chip PLL, the available timing margin diminishes noticeably.

How to Read a Timing Report and Triage Violations

Diagnosing timing violations requires a systematic approach. Consider the following excerpt from a Synopsys PrimeTime or Design Compiler timing report: 

  Point                                                   Incr       Path
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------
  clock core_clk (rise edge)                              0.00       0.00
  clock network delay (ideal)                             0.00       0.00
  u_act_sram/u_macro/CLK (TS1N28HPC_SP_4096X32_BM)       0.00       0.00 r
  u_act_sram/u_macro/Q[0] (TS1N28HPC_SP_4096X32_BM)      1.82 &     1.82 r
  u_router/act_col_data[0] (act_router)                  0.48 &     2.30 r
  u_mac_array/pe_inst_7_7/act_in[0] (tinyedge_pe_7_7)     0.02 &     2.32 r
  u_mac_array/pe_inst_7_7/U124/ZN (INV_X2)                0.15 &     2.47 f
  u_mac_array/pe_inst_7_7/u_mult/U45 (DW02_mult)          3.45 &     5.92 r
  u_mac_array/pe_inst_7_7/u_accum/U88 (ADD_X4)            2.85 &     8.77 f
  u_mac_array/pe_inst_7_7/accum_reg[0]/D (DFFHQX1)        0.18 &     8.95 f
  data arrival time                                                  8.95

  clock core_clk (rise edge)                              8.00       8.00
  clock network delay (propagated)                        0.35       8.35
  clock uncertainty                                      -0.25       8.10
  u_mac_array/pe_inst_7_7/accum_reg[0]/CK (DFFHQX1)                  8.10 r
  library setup time                                     -0.12       7.98
  data required time                                                 7.98
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------
  data required time                                                 7.98
  data arrival time                                                 -8.95
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------
  slack (VIOLATED)                                                  -0.97

Follow this four-step diagnostic procedure when inspecting failing paths:

  1. Check the Slack and Margins: Review the constraint target. In this run, the designer applied an aggressive 8.0 ns clock target (to maintain a 20% guardband over the 10.0 ns system specification), leading to a violation of \(-0.97\text{ ns}\).
  2. Examine Delay Hops (Cell vs. Net): Identify lines with the & annotation, which designates annotated post-synthesis or back-annotated RC values. Check for disproportionate increases:
    • u_act_sram/u_macro/Q[0] takes \(1.82\text{ ns}\) out of the budget.
    • The routing net u_router/act_col_data[0] takes \(0.48\text{ ns}\), pointing to severe routing capacitance or high logical fanout.
  3. Analyze High-Fanout Nets and Slew Rates: Check transition times. If an inverter (like INV_X2) shows an incremental delay of \(0.15\text{ ns}\), its load pin capacitance likely exceeds its drive capabilities, causing a slow transition slew that compounds delays down the logic cone.
  4. Review Logic Depth: The path traverses from an SRAM read directly through a multiplier block (DW02_mult, \(3.45\text{ ns}\)) and an adder block (\(2.85\text{ ns}\)). This is an architectural flaw: attempting to complete an SRAM read, an \(8\times8\) multiply, and a 32-bit accumulate all within a single cycle.
---

11.6 Worked Timing Closure Example: The TinyEdge-NPU Critical Path

To understand how static timing analysis (STA) drives design decisions, we walk through three sequential closure iterations on the TinyEdge-NPU. Synthesized in a foundry 28nm low-power process (28LP, 0.9V nominal, 1P8M metal stack), the core operates at a nominal target frequency of 100 MHz (\(T_{\text{clk}} = 10.00\text{ ns}\)). To maintain reliability across process-voltage-temperature (PVT) variations and dynamic voltage-frequency scaling (DVFS) drops to 0.81V, our sign-off criteria require closure at the SSG_0p81V_125C_rcworst corner with 350 ps of clock uncertainty (accounting for PLL jitter and intra-die variation) and an additional 150 ps design margin.

graph TD A["Initial Baseline STA: WNS = -0.42 ns"] --> B["Iteration 1: Microarchitecture"] B -->|Pipeline Adder Tree & Segment Broadcast| C["Intermediate STA: WNS = -0.27 ns"] C --> D["Iteration 2: SRAM Wrapper Interface"] D -->|Add Wrapper Retiming Stage & Pre-Decode| E["Post-CTS STA: Setup WNS = +0.18 ns, Hold WNS = -0.18 ns"] E --> F["Iteration 3: Physical ECO & CTS Tuning"] F -->|Useful Skew & Delay Buffer Insertion| G["Sign-off Timing Closed: Setup +0.22 ns, Hold +0.06 ns"]

Iteration 1: Baseline Architecture—Adder Tree Depth and Broadcast Congestion

The initial TinyEdge-NPU RTL calculated a full row-column product in a single clock cycle. Each of the 64 INT8 multipliers fed an unpipelined, 6-level adder-compressor tree terminating in a 32-bit accumulation register. The 8-bit weight broadcast net traversed all eight columns of the \(1\text{ mm}^2\) floorplan from a centralized weight unpacker register without intermediate repeaters.

After placement and preliminary global routing, PrimeTime reported severe setup violations on all 32 bits of the accumulator registers:

  data arrival time                                                 -9.92
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------
  slack (VIOLATED)                                                  -0.42

The report isolates two fundamental culprits:

  • Broadcast Wire Delay: The single net net_w_col0_bcast[7] has a fanout of 64 spread across a 780 μm run, accounting for 1.84 ns (over 18% of the entire cycle) due to wire resistance and total capacitive loading (\(C_{\text{pin}} \approx 180\text{ fF}\), \(C_{\text{wire}} \approx 140\text{ fF}\)).
  • Logic Cascading: An INT8 multiply combined with a 6-level reduction tree and final 32-bit accumulation spans 13 logic levels without an isolating register, contributing 6.98 ns of gate and local net delay.

The Fix: Cell sizing and localized buffer insertion cannot reclaim 420 ps over this topology. We modified the microarchitecture by inserting a pipeline register boundary between the partial-product reduction stage (the multipliers) and the adder tree. In parallel, we pipelined the weight broadcast network: the central controller registers broadcast to row-level pipeline registers (generating an H-tree-like routing topology), isolating long-wire capacitance.

Microarchitectural Insight: Never attempt to resolve an architectural logic depth deficit exceeding 5% of clock period with physical synthesis cell sizing alone. Inserting pipeline registers across natural mathematical boundaries (e.g., between multiplier arrays and compressor trees) cuts wire length exponentially and re-centers cells in their optimal delay-power curves.

Following RTL re-synthesis and placement legalization, the MAC adder-tree path slack improved from -0.42 ns to +1.28 ns. However, exposing this path unmasked the next critical timing bottleneck in the design.

Iteration 2: SRAM Macro Access and Ingestion Path

With the internal MAC pipeline resolved, the new worst path shifted to the boundary between the 32 KB Weight SRAM macro and the first processing rank of the MAC array. The 32 KB memory is organized as two instances of single-port 16 KB SRAM macros.

At 0.81V and 125°C, the macro access time (\(T_{\text{AA}}\)) degrades to 4.82 ns, absorbing over 48% of the available 10.00 ns period. Following the macro output pins, the read data passed combinatorially through:

  1. An asymmetric routing run over the analog memory collar (\(420\text{ }\mu\text{m}\)).
  2. An INT8 dequantization barrel shifter and zero-point clamping multiplexer logic (0.74 ns gate delay).
  3. Floorplan distribution wiring into the MAC array boundary (\(610\text{ }\mu\text{m}\), contributing 1.78 ns delay).

The Fix: We added an architectural output retiming register stage embedded directly inside the SRAM wrapper layout. By converting the memory subsystem into a pipelined read protocol (2-cycle read latency instead of 1-cycle), the raw memory access was isolated to its own clock phase. Address decode paths into the SRAM were also split using address pre-decoding registers clocked on the negative edge of the system clock.

This decoupling cut the SRAM read interface path into two distinct components: the memory read cycle (\(4.82\text{ ns} + \text{local net} = 5.25\text{ ns}\), giving \(+3.75\text{ ns}\) slack) and the dequantization/distribution cycle (\(3.12\text{ ns}\), giving \(+5.88\text{ ns}\) slack). The worst negative setup slack (WNS) across the entire digital core improved to +0.18 ns.

With all functional paths demonstrating positive setup slack, full Clock Tree Synthesis (CTS) was executed using a multi-corner CTS optimization methodology. Extracting parasitics with sign-off RC extraction engines at the fast-fast corner (FFG_0p99V_m40C_rcbest) unmasked substantial hold violations across the newly added pipeline stages:
