The root cause was clock skew induced by physical asymmetry. The multiplier pipeline registers were physically located on CTS branch 3, which had an insertion delay of 410 ps under FFG_rcbest. The receiving adder-tree registers were situated on CTS branch 5, which traversed an additional clock-gating cell (ICG) and displayed an insertion delay of 690 ps. This created 280 ps of positive clock skew (\(\text{Latency}_{\text{capture}} - \text{Latency}_{\text{launch}}\)). Because the registers were placed adjacently, data propagation required only 150 ps (\(0.11\text{ ns Q}\to\text{Q} + 0.04\text{ ns wire}\)), violating the minimum delay condition by 180 ps.

Across the core, hold time analysis reported:

  • Hold WNS: -0.18 ns
  • Hold TNS: -4.20 ns across 38 violating endpoints
  • Setup WNS at target corner: +0.05 ns (degraded from +0.18 ns due to localized OCV derates)

The Fix: We executed an Engineering Change Order (ECO) loop applying two automated techniques:

  1. Useful Skew (Clock Scheduling): Rather than padding data lines with large delays that inflate power consumption, CTS buffers on capture clock pin branches were rebalanced. Delaying launch paths with small inverter pairs lowered the local skew from 280 ps to 45 ps without degrading the setup slack at the worst-case corner.
  2. Delay Buffer Insertion: For the remaining 14 violating instances where clock balancing had zero setup headroom, the physical design tool inserted dedicated delay cells (DLY4D1BWP) possessing low temperature-inversion sensitivity. These cells increased data path delay by 110 ps without driving routing congestion over metallization limits.

Post-ECO verification confirmed that all hold violations were eliminated without degrading max-delay constraints.

Timing Closure Progress Summary

The progression through these three iterations demonstrates how timing closure metrics evolve from RTL planning down to sign-off ECOs:

Iteration Primary Bottleneck Dominant Corner Setup WNS (ns) Setup TNS (ns) Hold WNS (ns) Hold TNS (ns) Resolution Mechanism
Baseline Multiplier tree depth & broadcast nets SSG / 0.81V / 125°C / rcworst -0.42 -13.44 +0.02 0.00 RTL: Insert MAC pipeline stage; segment broadcast nets
Iteration 1 SRAM access (\(T_{\text{AA}}\)) + dequant path SSG / 0.81V / 125°C / rcworst -0.27 -2.16 +0.01 0.00 Wrapper: Add output retiming register; pre-decode addresses
Iteration 2 CTS clock skew on fast pipeline stages FFG / 0.99V / -40°C / rcbest +0.05 0.00 -0.18 -4.20 Physical: Useful skew balancing; DLY cell insertion
Sign-off (It. 3) Residual parasitics & variation margins All MCMM Views Closed +0.22 0.00 +0.06 0.00 Sign-off verified: Ready for tape-out mask generation

What the Iterations Teach: Systematic Triage Order

The progression of closing the TinyEdge-NPU critical path illustrates the golden rule of timing convergence: always address timing violations in descending order of physical hierarchy and implementation leverage.

Engineers frequently waste design cycles attempting to close a -400 ps setup violation inside synthesis or place-and-route by adjusting cell drive strengths or swapping threshold-voltage (\(V_t\)) libraries. Such attempts inevitably fail or generate severe power/congestion penalties because cell-level optimization can only recover small margins (typically 50–100 ps in 28nm).

As shown below, high-impact closure follows a strict three-tier triage hierarchy:

  • Tier 1 — Microarchitecture (Leverage: >500 ps): Address combinational logic depth, pipeline boundaries, and massive broadcast fanouts via architectural restructuring.
  • Tier 2 — Macro and Interface Boundaries (Leverage: 200–500 ps): Isolate analog and hard-macro IP margins (\(T_{\text{AA}}\), setup/hold times) using dedicated wrapper registers, pipeline stages, or multi-cycle path definitions where mathematically permissible.
  • Tier 3 — Physical and Clock Optimization (Leverage: <200 ps): Clean up localized hold violations, boundary skew, and manufacturing-induced wire parasitics using useful skew, buffer insertion, and drive-strength sizing.

Adhering to this hierarchy guarantees that each iteration permanently clears a class of violations rather than shifting the bottleneck across the floorplan.

11.7 Power Analysis and Optimization

For an edge-tier IP like the TinyEdge-NPU, power sign-off is not an afterthought run at the end of the tapeout schedule; it dictates architecture, logic synthesis strategies, and physical cell selection. Operating within an aggressive envelope of <5 mW active power at 100 MHz and <100 μW deep-sleep power in a 28nm planar process (such as TSMC 28HPC+ or GF 28SLP) requires an accounting process that correlates RTL simulation vectors with sign-off power models.

11.7.1 Vector-Driven Switching Activity: SAIF and FSDB Workflows

Static power estimation based on default toggle rates (e.g., assuming a uniform 10% or 20% activity factor across all registers) fails completely on neural network workloads. A convolutional or depthwise-separable layer has phase-dependent activity: weight buffers stream during filter loading, MAC pipelines toggle at near 90% during kernel execution, and activation SRAMs burst write during non-linear pooling/quantization phases. Between inferences, the core sits in micro-sleep, listening for sensor trigger thresholds via the always-on (AON) block.

flowchart TD A[RTL and Gate Simulation] --> B[Keyword Workload Vectors] B --> C[SAIF and VCD Activity] C --> D[Power Analysis Tool] D --> E[Power by Block Report] E --> F[Budget Check vs 5 mW]

To accurately capture switching activity for the TinyEdge-NPU's target keyword-spotting (KWS) task, such as running a 1-second 12-class Google Speech Commands convolutional neural network with 16 kHz audio and 40-band Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC), we rely on dynamic activity tracking files:

  • VCD (Value Change Dump): IEEE 1364 standard format. Uncompressed and prohibitively large. A 100 ms gate-level simulation run of the TinyEdge-NPU generates gigabytes of data. Use only for tiny unit-level sub-blocks.
  • FSDB (Fast Signal Database): Highly compressed, binary trace format native to Verdi/VCS. It retains full temporal waveform fidelity, allowing time-based power profiling (Peak Power, Cycle-Accurate Dynamic Power).
  • SAIF (Switching Activity Interchange Format): An aggregated statistical summary capturing toggling counts (TC), static high/low probabilities (T1, T0), and unknown states (TX) for every net and pin over a defined measurement window. SAIF eliminates temporal resolution but provides fast, memory-efficient average power calculation in tools like Synopsys PrimeTime PX or Cadence Voltus.

The standard workflow involves loading weights, running a calibrated 100 ms KWS inference window in gate-level simulation with annotated timing (SDF), and dumping activity across a defined time window:

// Verilog testbench activity capture snippet
initial begin
  // Wait until input MFCC feature buffer is loaded and core starts
  @(posedge tb.dut.u_core.start_inference);
  
  $fsdbDumpfile("tinyedge_kws_active.fsdb");
  $fsdbDumpvars(0, tb.dut.u_core);
  
  // Log activity across full 5-layer inference pass (~420,000 clock cycles)
  @(posedge tb.dut.u_core.inference_done);
  $fsdbDumpoff;
  $finish;
end

The resulting FSDB or translated SAIF is read into the power analysis environment alongside the gate-level netlist and Liberty (.lib) timing and power characterization libraries (including non-linear power models, NLPM, or Composite Current Source, CCS, power models).

11.7.2 Leakage vs. Dynamic Power Split in 28nm

At the 28nm node, leakage is dominated by two physical mechanisms: subthreshold leakage (\(I_{sub}\), flowing from drain to source through a weakly inverted channel) and gate dielectric tunneling (\(I_{gate}\), traversing the high-k metal gate stack). Dynamic power consists of capacitive charging/discharging (\(P_{cap} = \alpha C V_{DD}^2 f\)) and internal cell short-circuit switching (\(P_{sc} = V_{DD} I_{sc}\)).

The process foundry offers multiple threshold voltage (\(V_t\)) variants. Balancing dynamic performance against leakage requires a disciplined threshold distribution across the cell inventory:

  • High-Vt (HVT): Lowest subthreshold leakage (e.g., ~1.2 pW/gate), but slowest switching speed. Used extensively in non-critical control logic, configuration registers, AXI-Lite registers, and the AON domain.
  • Standard-Vt (SVT): Balanced speed and leakage (~8 pW/gate). The primary workhorse for the 8×8 MAC array and pipeline staging.
  • Low-Vt (LVT): High drive current, fast switching, but severe leakage (~60–80 pW/gate). Restricted to less than 3% of total cell count to close timing on tight speed paths (e.g., the last stages of the 32-bit accumulators).
flowchart TD A[Standard Cells] --> B[Combinational Logic] A --> C[Sequential Flops] B --> D[Dynamic Power Dominant] C --> E[Leakage Contribution] F[SRAM Macros] --> G[Leakage Dominant]

11.7.3 TinyEdge-NPU Worked Power Budget Table

During active inference at 100 MHz (\(V_{DD} = 0.9\text{V}\), \(T = 25^\circ\text{C}\) typical condition, scaling to \(85^\circ\text{C}\) worst-case thermal envelope), the TinyEdge-NPU consumes an average of 3.78 mW, comfortably beneath the 5.0 mW target specification. The power dissipation breakdown reveals the dominance of the memory subsystems and datapath:

Block / Subsystem Instance Count / Gate Count Dynamic Power (mW) Leakage Power @ 85°C (mW) Total Power (mW) Percentage of Total
8×8 MAC Array (Datapath) 64 INT8 MACs (~48k GE) 1.45 0.082 1.532 40.5%
Weight SRAM (32 KB) 2 × 16 KB single-port instances 0.98 0.045 1.025 27.1%
Activation SRAM (16 KB) 2 × 8 KB two-port instances 0.62 0.028 0.648 17.1%
Clock Network (CTS Tree) ~1,200 clock buffers / inverters 0.38 0.009 0.389 10.3%
Control Unit & Sequencer FSM, decoders, addr-gen (~14k GE) 0.11 0.018 0.128 3.4%
Bus Interfaces (AXI-Lite) Protocol adapters, CSRs (~8k GE) 0.04 0.012 0.052 1.4%
Always-On (AON) Domain 32 kHz timer, wake logic (~1.5k GE) 0.002 0.004 0.006 0.2%
Total TinyEdge-NPU Core ~72k Logic Gates + 48 KB SRAM (S configuration) 3.582 mW 0.198 mW 3.780 mW 100.0%

In Deep Sleep mode, the core \(V_{DD}\) rail is gated by an external PMIC or on-chip power switches (headswitches), leaving only the AON block powered and SRAMs in retention mode (biased at retention voltage \(V_{ret} = 0.65\text{V}\)). The resulting leakage stays well below the 100 μW ceiling at 46.8 μW at \(25^\circ\text{C}\) (rising to ~82 μW at \(85^\circ\text{C}\)).

11.7.4 Clock Gating and Operand Isolation Effectiveness

Uncontrolled clock distribution is catastrophic to battery life. Dynamic power optimization in the TinyEdge-NPU uses two aggressive front-end techniques implemented during synthesis:

Integrated Clock Gating (ICG): Automated ICG cell insertion (e.g., negative-edge latched clock gates with an integrated AND gate) is enforced by setting a low fanout threshold during compile. By forcing synthesis to instantiate ICGs for register banks down to a width of 4 bits, dynamic power drops drastically across control pipelines:

# Synopsys Design Compiler clock gating setup
set_clock_gating_style -positive_edge_logic {integrated:TLATNTSCA_X2} \
                       -control_point before \
                       -minimum_bitwidth 4 \
                       -max_fanout 64
compile_ultra -gate_clock

In the 8×8 MAC array, hierarchical clock gating disables clock feeds down to individual accumulator banks whenever the corresponding weight matrix element or incoming activation equals zero. Since ReLU activations introduce 40%–60% sparsity in typical KWS models, this achieves an effective clock gating efficiency of 92.4% (meaning the average flip-flop clock pin toggles on only 7.6% of core clock cycles during active inference).

Operand Isolation: Multipliers are combinational logic monsters; even when their outputs are unused, changes on their input buses cause internal nodes to switch dynamically, dissipating wasteful energy across deep XOR trees. By inserting operand isolation cells (AND or OR gates driven by an enable signal) directly upstream of the multiplier inputs, we freeze the datapath inputs whenever the MAC stage is stalled or operating on cached zero values:

# RTL Compiler / Genus operand isolation directive
set_db operand_isolation_effort high
set_db [get_cells -hier *u_mult*] operand_isolation true

This technique saves 0.32 mW (approximately 18% of the raw MAC array power) with a negligible area penalty of under 1,200 logic gates across the array.

---

11.8 Sign-Off Static Timing Analysis (STA)

Closing timing on the TinyEdge-NPU means verifying that setup (\(T_{su}\)) and hold (\(T_h\)) conditions are satisfied across all operating conditions, manufacturing process spreads, interconnect extraction variations, and functional modes. Relying on a single corner or basic best-case/worst-case checks is a recipe for post-silicon failure.

11.8.1 Multi-Corner Multi-Mode (MCMM) Setup

The sign-off STA environment must evaluate every intersection of operational mode and process-voltage-temperature (PVT) corner. For TinyEdge-NPU, we define three primary operational modes and five critical physical corners, yielding a multi-dimensional analysis matrix.

flowchart TD subgraph MODES[Operating Modes] A[Mission Mode] B[Scan Mode] C[Sleep Mode] end subgraph CORNERS[PVT Corners] D[Slow 0.81V 125C] E[Typical 0.9V 25C] F[Fast 1.1V Minus 40C] end A --> D A --> E B --> F C --> E
Operational Modes:
  1. Mission (Active Inference) Mode: Core clock active at 100 MHz, AON clock at 32 kHz. Both SRAM arrays actively accessed. AXI-Lite bus functional up to 50 MHz.
  2. Scan/DFT Shift Mode: Core clock routed to test clock pin running at 25 MHz. Test enable active. Clock gating cells bypassed into transparent state.
  3. Scan Capture Mode: At-speed scan capture (100 MHz launch and capture pulses to detect transition delay faults).
PVT and Extraction Sign-off Corners:
  • Slow Corner (Setup Analysis): Process: SSG (Slow NMOS, Slow PMOS, Global), \(V_{DD} = 0.81\text{V}\) (Nominal 0.9V − 10%), \(T = 125^\circ\text{C}\), RC Corner: Cmax (maximum parasitic capacitance, minimum interconnect resistance).
  • Cold-Slow Corner (Setup Analysis with Temperature Inversion): Process: SSG, \(V_{DD} = 0.81\text{V}\), \(T = -40^\circ\text{C}\), RC Corner: RCmax. (In 28nm devices operating at sub-1.0V, mobility improvements at cold temperatures can be outweighed by threshold voltage increases, making \(-40^\circ\text{C}\) slower than \(125^\circ\text{C}\) on standard threshold cells).
  • Fast Corner (Hold Analysis): Process: FFG, \(V_{DD} = 0.99\text{V}\) (Nominal 0.9V + 10%), \(T = -40^\circ\text{C}\), RC Corner: Cmin (minimum capacitance, maximum wire resistance).
  • Hot-Fast Corner (Hold Analysis): Process: FFG, \(V_{DD} = 0.99\text{V}\), \(T = 125^\circ\text{C}\), RC Corner: RCmin.
  • Typical Corner (Power & Nominal Checks): Process: TT, \(V_{DD} = 0.90\text{V}\), \(T = 25^\circ\text{C}\), RC Corner: Typical.

11.8.2 Hold Closure and Variation at Low Voltage

Hold time closure at 0.81V–0.99V is considerably more hazardous than at mature 65nm or 180nm nodes. Because cell propagation delay sensitivity (\(\partial t_d / \partial V_{DD}\)) increases non-linearly at reduced voltages, local supply noise and random dopant fluctuations cause dramatic delay disparities between physically adjacent launch and capture paths.

Traditional flat On-Chip Variation (OCV) derating, applying a blanket margin like ±10% to all cells, is excessively pessimistic and can stall design closure. Instead, sign-off for the TinyEdge-NPU uses Parametric OCV (POCV) or Advanced OCV (AOCV) backed by Liberty Variation Format (LVF) tables. AOCV adjusts derates dynamically based on path depth (stage count) and cell bounding-box area:

# PrimeTime configuration for AOCV / POCV sign-off
set_app_var read_parasitics_load_locations true
read_aocv ${TECH_DIR}/aocv_table_28nm.aocv

set_timing_derate -aocv -early
set_timing_derate -aocv -late

# Common Path Pessimism Removal (CPPR / CRPR) MUST be enabled
set_app_var timing_remove_clock_reconvergence_pessimism true

Common Path Pessimism Removal (CPPR): As illustrated below, clock launch and capture paths share common clock routing from the PLL/oscillator input through several levels of the clock distribution spine down to the divergence point.

flowchart TD A[Clock Source] --> B[Shared Clock Tree] B --> C[Divergence Point] C --> D[Launch Path] C --> E[Capture Path] D --> F[Reconvergence Point] E --> F F --> G[CPPR Credit Removes Shared Delay]

Without CPPR, the STA engine pessimistically applies an early derate factor to the launch portion of the common spine and a late derate factor to the capture portion for hold checks. CPPR identifies the exact clock divergence pin, calculates this artificial timing error, and adds it back as a positive credit to the Slack equation:

\[\text{Slack}_{hold} = (T_{launch\_clk\_shared} + T_{launch\_clk\_unique} + T_{cq\_min} + T_{data\_min}) - (T_{capture\_clk\_shared} + T_{capture\_clk\_unique} + T_h) + \text{Credit}_{CPPR}\]

Where \(\text{Credit}_{CPPR} = T_{capture\_clk\_shared} - T_{launch\_clk\_shared} \ge 0\).

11.8.3 Crosstalk and Signal Integrity (SI) Checks

With 28nm pitch scaling, interconnect aspect ratios are taller and narrower. Lateral coupling capacitance (\(C_{coupling}\)) between adjacent metal runs often exceeds the area capacitance (\(C_{ground}\)) to the underlying substrate (\(C_{coupling} / C_{total} > 65\%\)). STA must run in full Signal Integrity (SI) mode to capture two critical crosstalk artifacts:

  1. Delta-Delay (Δt): When an "aggressor" net transitions simultaneously with an adjacent "victim" net:
    • Opposite direction: Coupling capacitance charges to \(2 \times V_{DD}\) through the Miller effect, causing severe delay push-out (threatening setup time).
    • Same direction: Coupling capacitance demands zero net charge transfer, causing delay pull-in (threatening hold time).
  2. Glitch Analysis: An aggressor transitions while the victim is quiescent (static high or low). If the cross-coupled charge injection exceeds the receiver cell's switching threshold and noise-immunity duration, a false pulse propagates. If this glitch hits the clock, reset, or write-enable pin of an SRAM, it causes hard data corruption.
# PrimeTime SI crosstalk configuration commands
set_app_var si_enable_analysis true
set_app_var si_filter_accum_slack_threshold 0.01
set_app_var si_xtalk_composite_aggressor_mode true

# Check for both functional glitches and delay impacts
check_si -alerts
report_si_bottlenecks -cost_type delta_delay
report_noise -slack_lesser_than 0.0

11.8.4 Sign-Off STA Checklist

Before freezing the netlist and streaming out GDSII, the design must cleanly pass this non-negotiable verification matrix:

  • [ ] Worst Negative Slack (WNS) ≥ 0.000 ps across all MCMM scenarios (no setup violations).
  • [ ] Total Negative Slack (TNS) = 0.000 ps across all corners.
  • [ ] Hold Slack (Min Path Slack) ≥ 0.000 ps at all fast/slow hold corners, incorporating POCV/LVF.
  • [ ] Zero Unconstrained Endpoints: Verified via check_timing -verbose. Every register, output port, and macro input must trace back to a valid clock reference.
  • [ ] Maximum Transition (Slew) Violations: Zero violations under worst-case limits (typically \(\le 150\text{ ps}\) for 28nm core logic clock nets, \(\le 300\text{ ps}\) for data pins).
  • [ ] Maximum Capacitance Violations: Zero pin loading violations against max_capacitance attributes in the cell libraries.
  • [ ] Clock Gating Setup and Hold: Every ICG enable pin satisfies setup and hold requirements relative to the incoming clock edge (avoiding output clock truncation or glitches).
  • [ ] Dynamic Noise & Glitch: No glitches exceeding the \(V_{IL} / V_{IH}\) noise margin thresholds on any asynchronous reset, scan-enable, or memory control pin.

11.8.5 What to Do When the Last 20 ps Will Not Close

Every complex tapeout eventually reaches a point where generic PnR/synthesis commands can no longer close the final timing gap. You are looking at a setup violation of \(-20\text{ ps}\) on the critical accumulator chain in the MAC array at the SSG_0.81V_125C corner, and automated place-and-route optimization has plateaued. Do not randomly apply artificial timing exceptions. Use these systematic interventions:

  1. Cell VT Swapping: Identify non-critical pins on the same track and confirm whether the launch or critical receiver logic is implemented using SVT or HVT cells. Swap the single gating standard-cell driver to an equivalent LVT or eLVT (Ultra-Low-Vt) footprint. This lowers intrinsic cell delay by 30–50 ps at the cost of a micro-amp of localized leakage. Ensure that the adjacent hold timing in the fast corners still maintains positive margin.
  2. Driver Sizing and Wire Widening: Inspect the RC decomposition report. If net delay constitutes >40% of the path delay, the net is likely routed on thin metal layers (e.g., M1–M3) with high resistance. Force the router to up-size the driver to an \(X4\) or \(X8\) drive strength and assign the net an NDR (Non-Default Rule) property specifying \(2\times\) width, \(2\times\) spacing on higher, lower-resistance metal (M4 or M5). This mitigates both \(RC\) delay and cross-talk coupling.
  3. Useful Skew (Clock Scheduling): If the capture flip-flop has positive slack on its outgoing timing path (the downstream register has \(+180\text{ ps}\) of setup margin), you can intentionally borrow time. Insert an explicit buffer delay into the capture clock pin (or adjust its CTS target latency) to push the capture clock edge out by 40 ps. This turns a \(-20\text{ ps}\) setup violation on the incoming path into a safe \(+20\text{ ps}\), while keeping downstream setup and local hold safely positive: \[\text{Slack}_{new} = \text{Slack}_{orig} + \Delta T_{capture\_skew}\]
  4. Logic Restructuring / Datapath Cloning: If the critical path traces through an accumulator adder carry-chain where a high-fanout control signal (such as an overflow saturation clamp or zero-skip bit) acts as an input, clone the upstream driver logic to decouple data and control paths. Alternatively, push late-arriving control inputs closer to the output multiplexer stage using balanced Shannon expansion in the RTL.
---

11.9 Best Practices and Common Pitfalls in Synthesis and STA

IP-level development differs fundamentally from full-chip SoC design. An IP provider does not control the final chip environment, package constraints, or floorplan. Synthesis constraints must therefore be clean and defensively engineered.

11.9.1 Synthesis and STA Comprehensive Checklist

The table below summarizes the operational gates required during the synthesis and static timing cycle of the TinyEdge-NPU core before handing delivery collaterals (netlist, UPF, DEF, timing models) over to SoC integration teams.

11.9.2 Common Mistakes and Traps in Sub-Micron IP Implementation

Modern synthesis engines will gladly optimize for impossible goals if directed by poorly crafted constraints, generating massive area inflation, unroutable congestion, or unclosable paths in the process.

1. The Over-Constraining Fallacy

Engineers often attempt to build safety margin into synthesis by arbitrarily inflating clock constraints. For example, specifying a 150 MHz clock period (6.67 ns) for the TinyEdge-NPU's 100 MHz (10.0 ns) operational target. In 28nm processes, this 33% over-constraint triggers aggressive gate sizing, massive parallel logic duplication, widespread insertion of high-leakage LVT cells, and aggressive buffer tree creation. The result is an explosive increase in static leakage and dynamic power, and a routing congestion disaster during physical place-and-route.

Best Practice: Constrain the IP to its realistic operating target clock frequency (10.0 ns for TinyEdge-NPU). Model uncertainty cleanly using set_clock_uncertainty (e.g., 50 ps for PLL jitter, plus an initial 100 ps for synthesis margin that is dropped back to 40 ps during post-CTS STA sign-off), rather than manipulating the clock period itself. 
# Incorrect Approach (DO NOT DO THIS):
create_clock -name CORE_CLK -period 8.0 [get_ports clk_core] ;# DANGEROUS: 20% over-constraining via clock period manipulation

This ad-hoc approach creates catastrophic side effects. When you arbitrarily squash the clock period from 10.0 ns to 8.0 ns, you distort multicycle path relationships, artificially compress the available budget for multi-cycle memory accesses to the 32 KB weight and 16 KB activation SRAMs, and force the synthesis tool to insert aggressive, wide-gate, low-\(V_t\) sizing trees. In TinyEdge-NPU, this manifested as a 23% explosion in static leakage power within the MAC accumulator tree, completely blowing the <100 μW sleep/standby leakage budget. And hold-time analysis is severely degraded because the clock edge relationships against external interfaces (such as the AXI-Lite bus running at an independent phase) become fundamentally unaligned with reality.

The correct approach maintains the true 10.0 ns clock period and manages timing margins systematically through explicit uncertainty modeling. Tool uncertainty budgets should decouple random physical jitter (intrinsic to the phase-locked loop or clock generator) from margin buffers allocated for pre-route net capacitance estimation, On-Chip Variation (OCV), and tool correlation divergence. 

# ==============================================================================
# CORRECT SDC METHODOLOGY: Explicit Uncertainty Modeling (TinyEdge-NPU)
# Target: 100 MHz (10.0 ns period) at 28nm Bulk CMOS
# ==============================================================================

# 1. Define True Period Across All Design Modes
create_clock -name CORE_CLK -period 10.000 [get_ports clk_core]

# 2. Synthesis Margin Budget:
#    - Intrinsic PLL Jitter: 50 ps (Peak-to-Peak random + deterministic jitter)
#    - Pre-CTS Synthesis Margin: 100 ps (absorbs wire parasitics and OCV before tree synthesis)
#    Total Setup Uncertainty = 150 ps
set_clock_uncertainty -setup 0.150 [get_clocks CORE_CLK]

#    - Hold Uncertainty: 50 ps (guards against fast-path skew variations)
set_clock_uncertainty -hold 0.050 [get_clocks CORE_CLK]

# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Post-CTS and Sign-Off Transition (Applied in Sign-Off Scripts)
#    Once real clock network parasitics and clock trees are fully synthesized:
#    - Intrinsic PLL Jitter remains 50 ps
#    - Synthesis Margin drops from 100 ps down to 40 ps (POCV/AOCV covers local variation)
#    Total Sign-Off Setup Uncertainty = 90 ps
# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# set_clock_uncertainty -setup 0.090 [get_clocks CORE_CLK]
# set_clock_uncertainty -hold  0.030 [get_clocks CORE_CLK]

By modeling timing margin through set_clock_uncertainty, downstream place-and-route engines keep edge placements physically realistic. Critical path optimizations focus on high-fanout nets and complex arithmetic paths, such as the INT8 two's complement sign-extension and multiply-add logic, without warping input/output delays, multicycle paths, or clock-domain crossing interfaces.

Missing Exceptions on Configuration and Power-State Paths

A pervasive design flaw in deeply integrated IP cores is failing to communicate architectural multicycle and quasi-static behavior to the timing engine. In TinyEdge-NPU, dozens of control registers reside in the AXI-Lite register file to configure execution modes: activation clipping limits, pooling strides, INT8 weight scaling offsets, and clock-gating override masks. These bits are programmed during network layer initialization and remain completely static throughout tensor execution (often hundreds of thousands of cycles).

If left unconstrained, the timing engine treats register write updates to internal MAC saturation arithmetic as single-cycle timing paths that must resolve in 10.0 ns under worst-case PVT corners. The synthesis tool responds by inserting power-hungry, high-drive buffers along non-critical configuration buses. Every quasi-static configuration bus must be declared using explicit false-path or multi-cycle exceptions: 

# Declare quasi-static configuration paths as false paths for timing optimization
set_false_path -from [get_pins u_regfile/u_cfg_regs*/Q] \
               -to   [get_pins {u_mac_array/pe_*/*}]

Similarly, dynamic power-state transition signals driven by the power management unit (PMU), such as warm-state wake signals and power-gate enable handshakes, require relaxed multicycle assertions. Treating power-down handshakes as single-cycle paths wastes physical area by padding cells to meet race conditions that the architectural protocol already tolerates by design.

flowchart LR subgraph AON_DOMAIN ["Always-On (AON) Domain (32.768 kHz / Async)"] PMU[Power Management Unit] WAKE_REG[Wake-up Register] end subgraph ISOLATION_BARRIER ["Physical & Logical Boundary"] ISO[Isolation Cells] LS[Level Shifters] SYNC[Double-Flop Synchronizer / CDC FIFO] end subgraph CORE_DOMAIN ["Core NPU Domain (100 MHz VDD_CORE)"] CORE_CTRL[Array Controller] MAC_ENGINE[8x8 INT8 MAC Array] SRAM_W[Weight SRAM 32KB] end PMU -->|pwr_ack| ISO WAKE_REG -->|async_wake_req| SYNC SYNC --> CORE_CTRL ISO --> CORE_CTRL CORE_CTRL --> MAC_ENGINE MAC_ENGINE <--> SRAM_W classDef aon fill:#ffe6cc,stroke:#d79b00,stroke-width:2px; classDef iso fill:#fff2cc,stroke:#d6b656,stroke-width:2px,stroke-dasharray: 5 5; classDef core fill:#d5e8d4,stroke:#82b366,stroke-width:2px; class AON_DOMAIN aon; class ISOLATION_BARRIER iso; class CORE_DOMAIN core;

Unmodeled Clock-Domain Crossings Between Core and Always-On Domains

Sub-micron, energy-scavenging architectures rely extensively on split-rail, multi-domain topologies. TinyEdge-NPU isolates its primary compute matrix inside a switchable power and clock domain (VDD_CORE, 100 MHz CORE_CLK) while maintaining an Always-On (AON) domain powered by an unswitched rail (VDD_AON) running an asynchronous slow clock (32.768 kHz or asynchronous AXI-Lite host clock). A critical failure in static timing configuration occurs when designers fail to define explicit clock-group relationships or neglect physical synchronizer constraints across this boundary.

Without defining set_clock_groups -asynchronous, static timing analysis (STA) attempts to resolve phase timing between the 32 kHz wake-up clock and the 100 MHz compute clock. The tool discovers arbitrary pico-second timing closures, throwing tens of thousands of catastrophic timing violations across synchronizer flip-flops. Conversely, simply blanket-declaring a global set_false_path across the clocks without binding explicit constraints on synchronizer structures introduces silent functional bugs. Synchronizer flip-flops must be constrained with set_max_delay to limit data-path skew between handshake bits and placed strictly adjacent in physical layout using specific keep-together directives to eliminate multi-cycle metastability hazards.

Relying on a Single PVT Corner (The "Typical-Case" Fallacy)

At advanced geometries, including the 28nm bulk CMOS node used for TinyEdge-NPU, the assumption that standard slow-corner (SS/0.9V/125°C) analysis bounds worst-case delay while fast-corner (FF/1.1V/-40°C) bounds hold-time is dangerously obsolete. Non-linear sub-threshold conduction, random dopant fluctuation, and temperature inversion fundamentally invalidate single-corner or two-corner sign-off.

Engineering Rule of Thumb: In sub-40nm planar and FinFET nodes, temperature inversion causes cells to exhibit longer propagation delays at low temperatures (-40°C) than at high temperatures (125°C) when operating at low supply voltages (\(V_{DD} \le 0.9\text{V}\)). A path that passes setup timing comfortably at SS / 0.9V / 125°C can violate timing decisively at SS / 0.9V / -40°C.

Relying on simplistic worst-case margins forces either functional failure in cold environments or severe over-design that destroys power efficiency. TinyEdge-NPU requires a Multi-Corner Multi-Mode (MCMM) framework that captures:

  • Setup sign-off (Max delay): Evaluated across both high-temp (SS / 0.81V / 125°C) and inverted low-temp (SS / 0.81V / -40°C) conditions.
  • Hold sign-off (Min delay): Evaluated at extreme fast-leakage corners (FFG / 0.99V / -40°C and FFG / 0.99V / 125°C) using Advanced On-Chip Variation (AOCV) or Parametric On-Chip Variation (POCV) models to prevent clock-tree hold buffers from dominating total core area.
  • Leakage/Sleep sign-off: Checked at worst-case high temperature (FF / 0.99V / 125°C) to ensure standby sleep current stays below the strict 100 μW operational ceiling.

11.10 Chapter Summary

Transforming an architectural concept into clean, tape-out-ready GDSII requires bridging register-transfer abstractions with physical silicon reality. Throughout this chapter, the TinyEdge-NPU served as an empirical benchmark, illustrating how microarchitectural partitioning, RTL micro-optimizations, floorplanning, dynamic and static power isolation, Clock Tree Synthesis, and Multi-Corner Multi-Mode static timing sign-off converge. Achieving competitive performance within a sub-5 mW active envelope at 28nm is not the result of downstream tool automation; it is driven by deliberate frontend decisions, such as clock gating, memory banking, operand isolation, and rigorous, uncorrupted timing constraints. With physical closure achieved and the final timing, power, and physical verification sign-offs locked, the silicon IP core is formally prepared to transition from implementation into the exhaustive validation domain of post-silicon bring-up and qualification.

Key Takeaways

  • SDC constraints are a design artifact, not an afterthought: clocks, IO delays, false paths and multicycle paths must describe the real TinyEdge-NPU behavior, or synthesis will optimize the wrong thing.
  • The 8x8 MAC adder tree and the SRAM read-to-MAC path are the timing-critical structures; structure the datapath and pipeline them deliberately instead of hoping the tool fixes them.
  • Triage timing violations in order: worst slack first, then the structural cause, then the fix. And re-check after every change.
  • Power is a sign-off metric, not a report: vector-driven activity from the real keyword-spotting workload is what makes the <5 mW active budget believable.
  • Close STA across multiple corners and modes, and never fake margin by shrinking the clock period. Model uncertainty explicitly.

Chapter 12: Physical Design

This chapter takes the synthesized TinyEdge-NPU netlist to a manufacturable layout: floorplanning a small accelerator, placement, clock-tree synthesis and routing, power planning and low-power implementation, DRC/LVS sign-off, and a full section on planning the testchip that proves the IP in real silicon. The worked examples use the S configuration (48 KB SRAM: 32 KB weights + 16 KB activations; §3.9).

12.1 Physical Design as an IP Contract: From Gates to Silicon

The journey from an elaborated, synthesized gate-level netlist to a verified, signoff-clean GDSII/OASIS layout marks the boundary between theoretical logic and physical reality. In ASIC product development, physical design is often treated as the downstream execution phase of an architectural specification. In semiconductor IP development, however, physical design is an intrinsic part of the product specification. The physical implementation choices made for the TinyEdge-NPU do not remain confined to a single tapeout; they propagate downstream to every licensee who integrates the IP into an application processor, an edge microcontroller, or a sensor hub subsystem.

When an IP company delivers a "soft" IP core, the customer receives synthesizable SystemVerilog alongside a Reference Implementation Methodology (RIM) kit: synthesis scripts, floorplan guidelines, UPF power intent definitions, SDC timing constraints, and physical design scripts (typically for Cadence Innovus or Synopsys IC Compiler II). If the IP vendor fails to prove that the core closes timing with clean routability at a realistic utilization in the target foundry node (here, TSMC 28nm HPC+), the soft IP is effectively broken. Customers cannot afford to spend months debugging routing congestion, pin blockages, or clock tree divergence originating from poorly structured internal hierarchies or unrealistic floorplan assumptions. For "hard" IP delivery, where the customer instantiates a pre-routed, GDSII macro, the layout, pin pitch, metal stack selection, and power grid design become immutable physical contracts.

Key Concept: The Hard vs. Soft IP Handoff Contract
A soft IP core must be designed for portability and integration elasticity. Its pin placements, power delivery requirements, and boundary keepouts must tolerate neighboring macros and top-level routing channels. A hard IP block must be designed for plug-and-play determinism, guaranteeing zero internal DRC/LVS violations, closed internal timing across all signoff corners, minimal IR drop, and calibrated pin parasitics encapsulated inside an accurate LEF/DEF and Liberty (.lib) timing model.

Every decision made in the floorplan and place-and-route (P&R) stages directly influences the customer's top-level integration effort:

  • Pin Placement and Metal Layer Budgets: Exposing IP interface pins on dense lower metal layers (such as M2 or M3 in a 28nm process) creates severe routing blockages at the SoC level. Interface pins must be placed on intermediate metal layers (M4 or M5), with well-defined pin pitches, uniform track alignment, and clear keep-out regions that prevent top-level route-over signals from coupling into sensitive internal critical paths.
  • Boundary Protection and Halos: Standard cell logic cannot butt up directly against memory macros or IP tile boundaries without risking boundary DRC violations, N-well proximity effects, or stress-induced performance shifts. Explicit placement halos, routing halos, and well-tap cell strategies must be embedded into the floorplan collateral.
  • Power Grid Alignment: The pitch, width, and layer assignments of internal VDD and VSS straps must seamlessly snap to the standard SoC power mesh pitches (e.g., matching the pitch of upper-level M7/M8 global distribution grids) to avoid irregular via arrays or localized electromigration (EM) hotspots at the macro boundary.

12.2 Floorplanning a Small Accelerator

12.2.1 Aspect Ratio, Die Size, and Area Budgeting

The TinyEdge-NPU targets ultra-low-power edge devices, establishing a strict silicon area ceiling of ~1.0 mm² in a foundry 28nm HPC+ (High Performance Compact) logic process. The chosen aspect ratio is 1:1 (a 1000 µm × 1000 µm bounding box), which provides the optimal perimeter-to-area ratio, simplifies top-level floorplanning in a multi-core SoC, and balances horizontal and vertical routing resources across the symmetrical 8x8 MAC datapath.

To establish an achievable floorplan, we construct a rigorous area budget before committing cells to coordinates. In 28nm technology, high-density standard cell logic achieves an effective raw gate density of approximately 800 to 1,000 kGates/mm² at 100% density. However, target standard-cell core utilization must not exceed 65% to 70% to reserve space for clock tree synthesis (CTS) buffer insertion, scan chain reordering, hold-fixing delay cells, and routing channels around memory macros.

12.2.2 Dataflow-Driven Macro Placement

The placement of large memory macros governs the performance of an AI accelerator. The physical floorplan must mirror the logical dataflow: streaming weights into local storage, broadcasting them to the compute array, stepping activations synchronously through the processing grid, and exporting accumulated partial sums to local SRAM or external system memory.

In this architecture, the physical floorplan uses a "C-shaped" standard-cell channel wrapped around three hard macro blocks:

  • North-West Quadrant (Weight SRAM): The 32 KB Weight memory is instantiated as two distinct 16 KB single-port SRAM macros placed side by side. Their interface pins face south toward the MAC array standard cell territory. This orientation minimizes the length of the highly congested weight distribution bus.
  • South-West Quadrant (Activation SRAM): The 16 KB pseudo-dual-port Activation SRAM is placed along the southern perimeter, with pins facing north-east toward the activation input registers of Row 0–7 of the MAC array. This isolates the read/write streaming traffic from the weight loading traffic.
  • Center-East Core (8x8 MAC Array Standard Cells): The 64 Processing Elements (PEs) are confined using soft placement guides into a rectangular block in the right-center region. This places the MAC engines directly adjacent to both the memory outputs and the post-processing requantization block, guaranteeing that no point-to-point critical path spans more than 400 µm of wire length.
  • North Boundary (Interfaces & AON Island): The AXI-Lite control interface, configuration registers, and the Slow Always-On (AON) power island are aligned along the northern perimeter. This provides clean, short escape routes for interface pins to the top-level SoC interconnect, preventing system-level routing from crossing the internal compute datapath.

12.2.3 Mitigating Timing Penalties via Floorplan Iterations

Early floorplanning iterations often suffer from routing congestion and timing violations caused by naive macro orientation. In Iteration 1 of the TinyEdge-NPU floorplan, the two 16 KB Weight SRAMs were placed along opposite boundaries (one on the North edge, one on the South edge), with the MAC array sandwiched between them. While this appeared visually balanced, static timing analysis (STA) revealed severe setup violations along the weight update path:

# Initial Timing Failure: Weight SRAM to Row-7 MAC register
Endpoint:    u_core/u_mac_array/pe_inst_7_7/weight_reg_reg[7]/D
Path Group:  core_clk (100 MHz, Target Period: 10.0 ns)
Required:     9.65 ns (accounting for 350 ps setup margin + jitter)
Arrival:     11.20 ns
Slack:       -1.55 ns  (VIOLATION)

The root cause was excessive wire latency: the weight broadcast bus was forced to route across the entire 1 mm die height, competing with activation routing tracks. By consolidating the two Weight SRAMs into an abutted bank on the North-West perimeter and rotating their orientations so their pin channels opened directly into the standard-cell routing area, wire lengths were cut by 55%. Inserting a 15 µm halo around the SRAM macros also eliminated localized routing blockages, driving the post-floorplan zero-wire-load slack from -1.55 ns to +1.20 ns.

12.3 Placement, Clock-Tree Synthesis (CTS), and Routing

12.3.1 Placement Optimization and Density Targets

Standard cell placement translates logic gates into legal, site-aligned locations while optimizing wirelength, timing, and dynamic power. For the TinyEdge-NPU, setting a single global target density is insufficient due to structural variations across the design hierarchy:

  • MAC Array Placement Bounds: The 8x8 MAC array contains 64 parallel 8-bit multipliers, input pipeline stages, and wide 32-bit adders. Standard cell density inside the MAC placement region must be bounded between 68% and 72%. If density rises above 75%, local pin density explodes, creating localized routing congestion (GCell pin density overflow). If density drops below 60%, interconnect wirelengths increase, degrading dynamic switching power.
  • Memory Pin Channel Keepouts: The corridors directly in front of the SRAM pin interfaces must be protected with partial placement blockage regions (density restricted to 30%–40%). This leaves vertical and horizontal routing tracks open for the wide buses exiting the memories.
  • AON Island Isolation: The Always-On power domain requires a physical keepout boundary. Level shifters and isolation cells must be placed along the domain perimeter using dedicated fence regions (`create_voltage_area` and `create_bound_step`).
# Cadence Innovus / Synopsys ICC2 Placement Constraint Snippet
create_placement_blockage -type soft -density 35 \
    -coordinates {50 350 450 420} -name pb_sram_pin_channel

create_voltage_area -name VA_AON -region {50 850 250 950} \
    -guard_band {5 5} -target_utilization 0.50

create_inst_group -name grp_mac_array
add_to_inst_group grp_mac_array [get_cells u_core/u_mac_array/*]
create_guide -name guide_mac_array -area {500 200 950 650} grp_mac_array

12.3.2 Clock-Tree Synthesis (CTS) for Dual-Domain Accelerators

The TinyEdge-NPU employs two distinct clock domains: the primary core_clk operating at 100 MHz (10.0 ns period) and the low-frequency always-on clock aon_clk operating at 32.768 kHz. While 100 MHz is not exceptionally fast for 28nm technology, minimizing clock skew across the 64 processing elements is critical. The high concentration of flip-flops in the MAC array creates significant risk of hold-time violations under fast/cold PVT signoff corners (e.g., FF / 0.99V / -40°C).

The CTS architecture utilizes a symmetrical H-tree topology for the core array, coupled with multi-threshold inverter/buffer pairs:

  • Target Clock Skew: < 40 ps globally across the core_clk domain; < 20 ps locally within any single MAC Processing Element row.
  • Target Insertion Delay (Latency): < 650 ps across all corners, ensuring that environmental variations do not produce wide latency spreads.
  • Clock Buffer Selection: Medium-drive, balanced-slew clock tree inverters (e.g., CLKINV_X8, CLKINV_X12) are utilized. Fast, single-stage high-drive buffers (such as CLKBUF_X32) are avoided because they cause inductive supply bounce during simultaneous clock switching events across the 64 MAC blocks.
# CTS Specification in Synopsys ICC2 Tcl Format
create_clock_tree_spec -name CTS_CORE \
    -clocks [get_clocks core_clk] \
    -target_skew 0.035 \
    -target_latency 0.600 \
    -max_transition 0.120 \
    -leaf_rules [get_clock_routing_rules LEAF_NDR] \
    -root_rules [get_clock_routing_rules ROOT_NDR]

# Non-Default Rule (NDR) to prevent crosstalk and EM on clock trunks
create_routing_rule ROOT_NDR \
    -widths {M5 0.100 M6 0.100} \
    -spacings {M5 0.100 M6 0.100}

set_clock_tree_references -clocks [get_clocks core_clk] \
    -references [list CLKINV_X8 CLKINV_X12 CLKINV_X16]

For the 32 kHz aon_clk domain, skew requirements are relaxed (< 2.0 ns), but absolute dynamic and static leakage is paramount. High-threshold voltage (HVT) or ultra-high-threshold voltage (UHVT) delay buffers are used exclusively to build this tree, minimizing static leakage power while the rest of the accelerator core is powered off via MTCMOS power gates.

12.3.3 Routing, Signal Integrity, and Metal-Layer Guidance

The routing strategy for the TinyEdge-NPU is mapped to a standard 28nm 1P8M (one poly, eight metal layers) BEOL (Back End of Line) stack:

  • M1 and M2: Reserved strictly for standard cell internal pin access, intra-cell connections, and very short local flylines. Global and cross-tile routing across M1/M2 is completely prohibited.
  • M3 and M4: Dedicated to intermediate cell-to-cell routing within the MAC array and local signal connections between the DMA control logic and SRAM interfaces.
  • M5 and M6: Reserved for high-speed, critical buses. This includes the 64-bit weight broadcast buses and activation streaming connections. To eliminate crosstalk and prevent timing variability, these lines are routed using Non-Default Routing (NDR) rules (double-width, double-spacing).
  • M7 and M8: Thick, low-resistance top-metal layers assigned to the global Power Distribution Network (PDN). M7 forms vertical straps for VDD/VSS grids; M8 forms horizontal straps. A dense via array stitches M7/M8 down through intermediate layers to create a rigid, low-impedance mesh that controls transient IR drop when the 64 MAC multipliers switch simultaneously.
Signal Integrity Note: Shielding the Weight Broadcast
When weights update during neural network layer transitions, 64 bits toggle simultaneously across 500 µm of interconnect. In a 28nm node, parallel lines on M5 running together over this distance can induce severe capacitive cross-coupling (Miller effect), degrading slew rates and injecting crosstalk glitches into adjacent control paths. The weight broadcast bus must be interleaved with dedicated VSS shielding lines (e.g., VSS-Signal-Signal-VSS) whenever parallel runs exceed 150 µm.
