12.3.4 Step-by-Step Quality and Sanity Checks

To avoid costly iterations late in the physical design cycle, the engineer must execute systematic verification checks after each major phase:

  1. Post-Floorplan Checks:
    • Verify all macro orientations guarantee unobstructed pin egress toward standard-cell areas.
    • Confirm memory macro halos (minimum 10 µm for TSMC 28nm) are strictly enforced to prevent standard cells from interfering with SRAM well structures.
    • Run early boundary flyline analysis to confirm that no critical signals traverse the entire core diagonally.
  2. Post-Placement Checks:
    • Analyze the global routing congestion map. Maximum Horizontal and Vertical GCell overflow must be strictly less than 0.5% with no congested spots greater than a 2×2 cluster.
    • Verify cell density distribution: standard-cell density in the MAC array must not exceed 72%; macro pin channels must stay below 40%.
    • Check high-fanout nets (HFN): ensure clock, resets, and scan enables are properly buffered and not driving unmanaged loads.
  3. Post-CTS Checks:
    • Inspect the clock skew report: global skew < 40 ps; local PE cluster skew < 20 ps.
    • Verify transition times (slew): clock pin transition times must be less than 100 ps on all leaf nodes at nominal operating conditions.
    • Perform preliminary hold-time analysis under the Fast-Fast (FF / 0.99V / -40°C) corner. Flag any paths with negative hold slack exceeding 150 ps, which could overwhelm the detail router with delay-buffer insertion.
  4. Post-Routing Checks:
    • Ensure zero DRC violations, zero open nets, and zero layout-versus-schematic (LVS) shorts.
    • Verify process antenna rules: all long metal lines running to standard cell gate inputs must incorporate routing layer hopping or reverse-biased antenna diodes directly adjacent to the input pins.
    • Run static and dynamic IR drop simulations: static drop must not exceed 1.5% of the VDD rail (13.5 mV on a 0.9V nominal supply); worst-case dynamic IR drop must remain below 3% (27 mV) during peak neural processing burst cycles.

12.4 Power Planning and Low-Power Implementation

Physical implementation of an edge AI accelerator in a 28nm bulk planar process (such as TSMC 28HPC+ or Samsung 28LPP) requires tight co-design of the physical power distribution network (PDN) and the logical power architecture. For the TinyEdge-NPU, the floorplan occupies roughly \(1.0\text{ mm} \times 1.0\text{ mm}\) (\(1.0\text{ mm}^2\)). In this footprint, the design must cleanly support a continuous active power budget below \(5\text{ mW}\) at \(100\text{ MHz}\) and an aggressive deep-sleep target below \(100\ \mu\text{W}\). Achieving both extremes demands a low-resistance global power grid paired with power gating, fine-grained retention, and strict domain partitioning.

Power Grid Architecture and Target Budgets

The TinyEdge-NPU employs an 8-metal layer back-end-of-line (BEOL) stack (M1–M8). Lower layers (M1–M3) handle local intra-cell connections and macro pin breakouts. Intermediate layers (M4–M5) carry orthogonal signal routing and local power rails, while thick upper metals (M6–M8) form the low-impedance power distribution backbone.

The core operates at a nominal \(V_{\text{DD}} = 0.9\text{ V}\). For low-power 28nm edge devices, timing margin degradation accelerates non-linearly if supply droop exceeds \(7\%\). We establish the following sign-off budgets across worst-case PVT corners (Slow-Slow, \(0.81\text{ V}\), \(125^\circ\text{C}\)):

  • Static IR-Drop Target: \(\le 1.5\%\) of nominal supply (\(13.5\text{ mV}\)).
  • Dynamic IR-Drop Target: \(\le 5.0\%\) of nominal supply (\(45.0\text{ mV}\) worst-case cumulative droop).
  • Effective Target Impedance (\(Z_{\text{target}}\)): Derived from the peak switching current. For an 8x8 INT8 MAC array and companion SRAM interfaces running at \(100\text{ MHz}\), peak burst current reaches \(I_{\text{peak}} \approx 18\text{ mA}\). With a \(45\text{ mV}\) dynamic margin: \[Z_{\text{target}} = \frac{\Delta V_{\text{max}}}{I_{\text{peak}}} = \frac{0.045\text{ V}}{0.018\text{ A}} = 2.5\ \Omega\] over a bandwidth up to the clock edge frequency (\(\sim 1\text{ GHz}\)).

The physical power mesh uses dual rings around the macro boundaries and a cross-hatch strap pattern:

  • Top Distribution (M7 & M8): Global grid running at a \(30\ \mu\text{m}\) pitch. M8 (\(1.2\ \mu\text{m}\) thick, \(2.0\ \mu\text{m}\) width) runs horizontally, carrying unswitched \(V_{\text{DD\_AON}}\) and \(V_{\text{SS}}\). M7 (\(0.8\ \mu\text{m}\) thick, \(1.5\ \mu\text{m}\) width) runs vertically, distributing switched core power (\(V_{\text{DD\_CORE}}\)) and \(V_{\text{SS}}\).
  • Intermediate Mesh (M5 & M6): M6 straps (\(0.4\ \mu\text{m}\) width, \(10\ \mu\text{m}\) pitch) drop power down to standard cell rows and memory halos. M5 provides high-density routing over the MAC array tiles.
  • Standard Cell Rail (M1): Standard cell rows are \(0.6\ \mu\text{m}\) high (9-track libraries). The continuous M1 power rail (\(0.06\ \mu\text{m}\) width) connects to cell \(V_{\text{DD}}\) and \(V_{\text{SS}}\) pins, strapped by regular via stacks up to M5 every \(5\ \mu\text{m}\) to prevent localized rail collapse.

Decoupling Capacitance (DCAP) Allocation

Dynamic switching of the 64 INT8 multiply-accumulate units induces high \(di/dt\) transient events at every positive clock edge. To suppress inductive voltage droop without introducing unacceptable leakage, decoupling capacitance is inserted through a tiered strategy:

  • SRAM Boundary DCAP: Dedicated decap halos surrounding the 32 KB Weight SRAM and 16 KB Activation SRAM macros, filtering high-current precharge pulses.
  • Filler DCAP Cells: Standard cell DCAP (poly-gate and thin-oxide capacitors) placed automatically in empty cell sites across the switchable core domain. These yield approximately \(18\text{ pF}\) of distributed capacitance.
  • Leakage vs. Droop Trade-off: Thin-oxide DCAPs exhibit non-trivial gate tunneling leakage at 28nm (\(\sim 0.8\text{ pA}/\mu\text{m}^2\)). In the switchable core domain, this leakage is completely eliminated during sleep by power-gating. In the Always-On (AON) domain, thin-oxide decaps are strictly forbidden; low-leakage metal-oxide-metal (MOM) fringe capacitors or thick-oxide IO capacitors are deployed instead.

Power Gating Architecture: Header Switches

We isolate the primary power consumer, the \(8\times8\) MAC array, input/output accumulators, and weight buffers, using distributed coarse-grained PMOS header switches. PMOS headers were chosen over NMOS footers because keeping a continuous, unified ground (\(V_{\text{SS}}\)) substrate plane eliminates substrate noise injection into sensitive retention latches and avoids back-bias shifts in adjacent un-gated standard cells.

flowchart TD subgraph AON_Domain ["Always-On Power Domain: VDD_AON / Continuous VSS"] PMU[Power Management Unit] AON_CTRL["Wakeup Logic & AXI-Lite Regs"] ISO_CTRL[Isolation Controller] RET_CTRL[Retention Controller] end subgraph Power_Switches ["Distributed PMOS Headers"] SW_CHAIN[Daisy-Chained Sleep Transistors] end subgraph Gated_Domain ["Switchable Domain: VDD_CORE"] MAC[8x8 INT8 MAC Array] DATAPATH["Quantization & Normalization"] CFG_REGS[Config Registers with Retention Latches] end subgraph Memory_System ["Memory Domain: Dual-Rail Array"] SRAM_W[32 KB Weight SRAM] SRAM_A[16 KB Activation SRAM] end PMU -->|SLEEP_EN Chain| SW_CHAIN PMU -->|SAVE / RESTORE| RET_CTRL PMU -->|ISO_EN| ISO_CTRL SW_CHAIN -->|Gated Power Rail| MAC SW_CHAIN -->|Gated Power Rail| DATAPATH SW_CHAIN -->|Gated Power Rail| CFG_REGS RET_CTRL -->|Shadow Register Clock| CFG_REGS ISO_CTRL -->|Clamp Signals to 0| MAC MAC -->|Clamped Outputs| AON_CTRL PMU -->|Periphery Cutoff / Bias| SRAM_W PMU -->|Periphery Cutoff / Bias| SRAM_A

The PMOS header array is embedded in dedicated standard-cell rows across the core fabric. Key design parameters include:

  • Total Switch Width and IR Impact: Sized for an equivalent on-resistance (\(R_{\text{on}}\)) of less than \(0.4\ \Omega\) across the entire block. The aggregate saturation resistance induces less than a \(6\text{ mV}\) drop at peak operational current (\(18\text{ mA}\)).
  • In-Rush Current and Daisy-Chaining: Turning on all power switches simultaneously would cause an uncontrolled surge current (\(I_{\text{inrush}} > 120\text{ mA}\)), collapsing \(V_{\text{DD\_AON}}\) and inducing brownout resets on active registers. The sleep signal (`SLEEP_N`) is routed through a 16-stage buffer tree (daisy chain) spanning the cell array. This throttles the turn-on ramp over a \(1.2\ \mu\text{s}\) interval, capping the maximum in-rush current at \(8.5\text{ mA}\). This 1.2 µs figure is the cold power-up ramp from 0 V, with the full 16-stage daisy chain sequencing the switch segments; it is not the retention wake-up ramp (see the Wakeup Latency item below and Chapter 7, §7.5).
  • Wakeup Latency: At a core clock of \(100\text{ MHz}\) (\(10\text{ ns}\) cycle), a \(1.2\ \mu\text{s}\) cold power-up sequence translates to 120 clock cycles. Acceptable for a cold power-up, which happens once at power-on, but far outside the ≤64-cycle retention wake-up budget. The retention wake-up ramp is different: the SRAM arrays are already held at the 0.65 V data-retention voltage, so the rail only has to rise from 0.65 V to the 0.90 V operating voltage, and that ramp fits the 28-cycle window inside the 64-cycle wake-up budget (Chapter 7, §7.5). The 120-cycle figure must never be quoted as the wake-up latency.

Isolation and Retention Strategy (<100 µW Target)

To meet the \(100\ \mu\text{W}\) deep-sleep budget, the physical implementation enforces strict interface and state boundaries:

  1. Isolation Cells (ISO): Every signal crossing from the switchable \(V_{\text{DD\_CORE}}\) domain into the unswitched \(V_{\text{DD\_AON}}\) domain is buffered through standard clamp cells (AND-type isolation cells clamped to ground). This eliminates floating inputs that would otherwise cause high intermediate-voltage shoot-through currents in the AON domain logic.
  2. Retention Flip-Flops (RFF): Hardware registers containing layer configuration, base memory addresses, INT8 scale factors, and bias offsets (totaling 284 bits) use balloon-latch retention flip-flops. The retention latches are powered by a dedicated \(V_{\text{DD\_RET}}\) rail derived from \(V_{\text{DD\_AON}}\), while the main register flip-flop is on \(V_{\text{DD\_CORE}}\). Prior to asserting `SLEEP_N`, the AON controller triggers `SAVE` (1 cycle). On wake-up, it strobes `RESTORE` (1 cycle), bypassing external memory re-initialization.
  3. SRAM Sleep Management: The 32 KB Weight and 16 KB Activation SRAMs are equipped with dual-rail power architectures: the peripheral logic is powered by switchable \(V_{\text{DD\_CORE}}\), while the bitcell array is tied to an internal retention power rail (\(V_{\text{DD\_RET\_SRAM}}\)). In sleep mode, peripheral power is disconnected, and the bitcell array is clamped via internal diode regulators to \(0.65\text{ V}\) (data-retention voltage, or DRV). This cuts SRAM leakage by \(78\%\) while preserving weights.
Deep-Sleep Power Budget Breakdown (Nominal 28nm HKMG, 25°C):
• Gated Logic (\(V_{\text{DD\_CORE}}\) off, reverse-biased headers): \(0.8\ \mu\text{W}\)
• SRAM Arrays (Retention mode at \(0.65\text{ V}\), 48 KB total (S configuration)): \(64.2\ \mu\text{W}\)
• AON Logic (~5,200 gates active at \(32.768\text{ kHz}\)): \(3.1\ \mu\text{W}\)
• RFF Balloon Latches (284 bits retain mode): \(1.4\ \mu\text{W}\)
• Total Standby Leakage: \(69.5\ \mu\text{W}\) (Well within the \(< 100\ \mu\text{W}\) specification).

UPF Implementation and Verification Flow

Power intent is defined formally in IEEE 1801 (UPF 2.1). Below is the production-grade UPF snippet driving synthesis and place-and-route for the TinyEdge-NPU: 

## TinyEdge-NPU Core Power Intent (UPF 2.1)
create_power_domain PD_AON -include_scope
create_power_domain PD_NPU -elements {u_mac_array u_datapath u_acc u_weight_sram u_act_sram u_dma}

# Define Supply Ports and Nets
create_supply_port VDD -direction in
create_supply_port VSS -direction in

create_supply_net VDD_AON   -domain PD_AON
create_supply_net VSS       -domain PD_AON
create_supply_net VDD_CORE  -domain PD_NPU
create_supply_net VSS       -domain PD_NPU -reuse

set_domain_supply_net PD_AON  -primary_power_net VDD_AON  -primary_ground_net VSS
set_domain_supply_net PD_NPU -primary_power_net VDD_CORE -primary_ground_net VSS

# Define Power Switch (Header) for PD_NPU
create_power_switch pwr_switch_core \
  -domain PD_NPU \
  -switch_on_condition {switch_on !sleep_b} \
  -input_supply_port {in VDD_AON} \
  -output_supply_port {out VDD_CORE} \
  -control_port {sleep_b sleep_b_ctrl}

# Isolation Strategy: Clamp outputs of PD_NPU to 0 when sleeping
set_isolation iso_core_to_aon \
  -domain PD_NPU \
  -isolation_power_net VDD_AON \
  -isolation_ground_net VSS \
  -clamp_value 0 \
  -applies_to outputs

set_isolation_control iso_core_to_aon \
  -domain PD_NPU \
  -isolation_signal u_pmu/iso_en \
  -isolation_sense high \
  -location parent

# Retention Strategy: Save config registers across power cycles
set_retention ret_core_cfg \
  -domain PD_NPU \
  -retention_power_net VDD_AON \
  -retention_ground_net VSS

set_retention_control ret_core_cfg \
  -domain PD_NPU \
  -save_signal    {u_pmu/ret_save    high} \
  -restore_signal {u_pmu/ret_restore high}

Low-power formal checks (such as Synopsys VC LP or Siemens Questa PowerCheck) verify this intent continuously. Static checks verify:

  • Every output port from `PD_NPU` to `PD_AON` has an isolation cell mapped to an unswitched supply.
  • No unbuffered level-shifters bridge disparate voltage domains.
  • All retained registers receive continuous supply (`VDD_AON`) during simulation of power-down events.
  • No push-pull standard cell inputs float when the `sleep_b_ctrl` signal transitions low.
---

12.5 DRC, LVS, and Sign-Off at 28nm

Transitioning from 40nm/65nm nodes to 28nm marks the boundary where geometric planar layout rules transition into stress-engineered and lithography-constrained design rules. At 28nm, lithographic patterning requires high-numerical-aperture immersion (193nm ArFi) lithography with extensive optical proximity correction (OPC). Physical verification is no longer merely an exercise in finding design-rule check (DRC) violations. It dictates yield, device longevity, and functional immunity to parasitic electrostatics.

What DRC and LVS Actually Check at 28nm

Traditional DRC evaluates two-dimensional polygon width and spacing. At 28nm, DRC encompasses multi-layer dependency checks, stress-induced variation rules, and double-patterning or gridded rules on critical layers:

  • OD (Oxide Diffusion) Spacing and Jog Rules: The layout must account for the Length-of-Diffusion (LOD) effect and shallow trench isolation (STI) stress. Moving an active diffusion edge \(50\text{ nm}\) closer to a channel alters PMOS hole mobility by up to \(8\%\). DRC decks evaluate context-dependent active area spacing rules across standard cell boundaries.
  • End-of-Line (EOL) and Enclosure Checks: Metal wires terminating facing another metal line must maintain enlarged keep-out distances to prevent dielectric bridging caused by line-end pull-back during optical lithography. Via enclosures on M1–M4 must follow asymmetrical rules (e.g., minimum end-of-line enclosure \(\ge 15\text{ nm}\), side enclosure \(\ge 2\text{ nm}\)).
  • Antenna Ratios: During fabrication, reactive ion etching (RIE) charges floating metal runs. If a long metal wire connects to a thin-oxide gate without an intermediate reverse-biased junction, the trapped charge discharges through the gate oxide, permanently puncturing the dielectric. Antenna ratios at 28nm are notoriously tight (\(\text{Area}_{\text{metal}} / \text{Area}_{\text{gate}} \le 200:1\) on intermediate routing layers).
  • Layout Versus Schematic (LVS): LVS extracts device instances, pin geometries, and nodal interconnects from GDSII/OASIS data to compare against the final structural CDL/SPICE netlist. At 28nm, LVS also measures analog layout parameters (well-proximity distance, source/drain perimeters, LOD parameters \(SA, SB\)) and updates circuit performance models for parasitic simulation.

Common Violations in Low-Power Accelerators

The physical layout of the TinyEdge-NPU, with its dense MAC matrix flanked by memory blocks, repeatedly trips three specific categories of violations:

  • Antenna Violations on Clustered Broadcast Busses: The control lines (`weight_valid`, `accum_en`, and weight configuration busses) fan out from the central controller to all 64 MAC execution units. These signals run continuously on M4 and M5 for over \(800\ \mu\text{m}\). As these layers are patterned before higher metals are deposited, the long wires act as antennas connected to the thin gate oxides of the multiplier inputs. Resolution: The router must either automatically insert antenna diodes directly adjacent to the input gates or force the wire up to M7 via a reverse "jog", breaking the antenna length at intermediate metal processing steps.
  • Minimum-Area Metal Islands: Automated routing over tightly packed memory pin interfaces frequently produces short, isolated metal jogs that satisfy minimum width and spacing but fail the minimum area rule (\(\text{Area} < 0.04\ \mu\text{m}^2\) on M2/M3). Resolution: The post-route optimization engine must execute metal-expansion passes or use rule-aware patch-filling scripts.
  • SRAM Abutment, Well-Taps, and Boundary Halo Violations: The 32 KB and 16 KB compiled memory blocks feature strict external implant and well enclosure requirements. Placing standard cells directly against memory macros without a transition region produces N-well/P-well design-rule errors and violates DRC well-tap distance limits (\(\le 15\ \mu\text{m}\) to the nearest tap). Resolution: Memory macros must be bounded by dedicated boundary cells, end-cap cells, and a minimum routing halo of at least \(3.5\ \mu\text{m}\).
flowchart LR GDS["Post-P&R GDSII / OASIS"] --> FILL["Dummy Metal & Poly Fill"] FILL --> DRC[Calibre / Pegasus DRC] FILL --> LVS[Calibre / Pegasus LVS] GDS --> ERC[Electrical Rule Checks] DRC -->|Clean| AGG[Sign-off Aggregation] LVS -->|Clean| AGG ERC -->|Clean| AGG FILL --> EXT[Parasitic Extraction QRC/StarRC] EXT --> SPEF[Annotated SPEF] SPEF --> DYN_IR[Voltus / RedHawk Dynamic EM/IR] DYN_IR -->|Clean| AGG DRC -.->|Violations| ECO[Automated ECO Loop] LVS -.->|Violations| ECO DYN_IR -.->|Excessive Droop| ECO ECO -->|Route Patching / Diode Insertion| GDS

Electrical Rule Checks (ERC)

Unlike geometric DRC, Electrical Rule Checks evaluate non-functional or hazardous electrical configurations across physical domains:

  • Substrate and Well Continuity: Asserts that every standard cell P-substrate connection ties back to the true primary \(V_{\text{SS}}\), and all N-wells connect cleanly to their proper voltage supplies without forming isolated floating well islands.
  • Cross-Domain Sneak Paths: ERC highlights scenarios where an unpowered PMOS drain in the gated domain connects across an un-isolated gate in the always-on domain, forming a forward-biased PN junction with the substrate that drains supply rails during deep sleep.
  • Thin-Oxide Over-Voltage Checks: Identifies standard cells accidentally tied directly to an unbuffered \(1.8\text{ V}\) IO pad line without a voltage-divider or thick-oxide ESD clamp.

Metal Fill and CMP Sign-Off

To enable uniform planarization during Chemical-Mechanical Polishing (CMP) and prevent dishing or erosion of dielectric layers, foundry specifications impose strict metal density limits across all layers (typically \(25\%\) to \(75\%\) density within a moving \(20\ \mu\text{m} \times 20\ \mu\text{m}\) analysis window). Metal fill insertion at 28nm is non-trivial:

  • Dummy Fill Strategy: Non-functional metal shapes (perforated or staggered rectangles) are placed systematically across empty routing channels. Fill is connected to ground (\(V_{\text{SS}}\)) or left floating based on layer-specific foundry models.
  • Impact on Timing: Dummy metal placed too close to critical parallel signals, such as the high-speed adder trees within the MAC tiles, adds parasitic coupling capacitance (\(C_{\text{cross}}\)), increasing clock-to-output delays and inducing crosstalk noise. Sign-off flows require metal fill insertion to be performed before final parasitic extraction (RC Extraction), ensuring that timing closure (STA) reflects actual post-fill parasitics.

Electromigration and IR Drop (EM/IR) Sign-Off

Physical sign-off concludes with dynamic, vector-driven EM/IR analysis:

  • Electromigration (EM): High current density creates atomic migration along the aluminum or copper lattice, resulting in downstream voids or neighboring shorts. EM sign-off requires evaluating: \[J_{\text{RMS}} \le J_{\text{spec\_RMS}} \quad \text{and} \quad J_{\text{AVG}} \le J_{\text{spec\_AVG}}\] Every power tap, macro power pin via stack, and primary clock wire must pass EM analysis over a continuous 10-year operating lifetime at \(105^\circ\text{C}\) junction temperature.
  • Static vs. Dynamic IR: Static IR validates that the time-averaged \(I_{\text{RMS}} \times R_{\text{mesh}}\) drop does not degrade nominal voltages across standard cell clusters. Dynamic IR incorporates instant peak currents (\(di/dt\)), internal decap charge delivery, and package parasitics (\(L_{\text{package}}, R_{\text{package}}\)) through high-coverage simulation vectors.
---

12.6 Worked Sign-Off Example: TinyEdge-NPU

To demonstrate the physical sign-off procedure on the TinyEdge-NPU, we evaluate the final post-layout design through an industry-standard physical verification flow. The TinyEdge-NPU macro occupies approximately 1.02 mm×0.98 mm of silicon area in a commercial 28nm High-K Metal Gate (HKMG) process. Operating at a nominal core voltage of 0.90 V and a clock frequency of 100 MHz, the macro houses an 8×8 INT8 MAC array, control state machines, 16 KB of activation SRAM, and 32 KB of weight SRAM. At this density, geometric deviations, subtle layout-versus-schematic mismatches, parasitic coupling, and power delivery weaknesses can render silicon completely non-functional or degrade reliability over time.

Physical sign-off is not an open-ended optimization phase; it is an unforgiving, rule-bound gating process. The layout must pass foundry-certified rule decks across every physical and electrical verification domain before generating the final customer-facing GDSII/OASIS release package. The verification flow follows a structured, closed-loop execution pattern where each failure triggers specific ECO (Engineering Change Order) loops, as shown in the sign-off flow below.

flowchart TD A[Routed Post-CTS GDSII / OASIS] --> B["DRC & Antenna Check"] B -->|Violations Found| C["ECO Routing & Diode Insertion"] C --> B B -->|DRC / Antenna Clean| D["LVS & ERC Verification"] D -->|Mismatch / ERC Error| E[Schematic / Well-Tap ECO] E --> D D -->|LVS / ERC Clean| F[Dummy Metal Fill Insertion] F --> G["Fill DRC & Density Check"] G --> H[Full-Chip Parasitic Extraction RC] H --> I["Static & Dynamic IR / EM Sign-Off"] I -->|IR / EM Breach| J[Power Grid / Decap Refinement] J --> H I -->|All Sign-Off Targets Met| K[Final Sign-Off Archive Freeze]

12.6.1 Design Rule Checking (DRC) and Iterative Resolutions

The 28nm foundry deck enforces more than 4,200 individual geometric rules covering minimum width, spacing, area, enclosure, end-of-line spacing, and complex multi-patterning constraints. The initial full-chip DRC pass on the TinyEdge-NPU unmasked two significant physical violations that required structural layout ECOs.

  • Antenna Ratio Violation on Weight Broadcast Net: The broadcast net weight_bcast_row[3][7:0] traverses nearly 820 µm along Metal 3, routing from the central weight buffer across all eight processing elements in Row 3. During metal fabrication, reactive-ion etching (RIE) accumulates charge along long, unconnected metal runs. The antenna ratio, defined as the conductive area of the metal pattern divided by the thin gate-oxide area of the receiving inputs, reached 418:1 on this net. The foundry deck limits the maximum allowed antenna ratio on Metal 3 to 200:1 to prevent electrostatic breakdown of the delicate 28nm gate dielectrics.
    Resolution: The violation was resolved via a hybrid approach. First, an automated routing jumper hopped the signal up to Metal 4 close to the driving pin, breaking the long Metal 3 antenna receiver trace during intermediate processing steps. Second, dedicated reverse-biased antenna diodes (diffusion clamps) were instantiated directly adjacent to the input gate pins of the downstream MAC cells. This lowered the effective post-ECO antenna ratio to 74:1, well within the safety margin.
  • Metal Minimum-Area Violation near SRAM Abutment: A minimum-area violation (rule M2.A.1, requiring a minimum planar area of 0.055 µm² for any isolated Metal 2 island) appeared along the interface between the standard cell logic corridor and the 32 KB weight SRAM macro. The auto-router had snapped a set of Metal 2 horizontal signal tracks to the SRAM pin blockages, but subsequent pin-trimming operations left three disconnected, floating stubs measuring only 0.034 µm².
    Resolution: Rather than relying on automated fill to patch the defect, the layout engineer executed a manual ECO in the layout editor, retracting the truncated tracks back to their driving standard cell pins and snapping them to the nearest valid track pitch, eliminating the runt geometry entirely.

A second iteration of the DRC deck confirmed zero errors across all layers, satisfying both base-layer FEOL (Front-End of Line) and BEOL (Back-End of Line) criteria.

12.6.2 Layout Versus Schematic (LVS) and Device Recognition

LVS verifies that the electrical network realized in the physical layout matches the logical connectivity specified in the structural netlist. For the TinyEdge-NPU, the sign-off netlist comprised 184,210 standard cells (roughly 740,000 transistors) alongside the two embedded SRAM macros. The LVS extraction engine extracted the geometric components into an equivalent SPICE netlist using foundry device-recognition layers.

The SRAM macros were treated as hierarchical black boxes during early development, but for final physical sign-off, they were verified using full schematic-versus-layout views matching the memory vendor's certified macro CDL (Circuit Description Language) netlists. Special attention was paid to:

  • Power Domain Isolation: TinyEdge-NPU includes a core logic domain (VDD_CORE, 0.90 V nominal), a dedicated low-leakage memory array domain (VDD_MEM, 0.90 V nominal), and a sleep retention domain (VDD_RET, capable of collapse to 0.65 V during sleep). LVS validated that power and ground routing for each domain remained strictly separated, with no shorts between the standard cell logic rails and the macro power rings.
  • Well-Tap and Substrate Contacts: 28nm DRC/LVS rules mandate continuous bulk connection to avoid latch-up. The physical layout incorporates dedicated tap cells placed on a uniform 20 µm checkerboard pitch. LVS verified that all NMOS bulks connect unambiguously to VSS and all PMOS bulks connect to their respective VDD supply rails.
  • Dummy and Decoupling Capacitance (Decap) Cells: Fillers containing poly and active gate layers (decap cells) were matched against the structural netlist to guarantee that added decoupling capacitance did not induce gate-leakage shorts or unmapped net terminations.

The final extraction output reported a 1:1 topological match: 0 unmatched nets, 0 unmatched instances, and 0 pin discrepancies.

12.6.3 Electrical Rule Checking (ERC)

While LVS confirms that layout mirrors schematic, Electrical Rule Checking (ERC) looks for inherently dangerous electrical topologies that may be structurally matched but electrically invalid. Running the foundry sign-off ERC deck over the TinyEdge-NPU verified three core parameters:

  1. Well Bias and Floating Gates: All N-wells and P-substrates were evaluated for resistive path limits back to power pads. The maximum calculated resistance from any diffusion tap to the farthest transistor channel was 18.4 Ω, safely below the 50 Ω foundry latch-up limit. No floating MOS gates were discovered.
  2. Cross-Domain Sneak Paths: Because the NPU switches between an active mode (<5 mW) and a deep sleep state (<100 µW), isolation cells border the power-gated core logic. The ERC deck evaluated whether any un-isolated signal traced directly from a powered-down VDD_CORE driver to an active VDD_MEM peripheral receiver. The tool flagged zero unprotected boundary crossings, validating that all isolation cells are powered by the persistent VDD_RET rail and correctly clamped to logic zero during sleep.

12.6.4 Metal Fill Insertion and Parasitic Integrity

To avoid chemical-mechanical polishing (CMP) dishing and erosion during wafer fabrication, metal density across each layer (Metal 1 through Metal 7) must remain within strict planar windows, typically between 25% and 70% within any sliding 50 µm×50 µm window. The un-filled TinyEdge-NPU layout exhibited local metal density valleys as low as 14% on Metal 4 and Metal 5 in the routing channels between the MAC array and the SRAM blocks.

Automated track-based, dummy-metal fill was synthesized across all metal layers. Dummy metal features were instantiated as floating and tied fill patterns, using staggered geometries to minimize parasitic side-wall capacitance to adjacent active signal traces. Following fill generation, a full-chip parasitic extraction (RC extraction) was performed. A delta-analysis comparing post-fill vs. pre-fill parasitics demonstrated an average total capacitance increase of only 3.8% on critical signal nets. Setup timing on the 100 MHz clock domain (10.0 ns period) absorbed this delta cleanly: the worst-case slack on the critical activation accumulation path decreased from +182 ps to +146 ps, preserving timing closure without secondary buffer insertion.

12.6.5 Electromigration (EM) and Power Integrity (IR Drop)

Power integrity determines whether the core logic receives adequate voltage under peak switching current, and whether long-term metal degradation from electromigration will compromise the IP's 10-year operating lifetime. The power grid on TinyEdge-NPU utilizes an orthogonal mesh with Metal 1 standard cell rails, thick vertical Metal 5 straps, and ultra-thick horizontal Metal 6/Metal 7 global distribution layers.

The sign-off analysis evaluated both static and dynamic IR drop at the worst-case corner (Slow-Slow, 125°C, \(V_{DD} = 0.81\text{ V}\), reflecting a nominal 0.90 V supply degraded by a 10% external source tolerance).

  • Static IR Drop: Evaluated using the average peak power consumption of 4.82 mW during uninterrupted 8×8 matrix multiplications. The maximum static IR drop was observed near the geometric centroid of the MAC array, recording a peak drop of 11.4 mV (representing 1.27% of nominal \(V_{DD}\)). This easily satisfied the static sign-off threshold of ≤2.0% (18.0 mV).
  • Dynamic IR Drop: Dynamic analysis utilized a gate-level activity vector (VCD) capturing the highest-stress scenario: a simultaneous wake-up burst where all 64 MAC units transition from zero to full accumulation while the weight SRAM completes an eight-word burst read. The peak transient current reached 21.6 mA over a 250 ps window. The worst dynamic IR drop was measured at 29.8 mV (3.31% of \(V_{DD}\)), safely below the strict IP sign-off threshold of ≤5.0% (45.0 mV). Simultaneous ground bounce (\(V_{SS}\) rail rise) peaked at 14.2 mV.
  • Electromigration (EM) Compliance: EM evaluations were executed at 105°C continuous junction temperature over a 10-year operating model:
    • Signal EM: The highest RMS current density occurred on the root net of the balanced H-tree clock network. The measured \(J_{RMS}\) was \(3.2 \times 10^5\text{ A/cm}^2\) against a foundry reliability limit of \(7.5 \times 10^5\text{ A/cm}^2\), yielding an EM margin of 2.34× (a 57% safety buffer).
    • Power Rail EM: Standard-cell Metal 1 rail currents were evaluated for peak DC current limits under maximum toggle conditions. The worst-case current density showed an EM margin of 1.78× against voiding and hillock formation thresholds.

12.6.6 Sign-Off Verification Checklist

The following checklist summarizes the definitive status of the TinyEdge-NPU physical sign-off audit. Every metric represents a hard gate; a single failure prevents foundry release.

Sign-Off Check Target Specification Achieved Value Foundry Tool / Deck Status

Antenna Ratio Ratio ≤ 200:1 (M1–M7) Max Ratio: 74:1 (M3 net) Calibre PERC / Antenna Deck PASS

Sign-Off Engineering Takeaway: Never run metal fill as a disconnected cosmetic step. Because fill introduces sidewall and vertical coupling capacitance that directly impairs dynamic power, setup timing, and IR drop, the post-fill database must always be re-extracted and fed back through the final static timing analysis (STA) and power-integrity loops before freezing the design.

For an IP deliverable, sign-off is fundamentally different than it is for a monolithic SoC. A full-chip SoC team signs off against a single fixed floorplan, pad frame, and packaging configuration. In contrast, an IP team signs off against a rigorous contract of portability and integration tolerance. When TinyEdge-NPU is designated "sign-off clean," the development organization legally and technically warrants that the hard macro will introduce zero DRC errors, will not collapse the host SoC's local power mesh, will not fail under 10 years of peak-load electromigration stress, and will deliver its documented operating frequency within standard foundry margins. Sign-off is the boundary where design engineering ends and formal commercial warranty begins.

12.7 Why a Testchip Is Imperative for New Semiconductor IP

No tier-one semiconductor customer licenses high-performance or ultra-low-power silicon IP based purely on datasheets, RTL simulation logs, or FPGA demonstrations. While pre-silicon verification demonstrates functional correctness under idealized abstraction layers, it fundamentally fails to prove the non-linear physical realities of deep submicron fabrication. For an edge AI processor like the TinyEdge-NPU, which operates at the tight intersection of sub-milliwatt power budgets, dense SRAM arrays, and localized high-density dynamic switching, a testchip is not a luxury; it is the sole prerequisite for commercial viability.

Simulation and emulation tools rely on abstracted models (Liberty timing files, LEF/DEF physical abstracts, and extracted SPICE netlists). These models are approximations calibrated against standard foundry test vehicles, not custom architectures executing concurrent tensor computations. An FPGA prototype confirms that your microarchitecture executes keyword-spotting neural networks without mathematical drift, but it runs on an entirely decoupled manufacturing process (typically a mature, high-leakage FPGA fabric with rigid look-up tables and segmented routing channels) that bears zero physical resemblance to a target low-power foundry node such as 28nm HKMG (High-k Metal Gate).

Key Takeaway: An FPGA demonstrates that the algorithm works in logic; a testchip demonstrates that the circuits survive physics. A testchip delivers empirical, unarguable validation of four physical vectors that software cannot replicate:
  • Silicon-Proven Power Signatures: In the TinyEdge-NPU, the active power budget is strictly bounded at <5 mW at 100 MHz, with sleep leakage capped at <100 μW. EDA power analysis tools (such as Cadence Joules or Synopsys PrimePower) depend on gate-level toggle densities (SAIF/VCD vectors). These tools routinely exhibit estimation variances of ±25% to ±40% when calculating localized dynamic capacitance (\(C_{eff}\)) and dynamic clock-gating efficiency. Silicon measurement under actual workloads (e.g., continuous 1-second audio frame inference using a Deep Neural Network or Temporal Convolutional Network) provides true milliwatt-per-in-flight-MAC metrics across operating temperatures (\(-40^\circ\text{C}\) to \(+125^\circ\text{C}\)).
  • True SRAM Yield, Retention, and \(V_{min}\): The TinyEdge-NPU integrates 48 KB of on-chip memory (S configuration: a 32 KB weight buffer and a 16 KB activation buffer). Memory compiler SPICE models provide statistical approximations of bitcell stability, but they cannot predict exact static noise margins (SNM) in the presence of real localized intra-die variations, lithographic line-edge roughness (LER), and random dopant fluctuation (RDF). A testchip validates the true minimum operating voltage (\(V_{min}\)) of the SRAM bitcells, quantifying the retention floor during deep-sleep states where power-gating headers leak current.
  • Critical Path Timing Margins and Dynamic IR Drop: Static Timing Analysis (STA) operates on conservative global corner calculations (e.g., SSG / 0.81V / 125°C). However, when all 64 Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) engines in an 8×8 array toggle simultaneously on a heavy weight matrix burst, the instantaneous current demand (\(di/dt\)) generates high-frequency power-distribution-network (PDN) droop. A testchip reveals whether dynamic IR drop induces local clock jitter or path degradation that violates setup time on the actual silicon grid, exposing hold-time vulnerabilities that STA derating factors (AOCV/POCV) may have missed.
  • Analog and IO Subsystem Boundary Dynamics: Package parasitics (wirebond inductance, trace capacitance, pad-ring series resistance) distort edge rates and cause ground bounce during concurrent bus transitions. Validating physical IO behavior, particularly standard low-voltage CMOS IOs interfacing to off-chip host MCUs via AXI-Lite, ensures that drive strengths, slew rates, and ESD clamp leakage conform to operational targets without triggering parasitic substrate injection.

12.8 Tapeout Vehicle Strategies: Standalone, MPW, or Piggyback

Bringing a physical prototype to silicon requires selecting an appropriate tapeout vehicle. The decision directly impacts organizational burn rate, delivery schedules, and the fidelity of your characterization data. The three dominant paths are: a dedicated standalone maskset, a Multi-Project Wafer (MPW) shuttle, and a piggyback integration onto a partner or customer tapeout.

Strategy Mask / Fab Cost (28nm) Turnaround Schedule Area Constraints Risk Profile Schedule & Die Control Best Fit for TinyEdge-NPU
Standalone Run $600k – $1.2M+ (full mask tooling) Fastest fab time: ~10–12 weeks Unconstrained (entire wafer reticle, ~26×33 mm) High financial risk; complete liability for mask floor failures Absolute control over run dates, splits, and process skews Poor: Economically unjustifiable for validating a 1 mm² early-stage IP block.
MPW Shuttle (e.g., Europractice, MOSIS, TSMC Shuttle) $80k – $160k (standard slot) Slow to moderate: fixed schedule, ~14–18 weeks Strictly bounded (typically 1.5×1.5 mm, 2×2 mm, or 3×4 mm blocks) Low financial exposure; shared reticle costs across multiple tenants Low control; strict non-negotiable tapeout freeze dates; no wafer split control Optimal: Low-cost path delivering 40–100 packaged parts—sufficient for full characterization.
Piggyback (SoC Partner Integration) $0 – $50k (internal cost-share / license discount) Tied directly to host SoC tapeout milestones Variable: restricted to leftover "white space" on partner floorplan High operational risk: host SoC bugs, ESD faults, or pin limitations can brick IP testability Zero control: subservient to partner tapeout delays, fab choices, and package constraints Conditional: Viable only if an anchoring customer demands in-system validation and provides dedicated pins.

Selecting the Strategy for TinyEdge-NPU

For an IP startup or internal corporate R&D group developing the TinyEdge-NPU, the MPW shuttle is the mathematically and operationally correct strategy. The core IP occupies ~1.0 mm² in a standard 28nm process (including test harnesses). A standard 1.5 mm × 1.5 mm (2.25 mm²) or 2.0 mm × 2.0 mm (4.0 mm²) MPW block provides ample die area for the NPU, dedicated memory test matrices, process monitors, and a full pad ring.

Piggybacking is tempting because it eliminates mask fees, but it introduces shared fate. If the host SoC fails to exit reset due to a defect in their power-management unit (PMU) or clock generator, the TinyEdge-NPU cannot be initialized, rendering your silicon characterization effort a total loss. An MPW preserves architectural isolation: every pin, power supply, and test structure is under your direct instrumentation control.

12.9 Testchip Architecture: What Goes on the Die (and What Stays Off)

A testchip is an instrumentation instrument, not a commercial product. Its architectural focus shifts from production software conveniences (such as high-throughput interconnects and complex DMA controllers) to observability, controllability, structural isolation, and process validation.

1. The Core Under Test (DUT)

The primary instance of the TinyEdge-NPU core must represent the production physical synthesis, place, and route baseline. It includes the 8×8 INT8 MAC datapath, microcode sequencer, activation function pipelines (ReLU/Sigmoid approximations), and AXI-Lite register bank. It is strongly advised to instantiate two variations of the core if MPW area permits (e.g., inside a 2×2 mm footprint):

  • Instance A (Nominal Design): Balanced track library, standard nominal threshold-voltage (SVT) and low-threshold-voltage (LVT) mix targeted for maximum energy efficiency at 100 MHz.
  • Instance B (Aggressive Low-Leakage Design): High-threshold-voltage (HVT) dominant library using extensive multi-channel length cells, targeted for aggressive power reduction in always-on acoustic detection.

2. SRAM Test Structures and Characterization Blocks

Memory arrays dominate the area of the TinyEdge-NPU. Do not test memory solely through the core logic pipeline; processor pipeline stalls or decoding bugs will blind your memory validation. Implement:

  • Direct BIST Engine: A programmable, hardwired Built-In Self-Test (BIST) controller running standard March C+, March SS, and retention algorithms. The BIST must run at full target clock frequency (100 MHz+) and report pass/fail status, bit-error counts, and failing address coordinates via a simple register interface.
  • Split-Rail Isolation: Run the memory power domain (\(V_{DD\_MEM}\)) on an isolated physical rail separate from the standard logic core (\(V_{DD\_CORE}\)). This permits shmoo-plot characterization of memory \(V_{min}\) independently from standard logic cell collapse.
  • Direct Access Memory Bypass: A low-speed multiplexed debug mode allowing direct, deterministic read and write access to the 32 KB weight and 16 KB activation arrays directly from the test interface, bypassing all NPU pipeline staging.

3. Process Monitors (Ring Oscillators & PCM)

To correlate post-silicon silicon behavior back to foundry wafer sorting data (e.g., where the die sits within the nominal/fast-fast/slow-slow distribution), integrate an autonomous Process Characterization Monitor (PCM) block consisting of multiple, muxed Ring Oscillators (ROs):

  • Inverter Chains Across Cell Variants: Implement identical 101-stage inverter ring oscillators using Ultra-Low-Vt (ULVT), Low-Vt (LVT), Standard-Vt (SVT), and High-Vt (HVT) standard cells. Measuring their output frequencies via a clock divider reveals the local silicon process corner.
  • Interconnect/Parasitic Monitors: Include ring oscillators loaded with dense metal tracks across multiple back-end-of-line (BEOL) layers (e.g., dense Metal 2 routing vs. thick top-level Metal 7/8 routing) to measure real resistance-capacitance (RC) extraction skew.
  • N-input Gate Chains: Include NAND- and NOR-dominated ring oscillators to detect asymmetric PMOS versus NMOS manufacturing skews.

4. DFT, Observability, and Debug Hooks

Silicon debug without internal visibility is an expensive exercise in guessing. The testchip requires deep hardware observability:

  • Scan Infrastructure: Insert full scan chains via automated test pattern generation (ATPG) with an on-chip compression decompressor (e.g., Synopsys TestMAX or Siemens Tessent). Target >99% structural fault coverage. Ensure an uncompressed scan mode is accessible through low-speed IOs in case the compression logic malfunctions.
  • JTAG to AXI-Lite Debug Bridge: Implement a standard IEEE 1149.1 JTAG Test Access Port (TAP) coupled to an internal master bridge. This allows an external automated test equipment (ATE) system or host PC running OpenOCD via an FTDI FT2232H USB bridge to read and write every NPU configuration register and memory space deterministically.
  • Critical Node Multiplexer: Route internal critical path timing signals, clock-gating enable flags, power-switch acknowledge lines, and the SRAM memory-sense-amplifier strobe signals out to high-speed digital output pads for oscilloscope probing.

5. What to Ruthlessly Leave Out

Every additional subsystem adds tapeout risk, physical routing congestion, and debugging overhead. Exclude:

  • Complex embedded processor cores (e.g., quad-core application-class RISC-V or ARM Cortex-A) unless strictly necessary as a simple driver; a lightweight 2-pin JTAG-to-bus state machine is infinitely safer.
  • Complex multi-master crossbars and peripheral ecosystems (USB 3.0, PCIe, MIPI, high-performance DMAs).
  • On-chip high-frequency PLLs: Analog Phase-Locked Loops are notoriously sensitive to substrate noise, power supply ripple, and loop-filter layout errors. Instead, design the testchip to accept an external high-frequency differential or single-ended reference clock driven directly by a laboratory signal generator. If a PLL is under test, provide a physical hardware multiplexer to bypass it entirely via a dedicated external pin.

12.10 Floorplanning, Power Delivery, and Packaging

The physical floorplan of an MPW testchip dictates whether post-silicon instrumentation succeeds. A flawed pad frame or a poorly decoupled power distribution network will corrupt both performance and energy characterization.

Die Size, Pad Rings, and Floorplan Topography

Assuming a TSMC 28HPC+ MPW allocation of 1.5 mm × 1.5 mm, the total gross silicon real estate is 2.25 mm². The layout must be strictly floorplanned into clearly bounded modular zones:

  • Core-Limited vs. Pad-Limited Regimes: The TinyEdge-NPU core, with memories and test harnesses, consumes roughly 1.1 mm². In a standard wirebond configuration, standard IO pad cells measure roughly 60–80 μm in height with a 50–60 μm pitch. A peripheral ring containing 50 to 64 pads consumes significant perimeter area, driving the die near a pad-limited threshold. It is essential to use a staggered-pad frame or dual-row inline bond pads if additional IO signals are required.
  • Subsystem Placement: Place the TinyEdge-NPU core centrally. Anchor the 32 KB weight SRAM and 16 KB activation SRAM blocks against the core datapath to keep internal interconnect wires short, mitigating routing congestion over the MAC array. Position the Process Characterization Monitors in an isolated corner of the die, spaced at least 150 μm away from dynamic switching logic to isolate them from substrate noise.

Power Delivery Network (PDN) and Domain Isolation

To measure the distinct power profiles of memory, logic, and analog circuitry, isolate the power distribution network into at least four structurally separated power domains. Never merge these domains on-chip:

  1. VDD_CORE (Nominal 0.9V, operational range 0.7V–1.05V): Supplies solely the 8×8 MAC array, sequential controllers, and standard digital standard-cell logic.
  2. VDD_MEM (Nominal 0.9V, range 0.75V–1.1V): Dedicated power to the bitcells and peripheral logic of the 32 KB and 16 KB SRAM arrays. Separating this rail allows precise detection of memory-specific leakage and independent characterization of the memory minimum operating voltage (\(V_{min}\)).
  3. VDD_IO (1.8V or 3.3V): Powers the peripheral IO pad ring drivers and level-shifters.
  4. VDD_SENSE: Clean, isolated supply rail dedicated exclusively to the ring oscillators and any on-chip analog thermal/voltage telemetry sensors.

To mitigate high-frequency \(L \cdot (di/dt)\) supply bounce during neural network matrix processing bursts, pack all unused core area with standard decap cells (dense thin-oxide capacitor cells). Target an on-chip decap budget sufficient to supply localized charge during the first 2–5 clock cycles of an inference burst before external board-level capacitors can respond.

ESD Strategy and Grounding

Every IO pad must feature electrostatic discharge (ESD) protection networks capable of surviving 2000V Human Body Model (HBM) and 500V Charged Device Model (CDM) events. Dedicated back-to-back anti-parallel diode pairs must bridge the independent ground networks (VSS_CORE, VSS_MEM, VSS_IO) to provide unified ESD discharge paths without compromising low-noise signal returns during precision current measurements. Kelvin sense pads (force/sense line pairs) should be included for both VDD_CORE and VDD_MEM to allow accurate board-level supply regulation directly at the die perimeter, canceling out package lead-frame resistance.

ESD, Latch-Up, and Seal-Ring Rules for the Hard-Macro Deliverable

The pad-ring protection above belongs to the testchip. The hard macro delivered to licensees has no pads of its own. Its boundary is a set of internal signals crossing into the customer's pad ring, so the macro cannot provide ESD protection itself. What it must do is specify it: the integration guide states the ESD ratings the boundary is designed to tolerate, and the licensee's pad ring supplies the clamps. Conflating the two is a common integration failure, so the rules below are part of the deliverable, not an afterthought.

  • Latch-up (JEDEC JESD78). The parasitic PNPN structure formed by every NMOS/PMOS pair in bulk CMOS can latch into a self-sustaining short if a transient forward-biases either emitter beyond ~0.6 V. Prevention is layout, not circuitry: continuous guard rings (P+ in the P-substrate tied to VSS, N+ in the N-well tied to VDD) around the macro perimeter and around each SRAM macro, and dense substrate/well taps throughout the standard-cell area. The tap-spacing rule specified in Chapter 14 (§14.3.2), no diffusion edge more than 15 µm from its tap, keeps the lateral substrate resistance low enough that the ±100 mA JESD78 trigger currents cannot develop the forward bias. Latch-up sign-off runs the foundry's ERC latch-up deck over the delivered GDS, not over a schematic abstraction.
  • Seal ring. The delivered macro GDS includes a continuous seal ring around its perimeter: a stacked-metal ring on every routing layer, tied to VSS, with no gaps. It serves two purposes: a moisture and mobile-ion barrier protecting the edge circuitry, and a crack stop that prevents scribe-line damage from propagating into the macro during wafer dicing. The seal ring is part of the deliverable GDS; the integrator must not remove it, re-route through it, or place circuitry inside its keep-out. Minimum seal-ring-to-circuit spacing follows the foundry design-rule manual, and LVS must include the seal ring as a recognized structure rather than flagging it as a floating-metal violation.
  • ESD at the macro boundary. Signals routed directly from customer pads into the core must pass through the customer's pad-ring clamps first; the macro's own boundary carries no HBM clamps, because a clamp inside the macro would dump ESD current into the core ground network. Where a pad signal enters the macro, the integration guide requires either a series resistor or a secondary clamp at the boundary, and it states the CDM/HBM ratings the boundary is qualified to (≥500 V CDM, ≥2 kV HBM, per Chapter 14) as system-level ratings achieved by the pad ring, not as properties of the macro alone.
  • Antenna rules. Long metal routes into the macro accumulate plasma-etch charge during fabrication; the deliverable enforces the foundry's antenna ratio rules on every input pin (diode insertion or metal jumpers where a route exceeds the allowed antenna ratio), checked by the antenna DRC deck as part of sign-off.

Sign-off for all four items is electrical, not visual: ERC for floating wells and tap coverage, guard-ring continuity checks, antenna DRC, and an LVS run that includes the seal ring. A hard macro that passes DRC/LVS but was never run through the latch-up and antenna decks is not sign-off clean.

Packaging Choice: QFN vs. BGA

Packaging selection involves balancing thermal performance, lead parasitics, manufacturing simplicity, and test socket availability.

Parameter Plastic Quad Flat No-Lead (QFN-48 / QFN-64) Fine-Pitch Ball Grid Array (FBGA-81 / FBGA-100)
Assembly Cost & Turnaround Lowest cost; fastest packaging turnaround (~1–2 weeks) Moderate-to-high cost; substrate tape design required (+2–4 weeks)
Lead Inductance (\(L_{pkg}\)) Moderate (~1.0–1.5 nH per bond wire + lead frame) Low (0.3–0.8 nH for wirebond-to-substrate, <0.1 nH for flip-chip)
Board-Level Test Sockets Inexpensive, reliable high-frequency spring-pin sockets readily available ($500–$1,500) Expensive high-frequency elastomer or pogo-pin sockets ($3,000–$7,000)
Thermal Ground Path Excellent: massive exposed copper ground paddle directly underneath die Good: thermal vias through package substrate core down to solder balls
Suitability for 100 MHz TinyEdge-NPU Ideal: 100 MHz clock rates and <5 mW power draw do not hit package parasitic limits. Overkill: Adds substrate tape engineering cost without measurable electrical benefit.

For the TinyEdge-NPU testchip, an open-cavity or transfer-molded 64-pin QFN (9×9 mm body, 0.5 mm pitch) with an exposed ground pad is the optimal choice. The exposed ground slug delivers near-zero ground resistance and optimal thermal conduction, while 64 pins provide sufficient allocation for four split-rail power pairs, dedicated analog sensing nodes, the full JTAG interface, clock inputs, and wide parallel debug ports.

12.11 Cost, Execution Schedule, and Pre-Tapeout Checklist

A rigorous tapeout demands realistic financial modeling, structured milestones, and strict adherence to physical verification signoff criteria.

Realistic 28nm MPW Cost Breakdown

The following budget reflects commercial, real-world costs for an engineering run of a 28nm MPW vehicle through standard broker/foundry channels:

  • Foundry MPW Shuttle Slot (1.5 × 1.5 mm, TSMC 28HPC+): $95,000 – $130,000 (yields ~40 to 80 bare dies depending on cut strategy).
  • Assembly & Packaging (QFN-64 tooling, wirebonding, 50 packaged units): $8,000 – $15,000.
  • Custom Characterization PCB (Design, 8-layer fab, assembly, precision current sense amplifiers): $10,000 – $18,000.
  • High-Performance Compression Test Sockets (2× for lab bring-up boards): $2,500 – $4,000.
  • Laboratory Bench Logistics & Incidental Tooling: $5,000.
  • Total Budgetary Commitment: ~$120,500 – $172,000.

Engineering Caveat: The "Silent" Killers of First Silicon
Do not let DRC/LVS purity lull you into a false sense of security. The most catastrophic testchip failures typically bypass static rule decks entirely: floating input tie-offs causing multi-milliamp crowbar currents, inverted reset polarities holding state machines in perpetual initialization, uncharacterized package bondwire inductance triggering local supply bounce during parallel MAC firing, and un-isolated analog testpoints loading high-impedance internal nodes. Treat functional bring-up collateral with the same rigorous design reviews applied to the silicon core itself.

Executing a successful testchip program requires treating the test vehicle not as a disposable prototyping experiment, but as a flight-grade production tapeout executed on an accelerated timeline. Best practices dictate strictly freezing architectural scope early, deliberately avoiding bleeding-edge cell libraries unless strictly necessary for PPA objectives, maintaining continuous automated regression testing on sign-off decks, and reserving a physical "safety zone" on silicon for manual focused-ion-beam (FIB) pad modifications should unexpected logic bugs emerge. By standardizing these physical, electrical, and operational controls, the engineering team guarantees that first silicon delivers deterministic, repeatable correlation data rather than an unresolvable post-mortem investigation.

Chapter 12 has charted the complete trajectory required to translate the TinyEdge-NPU from high-level register-transfer logic into physically realized, fully packaged, and empirically validated 28nm silicon. By balancing rigorous microarchitectural floorplanning, targeted scan and memory DFT insertion, disciplined low-power power-grid distribution, and meticulous sign-off verification, the team eliminates the operational blind spots that routinely jeopardize modern semiconductor tapeouts. The physical testchip stands as the ultimate arbiter of engineering execution, closing the loop between pre-silicon EDA abstractions and real-world silicon physics, proving out sub-5 mW edge-AI inference capability, and laying an unshakable foundation for full-scale commercial IP licensing.

Key Takeaways

  • Floorplanning is dataflow planning: put the MAC array, SRAMs and IO where the weights and activations actually travel, and the timing follows.
  • Power planning is part of the floorplan, not an afterthought: IR drop, power gating, isolation and retention decide whether the <100 uW sleep target is real.
  • DRC/LVS sign-off is a gating process with a checklist; run it early and often, not once at the end.
  • A testchip is the cheapest way to buy certainty for a new IP: MPW shuttles make silicon proof affordable for a small accelerator like TinyEdge-NPU.
  • Plan the testchip as a product, DUT, SRAM test structures, process monitors, DFT hooks and packaging, and freeze that plan before tape-out, not during it.

Chapter 13: Silicon Validation & Characterization

This chapter covers the journey from tape-out to first silicon and the testchip-based validation that earns an IP its silicon-proven status: wafer sort and package test, bring-up, functional, performance and power validation, characterization across PVT, correlation between simulation, FPGA and silicon, and debugging the issues real silicon always finds. The testchip is the S configuration (48 KB SRAM: 32 KB weights + 16 KB activations; §3.9).

13.1 From Tape-Out to First Silicon: Redefining "Working Silicon"

The twelve weeks between the tape-out sign-off call and the arrival of the first packaged test chips at the lab bench are an uneasy hiatus in the life of a semiconductor IP team. In pre-silicon design, every signal is observable, clock edges are deterministic abstractions, and the environment is governed by discrete-event simulators running SystemVerilog testbenches. When the physical silicon arrives, fabricated in a 28nm bulk CMOS process, bumped, diced, and bonded into a 48-pin QFN, the team encounters an unforgiving analog reality: process corners, parasitic package inductances, supply rail bounce, thermal gradients, and physical defect densities.

For an ASIC product company, the phrase "the chip works" means that the device powers on, boots an operating system, runs user-facing applications, and survives within a consumer thermal and battery envelope. For a semiconductor IP vendor licensing the TinyEdge-NPU, the definition is fundamentally different and far more rigorous.

An IP vendor does not sell a standalone packaged component; you sell an integration database (RTL, UPF power intent, SDC timing constraints, Liberty models, GDSII macros, and integration test suites) that must function predictably inside dozens of third-party SoC environments. A single internal test-chip run must prove that:

  • The Architecture and Microarchitecture are Structurally Sound: The 8×8 INT8 MAC array must achieve bit-exact mathematical parity with the reference fixed-point software model across millions of synthetic and real neural network activation vectors.
  • The Silicon Matches Static Timing Analysis (STA) and Power Models: The design must run cleanly at its target frequency (100 MHz core clock at nominal 0.9V) and scale across the full operating range without timing degradation, while validating that active dynamic power remains below 5.0 mW and sleep-state leakage stays within the 100 μW budget.
  • Operating Voltage and Process Margins are Broad: The IP must prove wide margins across Process, Voltage, and Temperature (PVT) variations. If the IP only functions between 0.88V and 0.92V on typical-typical (TT) silicon, it will cause unacceptable yield fallout when dropped into a licensee's massive SoC fabricated across slow-slow (SS) or fast-fast (FF) wafer lots.
  • DFT and Test Infrastructure are Production-Grade: The ATPG (Automatic Test Pattern Generation) vectors, scan chains, and built-in self-test (BIST) engines must reliably isolate physical defects without over-testing or inducing destructive instantaneous current transients (\(di/dt\)).
The Real Cost of a Silicon Re-Spin: In a mature 28nm planar process, fabricating a full mask set costs between $800,000 and $1.5 million and consumes 10 to 14 weeks of fab time. A metal-only ECO spin, modifying only the top 3–4 metal layers to fix routing or logic tie-offs using pre-placed spare gate cells, costs roughly $200,000 to $350,000 and requires 4 to 6 weeks. For an IP startup, an unbudgeted mask re-spin can permanently exhaust the runway and miss customer SoC integration windows.

13.2 Wafer Sort and Package Test

Silicon characterization does not begin on the lab bench with a microcontroller and an oscilloscope; it begins on the manufacturing floor using Automated Test Equipment (ATE) such as the Advantest V93000 or Teradyne UltraFLEX. Testing is split into two distinct, sequential phases: Wafer Sort (also known as Circuit Probe or CP) and Package Test (Final Test or FT).

Wafer Sort: Screening Raw Silicon

Wafer sort tests the fabricated dies while they are still integral to the 300 mm silicon wafer. A probe card, containing an array of microscopic vertical or cantilever tungsten needles, physically docks with the die's exposed bond pads or micro-bumps. Because probe needles exhibit significant contact resistance (\(0.5\,\Omega\text{ to }2.0\,\Omega\)) and mutual inductance, high-speed interfaces cannot be evaluated at full performance during wafer sort. Instead, wafer sort focuses on structural defect screening, allowing the foundry to discard dead dies before incurring packaging costs.

The standard wafer sort test suite for the TinyEdge-NPU test chip comprises:

  1. Continuity and Open/Short (OS) Testing: With all power supplies grounded, small negative currents (e.g., \(-100\,\mu\text{A}\)) are driven into each signal pin to forward-bias the electrostatic discharge (ESD) protection diodes. A voltage response between \(-0.3\text{V}\) and \(-0.8\text{V}\) confirms physical contact; an open circuit yields a supply rail clamp, while a short reads near \(0.0\text{V}\).
  2. Power Grid Integrity and Quiescent Current (\(I_{\text{DDQ}}\)): Supplies are brought to nominal levels (0.9V core, 1.8V I/O). The device is clocked into specific internal states where CMOS logic is statically stable. If quiescent leakage exceeds the baseline (e.g., \(>5\,\text{mA}\) on a core where \(80\,\mu\text{A}\) is expected), the die is flagged for gate oxide rupture, bridging defects, or metal slivers.
  3. SRAM Built-In Self-Test (MBIST): The TinyEdge-NPU integrates 32 KB of weight SRAM and 16 KB of activation SRAM (S configuration), which together account for more than 40% of the die area. At wafer sort, the dedicated hardware MBIST controller executes standard algorithms (e.g., March C+, March SS, and Checkerboard patterns). The March C+ engine exercises transitions (\(w0 \rightarrow r0 \rightarrow w1 \rightarrow r1 \rightarrow w0\)) across all address spaces to screen for stuck-at bits, transition faults, address decoder faults, and inter-cell coupling.
  4. Stuck-At Scan ATPG: Scan chains are shifted at conservative tester frequencies (typically 10 MHz to 25 MHz). The tester loads deterministically generated patterns into flip-flops, asserts a single capture clock, and shifts out the captured response to check for logic nodes stuck permanently at \(V_{\text{DD}}\) or \(V_{\text{SS}}\).
  5. At-Speed Delay Fault Testing: Using on-chip clock generation (such as an internal PLL or an on-chip clock controller), scan patterns are shifted in at low frequency, followed by two fast clock pulses at the rated 100 MHz speed to detect slow-to-rise and slow-to-fall transition faults caused by resistive vias or partial gate bridging.
  6. Fuse Programming and Trimming: Any die-specific trimming (such as calibrating internal reference currents or blowing eFuses to burn a unique 64-bit die identifier) is executed during wafer sort.

Test Program Structure and Binning

ATE control software organizes execution into a modular tree where tests are ordered strictly by execution cost and failure probability. Fast parametric checks (OS, shorts) run first; long-duration digital vectors (MBIST, ATPG) run only on surviving silicon. The outcome of this flow maps each die into a discrete Bin:

  • Hard Bins (Hardware Bins): Physical bins or bins reported in the wafer map wafer file, typically limited by tester mechanics to numbers 1 through 8. Bin 1 is universally reserved for passing dies (Known Good Die, or KGD).
  • Soft Bins (Software Bins): Granular software categories mapped inside the ATE datalogging system. For example, Soft Bin 101 may indicate a failure in the 32 KB weight SRAM at March C+ step 4, while Soft Bin 205 indicates a transition-delay failure in the accumulator path of the MAC array.

For the TinyEdge-NPU test chip (~1.2 mm × 1.2 mm including I/O pads and seal ring on a 300 mm wafer), approximately 44,000 raw dies exist per wafer. In a mature 28nm node with an average defect density \(D_0 \approx 0.08\,\text{defects/cm}^2\), Murphy's yield model predicts an initial wafer-sort yield exceeding 94%:

\[Y = \left(\frac{1 - e^{-A \cdot D_0}}{A \cdot D_0}\right)^2 \approx 98.8\% \quad (\text{idealized random defects})\]

Accounting for systematic edge-die fallout, reticle field anomalies, and parametric margin losses, typical wafer sort yields 91% to 94% acceptable dies for the TinyEdge-NPU.

The Transition to Package Test (Final Test)

Dies identified as Bin 1 are sawn from the wafer, inspected via automated optical inspection (AOI), and mounted into standard packages, in our case a 48-pin Quad Flat No-Leads (QFN-48, 6×6 mm body, 0.4 mm pitch).

Package test serves a different engineering purpose than wafer sort: it screens for assembly defects (such as wire bond liftoff, package tilt, voiding, or substrate delamination) and validates the complete chip at speed under realistic capacitive and inductive loading. Package Test is where temperature corner validation occurs. Using thermal-forcing heads (such as Temptronic or Thermostream units), the ATE exercises the packaged TinyEdge-NPU at three thermal insertion points:

  • Cold (\( -40^\circ\text{C} \)): Slowest transistor subthreshold turn-off, maximum leakage sensitivity for certain memory topologies, highest carrier mobility (fastest logic, worst-case hold time violations).
  • Ambient (\( +25^\circ\text{C} \)): Golden reference calibration point.
  • Hot (\( +125^\circ\text{C} \)): Minimum threshold voltages, maximum junction leakage, lowest carrier mobility (slowest logic, worst-case setup time violations).

Only devices that pass this tri-temp matrix with complete register sweep, functional vector execution, and zero-error inferencing across nominal, VDDmin (0.81V), and VDDmax (0.99V) supply rails are designated as golden engineering samples for lab bring-up.

---

13.3 Bring-Up Strategy and Checklist

When the anti-static tubes containing the first 25 packaged TinyEdge-NPU engineering samples arrive in the validation lab, standard operating procedure dictates a disciplined, stepped bring-up methodology. An uncontrolled application of power on uncharacterized silicon can trigger latch-up, rupture gate oxides, or fuse bond wires, permanently destroying debugging evidence.

Lab Bench Setup and Instrumentation

The bring-up bench must be designed to avoid common grounding and supply-integrity issues before silicon touches the board. Figure 13.3 illustrates the architecture of a dedicated validation bench.
