A.3 Operating Conditions and Design Corners

All timing, area, and power metrics must be verified and achieved across the defined operating conditions in the target 28nm LP process:

  • Slow-Slow Corner (SS): 0.81V Core VDD, 125°C Junction Temperature. Used for setup timing signoff (≥ 80 MHz target).
  • Fast-Fast Corner (FF): 0.99V Core VDD, -40°C Junction Temperature. Used for hold timing signoff and peak inrush current evaluation.
  • Typical-Typical Corner (TT): 0.90V Core VDD, 25°C Junction Temperature. Baseline for functional profiling, active power signoff (< 5.0 mW), and nominal clock frequency (100 MHz).
  • Deep Sleep Sub-Corner: 0.90V Core VDD, 25°C Junction Temperature with power switches engaged. Baseline for static leakage evaluation (< 100 μW).

Appendix B: Architecture Decision Record Examples

Note: These condensed summaries use standalone appendix numbering (ADR-001 through ADR-005); for full quantitative derivations and workload context, refer to Chapter 4 (§4.8).

Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) capture key architectural choices made during IP development, documenting the context, alternatives considered, trade-offs analyzed, and the rationale behind each decision. They ensure long-term architectural integrity and prevent teams from revisiting established choices without new technical justification.

ADR-001: Dataflow Architecture — Weight-Stationary vs. Output-Stationary

Status: Approved

Context:
The TinyEdge-NPU must deliver 6.4 GMAC/s throughput within a strict active power budget of < 5.0 mW in a 28nm LP process. Primary target workloads are edge speech processing models, specifically Depthwise Separable Convolutional Neural Networks (DS-CNN) for keyword spotting and shallow ResNets for acoustic event detection. In edge audio inference, SRAM access energy dominates logic compute energy: reading an 8-bit operand from a local 32-word register file costs approximately 0.05 pJ, whereas fetching that operand from a 64 KB SRAM macro consumes 2.1 pJ (a 42× difference). The architectural challenge is selecting a spatial processing element (PE) dataflow that minimizes the total energy dissipated in the memory hierarchy per MAC operation while sustaining high compute utilization.

Decision:
We adopt a Weight-Stationary (WS) 2D systolic dataflow for the TinyEdge-NPU core datapath.

In this architecture, static weight parameters are preloaded from the 64 KB Weight SRAM into local registers located inside each of the 64 Processing Elements (PEs). During computation, weights remain static across multiple cycles while input activations stream horizontally across the array rows, and partial sums accumulate vertically down the columns into output shift registers. For depthwise separable layers (the primary compute consumer in DS-CNN), the same kernel weights are reused across incoming acoustic spectrogram frames over time, maximizing local weight reuse.

Consequences:

  • Positive: Weight SRAM access is reduced to zero during execution phases once the array is primed, cutting aggregate memory read power by 42% compared to direct memory-fed architectures.
  • Positive: Simplifies activation broadcasting logic across PE rows, keeping wire capacitance low.
  • Negative: Each PE requires an additional 8-bit shadow register and multiplexer to support concurrent background pre-loading of upcoming filter weights, increasing the physical area of the 64-MAC array by roughly 8,200 μm² (~0.8% of the total IP area).
  • Negative: Partial sums must propagate down array columns, necessitating 32-bit inter-PE accumulator routing paths that complicate physical design place-and-route congestion near the array boundary.

Alternatives Considered:

  • Output-Stationary (OS): Accumulators remain stationary in each PE while both weights and activations stream continuously through the datapath. While this minimizes accumulator register switching energy and keeps partial sums local, it requires constant reading of weights from the SRAM buffer. Power modeling showed OS exceeded the 5.0 mW budget by 1.8 mW due to high SRAM read rates during 3×3 convolution filters.
  • Row-Stationary (RS): Maximizes reuse across both weights and activations simultaneously by mapping 1D convolution primitives onto 1D PE rows. While energy-optimal in large-scale server NPUs, the complex control state machines, variable line buffer structures, and multi-dimensional routing crossbars required exceeded our logic area budget by > 18% in the target 28nm node.

ADR-002: Arithmetic Precision Baseline — Native INT8 with Optional Sub-Byte INT4

Status: Approved

Context:
Edge-deployed keyword spotting systems are severely constrained by available on-chip SRAM capacity. The TinyEdge-NPU allocates 64 KB for weight storage (M configuration) to stay within a total die area of ~1.0 mm². Complete DS-CNN models targeting 12 keyword classes require approximately 48,000 to 60,000 parameters. A standard INT8 quantized network of that class fits tightly within the M configuration's 64 KB buffer (consuming ~58 KB). DS-CNN-M, at ~120,000 parameters, needs the L configuration's 128 KB weight buffer (§3.9). Moving entirely to INT4 precision would halve memory footprint to ~29 KB and double compute throughput to 2.0 GMAC/s. However, empirical accuracy assessments on the Google Speech Commands V2 dataset indicate that aggressive uniform INT4 post-training quantization leads to a 4.6% drop in Top-1 classification accuracy and elevates false-acceptance rates in low Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) environments (0 dB to +5 dB) to unacceptable levels for battery-powered voice wake-up products.

Decision:
Implement a native INT8 multiplier datapath with an optional, runtime-configurable dual-lane INT4 sub-byte execution mode.

The primary execution mode is native signed INT8×INT8 multiplication feeding a 32-bit accumulator. To support memory-constrained models, each 8-bit hardware multiplier is architected using a split-radix structure: it can either operate as a single 8-bit×8-bit multiplier or be reconfigured via datapath multiplexers to operate as two independent 4-bit×4-bit multipliers in a single cycle. When the core is placed in INT4 mode, weights are packed two per byte in SRAM, and the 64-PE array executes 128 INT4 MACs per cycle.

Consequences:

  • Positive: Preserves baseline INT8 accuracy (> 95.2% Top-1 on Google Speech Commands) with zero quantization-induced penalty, providing standard drop-in support for mainstream TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers (TFLM) workflows.
  • Positive: Provides a high-performance, low-power fallback mode for simpler acoustic tasks (such as simple presence detection or binarized event triggers), doubling throughput to 12.8 GMAC/s and cutting memory read operations by 50%.
  • Negative: Datapath area overhead: The split-multiplier logic, operand sign-extension multiplexers, and dual 16-bit intermediate accumulator trees increase total cell area of the 64 MAC units by 13.5% (approx. 14,000 μm²) relative to a pure INT8 baseline.
  • Negative: Increases compiler toolchain complexity. The compiler must parse layer-by-layer quantization profiles, pack 4-bit weights into contiguous 8-bit memory words, and insert mode-switch configuration writes into the command buffer.

Alternatives Considered:

  • Pure Native INT4-Only Architecture: Rejected because customer product teams require standard INT8 accuracy benchmarks for commercial voice interfaces. The loss of accuracy under adverse acoustic conditions would prevent deployment in smart home and hearable appliances without extensive retraining pipelines that customer engineering teams often cannot undertake.
  • Floating-Point Support (FP8 / Microscaling Formats): FP8 (E4M3 / E5M2) was evaluated for improved dynamic range. It was rejected because the floating-point alignment shifters, exponent handling, and normalization stages added 38% more dynamic switching power and 25% logic area overhead to each PE, violating both the < 5.0 mW power ceiling and the ~1.0 mm² area constraint in the 28nm LP process.

ADR-003: Control Interface — AXI-Lite Slave for Configuration, AXI4 Master for DMA

Status: Approved

Context:
The TinyEdge-NPU control plane is written once per layer (a handful of 32-bit register writes) while the data plane moves weights and activations continuously. The two traffic classes have opposite needs: configuration wants the narrowest, simplest, most easily verified slave interface, while DMA wants bursts and throughput. A single interface serving both would either over-provision the control path or starve the data path.

Decision:
Control and configuration go through one narrow, single-beat slave interface: AXI4-Lite, 12-bit address, 32-bit data (REQ-INT-01). Data movement uses a separate AMBA 4 AXI4 master for DMA with bursts up to 16 beats. Chapter 5 implements the control slave as a native AXI-Lite slave; the register map is the single interface contract, not a bridged variant of another bus.

Consequences:

  • Positive: The control slave has no burst, ordering, or out-of-order logic to verify; its formal property set is small and the UVM register model maps one-to-one onto the AXI-Lite transactions.
  • Positive: DMA throughput is independent of control traffic. A burst in flight never blocks a configuration write.
  • Negative: Hosts with no AXI-Lite fabric need a bridge wrapper, which adds one cycle of read latency and one more item to the integration guide.

Alternatives Considered:

  • A narrower single-beat peripheral bus: Considered and rejected: AXI-Lite already provides single-beat access with no burst logic required in the slave, and a second bus would need a bridge for AXI-only hosts.
  • AHB-Lite control slave: Rejected: no benefit over AXI-Lite for single-beat configuration traffic, and it would require a bridge for AHB-only hosts.

ADR-004: Sleep Strategy — Power-Gate Logic, Retain SRAM

Status: Approved

Context:
The sleep budget is < 100 μW with a wake-up latency of ≤ 64 cycles (REQ-PWR-02, REQ-PWR-04). Clock gating alone cannot meet the leakage budget at the SS/125°C corner, and a full power shutdown loses the model context held in SRAM, forcing a reload from flash on every wake-up.

Decision:
Power-gate the logic in PD_NPU (header switches collapse VDD_CORE) while the weight and activation SRAMs stay in a low-voltage retention mode that preserves tensor context. The always-on domain PD_AON holds the AXI-Lite registers and wake logic. Isolation cells clamp PD_NPU outputs during shutdown; level shifters bridge the retained-SRAM voltage to the core rail on wake-up.

Consequences:

  • Positive: Wake-up completes in ≤ 64 cycles. No model reload, no cold-boot initialization penalty.
  • Positive: Sleep leakage is dominated by SRAM retention rather than logic, which is the smaller and more predictable term.
  • Negative: Retention mode needs its own characterization (retention voltage vs. read margin) and a dedicated UPF verification pass; the isolation/level-shifter cells add floorplan constraints at the domain boundary.

Alternatives Considered:

  • Full shutdown with reload from flash: Rejected: wake-up would run to milliseconds (flash read + DMA), far beyond the 64-cycle budget, and the reload energy would exceed the energy saved by shutting the SRAMs off.
  • Clock gating only, no power gating: Rejected: subthreshold leakage at SS/125°C exceeds the 100 μW budget even with all-HVT logic in the always-on paths.

ADR-005: Scan Compression Ratio — 32:1 with 16 Scan Chains

Status: Approved

Context:
The design has roughly 45,000 flip-flops (Chapter 6) that must be observable through scan. Uncompressed scan would need 45,000 shift cycles per pattern, making production test time, and therefore ATE cost, the dominant per-unit test expense for a 1 mm² die that costs only ~$0.05 in silicon.

Decision:
Adopt scan compression at 32:1 (per ARC-08) with 16 internal scan chains of ~2,800 flops each, fed by an on-chip decompressor and observed through a compactor with a MISR signature. Stuck-at coverage target is ≥ 99.0% and transition coverage ≥ 95.0% (REQ-REL-03).

Consequences:

  • Positive: Test time per pattern drops by ~32× versus uncompressed scan, keeping test cost a small fraction of the die cost.
  • Positive: 16 chains keep individual chain length short, which bounds the scan shift power and the clock-tree load during scan mode.
  • Negative: Compression aliases some faults into the MISR signature, so diagnosis of a failing die needs an uncompressed bypass mode; the decompressor/compactor logic adds ~1% area.

Alternatives Considered:

  • No compression (16 chains, direct ATE access): Rejected: test time and ATE channel cost would exceed the silicon cost of the die itself.
  • 64:1 compression: Rejected: marginal test-time gain over 32:1, with measurably worse fault diagnosis granularity and a larger decompressor.

Appendix C: Review Checklists

Engineering sign-off gates require verifiable, binary criteria rather than subjective evaluations. The following five checklists represent mandatory quality gates for the TinyEdge-NPU IP core across its development lifecycle: Architecture Review, RTL Review, Verification Review, Tape-out Review, and IP Release Review. Each check specifies concrete acceptance criteria aligned with TinyEdge-NPU targets: INT8 precision, AXI-Lite slave interface, <5 mW active power at 50 MHz (28nm SLP/HPC), <100 μW sleep power, and ∼1 mm2 die target area. Note: the 50 MHz basis used in Appendices C–E is a low-power operating point, distinct from the 100 MHz nominal burst clock specified in Appendix A.

ARC-03 Memory Architecture & Bandwidth SRAM banking (32 KB weight buffer, 16 KB activation scratchpad; S configuration) provides conflict-free dual-port access for continuous streaming at 50 MHz. [   ]
ARC-04 Bus Protocol Compliance AXI4-Lite slave specification verified for configuration register access; zero wait-state decode for single-cycle control writes. [   ]
ARC-05 Power Budget Allocation Active power modeled <4.2 mW (leaving 16% margin against 5.0 mW limit); retention/leakage modeled <65 μW at 28nm typical conditions (0.9V, 25°C). [   ]
ARC-06 Clock Domain Crossing (CDC) Spec Explicit architecture defined for crossing between bus clock (pclk, 25–100 MHz) and core processing clock (npu_clk, 100 MHz); handshakes or quasi-static synchronizers specified. [   ]
ARC-07 Power Intent & Domain Definition UPF/CPF architecture splits core into two domains: PD_AON (always-on AXI-Lite wrapper/wake-up logic) and PD_NPU (power-gated NPU compute array and scratchpads). [   ]
ARC-08 DFT Architecture Specification Test methodology approved: scan compression ratio ≥32x, dedicated IEEE 1500 or standard JTAG test wrapper, memory BIST engine with full repair/bypass hooks. [   ]
ARC-09 Safety & Error Handling Register parity, activation buffer single-error-correct double-error-detect (SECDED) ECC, and protocol timeout counters documented with SW fault-handling flow. [   ]

Appendix D: Testchip Bring-up Checklist

Bringing up first silicon requires an uncompromising, phase-based sequence to prevent hardware destruction caused by power-rail shorts, clock over-driving, or race conditions. This sequential checklist governs the bring-up of the 28nm TinyEdge-NPU testchip from initial board unboxing to multi-corner characterization. Note: Appendices C–E use a 50 MHz low-power operating point for some checks, distinct from the 100 MHz nominal burst clock (Appendix A); the bring-up steps in this appendix use the 100 MHz nominal clock unless stated otherwise.

Seq Bring-up Phase Action & Test Procedure Pass Criterion Sign-off
01 Board Unpowered Resistance Measure impedance across VDD_CORE (0.9V), VDD_IO (1.8V), and VDDA_PLL (1.2V) rails to GND using DMM before inserting package. No shorts (>100 kΩ on core; >1 MΩ on I/O rails). [   ]
02 Socket Insertion & Seating Install TinyEdge-NPU QFN/BGA sample into socket under microscope; check pin-1 alignment and uniform package clamping force. Zero visual displacement, pins aligned, co-planarity confirmed. [   ]
03 Initial Power-on (Current Limit) Apply laboratory bench power supplies with compliance limits set to 120% of quiescent levels (VDD_CORE limit = 10 mA; VDD_IO limit = 15 mA). Rails settle to 0.90V ±2% and 1.80V ±2%; no current trips. Quiescent current <1 mA. [   ]
04 Clock Source Validation Enable external signal generator to clk_in at conservative frequency (10 MHz, 1.8V LVCMOS). Monitor duty cycle with high-Z probe. 10.0 MHz measured at test point; duty cycle 50 ±2%; jitter <20 ps RMS. [   ]
05 Reset Assertion & Release Assert aresetn (low for >1 μs), verify reset pin voltage level; release reset to high (1.8V) using logic analyzer trigger. Reset falls cleanly to 0V and transitions to 1.8V without ringing/glitches (<50 mV overshoot). [   ]
06 JTAG / Scan TAP Sanity Shift IDCODE instruction through JTAG/scan interface using host debugger (OpenOCD / Lauterbach). Returns exact 32-bit hardware identifier (e.g., 0x0BB1_0001); TDO transitions cleanly. [   ]
07 Control Register Read Issue an AXI-Lite single read via debug bridge to the ID register (offset 0x1C) and the REVISION register (offset 0x34). ID reads 0x54454E50 ("TENP") and REVISION reads the expected RTL revision (zero bus timeouts). [   ]
08 Control Register Write/Read Execute walking-ones and walking-zeros patterns across writable scratchpad config registers (offset 0x0010–0x001C). 100% bit-retention matches; zero stuck-at-0 or stuck-at-1 bits detected. [   ]
09 Scan Chain Structural Test Run production ATPG stuck-at pattern suite at 10 MHz scan frequency via tester or bring-up automated tool. 0 vector miscompares out of all patterns applied (≥99.2% expected coverage verified). [   ]
10 Memory BIST Execution Trigger built-in self-test on 32 KB weight SRAM and 16 KB activation scratchpads (S configuration) by writing START to the MBIST_CTRL register (offset 0x28). MBIST_DONE register (offset 0x2C) asserts; MBIST_FAIL register (offset 0x30) reads 0 for all instances. [   ]
11 First Inference (Synthetic) Load 1-layer synthetic 8-MAC kernel into SRAM; trigger TinyEdge-NPU run bit; poll IRQ_DONE status flag. Computation completes in expected cycles (±0 cycles); result vector bit-exact with SW model. [   ]
12 Real KWS Model Execution Upload complete Keyword Spotting acoustic model (12-layer depthwise separable CNN); execute acoustic inference frame (1 sec audio input). Inference latency ≤10 ms at 100 MHz; accuracy score matches software floating/INT8 simulator. [   ]
13 Active Power Validation Measure average current on VDD_CORE (0.9V) during continuous keyword detection inference at 100 MHz using precision digital power meter. Active core power strictly <5.0 mW at 100 MHz (REQ-PWR-01). [   ]
14 Sleep & Wake-up Power Check Assert PD_NPU sleep mode via register; verify power-switch shutoff; measure retention current; assert external wake-up pin. Sleep leakage power <80 μW (well within <100 μW limit); wake-up recovery ≤64 cycles (0.64 μs at 100 MHz). [   ]
15 PVT Corner Characterization Operate device in thermal chamber across voltage and temperature: 0.81V–0.99V, -20°C to +85°C; verify continuous inference execution. Zero algorithmic miscompares, zero hang-ups, shmoo plot confirms robust functional operating box. [   ]

Appendix F: Glossary of Semiconductor IP Terms

This glossary provides concise, unambiguous definitions for standard semiconductor engineering acronyms and terminology used throughout the specification, design, verification, and physical implementation of commercial IP blocks such as the TinyEdge-NPU.

Term Definition
AMBA / AXI Arm's on-chip bus standards: AMBA is the framework; AXI is the high-performance bus used for DMA data movement (AXI4 with bursts, AXI4-Lite for single-beat register access, used for the control registers).
ASIC Application-Specific Integrated Circuit — a chip designed for one product or product family, as opposed to a general-purpose processor or an FPGA.
ATE (Automated Test Equipment) Specialized, computer-controlled industrial test hardware designed to perform high-throughput parametric, functional, and timing measurements on packaged integrated circuits or un-diced wafers.
ATPG (Automatic Test Pattern Generation) An automated algorithmic process executed by EDA software that analyzes digital netlists to create optimized stimulus vectors for uncovering manufacturing defects via internal scan structures.
BIST (Built-In Self-Test) On-chip hardware circuitry (such as Memory BIST or Logic BIST) designed to generate test patterns and verify circuit integrity internally without relying exclusively on high-speed external ATE channels.
CDC Clock Domain Crossing — a signal path between two clock domains; requires synchronizers or handshakes to avoid metastability. See also RDC (Reset Domain Crossing).
Chiplet An individually manufactured, tested, and functional silicon die integrated alongside other heterogeneous dies within a single advanced package using high-density interconnect substrates.
DFM (Design for Manufacturability) The set of physical design optimizations—including metal density filling, via doubling, and lithographic spacing adjustments—applied to an IC layout to minimize yield loss caused by manufacturing variations.
DFT (Design for Testability) Structural hardware modifications incorporated into a digital design (e.g., scan chains, test wrapper cells, compression logic) to facilitate efficient post-silicon defect detection and fault isolation.
DPPM (Defective Parts Per Million) A critical quality metric quantifying manufacturing defect density, representing the number of non-functional parts shipped per one million components delivered to customers.
DRC (Design Rule Checking) The physical verification step that verifies whether a geometric layout adheres to all foundry-mandated manufacturing constraints, such as minimum metal widths, layer spacings, and enclosure rules.
DV (Design Verification) The systematic engineering process of confirming that an RTL implementation precisely satisfies its architectural and functional requirements across all specified corner conditions prior to tape-out.
EDA (Electronic Design Automation) The ecosystem of specialized software tools, workflows, and methodologies used to design, simulate, verify, synthesize, and physically lay out integrated circuits and electronic systems.
FIT (Failures in Time) A standardized reliability metric that denotes the projected number of component failures occurring per one billion operating device hours under nominal or accelerated conditions.
Formal Verification A mathematical, exhaustive verification methodology that checks an RTL design against specific assertions or architectural properties without requiring dynamic simulation test vectors.
GDSII (Graphic Data System II) The legacy binary database format (alongside its modern successor, OASIS) used to represent planar geometric shapes, text labels, and layer assignments for integrated circuit photomask fabrication.
Hard IP A reusable, licensed block of semiconductor intellectual property delivered as a fully verified, technology-specific physical layout (GDSII/OASIS) optimized for exact timing, power, and area targets.
HTOL (High-Temperature Operating Life) A reliability stress qualification procedure that subjects a sample of ICs to elevated temperatures and operating voltages to accelerate infant mortality and estimate long-term operational lifespan.
INT8 / Quantization 8-bit integer arithmetic, and the process (quantization) of converting a floating-point neural network to INT8 weights and activations with per-tensor or per-channel scale factors.
IP (Semiconductor Intellectual Property) A modular, reusable unit of logic, cell design, or functional chip architecture licensed to third parties for integration into larger System-on-Chip (SoC) or ASIC designs.
LVS (Layout Versus Schematic) The physical verification phase that compares the electrical netlist extracted from the geometric layout against the post-synthesis gate-level netlist to ensure device-level structural equivalence.
MAC (Multiply-Accumulate) The fundamental hardware arithmetic execution unit that computes the product of two operands and adds that product to an accumulation register in a single cycle or pipelined sequence.
MCMM Multi-Corner Multi-Mode — static timing analysis run across combinations of process/voltage/temperature corners and operating modes (mission, scan, sleep).
MPW (Multi-Project Wafer) A shared manufacturing run where multiple distinct designs from different teams or companies share a single lithographic mask set to amortize non-recurring engineering (NRE) prototype fabrication costs.
NPU (Neural Processing Unit) A domain-specific hardware accelerator optimized with parallel execution units and tailored memory hierarchies to compute neural network tensors and machine learning operations efficiently.
OCV On-Chip Variation — the statistical spread in transistor and wire delay across a die, modeled in STA by derating launch and capture paths.
PDK (Process Design Kit) A comprehensive suite of foundry-provided technological files, including device models, DRC/LVS runsets, standard cell libraries, and design rules required to build chips in a target fabrication process.
PPA Power, Performance, Area — the three-way trade-off that governs every IP design decision; often extended to PPAC (adding Cost).
PVT (Process, Voltage, Temperature) The combined spectrum of manufacturing variances, operational supply voltages, and ambient operating temperatures across which silicon timing, power, and functionality must be verified.
RTL (Register-Transfer Level) A high-level hardware description language abstraction (e.g., SystemVerilog, VHDL) that specifies the flow of digital signals between hardware registers and the logical operations applied to those signals.
Scan Chain A specialized test configuration formed by cascading storage flip-flops into serial shift registers during dedicated test modes, granting external ATE direct controllability and observability of internal states.
SDC (Synopsys Design Constraints) The semiconductor industry-standard format used to document functional timing constraints, clock declarations, input/output delays, false paths, and multicycle paths for synthesis and static timing analysis.
SoC System-on-Chip — a complete system (processors, memory, peripherals, accelerators) integrated on a single die.
Soft IP A reusable IP block delivered as synthesizeable RTL source code (or encrypted netlists) that allows downstream integrators to target different foundry processes and customize physical synthesis targets.
STA (Static Timing Analysis) A non-vector-based verification methodology that evaluates the propagation delays along all circuit paths in a netlist to prove whether design setups and hold constraints are satisfied across all PVT corners.
Tape-out The final milestone in the chip design cycle where the verified, clean physical layout database (GDSII or OASIS) is officially frozen and transferred to the silicon foundry for photolithographic mask production.
Testchip A dedicated silicon vehicle manufactured specifically to validate critical IP architectures, characterize post-silicon analog/digital performance, correlate power models, and de-risk silicon process features.
TOPS / GOPS Tera/Giga Operations Per Second — a peak-throughput unit for accelerators; one MAC counts as two operations, so 64 MACs at 100 MHz is 12.8 GOPS (0.0128 TOPS).
UPF Unified Power Format (IEEE 1801) — the standard language for describing power intent: power domains, switches, isolation, retention, and level shifters.
UVM (Universal Verification Methodology) A standardized, object-oriented SystemVerilog verification framework and class library designed to build scalable, reusable, constrained-random verification testbenches with structured coverage tracking.
Yield The percentage of fabricated integrated circuit dies on a wafer that pass all functional, parametric, and reliability test criteria relative to the total number of physical dies manufactured.
---

Appendix G: Recommended Tools and Further Reading

Executing an IP development program from architectural specification to signoff requires a solid toolchain and a rigorous theoretical foundation. Below is a curated catalog of industry-standard EDA tools, spanning both proprietary commercial platforms and mature open-source alternatives, followed by essential literature for the practicing IP designer.

Tool Ecosystem by Development Stage

Development Stage Commercial Platforms Open-Source / Emerging Alternatives
RTL Design, Lint, & CDC
  • Synopsys SpyGlass: Industry-standard structural linting, CDC (Clock Domain Crossing), and RDC (Reset Domain Crossing) analysis.
  • Siemens EDA Questa Lint: Fast syntax, semantic, and multi-clock verification engine.
  • Verilator: High-performance cycle-accurate C++/SystemC transpilator ideal for fast architectural bring-up and firmware co-simulation.
Dynamic Simulation & Coverage
  • Synopsys VCS: High-capacity native SystemVerilog, UVM, and mixed-signal simulator.
  • Cadence Xcelium: Multi-core parallel simulation engine optimized for complex, randomized testbenches.
  • Icarus Verilog: Open-source IEEE-1364 simulator suitable for module-level verification.
  • Cocotb: Coroutine-based Python verification framework for rapid interface testing.
Formal Verification
  • Cadence JasperGold: Comprehensive formal property verification, protocol checking, and formal coverage signoff.
  • Synopsys VC Formal: Native formal verification engine integrated into the VC verification platform.
  • SymbiYosys (sby): Front-end driver for formal verification utilizing Yosys, enabling SAT/SMT-based property checking with engines like Z3.
Logic Synthesis & STA
  • Synopsys Design Compiler / PrimeTime: The gold-standard synthesis optimization engine and signoff static timing analysis framework.
  • Cadence Genus / Tempus: Massively parallel synthesis and signoff timing/signal integrity analysis suite.
  • Yosys: Modular synthesis framework supporting Verilog-2005 elaboration and technology mapping.
  • OpenSTA: Gate-level static timing verifier capable of tracking setup/hold slacks across corner libraries.
Physical Design (P&R)
  • Synopsys IC Compiler II / Fusion: Production-grade placement, clock tree synthesis (CTS), routing, and in-design optimization.
  • Cadence Innovus: High-capacity place-and-route platform tailored for modern advanced FinFET nodes down to sub-3nm.
  • OpenROAD: Autonomous RTL-to-GDS physical implementation infrastructure designed for no-human-in-loop synthesis and layout.
Physical Verification & Signoff
  • Siemens EDA Calibre (nmDRC / nmLVS): Universal foundry-standard golden signoff engine for geometric and netlist physical verification.
  • Cadence Pegasus: Distributed DRC/LVS verification platform optimized for high-volume cloud execution.
  • Magic: Classical VLSI layout engine with integrated interactive DRC extraction.
  • KLayout: High-performance GDSII/OASIS mask data viewer with custom script-based DRC capabilities.
DFT & ATPG
  • Siemens EDA Tessent: Comprehensive test suite covering scan insertion, hierarchical ATPG, Logic BIST, and Memory BIST.
  • Synopsys TestMAX: Integrated scan synthesis, compression, and high-defect coverage pattern generation platform.
  • Fault: Academic, open-source ATPG and scan-chain analysis utility targeting deterministic stuck-at fault models.
Power Modeling & UPF
  • Synopsys PrimePower: Cycle-accurate vector-driven average and peak gate-level power profiling.
  • Ansys RedHawk-SC: Signoff dynamic voltage drop, EM (electromigration), and power grid integrity analysis.
  • OpenROAD Power Analysis: Native static power evaluation modules based on liberty cell files.
FPGA Prototyping
  • AMD Vivado ML: End-to-end synthesis, placement, and debugging suite for AMD/Xilinx UltraScale+ FPGA platforms.
  • Intel Quartus Prime Pro: Design environment for Intel Agilex and Stratix FPGA acceleration ecosystems.
  • NextPNR: Vendor-neutral, timing-driven FPGA place-and-route utility supporting open bitstream ecosystems.
Register Automation & Docs
  • No commercial tool listed for this stage.
  • PeakRDL: Open-source Python tool suite for compiling SystemRDL 2.0 register address maps into Verilog, C headers, and HTML docs.
  • Sphinx + Breathe: Automated generation of technical IP user guides directly parsed from source code annotations.

Further Reading: Key Standards and Foundational Texts

  1. IEEE Standard 1801-2018 (UPF — Unified Power Format): The definitive industry specification for defining multi-voltage power intent, power-gating switches, isolation cells, and level shifters across design flows.
  2. IEEE Standard 1500-2005 (Standard for Embedded Core Test): The standard mechanism establishing architectural wrapper boundaries, instruction registers, and test isolation interfaces for plug-and-play modular IP testing.
  3. UCIe (Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express) Specification (v1.0 & beyond): The open industry standard governing high-bandwidth, ultra-low latency, and low-power die-to-die physical layers, protocols, and test mechanisms across heterogeneously packaged chiplets.
  4. JEDEC JESD47 / AEC-Q100 Qualification Standards: The baseline qualification stress test protocols establishing environmental, electrical, and thermal reliability thresholds for commercial and automotive-grade integrated circuits.
  5. Arm AMBA Protocol Specifications (AXI4, AXI-Lite): The canonical interface standards governing synchronous, point-to-point on-chip control buses, pipelined data streaming channels, and interconnect protocols.
  6. Bhasker, J., & Chadha, R. (2009). Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs: A Practical Approach. Springer: A thorough, accessible guide covering liberty cell modeling, interconnect parasitic delay calculations, crosstalk noise, and timing signoff constraints.
  7. Keating, M., Flynn, D., Aitken, R., Gibbons, A., & Shi, K. (2009). Low Power Methodology Manual: For System-on-Chip Design (LPMM). Springer: The foundational text outlining power domains, architectural clock-gating, state retention techniques, dynamic voltage/frequency scaling, and signoff verification.
  8. Spear, C., & Tumbush, G. (2020). SystemVerilog for Verification: A Guide to Learning the Testbench Language Features (3rd ed.). Springer: The industry's most widely adopted instructional book covering object-oriented verification techniques, constrained-random stimulus generation, and functional coverage concepts.
  9. Wang, L.-T., Wu, C.-W., & Wen, X. (2006). VLSI Test Principles and Architectures: Design for Testability. Morgan Kaufmann: The definitive technical reference detailing scan-based logic testing, modern ATPG algorithms, embedded memory BIST, and boundary scan implementations.
  10. Hennessy, J. L., & Patterson, D. A. (2019). Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach (6th ed.). Morgan Kaufmann: Contains essential foundational chapters on domain-specific architectures (DSAs), tensor acceleration pipelines, and memory hierarchy trade-offs essential to engineering modern NPUs.

Appendix H: TinyEdge-NPU Register Map (Summary)

The register map is the software API of the IP (Chapter 5, "Register map"). This appendix is the one-page summary promised by Appendix C (REL-06) and Chapter 15. All registers are 32-bit, accessed through the control slave; unmapped addresses return SLVERR. Configuration writes take effect only at a layer boundary (shadow registers, latched when the FSM is in IDLE); every register has a defined reset value; the ID register is read-only and non-zero.

Offset Name Access Description
0x00CTRLRWBit 0: START (self-clearing). Bit 1: SOFT_RESET. Bit 2: IRQ_ENABLE.
0x04STATUSROBit 0: BUSY. Bit 1: DONE. Bit 2: ERROR. Bits 7:4: FSM state (debug).
0x08LAYER_DESC_PTRRWSystem-memory address of the layer descriptor list.
0x0CNUM_LAYERSRWNumber of layers to execute (1–16).
0x10IN_ADDRRWSystem-memory address of the input feature map.
0x14OUT_ADDRRWSystem-memory address of the output feature map.
0x18IRQ_STATUSRW1CBit 0: DONE. Bit 1: ERROR. Write-1-to-clear.
0x1CIDROIP identifier: 0x54454E50 ("TENP"). The RTL revision is reported in the separate REVISION register at 0x34.
0x20PERF_CYCLESROCycle count of the last completed inference.
0x24PERF_MAC_UTILROMAC array utilization of the last inference, in percent.
0x28MBIST_CTRLRWBit 0: START (self-clearing) — launches BIST on all SRAM instances. Bits 31:1: reserved.
0x2CMBIST_DONEROBit 0: DONE — set when BIST completes on all SRAM instances; cleared by the next MBIST_CTRL.START.
0x30MBIST_FAILROBit 0: weight SRAM fail. Bit 1: activation SRAM fail. 0 = all instances pass.
0x34REVISIONRORTL revision identifier (e.g. 0x00000001 for revision 1); changes with every RTL revision.

Notes. (1) The device identifier is read from ID at 0x1C (0x54454E50, "TENP") and the RTL revision from REVISION at 0x34. Appendix D step 07 reads these two registers. There is no DEVICE_ID or VERSION_REG register; offsets 0x00 and 0x04 are CTRL and STATUS. (2) MBIST_CTRL (0x28), MBIST_DONE (0x2C), and MBIST_FAIL (0x30) are the BIST registers used by Appendix D step 10. (3) IRQ_STATUS is write-1-to-clear; CTRL.START is self-clearing.

From clean architectural specification through rigorous verification, physical signoff, and silicon validation, world-class semiconductor IP is built on precision, repeatable methodology, and an uncompromising attention to detail.
